nuance.analogy: Chronometry is the engineering of a ruler, but for time instead of length.
nuance.etymology: From Greek chronos (time) and metron (measure), with the suffix -y.
common_mistakes: Confusing chronometry with chronology, which is about the order of events.
Stressing the first syllable instead of 'NAH'.

chronometry.etymology: From *chrono-* + *-metry* on the model of *chronometer*, q.v. ultimately from Ancient Greek *χρόνος* (“time”) and *μέτρον* (“meter, measuring device”).

senses.definition: Capable of being, or appropriate to be, cited.
senses.example: Only peer-reviewed articles are citable in our department's research papers.

core.definition: Able to be cited, or good enough to be used as a reliable source or authority.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, and "cite" sounds exactly like "sight." The ending -able is a reduced syllable, so it sounds like "uh-buhl."

nuance.connotation: Positive. It describes a source that is credible and worth referring to.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word mostly in academic, legal, and professional writing. A source is "citable" if it can be formally referenced in a paper or report. Both "citable" and "citeable" are accepted spellings, but "citable" is more common in American publishing.

distinctions.note: Quotable means memorable enough to be quoted, while citable means suitable as a formal source.
Credible describes trustworthiness in general, while citable is a narrower term about whether something can be formally referenced.

examples.everyday: My roommate asked if her blog post was citable for her class, and I told her it probably wasn't.
examples.professional: Before we publish the internal report, make sure every figure comes from a citable source.
examples.analytical: The author argues that only peer-reviewed work should count as citable evidence in a systematic review.

nuance.analogy: It is like a book with a clear call number in a library catalog, so anyone can find it and refer to it.
nuance.etymology: From cite (from Latin citare, "to summon or call forth") plus the suffix -able.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing "cite" as "cit" or "seet" instead of "sight."
Mistaking it for "quotable" when the sentence is about formal references in academic writing.

senses.definition: In a clement manner.

core.definition: In a merciful or lenient way, showing mercy toward someone who could punish them.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The middle syllable is reduced, and the final -ly sounds like 'lee'.

nuance.connotation: Positive but very rare. It sounds old-fashioned and is usually replaced by simpler words.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use clemently; many native speakers would not recognize it. In formal writing about punishment, use 'leniently', and when describing relief from harm, use 'mercifully'. You will mostly find clemently in older literature or dictionaries.

distinctions.note: Leniently is the standard adverb for judging or punishing gently.
Mercifully means in a way that spares someone pain; clemently focuses on a powerful person's gentle decision.

examples.everyday: The coach treated us pretty clemently after that terrible game, and I appreciated it.
examples.professional: The board handled the failed audit clemently and gave the team time to fix the issues.
examples.analytical: The philosopher argues that a ruler should govern clemently, since punishment alone only breeds fear.

nuance.analogy: Like a parent who sets the rules but chooses a softer tone when enforcing them.
nuance.etymology: From clement plus the adverb suffix -ly.
common_mistakes: Using clemently in everyday English where leniently or mercifully is more natural.
Confusing it with clearly or cleanly because of the similar spelling.

senses.definition: An ordained (female) Christian minister; a female member of the clergy.
A woman belonging to a clergyman's family.
senses.example: Growing up as the minister's daughter, she was the clergywoman of the family, always helping at church suppers.

core.definition: A woman ordained to lead Christian worship and church services, such as a priest, pastor, or minister.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and keep the r rhotic. The second part, 'woman,' is pronounced 'WOOM-un' with a secondary stress, so do not say 'wo-man' as in 'ho-man'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It names a role in a respectful, descriptive way, and it is widely used in American church and news writing.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use clergywoman for a woman who has been ordained as a pastor, priest, or minister, especially in Protestant churches where women are ordained. In many American congregations, people also say pastor or reverend, and they may simply use her title. Clergyperson is a gender-neutral alternative that many people prefer in formal writing.

distinctions.note: Clergyperson is gender-neutral and is often used when the gender is unknown or the writer wants to avoid assumptions, while clergywoman specifies a woman.
A nun is a woman in a religious community who has taken vows, but may not be ordained, while a clergywoman is ordained for ministry.

examples.everyday: My friend is a clergywoman at the Episcopal church, and she preaches on Sunday mornings.
examples.professional: The denomination appointed a clergywoman to lead the new outreach team.
examples.analytical: Scholars debating women's ordination often ask whether the clergywoman's authority is derived from the same source as a clergyman's.

nuance.analogy: A clergywoman is like a teacher who has been officially certified, with the same training and responsibility as any colleague.
nuance.etymology: From clergy (Late Latin clericus, from Greek klēros, lot or portion) plus woman.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the second part as 'wo-man' with two equal syllables, rather than 'WOOM-un' with a reduced final syllable.
Assuming every church accepts clergywomen; many Catholic and Orthodox churches do not ordain women.

traditions.view: Only men are ordained as priests and bishops, so clergywomen are not recognized in the ordained sense. Historic deaconesses existed in the early church, but they are not ordained clergy today.
The church teaches that only men can be ordained as priests, so there are no clergywomen in the ordained sense. Women serve in many ministries, but they are not clergy in the sacramental sense.

Many Protestant denominations, such as Methodists, Episcopalians, and many Lutherans, ordain women as pastors or priests. Other Protestant churches, including some Reformed, Baptist and Pentecostal groups, do not ordain women to pastoral leadership.

senses.definition: An elite group of intellectuals; learned people, the literati.
senses.example: The clerisy of the early republic wrote essays on law, science, and public virtue.

senses.definition: The clergy, or their opinions, as opposed to the laity.
senses.example: The clerisy opposed the reforms, arguing that the laity lacked the training to interpret scripture.

core.definition: An educated elite of intellectuals or writers who shape a society's ideas; in older usage, also the clergy.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The ending -isy is pronounced 'see', like the 'ci' in city, and the word has only three syllables.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly formal. It can carry a note of elitism when a writer uses it to describe an intellectual class.
nuance.usage_note: Clerisy is rare in American speech and appears mainly in academic, literary, or historical writing about intellectuals and culture. In conversation, Americans would say 'intellectual elite', 'intelligentsia', or 'academics'. The religious sense is old and seldom used today.

distinctions.note: Intelligentsia is the more common term for educated, often politically engaged intellectuals; clerisy is more historical and literary.
Literati are educated writers and scholars; clerisy suggests a more organized class with social influence.
Elite is a general term for a privileged group; clerisy specifically means educated intellectual or cultural leaders.

examples.professional: The strategy memo assumed that a small clerisy of researchers would set the standards for the field.
examples.analytical: Coleridge's idea of a clerisy imagined learned men who cultivate a nation's moral and intellectual life.

nuance.analogy: Like a library's curators, quietly deciding what a culture remembers and values.
nuance.etymology: From Medieval Latin clericia, clergy, related to clericus, cleric; the intellectual sense was revived by Samuel Taylor Coleridge in the early 1800s.
common_mistakes: Assuming it means only the clergy; in modern usage it usually refers to intellectuals.
Confusing it with clergy in spelling or meaning; clerisy has no -gy ending.

senses.definition: To hit or bash severely; to seriously harm or damage.
To overwrite (data) or override (an assignment of a value), often unintentionally or unexpectedly.
A beating.
A bash on say the head, typically with a tool or object rather than with fists.
A paste used by shoemakers to hide the cracks in leather.

core.definition: To hit someone hard, or to defeat them badly in a game, contest or argument.

pronunciation.tip: Stress is on the first syllable. The second syllable is a weak, r-colored 'er' that is nearly silent, so don't stress it as in 'klah-BURR'.

nuance.connotation: Negative or humorous; it suggests a hard beating or a lopsided defeat.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use clobber in casual sports talk and everyday conversation, as in 'we got clobbered in the second half.' It is informal and sometimes playful, so in serious writing use defeat or beat. The noun sense for clothes is mainly British slang; Americans say clothes or outfit. A natural reply is 'Ouch, that's rough.'

distinctions.note: Defeat is neutral and formal; clobber is informal and suggests a crushing, lopsided loss.
Beat is the common everyday word; clobber is stronger and more colorful.
Hit is a plain verb for striking; clobber suggests hitting hard enough to do serious damage.

examples.everyday: Our team got clobbered last night, so nobody is in the mood for trivia.
examples.professional: Our product team got clobbered in the quarterly review, so we're rethinking the launch plan.
examples.analytical: The critics clobbered the theory in one essay, but its core intuition survived in revised form.

nuance.analogy: Being clobbered is like a sudden wave that knocks you flat before you can get to your feet.
common_mistakes: Using the noun sense for clothes in American speech, where it sounds British and odd.
Using clobber in formal writing where defeat or beat is expected.

clobber.etymology: British slang from 1941; possibly of the sound of detonated bombs in the distance.

senses.definition: Close, near, nearby: in proximity (to).
senses.example: She lives close by us.

senses.definition: Close, near, nearby: in proximity (to).
senses.example: There isn't any good source of water close by.

senses.definition: Close, near, nearby: in proximity (to).
senses.example: The close-by family members tried to help.

core.definition: Near, not far away; in the same general area as the speaker or the place being discussed.

pronunciation.tip: Close is pronounced with an s sound here, not z, and the stress falls on by, so say klohs-BYE. Keep the word by clearly stressed, since it is the main word of the phrase.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and friendly. It is a practical word for location in everyday talk.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use close by for directions and locations: there is a coffee shop close by. It often comes at the end of a clause, and nearby is a very common one-word synonym. A natural reply is 'Great, let's go check it out' or 'Perfect, that saves us a drive.'

distinctions.note: Nearby is one word and very common, while close by is two words and often sounds a bit more conversational.
Around is vaguer and means somewhere in the general area, while close by means a short distance away.

examples.everyday: We're hungry, so let's grab a sandwich at the place close by.
examples.professional: The client's office is close by, so we can walk over for the review.
examples.analytical: A witness who was close by has more direct knowledge of the event than one who heard about it afterward.

nuance.analogy: Like a neighbor a few houses down the street, someone you can reach on foot in a minute.
nuance.etymology: Close from Latin clausus, shut or confined; by from Old English bī, near.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing close with a z sound as in KLOHZ, which makes the phrase less natural; use klohs.
Writing closeby as one word in formal writing; use close by or nearby.

senses.definition: A sudden heavy rainstorm.
A sudden downfall or shortcoming.

core.definition: A sudden, very heavy rainstorm that releases a large amount of water in a short time, often causing flash flooding.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, CLOUD, with a lighter secondary stress on 'burst'. Keep the r-colored vowel in 'burst' and do not add an extra vowel before the final st cluster.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative; it suggests danger, flooding or damage when describing weather, and it can describe a sudden disaster figuratively.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use cloudburst in weather reports, news and local conversation, especially in mountain and desert regions where storms come quickly. Figuratively it is used in writing for a sudden downpour of something, such as complaints, but it is less common in speech. For milder rain, say downpour or heavy rain. A natural reply is 'Did you get caught in that?'

distinctions.note: A downpour is heavy rain in general; a cloudburst implies a rain that is more sudden, more intense and briefer.
A thunderstorm is defined by thunder and lightning; a cloudburst describes very heavy rain, even without thunder.

examples.everyday: We got caught in a cloudburst on the drive home, so my shoes are still soaked.
examples.professional: The site inspection was delayed because a cloudburst flooded the access road, so we'll reschedule for next week.
examples.analytical: Climate models suggest more intense cloudbursts, which strains drainage systems designed for historical rainfall levels.

nuance.analogy: Like a bucket tipped over the sky, emptying in a few minutes.
nuance.etymology: From cloud and burst, describing a cloud that seems to break open and release its water.
common_mistakes: Writing 'cloud burst' as two words in formal writing; the standard form is usually one word.
Pronouncing 'burst' like 'bust' with a short u; it has an r-colored vowel.
Using cloudburst for a long, gentle rain; it means a sudden, intense downpour.

senses.definition: To stick together physically, by adhesion.
senses.example: Separate molecules will cohere because of electromagnetic force.

senses.definition: To be consistent as part of a group, or by common purpose.
senses.example: Members of the party would cohere in the message they were sending.

core.definition: To stick firmly together as one mass, or to fit together logically so that the parts form a unified whole.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, koh-HEER, and pronounce the final r clearly. Do not stress the first syllable or say 'koh-HEAR-ent' as if it were a different word.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is positive when describing a team or argument that holds together well and negative when a plan fails to cohere.
nuance.usage_note: In physical contexts, such as chemistry or materials, Americans use 'cohere' for particles that stick together. In everyday speech they say 'hold together' or 'make sense'. In business and academic writing, 'cohere' describes groups, plans, or ideas that come together into a unit.

distinctions.note: Adhere means to stick to an outside surface or to follow a rule; cohere means parts stick to each other or fit together as one whole.
Coalesce means to merge gradually into one body; cohere means to hold together as a unit that is already formed.

examples.everyday: After a rough start, our new roommates finally started to cohere as a household.
examples.professional: Once we agreed on the goals, the project team finally began to cohere.
examples.analytical: A theory must cohere with the evidence we already accept if it is to be credible.

nuance.analogy: Like wet sand in a bucket: the grains stick together and hold a shape as one piece.
nuance.etymology: From Latin cohaerere, 'to stick together', from co- 'together' plus haerere 'to stick'.
common_mistakes: Confusing it with 'adhere', which means to stick to an external surface or to follow rules.
Stressing the first syllable instead of the second.
Using it for a single person's logic; 'cohere' usually describes parts of a group or whole.

senses.definition: Synonym of ice pack (for healing)
senses.example: After the ankle sprain, the trainer wrapped a cold pack around it for twenty minutes.

core.definition: A pack filled with ice or a chemical gel, applied to an injury to reduce swelling and pain.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on PACK, and the vowel is the short a of 'cat', not the 'ah' of 'pock'. End with a clear, released k sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral: a practical first aid item used in homes, schools and sports settings.
nuance.usage_note: Americans often say ice pack or ice bag for the same item, and ice pack is more common in everyday speech. Reusable gel packs are kept in the freezer, and the pack should go between a towel and the skin, usually for about fifteen to twenty minutes. Never press it directly onto bare skin.

distinctions.note: The two are nearly interchangeable; ice pack is more common in everyday speech, while cold pack often refers to a reusable gel pack.
A heating pad supplies warmth to relax sore muscles, while a cold pack reduces swelling after an injury.

collocations: ice the sprain with a cold pack
keep a cold pack in the freezer

examples.everyday: Hold this cold pack on your ankle for twenty minutes; it'll help with the swelling.
examples.professional: Please put a cold pack in the first aid kit before the field trip.
examples.analytical: The evidence supports a cold pack for acute soft-tissue injuries, but prolonged direct contact can damage the skin.

nuance.analogy: Like a small winter blanket for a sore spot, one that cools instead of warms.
nuance.etymology: Cold from Old English ceald; pack from Middle Dutch pak, 'bundle'.
common_mistakes: Placing a cold pack directly on bare skin
Using cold pack and cold compress as identical, when a compress is usually a cloth soaked in cold water

senses.definition: A person who comforts someone who is suffering.
senses.example: My mother was a quiet comforter who always knew what to say at funerals.

senses.definition: A padded cover for a bed, duvet, continental quilt.
senses.example: On cold nights we pile an extra wool comforter on the bed.

senses.definition: A pacifier.
senses.example: The baby spit out the comforter again, so we gave her a clean one.

core.definition: A thick, quilted bed covering used on top of sheets, or a person who soothes someone in grief or distress.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. Both final syllables are weak and rhotic, so the word ends with two reduced 'ur' sounds.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. The bedding sense is practical and warm, and the person sense is compassionate, but it can sound old-fashioned when used of a person.
nuance.usage_note: In the United States, 'comforter' is the everyday word for a thick quilted bed covering, and it is sold in many sizes and fabrics. The sense 'pacifier' is mainly British slang for a baby's soother, and Americans say 'pacifier' instead. When it means a person who comforts, the word is formal and is used mostly in religious or literary contexts.

distinctions.note: A duvet is a soft filled inner cover that goes inside a separate duvet cover, while an American comforter is usually a single finished quilted piece.
A blanket is generally a single layer for warmth, while a comforter is thicker, usually filled, and used as a bed cover on its own.

examples.everyday: Can you grab another comforter from the hall closet? It's freezing in here tonight.
examples.professional: Our new bedding line includes a down comforter with a warranty, and it sells well during the winter.
examples.analytical: In John 14, the Greek term paraklētos is rendered 'Counselor' in the RSV, not 'Comforter' as in older translations, because it denotes an advocate called to one's side.

nuance.analogy: A comforter is like a warm hug that covers the whole bed: it wraps you up when you need rest.
nuance.etymology: From 'comfort' with the agent suffix '-er', one who or that which comforts.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'comforter' the bedcover with 'duvet', which is a different product in the US.
Using 'comforter' for a baby's pacifier, which Americans call a pacifier.
nuance.biblical_note: In the RSV, Greek paraklētos is usually translated 'Counselor' or 'Advocate', and in older versions it appears as 'Comforter', the name for the Holy Spirit. Key passages include John 14:16, where Jesus promises another Counselor to be with his disciples forever; John 14:26, where this Counselor is called the Holy Spirit, who teaches and reminds the disciples; and 2 Corinthians 1:3-4, where God is described as the Father of mercies and God of all comfort. These passages present the Spirit as one who stands beside believers in difficulty and helps them.

comforter.etymology: From Middle English *comfortour* et al, from Anglo-Norman *confortour*, from Old French *conforter*.

core.definition: The spiritual union of all believers in Christ, living and dead, sharing in God's life and praying for one another.

pronunciation.tip: In 'communion' the stress is on 'MYOON' and the ending is a quick 'yun'. In the phrase, 'of' reduces to 'uv', and 'saints' gets the stress.

nuance.connotation: Positive and reverent; suggests unity and fellowship across time.
nuance.usage_note: Americans hear this phrase mainly in church, especially from the Apostles' Creed, which many say weekly. It is not casual speech, and outside Christian circles most people will not know it. Avoid confusing it with the Communion service.

distinctions.note: Communion alone often means the sacrament of the Lord's Supper; communion of saints refers to the fellowship of believers.
Fellowship is the shared life of a local group; communion of saints is universal and includes the departed.
The church is the body of believers; the communion of saints stresses their unity and shared life.

collocations: believe in the communion of saints
fellowship of the communion of saints
the Church and the communion of saints

examples.everyday: When we say the Creed, I always think about the communion of saints, the people who prayed in this church before me.
examples.professional: This course explores how the communion of saints shapes Christian ideas of prayer, memory, and the afterlife.
examples.analytical: The doctrine of the communion of saints holds that death does not sever the bond among those united in Christ.

nuance.analogy: Like a family that stays one even when some members are in another room.
nuance.etymology: Latin communio sanctorum, which can mean both fellowship of holy persons and sharing in holy things.
common_mistakes: Confusing it with the sacrament of Communion.
Pronouncing 'communion' as 'kuh-MYOO-nee-on'; the ending is 'yun'.
Dropping the plural s: say 'saints', not 'saint'.
nuance.biblical_note: The phrase itself is not in the Bible, but the idea rests on Greek koinonia, 'fellowship,' and hagioi, 'saints.' 1 Corinthians 12:12-27 describes the church as one body whose members share one another's joys and sufferings. Hebrews 12:1 pictures believers surrounded by a great cloud of witnesses. Revelation 7:9-10 shows a multitude from every nation worshiping before the throne.

traditions.view: The Church includes the faithful on earth, souls being purified, and the saints in heaven, all united and able to help one another by prayer.
The Church is one living body on earth and in heaven. The living and departed pray for each other, especially in the Divine Liturgy.

Most affirm the communion of saints as the unity of all believers in Christ, and the Apostles' Creed is widely used. Many deny that departed saints should be invoked, though some, like Anglicans and Lutherans, remember them with thanks.

senses.definition: The state of having or being a companion.
senses.example: seek companionship

senses.definition: The state of being a journeyman.
An organized group of people.
senses.example: The retired teachers formed a companionship that met every Tuesday at the library.

core.definition: The friendly company of another person, or the comfort of being with someone you enjoy.

pronunciation.tip: Stress 'PAN' in the second syllable. The '-ion' ending is pronounced 'yun', not 'ee-un', and the final 'ship' is short and light.

nuance.connotation: Positive and warm. It suggests comfort, loyalty, and emotional support.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'companionship' to describe friendship, company for an older person living alone, or the comfort of a pet. It is more formal than 'company' and warmer than 'a friend around'. In casual talk, people often say 'company' or 'someone to hang out with'. In church, the word may refer to friendship in God's community.

distinctions.note: Friendship is the relationship itself; companionship focuses on the everyday presence and company that friends or partners provide.
Company is more general and casual, for example having people around; companionship suggests a closer, warmer bond.

examples.everyday: Our dog gives my dad a lot of companionship since Mom passed, and he is much happier with her around.
examples.professional: The remote onboarding program pairs new hires with a peer mentor to provide professional companionship during the first month.
examples.analytical: Ecclesiastes says that two are better than one, and the companionship it praises is not merely practical help but a shared life that gives both people strength.

nuance.analogy: Companionship is like a steady campfire on a cold night: it keeps you warm not by blazing, but by staying near.
nuance.etymology: From companion, from Old French compaignon, one who shares bread, from Latin com-, with, and panis, bread.
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable, as in 'kuhm-pan-YUN-ship' with a stressed 'yun'.
Pronouncing the '-ion' as 'ee-un' instead of the reduced 'yun'.
nuance.biblical_note: In Ecclesiastes 4:9-10 (RSV), the Preacher says that two are better than one, because they have a good reward for their toil, and if one falls, the other can lift him up. Proverbs 27:17 (RSV) says that iron sharpens iron, and one person sharpens another, describing the growth that comes through friendship. Psalm 55:13-14 (RSV) speaks of a close companion and familiar friend who shared sweet fellowship with the psalmist, showing that betrayal by a companion is especially painful.

senses.definition: A team; a group of people who work together for a common purpose.
senses.example: a company of knights

senses.definition: A group of performing artists who put on shows together.
senses.example: a company of actors

senses.definition: A unit of firefighters and their equipment.
senses.example: It took six companies to put out the fire.

senses.definition: An intelligence service.
senses.example: As he had worked for the CIA for over 30 years, he would soon take retirement from the company.

senses.definition: A specific aircraft or its airline, usually used in air traffic communications to refer conveniently to another aircraft operated by the same airline.
senses.example: Tower, company 2417 is holding short of runway two-seven, please advise.

senses.definition: A small group of birds or animals.
senses.example: A company of crows lifted from the cornfield as we drove past.

senses.definition: An entity having legal personality, and thus able to own property and to sue and be sued in its own name; a corporation.
senses.example: a financial services company

senses.definition: Any business, whether incorporated or not, that manufactures or sells products (also known as goods), or provides services as a commercial venture.
senses.example: Marconi set up the company who made the first radios.

senses.definition: The members of a partnership business who are not listed in the company's name; unnamed individuals in an entourage or other group.
senses.example: Smith, Capitano and Company

senses.definition: Companionship.
senses.example: I treasure your company.

senses.definition: One or more social visitor(s) or companion(s).
senses.example: Keep the house clean; I have company coming.

senses.definition: One or more other person(s) who are nearby, are approaching, or are (e.g. covertly) watching, especially if they may have hostile intentions (like adversaries or rivals).
senses.example: Get your guns ready: intel said there'd be no hostiles in the area, but it looks like we've got company.

senses.definition: The crew of a ship.
senses.example: a ship's company

senses.definition: A unit of approximately sixty to one hundred and twenty soldiers, typically consisting of two or three platoons and forming part of a battalion.
senses.example: the boys in Company C

core.definition: The presence of other people, or the people you spend time with; also a business firm.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, KUM-, and the middle syllable is a reduced schwa. Say it as two quick beats and end with a light 'ee', not 'com-PAN-ee' or 'KOM-pa-nee'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive; 'good company' is warm praise, while 'bad company' is negative.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use company for both people who are with you and for a business, and both uses are very common. To keep someone company means to stay with them so they are not alone. In work settings, 'What company do you work for?' is a normal small-talk question. If someone says 'We have company', they mean visitors have arrived.

distinctions.note: Company is the presence of people or a business; companion is one person who accompanies you.
A corporation is a formal legal entity; company is the everyday word for any business, large or small.
Firm is common in law and professional services; company is the general word for a business.

examples.everyday: Thanks for coming over, it's nice to have some company while I cook.
examples.professional: Our company is moving the reporting platform to the cloud next quarter, so please update your access requests by Friday.
examples.analytical: Lewis argues that good company refines the mind, since we learn to test our views against other people.

nuance.analogy: Company works like a mirror: other people reflect your ideas back to you, so they become clearer.
nuance.etymology: From Old French compaignie, from compain 'companion', from Late Latin companio, from com- 'with' + panis 'bread'.
common_mistakes: Using company to mean a single friend; say companion or friend, since company usually means people in general or a business.
Saying 'I have company' when you mean you work for a company, which can confuse listeners.

company.etymology: From Middle English *companye* (“a team; companionship”), from Old French *compaignie* (“companionship”) (Modern French: *compagnie*), possibly from Late Latin, but this word is not attested.

senses.definition: Containing a subset of words, succinctly described; abridged and summarized.
senses.example: The compendious textbook condensed three decades of research into a single two-hundred-page volume.

senses.definition: Briefly describing a body of knowledge.
senses.example: Her compendious lecture surveyed the entire history of statistics in under an hour.

core.definition: Briefly covering a large amount of material in a complete but compact form.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on PEN, the second syllable. The -dious ending is 'dee-uhs', with a clear ee sound in the middle and a reduced final vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive; it praises a work for being thorough yet concise. It sounds bookish, so in casual speech it can seem pretentious.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use compendious in conversation. You will see it in book reviews, academic writing or formal descriptions of reference works. In speech, say concise, comprehensive or thorough instead.

distinctions.note: Comprehensive means covering everything fully and can be long; compendious means covering a lot in a condensed form.
Concise describes brevity in general; compendious implies a broad body of knowledge squeezed into a compact form.
Succinct is common in speech and writing and describes brief, clear expression; compendious is more formal and focuses on the scope of content.

examples.everyday: This travel guide is pretty compendious, so you can look up almost anything about the national parks in one place.
examples.professional: The onboarding wiki is a compendious guide to our data pipelines, so new engineers can find answers without asking around.
examples.analytical: Because the author treats each school of thought in only a few pages, the book is compendious in scope but thin in argument.

nuance.analogy: A compendious book is like a well-packed carry-on: it holds everything you need in a small, organized space.
nuance.etymology: From Latin compendiosus 'shortened, brief', from compendium 'saving, shortening', from compendere 'to weigh together'.
common_mistakes: Confusing compendious with compendium: the adjective describes a work, while the noun is the collection itself.
Stressing the final syllable (kuhm-pen-DEE-us) instead of PEN, the stressed syllable.

compendious.etymology: From Old French *compendieux*, from Latin *compendiosus* (“advantageous, abridged, brief”), from *compendium*.

senses.definition: Compulsion.

core.definition: The tendency to act compulsively, driven by urges to perform repeated actions that one feels unable to resist; used especially in psychology.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on SIV, the third syllable, with a lighter stress on the first. The -ity ending is a short 'ih-tee', and the vowels in the middle are reduced.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes a pattern that causes distress or impairment, though as a research measure it is neutral.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use compulsivity mainly in psychology, psychiatry and research papers, for example in studies that compare impulsivity and compulsivity. In everyday conversation they say compulsiveness or compulsive behavior. Using compulsivity in casual talk can sound overly clinical.

distinctions.note: Compulsivity is more technical and research-oriented; compulsiveness is the everyday word for the same trait.
Impulsivity means acting quickly without thinking, while compulsivity means repeating acts to relieve an urge one cannot resist.

examples.everyday: My therapist said my nightly routine shows some compulsivity, but she thinks it is manageable.
examples.professional: The study measured compulsivity and impulsivity separately, since they predict different behaviors in patients.
examples.analytical: Compulsivity, unlike simple habit, persists even when the person recognizes the behavior as excessive and wants to stop.

nuance.analogy: Think of compulsivity as a smoke alarm that keeps going off even when there is no fire: the urge keeps sounding whatever the facts are.
nuance.etymology: From compulsive, from Latin compellere, to drive together, plus the abstract suffix -ity from Latin -itas.
common_mistakes: Using compulsivity in casual conversation, where compulsiveness sounds more natural.
Confusing compulsivity with impulsivity, which describes acting too quickly rather than repeating a ritual.

senses.definition: Having an excessively favorable opinion of one's abilities, appearance, etc. egotistical and vain.
senses.example: Nobody liked working with him because he was conceited and never admitted a single mistake.

senses.definition: Having an ingenious expression or metaphorical idea, especially in extended form or used as a literary or rhetorical device.
senses.example: The metaphysical poet's conceited comparison of two lovers to a drafting compass delighted his readers.

core.definition: Vain and full of pride in your own appearance, abilities or importance, often in an annoying way.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, SEE. The ending -ed is pronounced as a separate short syllable, 'tid,' not as a plain t sound.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It strongly criticizes someone for vanity or bragging.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use conceited in everyday talk to criticize people who brag or act superior, as in 'He's so conceited about his new car.' It is informal but not rude in most settings. For a harsher insult, people say 'stuck-up' or 'full of himself.' To be polite, speakers often choose 'confident' or 'proud' instead.

distinctions.note: Arrogant focuses on acting superior and dismissive of others. Conceited focuses on vanity and an inflated opinion of yourself.
Confident is positive and based on real ability. Conceited is negative and suggests you overrate yourself.

examples.everyday: Mike's so conceited about his new truck that he talks about it all night.
examples.professional: Nobody wants to work with a conceited lead who dismisses every suggestion from the junior engineers.
examples.analytical: The narrator's conceited voice undermines his claim to objectivity, which is part of what makes the novel unsettling.

nuance.analogy: Like a peacock that keeps turning around to show off, a conceited person keeps checking whether you noticed.
nuance.etymology: From conceit (noun), from Middle English conceite, with the past-participle suffix -ed.
common_mistakes: Confusing conceited with conceived, the past tense of conceive
Using conceited as a compliment for someone who is simply confident; it almost always sounds critical

senses.definition: To strongly criticize or denounce; to excoriate.
senses.example: The president condemned the terrorists.

senses.definition: To judicially pronounce (someone) guilty.
senses.example: The judge condemned the defendant after the jury returned a unanimous verdict.

senses.definition: To judicially announce a verdict upon a finding of guilt; To sentence.
senses.example: The judge condemned him to death.

senses.definition: To confer eternal divine punishment upon.
senses.example: Many preachers insist that unrepentant sinners will be condemned to eternal punishment.

senses.definition: To destine to experience bad circumstances; to doom.
senses.example: Too many people are condemned to a life of poverty.

senses.definition: To declare something to be unfit for use, or further use.
senses.example: The house was condemned after it was badly damaged by fire.

senses.definition: To adjudge (a building) as being unfit for habitation.
senses.example: The house was condemned after it was badly damaged by fire.

senses.definition: To adjudge (building or construction work) as of unsatisfactory quality, requiring the work to be redone.
senses.example: The inspector condemned the new wiring and ordered the electricians to redo it.

senses.definition: To adjudge (food or drink) as being unfit for human consumption.
senses.example: The health department condemned the shellfish and destroyed the entire shipment.

senses.definition: To declare (a vessel) to be unfit for service.
senses.example: The admiralty court condemned the captured schooner as a lawful prize of war.

senses.definition: To determine and declare (property) to be assigned to public use. See eminent domain.
senses.example: The city condemned three houses on Elm Street to make room for the highway.

senses.definition: To declare (a vessel) to be forfeited to the government or to be a prize.
senses.example: The admiralty court condemned the captured schooner as a lawful prize of war.

core.definition: To express strong disapproval of something, or to declare someone guilty and sentence them.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, DEM. The final m is clearly pronounced, and the b is silent, so the word has no b sound. The first syllable is a reduced schwa.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it expresses strong disapproval or a serious judgment against someone.
nuance.usage_note: In everyday American speech people use condemn for strong public disapproval, as in 'the mayor condemned the violence,' or in legal contexts for sentencing. In casual talk people might say 'I can't condemn him for that,' meaning they understand and don't blame him. Be careful, because the word is strong and can sound dramatic in ordinary conversation.

distinctions.note: Criticize is a general word for finding fault; condemn is much stronger and implies moral or public disapproval.
Sentence is the legal act of announcing punishment, while condemn can also mean finding someone guilty or expressing strong disapproval.

examples.everyday: I can't really condemn him for lying; he was scared and didn't know what to do.
examples.professional: The team condemned the outage publicly, but we still need to find the root cause in the logs.
examples.analytical: Paul argues that God condemned sin in the flesh, but he does not condemn those who are in Christ Jesus.

nuance.analogy: To condemn is to place a heavy stamp of disapproval on something, like a red seal on a document that cannot be undone.
nuance.etymology: From Latin condemnare, to sentence or to condemn, from com- 'completely' and damnare 'to harm, condemn'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the b in condemn, which is silent.
Using condemn for mild disagreement where criticize is more appropriate.
nuance.biblical_note: The Greek word behind 'condemn' is katakrinō, meaning to pass judgment against or to sentence. Romans 8:1 in the RSV says there is no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus. John 3:17 says God did not send his Son into the world to condemn the world, but to save it.

condemn.etymology: From Middle English *condempnen*, from Old French *condamner*, from Latin *condemnāre* (“to sentence, condemn, blame”), from *com-* + *damnāre* (“to harm, condemn, damn”), from *damnum* (“damage, injury, loss”).

senses.definition: Anything that improves the condition of something. (Can we add an example for this sense?)
senses.example: Compost is a natural soil conditioner that improves drainage and holds nutrients in the root zone.

senses.definition: Hair conditioner.
Fabric conditioner; fabric softener.
Someone who trains athletes or racehorses.
senses.example: The conditioner worked with the racehorse every morning, building its stamina before the Derby.

senses.definition: An agricultural machine that crimps and crushes newly cut hay to promote faster and more even drying.
senses.example: The farmer's conditioner crimped the cut alfalfa so it would dry before the afternoon rain.

core.definition: A product, such as hair conditioner or fabric softener, that makes hair or laundry softer and easier to manage.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, DISH. The final 'er' is a rhotic American r-colored vowel, not a long 'ee', and the middle syllables are reduced.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral. It is a practical product word used in shopping and home contexts.
nuance.usage_note: In everyday American English 'conditioner' almost always means hair conditioner, used after shampoo. For laundry, Americans say 'fabric softener', while 'fabric conditioner' is more British and rare. The older sense of anything that improves a condition is formal and uncommon.

distinctions.note: Shampoo cleans hair, while conditioner is applied afterward to soften and smooth it.
Fabric softener is the American word for the laundry product, while 'conditioner' normally refers to hair products.
Moisturizer is used for skin, while hair conditioner is designed specifically for hair.

examples.everyday: Do you know if this conditioner works well on curly hair?
examples.professional: Our product team is testing a new conditioner formula for the spring line before it goes to retail.
examples.analytical: The conditioner's effect is hard to isolate in the trial, since participants also changed their washing routines.

nuance.analogy: Like lotion after a shower: the shampoo cleans, and the conditioner makes everything softer and easier to comb.
nuance.etymology: From the verb condition, from Latin condicio, plus the agent suffix -er.
common_mistakes: Using 'conditioner' for laundry in the US; say 'fabric softener' instead.
Saying the word with an extra syllable, such as 'con-di-TION-er', instead of the standard 'kun-DISH-un-er'.

senses.definition: Of or pertaining to Congregationalism, Congregationalists or a Congregational church.

core.definition: Relating to Congregationalism, or to a church in which each local congregation governs itself through its own members.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on GAY, and the '-tional' ending is pronounced 'shuh-nul' with a light final l, not 'shuh-nal'. Many learners stress the first syllable or pronounce every vowel fully.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a descriptive term for church structure and carries no judgment about any church.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word mostly in religious contexts, such as a Congregational church or Congregational polity. Many older New England churches and the United Church of Christ have Congregational roots. In casual talk people more often say the church's name or say that it is 'a Congregational church' when explaining how it is run.

distinctions.note: Congregation is the noun for the group of worshippers. Congregational is the adjective describing a church or system of governance based on local self-rule.
Presbyterian churches are governed by elders in councils called presbyteries, while Congregational churches place final authority in the local membership.

examples.everyday: Our church is Congregational, so the members vote on who becomes the new pastor.
examples.professional: Because our church is Congregational, the annual budget has to be approved by a vote of the membership.
examples.analytical: A Congregational polity locates final authority in the local body of believers rather than in bishops or a synod.

nuance.analogy: It works like a town meeting, where residents make the decisions directly rather than a distant council or mayor.
nuance.etymology: From Latin congregatio, 'a gathering,' from congregare, 'to gather into a flock,' from con- 'together' and grex, gregis 'flock'.
common_mistakes: Using congregational as a noun for worshippers. The noun is congregation, and the adjective congregational describes the church or its structure.
Stressing the first syllable (KAHNG-gruh-GAY-shuh-nul) instead of GAY.
nuance.biblical_note: Congregationalism draws on the New Testament Greek word ekklesia, meaning 'assembly' or 'gathering of those called out,' which the RSV usually translates as 'church.' Matthew 16:18 has Jesus speaking of building his church on Peter's confession. Acts 15:22 describes the apostles and elders together with the whole church choosing men to send to Antioch, which Congregationalists read as evidence of communal decision-making. Congregationalists also point to Exodus 12:6, where the whole assembly of the congregation of Israel takes part in the Passover rite, as an Old Testament model of corporate worship.

traditions.view: The Orthodox Church is governed by bishops in a synodal structure, with the local bishop as the normal head of a local church. Congregational self-governance is not a recognized model of church order.

The Church is structured hierarchically, with the pope, bishops, and parish priests holding authority by apostolic succession. Local congregations are parishes under the pastoral authority of an appointed priest and their bishop, not self-governing bodies.

Congregationalists, Baptists in many forms, and some independent churches hold that each local congregation is self-governing under Christ. Presbyterians and Reformed churches use elders in representative councils, while Anglicans and Lutherans maintain episcopal or synodal structures, so Protestants differ among themselves on polity.

senses.definition: A relation between two numbers indicating they give the same remainder when divided by some given number.
The quality of being isometric — roughly, the same measure and shape.
Matrix similarity by an orthogonal matrix.
senses.example: In the proof, we established congruence between the two matrices using an orthogonal matrix.

senses.definition: The quality of agreeing or corresponding; being suitable and appropriate.
senses.example: The congruence between the design and the company's values made the brand feel authentic.

senses.definition: Any equivalence relation defined on an algebraic structure which is preserved by operations defined by the structure.
senses.example: In abstract algebra, congruence modulo n is preserved by addition and multiplication of integers.

senses.definition: A well-adjusted state or condition in which people are not lying to themselves or in denial.
senses.example: Her therapist believed that real congruence required her to admit her fears about the business.

core.definition: In mathematics, a relation showing that two figures have identical size and shape, or that two integers leave the same remainder when divided by a given number.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, KAHNG, with the a as in cot. The middle syllable is quick, and the ending is a reduced uns sound, not a full ence.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise term and sounds technical in everyday talk.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use congruence mainly in math classes, geometry, and academic writing. In ordinary speech people say 'agreement,' 'match,' or 'consistency.' Outside mathematics, the word can describe consistency between values and actions, but this use is less common.

distinctions.note: Similar figures have the same shape but may differ in size. Congruent figures match exactly in both size and shape.
Equality means the same value or amount. Congruence is a specific mathematical relation about shape or remainders.

examples.everyday: There is a real congruence between what she says and how she acts, and I like that about her.
examples.professional: The unit test checks for congruence between the expected output and the computed value within a small tolerance.
examples.analytical: The congruence 17 is congruent to 5 modulo 6 reveals a structure that ordinary subtraction hides.

nuance.analogy: Like two cookie cutters that cut out exactly the same shape.
nuance.etymology: From Latin congruentia, from congruere, 'to come together, agree', from com- 'together' and ruere 'to fall'.
common_mistakes: Using congruence in casual speech where agreement or match is more natural.
Confusing congruence with similarity: congruent shapes match exactly, while similar shapes only match in form.

congruence.etymology: From Middle English *congruence*, from Latin *congruentia* (“agreement”), from *congruēns*, present active participle of *congruō* (“meet together, agree”).

senses.definition: In a conscious manner; knowingly, volitionally.
senses.example: She consciously chose to forgive her brother, knowing exactly what he had done.

core.definition: On purpose and with awareness; deliberately, knowing what you are doing.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable. Say the 'sh' sound clearly, then 'us' as a reduced vowel, and end with 'lee'. Don't pronounce it as 'con-see-us-lee'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It emphasizes intention and awareness, which can sound careful or deliberate.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'consciously' mostly with verbs, as in 'I consciously chose not to reply' or 'She tries consciously to listen more.' It often implies effort, and it can sound like a correction, as in 'I'm not consciously ignoring you.' In casual speech, 'on purpose' is more common; 'consciously' sounds more reflective.

distinctions.note: Deliberately stresses careful planning. Consciously stresses awareness of what you are doing, even if it was not planned in advance.
Intentionally is the closest synonym, but consciously usually emphasizes awareness rather than the goal.
Unconsciously means without awareness or intention. It is the opposite of consciously.

examples.everyday: I know I shouldn't have said that, but I consciously chose not to bring it up at dinner.
examples.professional: We consciously included junior engineers in the design review to broaden our perspective.
examples.analytical: A philosopher might ask whether we can consciously choose our beliefs, or whether beliefs simply happen to us.

nuance.analogy: Like a driver who steers on purpose rather than letting the car drift on autopilot.
nuance.etymology: From the adjective conscious (from Latin conscius, 'knowing with oneself') plus the adverb suffix -ly.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'consciously' with 'conscientiously'. The first means deliberately or with awareness; the second means carefully and thoroughly.
Mispronouncing the middle as 'see-us' instead of 'shus'.

senses.definition: Rare form of conservatism.

core.definition: A rare spelling variant of conservatism: a political or social philosophy favoring tradition, stability, and gradual change over sudden reform.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on SUR. Note that the standard form conservatism is pronounced kun-SUR-vuh-tiz-um, and the -ism ending is an unstressed 'um' sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It names a political or social philosophy and sounds formal, but the spelling itself is unusual.
nuance.usage_note: Americans almost always write conservatism, not conservativism. You may see the rare form in older texts or in mistaken writing, but you should avoid it in your own work. Use conservatism in both speech and writing.

distinctions.note: Conservatism is the standard American spelling; conservativism is a rare variant with the same meaning.
Conservation means protecting natural resources; conservatism is a political or social philosophy.

examples.everyday: Grandpa's conservativism shows up in how he refuses to try any new recipes.
examples.professional: Her conservativism on budget matters shaped how the board approved the spending plan.
examples.analytical: Burke's conservativism, as usually read, treats custom and prejudice as sources of practical wisdom rather than as obstacles to reason.

nuance.analogy: Conservativism is like an old word spelled in an unusual way: it means the same thing as conservatism but looks strange on the page.
nuance.etymology: Formed from conservative (from Latin conservativus) plus the suffix -ism, with the rare spelling -ivism.
common_mistakes: Using the rare spelling conservativism in formal writing, where conservatism is standard.
Confusing conservatism with conservation, which refers to protecting natural resources.

senses.definition: To think about seriously.
senses.example: Consider that we’ve had three major events and the year has hardly begun.

senses.definition: To think about something seriously or carefully: to deliberate.
To think about whether one will do (an action); to weigh as a possible course of action.
senses.example: I’m considering going to the beach tomorrow.

senses.definition: To assign some quality to.
senses.example: Consider yourself lucky, but consider your opponent skillful.

senses.definition: To look at attentively.
senses.example: She sat there for a moment, considering him.

senses.definition: To take up as an example.
senses.example: Consider a triangle having three equal sides.

senses.definition: To debate (or dispose of) a motion.
senses.example: This body will now consider the proposed amendments to Section 453 of the zoning code.

senses.definition: To have regard to; to take into view or account; to pay due attention to; to respect.
senses.example: He never seems to consider the feelings of others.

senses.definition: To believe or opine (that).
senses.example: Most analysts consider that the rate cut is already priced in.

core.definition: To think carefully about something, especially before making a decision or judgment.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, SID. The final -er is a weak, reduced syllable, not a full 'air' sound; say it lightly with a slight r coloring.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive: it signals careful thought, and it is polite when you ask someone to think about something.
nuance.usage_note: Consider is one of the most common verbs in American English, used in meetings, emails and everyday talk. You can say 'Have you considered...?' or 'I'm considering a job offer' to show you are weighing options. The grammar pattern is consider plus a gerund, as in 'consider moving,' not 'consider to move.' In polite requests, 'Would you consider...?' is a gentle, respectful way to ask.

distinctions.note: Think about is broader and more casual; consider implies weighing options or reasoning.
Contemplate is more formal and often suggests quiet, extended reflection.
Ponder suggests slow, puzzled reflection, often on a hard question.

examples.everyday: Would you consider moving to Denver for the job, or is that too far from family?
examples.professional: Before we approve the vendor, we should consider the total cost of ownership over three years.
examples.analytical: A careful reader must consider whether the author's conclusion truly follows from the evidence presented.

nuance.analogy: Considering a choice is like holding it up to the light and turning it slowly to see every side.
nuance.etymology: From Latin considerare, 'to examine closely, contemplate'.
common_mistakes: Writing consider to do instead of consider doing, as in 'I am considering to move' instead of 'considering moving'.
Adding about after consider, as in 'consider about it'; just say 'consider it'.
Pronouncing the last syllable as a full 'air' sound instead of the reduced -er.

consider.etymology: From Middle English *consideren*, from Middle French *considerer*, from Latin *considero*.

senses.definition: Consciously thoughtful and observant (often of other people and their rights, needs, feelings and comfort).
senses.example: It was very considerate of you to give up your place for your friend.

senses.definition: Characterized by careful and conscious thought.
Synonym of consider.

core.definition: Careful not to hurt, inconvenience, or upset others; thoughtful about their needs and feelings.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on SID, and the ending is a weak 'it' sound, not 'ate'. The middle syllable is a quick American r, so say it as one smooth word.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It praises kindness toward others and rarely shifts meaning with context.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use it to praise someone who thinks about other people, as in 'That was really considerate of you.' It is common in everyday talk and workplace feedback, and it sounds warm rather than stiff. A natural reply is 'Thanks, I try to be.'

distinctions.note: Thoughtful can mean deep reflection or a nice gesture; considerate focuses on not inconveniencing or hurting others.
Polite is about manners and social rules; considerate is about actually noticing someone else's needs.

examples.everyday: Thanks for turning down the music, that was really considerate.
examples.professional: Thanks for sending the agenda early, that was considerate since people had time to prepare.
examples.analytical: Kant's ethics ask whether we treat others as ends in themselves, and a considerate person does this as a habit rather than a calculation.

nuance.analogy: Like walking quietly past a sleeping baby's room.
nuance.etymology: From Latin considerare, 'to examine closely'.
common_mistakes: Using it for a thinking process, as in 'a considerate analysis'; it describes behavior toward people, so use 'careful' or 'thorough' for analysis.
patterns: it is considerate of sb to do sth

senses.definition: Obvious or easy to notice.
senses.example: He was conspicuous by his absence.

senses.definition: Noticeable or attracting attention, especially if unattractive.
senses.example: He had a conspicuous lump on his forehead.

core.definition: Easy to notice, often because it stands out or looks out of place, sometimes in a way that draws unwanted attention.

pronunciation.tip: Primary stress falls on SPIK, and the ending '-ous' is a short 'us', not 'oh-us'. Say the middle syllables quickly and do not add an extra syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in most uses, but negative when it describes showing off, as in 'conspicuous consumption'.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word more in writing and formal speech than in casual talk, where 'obvious' or 'noticeable' is more common. The phrase 'conspicuous by its absence' is a common idiom for something important that is missing. It is standard American English.

distinctions.note: Obvious means easy to understand or see, while conspicuous adds that something stands out and draws attention.
Visible is neutral and simply means can be seen, while conspicuous means so easy to see that it catches your eye.

examples.everyday: Our new car's bright orange paint is pretty conspicuous in the parking lot.
examples.professional: The missing budget line was conspicuous in the report, so finance asked us to explain it.
examples.analytical: The author's silence on colonial labor is conspicuous, and it shapes how we read her whole argument.

nuance.analogy: Like a red sock in a drawer of white laundry: it is hard to miss.
nuance.etymology: From Latin conspicuus 'visible', from conspicere 'to look at, observe', from con- and specere 'to look'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable as 'con-SPIK-yoo-us' or 'kon-spih-KYOO-us'; the main stress is on SPIK.
Using 'conspicuous' for something that is merely good; it describes visibility, not quality.

conspicuous.etymology: From Latin *conspicuus* (“visible, striking”), from *cōnspicere* (“to notice”), from *con-* (“with, together”) + *specere* (“to look at”).

senses.definition: Capable of contraction.
(of a topological set) Able to be reduced to one of its points by a continuous deformation.
senses.example: In topology, a set is contractible if it can be continuously deformed to one of its points.

core.definition: Capable of being made smaller or drawn together, as in materials, tissues, or mathematical shapes.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on TRAK. The ending -ible is reduced to 'uh-bul' in American speech, not 'ih-bull' or 'eebul.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise technical term with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word mostly in physics, biology, materials science, and mathematics. In everyday talk, people say 'can shrink' or 'gets smaller.' The word is rare in general English, so using it outside technical settings may sound overly precise.

distinctions.note: Contractile describes living tissue that actively shortens, such as muscle; contractible is broader and can describe passive shrinking of a material or shape.
Compressible means it can be squeezed into less space by force; contractible can also mean shrinking through cooling or topological deformation.

examples.everyday: This foam is contractible, so it gets smaller when it cools down.
examples.professional: In the simulation, the membrane is contractible, so the model shrinks it under heavy stress.
examples.analytical: A subset is contractible when a continuous deformation shrinks it to a single point within itself.

nuance.analogy: A contractible shape is like a balloon that can be squeezed slowly down to one point without tearing.
nuance.etymology: From contract, with the suffix -ible, meaning capable of being.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'contractible' with 'contractile,' which refers to active shortening in living tissue.
Pronouncing the ending as 'ih-bull' rather than the reduced 'uh-bul.'

senses.definition: To distinguish things by contrasting their different qualities.

core.definition: To distinguish two things by setting them against each other and pointing out their contrasting qualities.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on STING, and the 'gw' sound is clear, as in 'language'. The final 'ish' is short, and the middle syllables are reduced.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it sounds technical and deliberate.
nuance.usage_note: This is a specialized academic verb used in philosophy, linguistics and scholarly writing. Americans rarely use it in speech; they say 'distinguish between' or 'contrast' instead. It works best in writing where the author wants to stress a deliberate, two-sided distinction.

distinctions.note: Distinguish is the everyday verb for telling things apart, while contradistinguish stresses the act of setting one thing against its opposite.
Contrast is common and general, while contradistinguish is formal and often used to define a term by its opposite.

examples.professional: The memo contradistinguishes the two budget options so the committee can vote on them clearly.
examples.analytical: Luther contradistinguishes the law from the gospel, treating each as a distinct way God addresses human beings.

nuance.analogy: Like placing two photos side by side so the difference between them becomes obvious.
nuance.etymology: From contra- 'against' and distinguish, from Latin distinguere 'to separate'.
common_mistakes: Using it as a casual synonym for 'distinguish' in everyday speech, where it sounds stiff.
Forgetting the preposition: 'contradistinguish A from B' is the usual pattern.

senses.definition: The vertical movement of heat and moisture, especially by updrafts and downdrafts in an unstable air mass. The terms convection and thunderstorm are often used interchangeably, although thunderstorms are only one form of convection. Towering cumulus clouds are visible forms of convection.
senses.example: Warm, humid air rising over the hot pavement drives convection that builds towering clouds.

senses.definition: The transmission of heat in a fluid by the circulation of currents.

core.definition: The transfer of heat through a fluid or gas by the movement of warmer, lighter currents rising and cooler ones sinking.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, VEK. The first and last syllables are weak, and the 'ti' in the ending sounds like 'sh'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise scientific or everyday kitchen term with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use convection in physics, weather forecasts and cooking, where a convection oven circulates hot air with a fan. In everyday talk people might say the oven is on convection. In weather contexts, a meteorologist may talk about convection building thunderstorms over the afternoon.

distinctions.note: Conduction transfers heat through direct contact without bulk movement of the material; convection requires the fluid to move.
Radiation transfers heat as electromagnetic waves and needs no medium; convection needs a fluid to carry the heat.

examples.everyday: Set the oven to convection so the cookies brown evenly on both racks.
examples.professional: The storm developed from strong convection over the Gulf, with cumulus towers building well above 30,000 feet.
examples.analytical: Convection in the mantle drives tectonic plate motion, so the planet's thermal history depends on fluid flow at depth.

nuance.analogy: Convection is like a pot of boiling water: hot water rises from the bottom, cools at the top, and sinks again in a loop.
nuance.etymology: From Latin convectio, a carrying together, from convehere, to carry together.
common_mistakes: Confusing it with convention, which means a formal meeting or accepted custom.
Using it to mean any kind of heat transfer; conduction and radiation are different processes.

convection.etymology: From Latin *convectiōnem*, from *convectiō* (“act of carrying”), from *convectus*, past participle stem of *convehō* (“to carry together”), combination of *com-* and *vehō*.

senses.definition: Relating to, or exhibiting, coprolalia.

core.definition: Involving coprolalia, the involuntary blurting of obscene or socially taboo words, often a symptom of Tourette syndrome.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on 'LAY', with secondary stress on 'koh'. The middle syllables reduce to weak 'pruh' and 'lik', so don't pronounce each vowel fully.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to clinical, but the subject is sensitive. It describes a medical symptom, not a person's character.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'coprolalic' mainly in medical, psychological, and educational contexts. Most people with Tourette syndrome never have this symptom, so do not use the word to describe someone who swears. In everyday speech, say that someone 'swears involuntarily' or 'has verbal tics'.

distinctions.note: Profane describes language that is deliberately vulgar, while coprolalic describes involuntary speech that the speaker cannot control.
Echolalic describes involuntarily repeating words that someone else has just said, while coprolalic describes blurting out taboo words.

examples.everyday: The doctor said his tics aren't coprolalic, so he isn't swearing on purpose.
examples.professional: The school nurse documented that the student's vocal tics were not coprolalic, which mattered for the accommodation plan.
examples.analytical: Coprolalic symptoms, though striking, occur in only a minority of people with Tourette syndrome.

nuance.analogy: Like a stuck radio that keeps playing the same unwanted station, regardless of what the listener wants.
nuance.etymology: From Greek 'kopros' (dung) plus 'lalia' (speech), coined in medical Latin and English usage.
common_mistakes: Using 'coprolalic' as a casual synonym for 'vulgar' or 'rude', when it is a clinical term.
Stressing the first syllable, as in 'KOH-pro-LAY-lik', rather than the second.

senses.definition: In general usage, an essential part of a thing surrounded by other essential things.
senses.example: the core of an apple or quince

senses.definition: The central part of a fruit, containing the kernels or seeds.
senses.example: the core of an apple or quince

senses.definition: The heart or inner part of a physical thing.
senses.example: The core of the apple was bitter, so we threw out everything except the flesh.

senses.definition: The anatomical core, muscles which bridge abdomen and thorax.
senses.example: Strengthening your core helps your back and posture during long hours at a desk.

senses.definition: The center or inner part of a space or area.
senses.example: The crowd gathered in the core of the plaza near the old fountain.

senses.definition: The most important part of a thing or aggregate of things wherever located and whether of any determinate location at all; the essence.
senses.example: the core of a subject

senses.definition: A technical term for classification of things denoting those parts of a category that are most easily or most likely understood as within it.
senses.example: Prototype theory says the core of a category holds its most typical members.

senses.definition: The set of feasible allocations that cannot be improved upon by a subset (a coalition) of the economy's agents.
senses.example: The core of this exchange economy consists of allocations no group of traders can improve upon.

senses.definition: A thematic aesthetic; objects related to a specific topic.
senses.example: Photographs of cottagecore focuses on countrysides or forests.

senses.definition: Particular parts of technical instruments or machines essential in function:
senses.example: I wanted to play a particular computer game, which required I buy a new computer, so while the game said it needed at least a dual-core processor, I wanted my computer to be a bit ahead of the curve, so I bought a quad-core.

senses.definition: The portion of a mold that creates a cavity or impression within the part (casting or molded part) or that makes a hole in or through the part.
senses.example: The mold's core creates the hollow channel inside the cast aluminum engine block.

senses.definition: Ellipsis of core memory (“magnetic data storage”).

An individual computer processor, in the sense when several processors (called cores or CPU cores) are plugged together in one single integrated circuit to work as one (called a multi-core processor).
senses.example: I wanted to play a particular computer game, which required I buy a new computer, so while the game said it needed at least a dual-core processor, I wanted my computer to be a bit ahead of the curve, so I bought a quad-core.

senses.definition: The material between surface materials in a structured composite sandwich material.
senses.example: a floor panel with a Nomex honeycomb core

senses.definition: A piece of ferromagnetic material (e.g. soft iron), inside the windings of an electromagnet, that channels the magnetic field.
senses.example: The soft iron core inside the coil channels the magnetic field and boosts the electromagnet's strength.

senses.definition: Hence particular parts of a subject studied or examined by technical operations, likened by position and practical or structural robustness to kernels, cores in the general sense above.
senses.example: Our analysis focused on the core of the dataset, the variables that drive most predictions.

senses.definition: The bony process which forms the central axis of the horns in many animals.
senses.example: The horn's bony core extends from the skull and is covered by a sheath of keratin.

senses.definition: A disorder of sheep caused by worms in the liver.
senses.example: The farmer treated several sheep for core after noticing their steady weight loss.

senses.definition: The central part of a protein's structure, consisting mostly of hydrophobic amino acids.
senses.example: The protein's core is packed with hydrophobic residues that avoid contact with water.

senses.definition: A cylindrical sample of rock or other materials obtained by core drilling.
senses.example: Geologists pulled a long core of basalt from the drill hole for laboratory analysis.

senses.definition: A miner's underground working time or shift.
senses.example: The miners finished their core and climbed back to the surface before dusk.

senses.definition: A deposit paid by the purchaser of a rebuilt part, to be refunded on return of a used, rebuildable part, or the returned rebuildable part itself.
senses.example: The auto parts store charged a core deposit on the rebuilt alternator, refundable when I returned the old one.

senses.definition: An aesthetic ending in the suffix -core, such as cottagecore, normcore, etc.
senses.example: Lots of my students now describe their dorm decor as cottagecore, all mismatched mugs and dried flowers.

senses.definition: The main and most diverse monophyletic group within a clade or taxonomic group.
senses.example: The core of this clade includes most of the species and shows the greatest diversity.

senses.definition: The inner part of a nuclear reactor, in which the nuclear reaction takes place.
The central fissile portion of a fission weapon.
senses.example: In a hollow-core design, neutrons escape from the core more readily, allowing more fissile material to be used (and thus allowing for a greater yield) while still keeping the core subcritical prior to detonation.

senses.definition: A hollow cylindrical piece of cardboard around which a web of paper or plastic is wound.
A tiny sample of organic material obtained by means of a fine-needle biopsy.
An atomic nucleus plus inner electrons (i.e. an atom, except for its valence electrons).
Forming the most important or essential part.
Deeply and authentically involved in the culture surrounding the sport.
To remove the core of an apple or other fruit.
To cut or drill through the core of (something).
To extract a sample with a drill.

core.definition: The central, essential part of something, the part that everything else depends on or is built around.

pronunciation.tip: One clear syllable with a strong 'r', like the 'or' in 'door' followed by a short 'r'. Do not add a second vowel sound, which would make it sound like 'kor-ee'.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral. It signals importance and fundamental value.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'core' everywhere: 'core values' in companies, 'core curriculum' in schools, and 'the core of the problem' in conversation. In school, 'core classes' are required courses. 'To the core' is an informal expression for thoroughly, as in 'a New Yorker to the core'. For a geometric middle, Americans usually say 'center' rather than 'core'.

distinctions.note: Center is the geometric or physical middle; core is the essential, inner part that matters most.
Heart is more emotional or poetic; core is more neutral and is common in business and academic English.
Nucleus is a technical term in physics and biology; core is the everyday word.

examples.everyday: Honesty is the core of how I was raised, so I try to tell my kids the truth even when it's hard.
examples.professional: Our core product is the reporting dashboard, so we are prioritizing its speed in the next release.
examples.analytical: Aristotle's account of essence picks out the core features that make a thing what it is.

nuance.analogy: Like the pit of a peach: everything else grows around it and depends on it.
nuance.etymology: From Middle English core, probably from Old French cor, from Latin cor 'heart'.
common_mistakes: Saying 'the core of the circle' for its center; say 'the center of the circle'.
Using a long 'o' with an extra vowel, like 'kor-ee'; it is one syllable, KORE.

core.etymology: From Middle English *core*, *kore*, *coor* (“apple-core, pith”), of origin.

senses.definition: Contrary to intuition or common sense.

core.definition: Seeming to contradict common sense or what most people would expect, even though it may turn out to be correct.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on TOO, the fourth syllable. Americans reduce the other vowels heavily, so 'intuitive' sounds like 'in-TOO-ih-tiv' with the 'tu' as 'too'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral, often used to introduce surprising results in a positive way.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word in science, statistics, business presentations, and news stories about surprising findings. A typical phrase is 'It sounds counterintuitive, but...', which is a natural way to introduce an unexpected idea. It is common in workplaces and academic talks, and it is less common in very casual talk.

distinctions.note: Surprising describes an emotional reaction, while counterintuitive specifically means it goes against what logic or common sense would suggest.
Illogical means it is wrong in reasoning, while counterintuitive can be logically correct but still seem wrong at first.
Unexpected describes something that was not foreseen, while counterintuitive describes something that feels wrong even after thinking.

examples.everyday: It sounds counterintuitive, but this recipe actually works better when you use less salt.
examples.professional: The A/B test showed a counterintuitive result: the simpler design converted better than the one with more features.
examples.analytical: Simpson's paradox is counterintuitive because the trend in the combined data can reverse the trend in each subgroup.

nuance.analogy: A counterintuitive result is like a ball that rolls uphill because of a hidden slope you did not see.
nuance.etymology: From counter- (against) plus intuitive, from Latin intuitus (contemplation).
