examples.everyday: My neighbor's son has epilepsy, and the school nurse always keeps his medicine ready.
examples.professional: Our health plan covers the epilepsy medication, which the pharmacy refills every month.
examples.analytical: Epilepsy is defined by recurrent, unprovoked seizures, not by any single seizure, which is why a second episode matters so much.

nuance.analogy: Like a faulty wire in a house that keeps tripping the breaker, even when nothing is overloaded.
nuance.etymology: From Greek epilepsia 'seizure', from epilambanein 'to seize upon'.
common_mistakes: Calling any seizure 'epilepsy', when epilepsy refers to the recurring condition.
Saying 'an epileptic' for a person; Americans prefer 'a person with epilepsy'.

epilepsy.etymology: Since 16th century; borrowed from French *épilepsie*, from Latin *epilēpsia*, from Ancient Greek *ἐπιληψίᾱ*, from *ἐπιλαμβάνω* (“to seize”), from *ἐπι-* (“upon”) + *λαμβάνω* (“to take”).

senses.definition: Equal distance.

core.definition: The condition of being at the same distance from two or more points, objects, or places.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on DIS, and the final '-ance' reduces to 'uns'. Do not stress the first or last syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is precise and can imply fairness when used about mediators or neutral positions.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'equidistance' mainly in mathematics, geography, planning, and diplomacy. In casual talk, people say 'the same distance from' or 'equal distance'. The word often describes a position that looks fair or neutral.

distinctions.note: Proximity means closeness in general, while equidistance means being exactly the same distance from two or more points.
Symmetry describes a balanced arrangement or mirror pattern, while equidistance describes only equal distances from reference points.

examples.everyday: Our friends picked a café with perfect equidistance from both our houses, so nobody had to drive far.
examples.professional: Maintain equidistance between the two vendors so the procurement decision looks fair to everyone involved.
examples.analytical: A mediator's claim to neutrality rests on equidistance from every party, not merely on the absence of obvious bias.

nuance.analogy: Like a campfire where everyone sits the same distance from the flame.
nuance.etymology: From equi-, 'equal', plus distance, from Latin distantia, 'separation'.
common_mistakes: Using 'equidistance' as an adjective; the adjective is 'equidistant'.
Saying 'equidistance to' instead of 'equidistance from' or 'equidistance between'.

senses.definition: The act of one who errs; sin.
senses.example: Scripture teaches that repentance restores us after our erring, however grave.

core.definition: The act of going astray or doing wrong, especially wrongdoing in a moral or religious sense; sin.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, AIR. The second vowel is a short 'ih', not 'ee'. The r is strong in General American, and the -ing ending is clear.

nuance.connotation: Negative in moral or religious use, suggesting a fault or sin, though it can be gentle in contexts of forgiveness.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use erring mostly as an adjective, as in erring child or erring brother, or in religious speech. The noun use is rare and formal. In church and Scripture settings, it means going morally astray. In everyday talk, you'd say mistake or wrong. Using erring as a noun in casual conversation sounds odd.

distinctions.note: Error names a mistake in general, often factual or practical; erring focuses on the act of going wrong, often moral or religious.
Sin is a stronger, deliberate moral or religious term; erring can suggest wandering off course, which may be less willful.
A mistake is an everyday, neutral term for something done wrong; erring is more formal and often carries a moral sense.

examples.everyday: My grandmother still says we should forgive our erring friends, even when they hurt us.
examples.professional: In the church newsletter we wrote about restoring erring members with gentleness rather than public shame.
examples.analytical: Hebrews presents Jesus as one who can sympathize with the ignorant and erring, which shapes how the epistle describes his priesthood.

nuance.analogy: Erring is like a hiker who leaves the marked trail: the path is still there, and the way back is open.
nuance.etymology: From err, from Latin errare, 'to wander, to stray'.
common_mistakes: Using erring as an everyday noun for ordinary mistakes; it sounds archaic and religious.
Confusing erring (AIR-ing) with earring, which is pronounced EAR-ing.
nuance.biblical_note: The Hebrew word shagah, 'to go astray, to err', and the Greek planaō, 'to lead astray, to wander', lie behind the idea. Hebrews 5:2 in the RSV describes the high priest as able to deal gently with the ignorant and erring, because he is himself beset with weakness. Psalm 95:10 describes a people who err in their hearts, pointing to a fault of the will as well as of understanding. Mark 12:24 has Jesus telling the Sadducees they are wrong because they do not know the Scriptures or the power of God.

senses.definition: One who practises eschatology.

core.definition: A person who studies or writes about eschatology, the theological doctrine of the last things.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on 'tah', the third syllable. The vowel in 'tah' is the 'ah' of 'cot', and the final syllable is a short 'ist'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and specialized; it can sound a bit formal or scholarly.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this term mainly in theology and religious scholarship, for example 'She is a respected eschatologist at the seminary.' Outside those contexts it would sound unusual. In general conversation people would say 'a scholar of end-times theology' instead.

distinctions.note: A theologian studies God and religious belief broadly, while an eschatologist specializes in the doctrine of the last things.

examples.everyday: My friend is an eschatologist, so she always has strong opinions about the end times.
examples.professional: The seminary invited an eschatologist to lead the faculty discussion on Revelation.
examples.analytical: The eschatologist argues that early Christian hope was shaped by expectations of imminent judgment.

nuance.analogy: An eschatologist is like a cartographer of the final chapter, mapping what the story is heading toward.
nuance.etymology: From Greek 'eschatos', last, plus '-logist', one who studies.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'eschatologist' with 'eschatology', the subject itself.
Stressing the wrong syllable, such as 'es-ka-TOL-o-jist'.

senses.definition: Having become a stranger, of one who formerly was close, as a relative, friend, lover, or spouse.
senses.example: He managed to become estranged from all of his friends.

core.definition: No longer close or on friendly terms with someone who was once close, especially a family member, spouse, or partner.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable and end on a 'jd' sound. The 'ed' ending is pronounced as a separate 'd' after the 'j' sound, so it is two consonants at the end.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It implies sadness or conflict between people who were once close.
nuance.usage_note: Americans commonly use 'estranged' when discussing family, especially in phrases like 'my estranged father' or 'estranged spouse.' It is neutral to serious in tone and is common in news, memoirs, and everyday talk about family conflict. Be careful with the sensitivity of the topic, and don't use it to describe strangers.

distinctions.note: 'Separated' in American legal usage means a formal living-apart arrangement, while 'estranged' describes emotional distance regardless of living arrangements.
'Distant' describes a relationship that is physically or emotionally far, while 'estranged' implies a once-close bond that has broken down.

examples.everyday: She doesn't talk about her estranged brother much, but she told me he lives in Ohio now.
examples.professional: The HR policy covers employees who are estranged from a family member and need to change their emergency contact.
examples.analytical: Scripture's parable of the prodigal son describes a father and son who become estranged, and then reconciled by the father's longing.

nuance.analogy: An estranged relationship is like a bridge that is still standing but no longer has anyone walking across it; the structure is there, but the traffic has stopped.
nuance.etymology: Past participle of 'estrange,' from Old French estranger, from Latin extraneus, 'foreign.'
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it with an 'ess' sound at the start ('ess-TRAYNJD') or changing the vowel to 'eh' at the start.
Using 'estranged' for people who never knew each other; it only describes people who were once close.
nuance.biblical_note: The Bible describes estrangement between God and humanity, and between people, without using this exact word. In Luke 15:11-32 the younger son leaves his father and lives far away until he returns, which illustrates the restoration of a relationship. In Ephesians 2:12 Paul describes Gentiles as once alienated from the commonwealth of Israel, a Greek word closely related to estrangement, and reconciled through Christ.

senses.definition: Life after death; the afterlife.
Immortality.
senses.example: Some ancient myths promised eternal life to heroes who conquered death itself.

core.definition: Life that continues forever with God, especially the unending life of the faithful after death, or in some uses, life in God's presence now.

pronunciation.tip: Stress ETER and LIFE, with the middle syllable reduced to a quick nul. Say the r clearly in the American way, with the tongue curled, and avoid adding an extra syllable in eternal.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It describes a hope and promise, and it is used warmly in church and faith contexts.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this phrase mostly in religious settings, such as church, sermons, funerals and Bible study. In casual talk it sounds heavy, so people often say heaven or the afterlife instead. A natural reply in a faith conversation is a simple Amen or I believe that too.

distinctions.note: Afterlife is a general word for existence after death in any belief system, while eternal life is a specifically Christian and Jewish idea of unending life with God.
Heaven is a place or state of being with God, while eternal life describes the quality of unending life itself.

examples.everyday: My neighbor told me she finds comfort in the idea of eternal life after her mother passed away.
examples.professional: In the pastor's sermon plan, the next point is what eternal life means for people who suffer now.
examples.analytical: John 17:3 defines eternal life in relational terms, as knowing God and Jesus Christ, rather than as mere endless duration.

nuance.analogy: Like a flame that never runs out of fuel, because its source is not the wick but something beyond it.
common_mistakes: Saying eternal live with a short i, which changes the meaning
Using it casually for a long time, as in This meeting feels like eternal life
nuance.biblical_note: The Greek phrase is zoe aionios, where zoe means life and aionios means of the age or eternal. In John 3:16 (RSV), believers should not perish but have eternal life. In John 17:3 (RSV), eternal life is described as knowing the only true God and Jesus Christ. In Matthew 25:46 (RSV), the righteous go into eternal life, set against eternal punishment.

senses.definition: Of or relating to a group of people having common racial, ancestral, national, religious or cultural origins.
Characteristic of a foreign or a minority group's culture.
senses.example: I like to eat ethnic food

senses.definition: Representative of a folk or traditional mode of expression.
senses.example: The festival featured ethnic music, with fiddles and drums played the way families have for generations.

senses.definition: (historical) Heathen, not Jewish, Christian, or Muslim.
senses.example: The sermon condemned the ethnic nations who worshipped idols rather than the true God.
senses.label: historical

senses.definition: An ethnic person, especially a foreigner or member of an immigrant community.
senses.example: Many ethnics in the neighborhood still speak their parents' language at home.

senses.definition: (in classical scholarship) The demonym of an Ancient Greek city.
senses.example: In the inscription, the poet is listed as an ethnic of Corinth rather than Athens.

core.definition: Relating to a group of people who share ancestry, culture, language, religion, or national origin.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and keep the th voiceless. The second syllable is short and light, so it sounds like 'nik', not 'neek'. Compare ethnicity, where the stress shifts to the -NIS- syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in academic and descriptive use, but it can sound othering when used to label food or people casually.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use ethnic to describe groups, neighborhoods, and cultural traditions, as in ethnic restaurant or ethnic identity. Some people find the phrase ethnic food loaded, so it is often better to name the cuisine, such as Thai or Ethiopian. The noun form, as in an ethnic, sounds dated and can be offensive, so avoid it.

distinctions.note: Race usually refers to physical characteristics and social classification, while ethnic refers to shared culture, ancestry, language, or origin.
National refers to citizenship or a country, while ethnic refers to a shared heritage that can cross national borders.
Cultural covers any shared customs or arts, while ethnic specifically points to a group defined by ancestry or origin.

examples.everyday: My neighbor's family brings some of their ethnic recipes to every block party, and everyone asks for them.
examples.professional: HR wants the survey results broken down by ethnic background, but we should also ask about language and religion.
examples.analytical: Ethnic identity is partly chosen and partly ascribed, which is why sociologists are cautious about treating ethnic groups as fixed categories.

nuance.analogy: Like a family accent: inherited, shaped by history, and not the same thing as where you currently live.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin ethnicus, from Greek ethnikos, 'pertaining to nations or peoples,' from ethnos, 'nation.'
common_mistakes: Using ethnic as a noun for a person, which sounds dated and can be offensive.
Stressing the second syllable, which makes the word sound like eth-NICK.
Using ethnic to mean exotic or foreign in a stereotyped way, when the word simply describes shared heritage.
nuance.biblical_note: The English word ethnic does not appear in Scripture, but its Greek root ethnos, meaning nation or people group, is common in the New Testament. In Matthew 28:19 Jesus tells the disciples to make disciples of all nations, and in Romans 1:5 Paul writes of the obedience of faith among all the nations. In both passages the Greek term refers to peoples beyond Israel, not to a modern ethnic category.

ethnic.etymology: From Middle English *ethnik*, from Latin *ethnicus*, from Ancient Greek *ἐθνικός* (“of or for a nation, heathen”), from *ἔθνος* (“a company", later "a people or nation, heathens”).

senses.definition: Agent noun of evaluate; one who evaluates.
senses.example: They were asked to program an expression evaluator that could determine the value of a numeric expression.

core.definition: A person or tool that judges the quality, value, or performance of something, such as a program, a candidate, a product, or a model.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on VAL, the first syllable of the root. The ending '-ator' is reduced to 'ay-ter' in American speech, with a clear r sound at the end.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a role and carries no emotional tone, though evaluators are often seen as impartial judges.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use evaluator in workplaces, schools, government programs, and research. A 'program evaluator' assesses whether a project works, and in data science an 'evaluator' can mean a component that scores models. In casual speech people often say 'the person who grades' or 'the reviewer'.

distinctions.note: An assessor usually measures value or risk for an official purpose, such as property tax or insurance, while an evaluator more often judges performance, quality, or effectiveness.
A reviewer usually writes a published opinion or critique, while an evaluator usually produces a formal, structured assessment for a client or organization.

examples.everyday: My sister works as a program evaluator for the county, so she mostly checks whether the afterschool programs are doing what they promise.
examples.professional: We hired an external evaluator to review the pilot, and her report will guide the funding decision next quarter.
examples.analytical: The evaluator's role raises a methodological question: can someone who designed the intervention judge its effects without bias?

nuance.analogy: An evaluator is like a home inspector: they examine the structure carefully and report on its real condition rather than its appearance.
nuance.etymology: From 'evaluate' (from French 'évaluer', from 'é-' and 'valuer', to value) plus the agent suffix '-or'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the final syllable, as in 'eh-val-yoo-AY-tor'
Confusing 'evaluator' with 'evaluation' when a person is meant
Using 'evaluator' for a casual opinion, which sounds stiff

senses.definition: A method or subroutine that handles an event.
senses.example: The button's click event handler updates the form before the page submits.

core.definition: A function in software that runs automatically in response to a specific event, such as a click or keypress.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress is on 'HAN' in 'handler', with a lighter stress on 'vent'. Pronounce the final 'er' as a soft, r-colored vowel, not a full 'ah'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical. It is a precise term in software development, with no emotional tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'event handler' in programming, web development and user interface design, usually in conversations among developers. In casual speech you may hear it when someone explains why a button does not work. It is rarely used outside technical contexts.

distinctions.note: A callback is any function passed to be run later, while an event handler is a callback specifically tied to an event.
A listener is the object or function registered to receive events, while an event handler is the code that runs when the event happens; in many APIs the terms overlap.

examples.everyday: When I tap that button, the app opens the menu, and that behavior comes from an event handler.
examples.professional: I added an event handler to the login form so it checks the password as soon as the user submits.
examples.analytical: An event handler decouples the user's action from the logic that responds to it, which makes the system easier to test and extend.

nuance.analogy: An event handler is like a waiter who only moves when a particular bell rings.
nuance.etymology: Compound of event (from Latin eventus) and handler, from handle (from Old English handlian).
common_mistakes: Saying 'handle' as a noun for the code; the noun is 'event handler' or 'handler'.
Stressing 'vent' too strongly, as in 'ih-VENT HAN-dler'; the main stress is on 'HAN'.

senses.definition: Obviously true by simple observation.
senses.example: It was evident she was angry, after she slammed the door.

core.definition: Obviously true or present; clear to anyone who looks or thinks about it.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, and the middle vowel is a weak schwa, so it sounds like two quick syllables after EH. Don't pronounce the final -ent as a full 'ent'; it is a reduced 'unt'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive; it presents something as plain and undeniable, which can sound confident or slightly superior depending on tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use evident often in both speech and writing, especially in phrases like 'it's evident that' or 'was evident to everyone.' In casual talk, 'obvious' is more common, and 'clear' is safer when you want to sound friendly. 'Evident' is especially common in reports, reviews and arguments.

distinctions.note: 'Obvious' is more casual and can sound dismissive ('That's obvious!'), while 'evident' is more measured and suits academic or formal contexts.
'Apparent' often means seeming to be true but possibly not, while 'evident' means actually shown by the facts.

examples.everyday: It was evident that my neighbor was tired after the long drive, so I offered to help with the groceries.
examples.professional: It's evident from the dashboard that conversion dropped after the pricing change, so let's review it in Thursday's meeting.
examples.analytical: It is evident from the text that the author assumes a shared moral framework that the argument itself never defends.

nuance.analogy: Like footprints in fresh snow: anyone who looks can see them without a lecture.
nuance.etymology: From Latin evidens, 'seen clearly,' from e- 'out' and videre 'to see.'
common_mistakes: Using 'evident' for 'evidence' as a noun: say 'the evidence is clear,' not 'the evident is clear.'
Pronouncing the stress on the last syllable or saying 'ee-VI-dent.'

evident.etymology: From Middle English *evident*, from Old French *evident*, from Latin *ēvidēns* (“visible, apparent, clear, plain”), from *ē* (“out”) + *videō* (“see”), present participle *vidēns*, deponent *videor* (“to appear, seem”).

senses.definition: Of or providing evidence.
A syntactic element (affix, clitic, or particle) that indicates evidentiality.
senses.example: The Quechua verb takes an evidential suffix that tells the listener how the speaker knows the event.

core.definition: Of or relating to evidence; serving to provide or support evidence for a claim.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on the -DEN syllable, and the 'tial' ending is pronounced as 'shul,' not as 'shee-ul.' Reduce the middle vowels to quick schwas, and do not say 'ev-ih-DEN-tee-al.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a precise, technical adjective with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use evidential mainly in academic writing, philosophy, law and linguistics, where it describes things that bear on proof. In everyday speech they say 'evidence-based' or 'relating to the evidence.' The word can also refer to a grammatical marker in linguistics, which is a separate technical sense.

distinctions.note: 'Evidential' tends to mean supporting or indicating, while 'evidentiary' is used more in legal and procedural contexts about admissible evidence.
'Evident' means obvious, while 'evidential' means related to providing evidence.

examples.everyday: Honestly, the photo is not really evidential, because anyone could have taken it at a different time.
examples.professional: The hospital's chart review has strong evidential value, so we should include it in the incident report.
examples.analytical: The historian's argument depends on a chain of evidential claims that each require independent support.

nuance.analogy: Like a receipt: it does not prove the purchase by itself, but it supports the claim that you bought something.
nuance.etymology: From Latin evidentia, 'clearness,' from evidens, 'seen clearly.'
common_mistakes: Confusing 'evidential' with 'evident'; 'evidential' describes what supports proof, not what is obvious.
Pronouncing the ending as 'shee-ul' instead of 'shul.'

senses.definition: The practice of being exclusive; a mentality or policy that excludes others.
senses.example: Her church's exclusivism made newcomers feel unwelcome, even when they shared the same faith.

senses.definition: The doctrine that one religion is the only true religion, or that one religious sect is the only true version of a larger religion.

core.definition: The attitude or policy of keeping others out of a group or privilege; in religion, the belief that only one faith or sect is true.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on SKLOO, the root syllable of exclusive, not on the weak -ism ending. Learners often stress the ex- or say the ending as a full 'izm'; keep it short and unstressed.

nuance.connotation: Usually negative, because it suggests shutting people out. In theology, the word can be used neutrally to name a doctrinal position, as in 'Christian exclusivism' versus 'inclusivism'.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use exclusivism mainly in academic writing, religious studies, and editorials, not in casual talk. In conversation they usually say 'elitist', 'cliquey', or 'they won't let anyone in'. In religious contexts, it is a neutral technical label for the claim that one tradition alone holds saving truth.

distinctions.note: Exclusivity is the quality of being limited to a few, as in 'the exclusivity of the deal'; exclusivism is an attitude or doctrine of keeping others out.
Elitism is the belief that a select group deserves power or privilege because it is superior; exclusivism focuses on the act of excluding outsiders.
In religion, inclusivism holds that outsiders may still be saved through the one true God, while exclusivism denies this.

examples.everyday: I'm tired of the exclusivism at that country club; they won't even let guests in for a drink.
examples.professional: The data team's exclusivism around the pipeline made it hard for other departments to contribute, so we opened read access.
examples.analytical: Religious exclusivism often rests on the claim that revelation is confined to one tradition, which raises hard questions about divine justice toward those outside it.

nuance.analogy: Like a velvet rope at a club: exclusivism is the policy of keeping the rope up.
nuance.etymology: From exclusive, from Latin excludere 'to shut out', plus the suffix -ism.
common_mistakes: Using exclusivism for a product's limited availability, where exclusivity is the normal word.
Stressing the ex- syllable instead of SKLOO, which makes the word hard to recognize.
nuance.biblical_note: The word itself is a modern theological label, not a biblical term. The closest scriptural basis for the debate is John 14:6, where Jesus calls himself the way, the truth and the life and says that the Father is reached through him, and Acts 4:12, where Peter says salvation is found in no other name under heaven. Christians disagree about whether these verses teach exclusive salvation through Christ alone or are compatible with a wider divine mercy.

traditions.view: The Orthodox Church understands itself as the fullness of the true faith, yet it has generally been cautious about stating that God's saving work is strictly confined to its visible boundaries.

The Church teaches that salvation comes through Christ and the Church, but Vatican II (Lumen Gentium, 1964) affirmed that those who, without fault, do not know the Gospel may be saved, softening the older axiom of no salvation outside the Church.

Many evangelical and Reformed Protestants hold that Christ alone is the way to God and that other religions do not save, while mainline and liberal Protestants more often accept inclusivist or pluralist positions; Lutherans and Reformed Christians also differ on how far God's grace extends.

senses.definition: A type of artificially intelligent software system that stores expertise concerning some subject matter in a knowledge base and attempts to answer questions or solve problems in a manner which simulates the thought processes of a human expert.
senses.example: Our hospital's expert system flags unusual lab results by comparing them to stored medical rules.

core.definition: A computer program that stores specialized knowledge as rules and uses them to answer questions or solve problems the way a human expert would.

pronunciation.tip: Both words are stressed, with EK and SIS getting the main stress. The t in expert is often soft or dropped in fast speech, and the -em in system is a reduced um sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical. It describes a classic type of artificial intelligence tool.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use expert system in computer science and AI courses, and in discussions of older rule-based AI from the 1970s and 1980s. Today people more often say machine learning model or AI assistant, so expert system can sound dated. It is also used for rule-based tools in medicine or tax software.

distinctions.note: An expert system relies on hand-written rules and a knowledge base; a machine learning model learns patterns from data.
A knowledge base is the stored collection of facts and rules; an expert system is the complete program that uses it to reason.

examples.everyday: My bank's phone line uses some kind of expert system to route my question to the right department.
examples.professional: We replaced the manual triage rules with an expert system built on the support team's decision guidelines.
examples.analytical: An expert system's competence is only as good as the knowledge base its engineers encoded, which limits its ability to handle novel cases.

nuance.analogy: It is like a very organized rulebook that answers questions by following the flowchart a senior specialist would use, but it never learns new rules on its own.
nuance.etymology: Expert from Latin expertus, having tried; system from Greek systema, a whole made of parts.
common_mistakes: Using expert system to mean any expert in a field; the phrase refers to a software system.
Pronouncing expert with a long e or a full t sound; the usual American form is EK-spurt.

conversation.text: An expert system encodes a specialist's knowledge as if-then rules and applies them through an inference engine.
MYCIN, an expert system for diagnosing bacterial infections, is a classic example from the 1970s.
Expert systems were brittle and expensive to maintain because every rule had to be written by hand.

senses.definition: The doctrine that moral statements such as "this is wrong" express a moral evaluation rather than a statement of fact.

core.definition: In philosophy, the view that moral statements like 'this is wrong' express an attitude or emotion rather than report a fact.

pronunciation.tip: Stress is on the second syllable, SPRES. The final syllable is a weak 'um', and the vowel in the middle is a reduced 'ih'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a technical term used in philosophy and ethics without emotional coloring.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use expressivism almost only in philosophy, ethics, and metaethics courses or papers. It is usually contrasted with cognitivism, the view that moral claims state facts that can be true or false. Outside academic discussion, people would describe the idea in plain words instead.

distinctions.note: Emotivism is a closely related, earlier form associated with A. J. Ayer and Charles Stevenson; expressivism is the broader family of views that includes it.
Cognitivism holds that moral statements can be true or false as statements of fact; expressivism denies this.

examples.everyday: My philosophy professor said that expressivism is why we argue about morals as if we were arguing about taste.
examples.professional: Our ethics seminar will compare expressivism with divine command theory for next week's reading.
examples.analytical: The expressivist must explain how moral disagreement is genuine if moral sentences express attitudes rather than beliefs about facts.

nuance.analogy: Saying 'murder is wrong' is like saying 'boo' at a bad movie: it expresses a reaction rather than describing the film.
nuance.etymology: Formed in English from express plus the suffix -ism, the term was popularized in twentieth-century metaethics.
common_mistakes: Using expressivism to mean simply 'being expressive' or emotional in ordinary life.
Confusing it with expressionism, which is an art movement.

senses.definition: Pertaining to or advocating expressivism, the doctrine that the primary function of moral sentences and sensation sentences (like "I am in pain") is to express an evaluative attitude, rather than stating a fact.
senses.example: The expressivist account of moral claims holds that murder is wrong conveys disapproval rather than a fact.

senses.definition: An advocate of expressivism.
senses.example: As an expressivist, she thinks ethical sentences reveal attitudes rather than describe the world.

core.definition: Relating to expressivism, the view that moral and emotional statements express attitudes rather than state facts.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on PRESS, and the -ist ending is short ist. Keep the middle syllables light, with a short i, and do not stress the -ive part.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It names a philosophical position without praise or criticism.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word almost only in academic philosophy, especially ethics and the philosophy of language. You will hear it in seminars, such as an expressivist account of moral claims. Most people never need it outside that setting.

distinctions.note: Emotivism, associated with A. J. Ayer, is a closely related earlier view; expressivism is the broader family that includes later views such as Simon Blackburn's.
Cognitivism holds that moral sentences state beliefs that can be true or false; expressivism denies that their main job is describing facts.

examples.everyday: My friend in philosophy says that when I say that was cruel, I am really just expressing disapproval, which sounds like an expressivist view.
examples.professional: In the AI ethics workshop, the speaker defended an expressivist reading of value judgments, so we spent an hour on that distinction.
examples.analytical: An expressivist must explain how moral disagreement can be genuine if moral sentences do not state facts that can be true or false.

nuance.analogy: Like saying ouch: the word expresses pain rather than describing a fact about the pain.
nuance.etymology: From expressivism, from express (from Latin exprimere, to press out) plus -ism.
common_mistakes: Confusing expressivist, a philosophical position, with expressive, meaning full of feeling.
Using expressivist as a noun for any emotional person; in the noun sense it means an advocate of the philosophical view.

senses.definition: Tending to expel or resulting in expulsion.
senses.example: The fire extinguisher has an expulsive force that pushes foam out at high pressure.

core.definition: Tending to force something out, or having the power to drive something out of the body or a container.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, SPUHL. The final -sive is a short siv, not seev, and the first syllable is a weak ik.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical; it describes a force or action rather than a person's behavior.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use 'expulsive' in everyday talk. It appears in medical texts (for example, expulsive contractions during childbirth) and in physics or ballistics writing about the force that pushes something out. In ordinary speech, say 'pushing out' or 'forcing out'.

distinctions.note: Explosive means blowing up or bursting violently; expulsive means forcing something out, with no suggestion of an explosion. The two words sound alike but are not interchangeable.
Expulsory is a rare variant that appears mainly in older texts; expulsive is the normal form in modern English.

examples.professional: The engineer measured the expulsive force of the piston to determine the seal's required strength.
examples.analytical: The essay argues that the expulsive logic of the policy, which removes members rather than persuading them, undermines the community it claims to protect.

nuance.analogy: Like a cork forced out of a bottle by pressure from inside.
nuance.etymology: From Latin expulsivus, from expellere (to drive out), from ex- (out) and pellere (to drive).
common_mistakes: Confusing expulsive with explosive, which changes the meaning from forcing out to blowing up.
Using expulsive as a noun; it is only an adjective.

senses.definition: Of, related to, or typifying extortion (“the practice of obtaining money or other property by the use of force or threats”).
senses.example: The extortionate racket demanded weekly payments from every shop owner on the block.

senses.definition: Greatly exceeding what is moderate or reasonable; exorbitant.
senses.example: The hotel charged extortionate prices for bottled water, nearly ten dollars a bottle.

core.definition: Far higher than is fair or reasonable, especially a price, fee, or demand; exorbitant.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on STOR, and the -tion is pronounced 'shun', with the t becoming sh. The final -ate is a weak 'ut' sound, so do not give it a full 'ayt' ending.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It implies that someone is taking unfair advantage of others, so it sounds like a complaint.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use extortionate in everyday talk about prices, rent, and fees, often with 'extortionate prices' or 'extortionate rent'. It sounds stronger than 'expensive' and suggests unfairness. It is common in news and conversation, but in polite talk people often soften it to 'really steep' or 'a lot'.

distinctions.note: Exorbitant means far beyond normal, focusing on size; extortionate adds a sense that the seller is taking unfair advantage.
Expensive is neutral and simply means high cost; extortionate is a strong complaint about unfairness.
Steep is informal and common in everyday talk about prices; it is less accusatory than extortionate.

examples.everyday: The hotel charged an extortionate fee for parking, so we just found a spot down the street.
examples.professional: The vendor's renewal quote is extortionate for a tool we barely use, so we're going to switch.
examples.analytical: Economists distinguish a fair markup from an extortionate one, although the line between them is contested.

nuance.analogy: Like a toll bridge that charges far more than the road is worth, taking advantage of the fact that you have no other way across.
nuance.etymology: From extortion, from Latin extorquere 'to wrench out', with the adjective ending -ate.
common_mistakes: Using extortionate for a moderately high price; it signals unfairness, so use 'expensive' for ordinary high prices.
Pronouncing the stressed vowel like 'store' with a long o sound; in General American it is closer to 'or'.

senses.definition: In an extrinsic manner.

core.definition: In a way that comes from outside something, rather than from its own nature.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on TRIN. Say the last two syllables quickly and lightly: "zik-lee," with the "ik" reduced.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: This word appears mainly in academic, legal, and philosophical writing. Americans would normally use "externally" or "from outside" in everyday speech. It is useful when describing how a value or motivation is applied from outside, for example in a research paper.

distinctions.note: Externally is the common everyday adverb meaning on the outside or from outside; extrinsically is narrower and suggests not belonging to the thing's nature.
Intrinsically means by its very nature; extrinsically is the opposite.

examples.everyday: My kids study only because we pay them, so they're motivated extrinsically.
examples.professional: The pilot program is evaluated extrinsically, using outside metrics rather than the team's own goals.
examples.analytical: The theologian argues that the sacrament's worth is not grasped if it is understood only extrinsically, as a mere social ritual.

nuance.analogy: Like a fence painted by a neighbor: the paint is applied from outside, not part of the wood itself.
nuance.etymology: Formed from extrinsic and the adverbial suffix -ally, from Latin extrinsecus, meaning from outside.
common_mistakes: Using "extrinsically" in casual conversation where "externally" or "from outside" is more natural.
Confusing it with "intrinsically", which means the opposite.

senses.definition: In an exultant manner.

core.definition: In a joyful, triumphant way; showing great happiness, often after a success or victory.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, ZULT, and the final -ly is a light 'lee.' Non-native speakers often stress the first syllable or add an extra vowel between the l and the t.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It describes joy at a victory or success, and it sounds heightened, so it fits writing and speeches better than casual chat.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use exultantly mainly in writing, storytelling, sports journalism and formal speech, where it adds drama. In everyday talk, people more often say 'with a big grin' or 'thrilled.' A natural reply to someone describing an exultant moment is simply 'That's great, I'm so glad it worked out.'

distinctions.note: Joyfully only says someone is happy; exultantly adds a sense of triumph or open celebration.
Triumphantly emphasizes winning over an opponent, while exultantly emphasizes the emotional outburst of joy.

examples.everyday: She waved her signed contract at us and shouted exultantly that she'd finally got the apartment.
examples.professional: When the budget approval came through, Maria exultantly forwarded the news to the whole team.
examples.analytical: The psalmist often speaks exultantly of God's deliverance even while enemies still surround him, so his joy is shaped by trust rather than by present safety.

nuance.analogy: Like a runner breaking the tape with both arms thrown up, exultantly means joy that is loud, open and visible.
nuance.etymology: From exultant plus the adverb ending -ly; exultant comes from Latin exsultare, to leap up for joy.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable as 'EX-ul-tant-ly' instead of 'ig-ZULT-ant-ly.'
Using it for quiet happiness; it implies open, energetic triumph.

senses.definition: To pass from a state of wakefulness into sleep.
To be affected by paresthesia; to go numb.
senses.example: My left leg has fallen asleep!

senses.definition: (poetic) To die.
senses.example: My grandmother told me that she was ready to fall asleep in the arms of God.
senses.label: poetic

core.definition: To begin sleeping; to pass from being awake into sleep, often without intending to.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second word, SLEEP, with a weaker stress on 'fall'. In fast speech, 'fall asleep' links into 'fawl-uh-SLEEP', with the 'a' reduced to a schwa.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it describes a normal daily event and can be used in both casual and formal settings.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'fall asleep' in everyday conversation, and it is perfectly neutral. You might say 'I fell asleep on the couch' or 'I can't fall asleep' when talking to friends or coworkers. A natural reply to 'Did you sleep well?' is 'Yes, I fell asleep right away' or 'Not really, I couldn't fall asleep.'

distinctions.note: 'Go to sleep' emphasizes the act of going to bed or the instruction to sleep; 'fall asleep' stresses the moment of passing into sleep.
'Doze off' is an informal term for falling asleep briefly and lightly, often while sitting up; 'fall asleep' is broader.
'Drift off' suggests a gentle, gradual slide into sleep; 'fall asleep' is more neutral.

collocations: fall asleep with the TV on

examples.everyday: I always fall asleep during movies after a big dinner.
examples.professional: The overnight data pipeline is still running, so I can't fall asleep until it finishes.
examples.analytical: Locke asks whether the self persists when we fall asleep, a question that tests the boundary between thought and unconsciousness.

nuance.analogy: Falling asleep is like a tide coming in: the shore of waking life slowly disappears under the water, often without you noticing the exact moment.
nuance.etymology: 'Fall' from Old English feallan, and 'asleep' from Old English on slæpe, meaning in sleep.
common_mistakes: Saying 'I fell to sleep' instead of 'I fell asleep'; the usual American phrase is 'fall asleep'.
Using a present-continuous form like 'I am fall asleep'; the correct form is 'I am falling asleep' or 'I fall asleep'.

senses.definition: Typical or characteristic of fall (autumn); autumnal.
senses.example: Next week, it will begin to feel a lot more fall-like.

core.definition: Resembling or typical of autumn, with cool air, shorter days or colorful leaves.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, FALL, and keep -like light but clear, rhyming with bike. The l at the start of like is clear, and the k ends the word crisply.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral: it usually describes pleasant cool weather, colors and seasonal mood.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use fall-like mainly in weather forecasts, conversation and seasonal writing, as in 'fall-like temperatures this weekend.' It is informal and friendly. For a more formal or literary tone, you can say autumnal.

distinctions.note: Autumnal is more formal and literary, often used in writing; fall-like is everyday American speech.
Fall alone can modify a noun, as in 'fall weather,' but fall-like emphasizes resemblance to the season.

examples.everyday: It feels so fall-like out today, so let's grab a hot cider and walk the park.
examples.professional: The forecast shows fall-like temperatures next week, so we should expect higher heating demand in the northeast.
examples.analytical: The poet's fall-like imagery of dying leaves and low light presents the season as a mirror of human aging.

nuance.analogy: Like a sweater that feels just right on a cool morning: it signals the season before the calendar does.
nuance.etymology: Fall from the earlier English phrase 'fall of the leaf'; -like from Old English -lic.
common_mistakes: Writing fall like with no hyphen when used as a single modifier.
Pronouncing the stress on like instead of on fall.

senses.definition: A category in the classification of organisms, ranking below ordo and above genus.
senses.example: In the taxonomic hierarchy, the familia sits between the order and the genus.

senses.definition: A taxon at this rank.
The paterfamilias, his legitimate descendants and their wives, all persons adopted into his family and their wives, and all slaves belonging to the household.
senses.example: In Roman law, the familia included the father's children, their spouses, and his slaves.

senses.definition: (historical) A household or religious community under one head, regarded as a unit.
senses.example: The monastery functioned as a familia, sharing one abbot's authority over all its members.
senses.label: historical

core.definition: The Latin name for the biological rank of family, between order and genus in the classification of organisms.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on MIL, and the final -ia is two light syllables, 'ee-uh', not 'ya'. Keep the vowel in the second syllable short and the vowel in the first syllable reduced.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: Americans use familia almost only in technical biology and taxonomy, often in Latin scientific names or older textbooks. In ordinary speech and in modern English biology, people say family. Using familia in everyday conversation would sound strange or pedantic.

distinctions.note: Family is the English word used in everyday speech and in modern biology, while familia is the Latin term for the same rank in classification.
A genus is a lower rank that contains closely related species, and it always sits below the familia in standard classification.

examples.everyday: My biology professor said the Latin word for that rank is familia.
examples.professional: The taxonomy manual lists each genus under its familia, following the Latin naming conventions.
examples.analytical: Linnaean ranks such as familia remained flexible for a long time before international codes fixed their positions in the hierarchy.

nuance.analogy: Like a folder that holds several related files, sitting above each file but below a larger cabinet drawer.
nuance.etymology: From Latin familia, meaning household or family group.
common_mistakes: Using familia as an ordinary English word for family in everyday speech.
Stressing the wrong syllable, as in fuh-MEE-lee-uh.

senses.definition: Someone or something that farms, as:
senses.example: Every farmer on this county road is watching the sky for rain this week.

senses.definition: A person who works the land and/or who keeps livestock; anyone engaged in agriculture on a farm.
senses.example: My uncle is a dairy farmer who gets up before dawn to milk the cows.

senses.definition: A baby farmer (operator of a rural orphanage).
senses.example: The Victorian baby farmer was charged after several infants in her care died.

senses.definition: (historical) One who takes taxes, customs, excise, or other duties, to collect for a certain rate per cent.
senses.example: a farmer of the revenues
senses.label: historical

senses.definition: (historical) The lord of the field, or one who farms the lot and cope of the crown.
senses.example: In medieval England, the farmer paid the lord a fixed rent for the right to work the manor's lands.
senses.label: historical

core.definition: A person who grows crops or raises livestock on a farm, usually as their job.

pronunciation.tip: Pronounce the r clearly and make the final syllable a reduced 'er' sound, not 'mar'. Do not add a long a sound after the r.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral; often associated with hard work, independence and rural life.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use farmer for anyone who runs a farm, from a small family operation to a large agribusiness, and it is the normal everyday word. Calling someone a farmer is respectful. The compound farmers' market is a very common term for a local outdoor market where growers sell produce directly to customers.

distinctions.note: A rancher usually raises cattle or other livestock on large open land, while a farmer grows crops and may also keep animals.
Agriculturalist is a formal word for a scientist or expert in agriculture, not a person who works the land.

examples.everyday: My uncle is a dairy farmer, so he's up before five every morning.
examples.professional: The county extension office runs workshops to help small farmers adopt drip irrigation.
examples.analytical: In the older agrarian ideal, the farmer appears as a figure of moral independence rather than merely an economic producer.

nuance.analogy: A farmer is like a gardener who plants for a living, working at the scale of whole fields.
nuance.etymology: From farm plus -er, meaning one who farms; farm comes from Old French ferme, a fixed rent or lease.
common_mistakes: Calling a hired worker a farmer; that person is usually called a farmhand or farmworker.
Saying cow farmer in casual speech; Americans more often say dairy farmer or cattle farmer.

farmer.etymology: From Middle English *fermour* (“a steward, bailliff, collector of taxes”), from Old French *fermier* (“a farmer, a lessee, husbandman, bailliff”), from Medieval Latin *firmarius* (“one to whom land is rented, a collector of taxes, deputy”), from *firma*;…

senses.definition: Causing death or destruction.
senses.example: a fatal wound; a fatal disease; that fatal day; a fatal mistake

senses.definition: Causing a sudden end to the running of a program.
senses.example: a fatal error; a fatal exception

senses.definition: A fatality; an event that leads to death.
senses.example: another fatal on the turnpike during rush hour

senses.definition: A fatal error; a failure that causes a program to terminate.
senses.example: The compiler reported a fatal error, so the program terminated immediately without saving.

core.definition: Causing death or serious destruction; in computing, causing a program or system to stop completely.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable. The t between vowels is often a quick flap, and the second syllable is a syllabic l with no extra vowel, so say FAY-tul, not FAY-tahl.

nuance.connotation: Negative, because it describes death, destruction, or a complete failure.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use fatal in news, medicine, and law, as in a fatal accident or a fatal overdose. In everyday talk they use it loosely for a severe flaw, as in a fatal mistake. In software, a fatal error is an error that stops the program, and a non-fatal error is one the program can recover from.

distinctions.note: Lethal describes something capable of killing, such as a dose or weapon, while fatal describes an outcome that actually causes death.
Deadly is more informal and emotional, often used for dangerous things in general, while fatal is more precise and often used in news or technical contexts.
Fateful means decisive or with important consequences, usually without implying death, while fatal means causing death or ending something.

examples.everyday: The doctor said the crash was not fatal, so he's going to be okay.
examples.professional: A fatal error in the deployment script stopped the pipeline before the data was loaded.
examples.analytical: Critics argued that the flaw was fatal, not merely inconvenient, because it undermined the whole argument.

nuance.analogy: A fatal flaw is like a crack in a dam: it may look small, but it can bring the whole structure down.
nuance.etymology: From Latin fatalis, decreed by fate, from fatum, fate.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the second syllable as a full vowel, as in FAY-tahl, when it is a quiet l.
Confusing fatal with fateful, which means decisive but not deadly, or with lethal, which describes the power to kill.

senses.definition: In a favorable manner.
senses.example: She looked favorably on people who gave freely their assistance.

core.definition: In a way that shows approval, or in a way that helps your interests or reputation.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on FAY, and the middle syllables are reduced to a quick 'ver-uh.' The final syllable is 'blee,' a long 'ee' sound.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It describes a favorable reaction or result.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'favorably' in business, reviews, and news writing, such as 'the proposal was received favorably.' In casual speech, people often use 'well' or 'nicely' instead. You often see it with verbs like 'compare,' 'view,' and 'react.'

distinctions.note: Well is the more casual, all-purpose word, while favorably is more formal and specifically suggests approval or a positive comparison.
Positively can describe an emotional or feel-good manner, while favorably focuses on judgment, comparison, or outcome.

examples.everyday: My landlord took the news about the repairs more favorably than I expected.
examples.professional: The board reviewed the budget favorably, so we can start hiring next quarter.
examples.analytical: Historians have often viewed the reform favorably, though the evidence for its success is mixed.

nuance.analogy: If a plant grows favorably, it has the sun, water, and soil it needs, and it thrives.
nuance.etymology: From 'favorable' (Latin favorabilis) plus the adverbial suffix '-ly.'
common_mistakes: Using 'favorably' when you mean 'nicely' in casual speech, which can sound too formal.
Using the British spelling 'favourably.'

senses.definition: Acting against or preventing fever.

core.definition: Reducing or preventing fever; used of medicines or remedies that bring down a fever.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the syllable 'fyoo,' which is the primary stress. The first syllables are reduced, and the 'g' is hard, as in 'fugal.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical. It is used in medicine and pharmacy.
nuance.usage_note: Americans mostly use this word in medical or pharmaceutical contexts, where it describes drugs or remedies. In everyday talk, people say 'fever reducer' or 'fever medicine.' The technical term 'antipyretic' is also common in clinical settings.

distinctions.note: Antipyretic is the more common technical term in American medicine for a fever-reducing drug.
Febrile means having a fever, the opposite condition, so do not confuse the two.

examples.everyday: My grandmother swears by her febrifugal tea, but I'd just take ibuprofen.
examples.professional: The pharmacist recommended a febrifugal medicine for the child's fever and told us the correct dose.
examples.analytical: Willow bark's febrifugal use in ancient medicine foreshadowed the later development of aspirin.

nuance.analogy: Like a thermostat turned down to cool a room that has become too warm.
nuance.etymology: From Latin 'febris,' fever, plus 'fugare,' to drive away.
common_mistakes: Confusing it with febrile, which means having a fever.
Stressing the first syllable instead of the 'fyoo' syllable.

senses.definition: To provide informational feedback to.
senses.example: His employees fed back a lot more than he wanted.

senses.definition: To convey by means of specialized communications channel.
senses.example: Customers fed back their complaints and some praise.

senses.definition: To return electrical current generated by some means (such as solar panels, regenerative braking) to the power grid.
senses.example: Our rooftop solar panels feed back surplus electricity to the grid during sunny afternoons.

core.definition: To pass your reactions, comments or results about something back to the people responsible for it so they can improve it.

pronunciation.tip: Stress back, the second word, since it carries the main emphasis. Keep feed short and light, and say the two words together so the d in feed links smoothly to the b in back.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and practical. It suggests a helpful, constructive exchange.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use feed back in workplaces, schools and customer service when reporting what they noticed or what worked. It is separable, so you can say feed the results back or feed back the results. In formal writing people often say provide feedback instead. A natural reply is thanks, I will take that into account.

distinctions.note: Give feedback is the usual noun phrase in most workplace contexts, while feed back is the verb form and sounds more active.
Report means to tell what happened in a formal or factual way, while feed back means to return reactions meant to help improve something.

examples.everyday: I will feed back to you after I talk to the landlord about the leak.
examples.professional: Please feed the test results back to the product team by Friday so they can adjust the release.
examples.analytical: In cybernetic systems, outputs feed back to shape the inputs that follow, which is why they can stabilize or amplify behavior.

nuance.analogy: Like sending a rough draft back to the writer with notes, so the next version improves.
nuance.etymology: Compound of the verb feed and the adverb back; the phrasal verb is recorded in modern English usage.
common_mistakes: Writing feedback as a verb, as in I will feedback you; say feed back to you or give you feedback.
Using a preposition incorrectly, as in feed back of the results; say feed back the results or feed the results back.

senses.definition: A woman; a wife; a young woman or girl.
senses.example: In the old novel, the proud femme ruled her household with quiet, unshakable authority.

senses.definition: A lesbian or other queer woman whose appearance, identity etc. is seen as feminine as opposed to butch.
senses.example: At the queer dance night, she identifies as a femme and her partner as butch.

senses.definition: A person whose gender is feminine-leaning, such as a feminine non-binary person.
senses.example: Many nonbinary folks in our group describe themselves as femme, not as women.

senses.definition: An effeminate or gay man.
senses.example: Some older men in that bar mocked him as a femme whenever he wore bright colors.

senses.definition: Pertaining to a femme; feminine, female.
senses.example: She loves her femme style, with flowing dresses and soft, romantic makeup.

senses.definition: Effeminate (of a man).
senses.example: His femme mannerisms drew teasing from the coaches, which he found exhausting.

senses.definition: Characteristic of a feminine lesbian or queer woman.
senses.example: Her style was more femme than butch.

senses.definition: To feminize.
senses.example: Critics say the brand's ad campaign tries to femme up its tough, rugged products.

core.definition: In LGBTQ+ communities, a feminine-presenting woman or person, often in contrast to butch.

pronunciation.tip: Pronounce it like 'fem,' rhyming with 'hem.' Americans do not use the French nasal vowel, so do not say 'fahm.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive within queer communities as a self-description; it can sound stereotyping or offensive if applied to someone without consent.
nuance.usage_note: Femme is used mainly in LGBTQ+ communities as a self-description, often in contrast to butch. Outside those communities it may sound confusing or stereotyping. Ask how someone describes themselves before using it, and avoid it in formal writing unless you are describing the community.

distinctions.note: Femme is more specific and tied to queer identity; fem is broader informal slang about presentation.
Feminine is the standard, neutral word; femme names a specific identity or role.

examples.everyday: My friend calls herself a femme, and she loves her red lipstick and vintage dresses.
examples.professional: The LGBTQ+ resource guide defines femme as a gender expression rather than a fixed identity, and it asks staff to use the term respectfully.
examples.analytical: The terms femme and butch developed within lesbian communities as ways of expressing desire and gender, and their meanings have shifted across decades.

nuance.etymology: From French femme 'woman,' from Latin femina.
common_mistakes: Using femme as a casual synonym for feminine when speaking to people outside queer contexts.
Pronouncing it like the French 'fahm' instead of the English 'fem.'

femme.etymology: From Middle English *femme*, itself borrowed from Old French *fame*, from Latin *femina* (“woman”).

senses.definition: A section of a European newspaper typically dedicated to arts, culture, criticism, and light literature.
An article published in such a section.

core.definition: A section of a European newspaper devoted to arts, culture, criticism, and light literature; also an article printed in that section.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, and say the ending as a short 'tahn.' The word comes from French, but American speakers normally anglicize the sounds rather than producing a nasal French vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a format and a tradition rather than an opinion.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use 'feuilleton' except when discussing European newspapers, literary history, or journalism. American newspapers do not have a feuilleton section; you would say 'arts section,' 'book review,' or 'cultural supplement.' If you mean a critical essay, the American word is usually 'essay' or 'column.'

distinctions.note: A 'column' is a regular opinion piece by one writer; a 'feuilleton' is a whole section that mixes criticism, culture, and light literature.
An 'essay' is a formal, extended piece of argument; a 'feuilleton' is usually shorter, more lively, and written for general readers.
A 'review' evaluates one book, film, or show; a 'feuilleton' can cover many cultural topics in a single article.

examples.everyday: My German friend reads the feuilleton every morning, but I usually just check the headlines.
examples.professional: Our translated interview ran in the feuilleton of a Berlin daily, so we need to get the reprint rights cleared.
examples.analytical: Benjamin's early essays first appeared in the feuilleton, where criticism, anecdote, and theory mixed freely for a general readership.

nuance.analogy: A feuilleton is like the culture pages of a newspaper, but written with the freedom of a magazine essay.
nuance.etymology: From French feuilleton, a diminutive of feuillet, 'leaflet,' from feuille, 'leaf.'
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the final syllable as 'ton' with a long vowel, or adding a French nasal sound that Americans rarely use.
Assuming a feuilleton is a novel published in installments; the word refers to a newspaper section or article type.

senses.definition: Rare and scarce; hard to find.

core.definition: Rare and scarce; not occurring often or easy to find.

pronunciation.tip: The main stresses fall on 'far' and 'between,' while 'and' reduces to a weak 'und' or 'uhn' in fast speech. Pronounce the r in 'far' clearly for American English.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes scarcity without judging it, though it often implies that something is valuable because it is rare.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this idiom in casual conversation and workplace talk to say that something is uncommon, such as good parking, good jobs, or sunny days. It is informal but acceptable in most settings. A natural reply is 'Tell me about it' or 'You're not kidding.'

distinctions.note: 'Rare' is a single neutral word and can be formal; 'few and far between' is more vivid and conversational.
'Scarce' describes a limited supply of something needed; it often sounds more formal or economic than the idiom.
'Uncommon' is milder and suggests something unusual rather than hard to find.

collocations: good jobs are few and far between
good parking is few and far between
rain is few and far between
such moments are few and far between
reliable plumbers are few and far between

examples.everyday: Decent parking downtown is few and far between, so just take the bus.
examples.professional: Senior data engineers with real production experience are few and far between in this market.
examples.analytical: Genuinely original arguments are few and far between in the literature on theodicy, where most works repeat familiar positions.

nuance.analogy: It is like rain in a desert: the moments arrive so rarely that each one feels precious.
common_mistakes: Saying 'few and far in between,' which mixes the idiom with a phrase that is not standard.
Using 'few' alone without the idiom, such as 'few and far' with no 'between,' which sounds incomplete.

few-and-far-between.etymology: Attested at least since the 17th century.

conversation.text: Good apartments in this price range are few and far between.
Days off have been few and far between since the launch.
Gas stations are few and far between on this highway, so fill up now.

senses.definition: To come to understand; to discover or find a solution; to deduce.
senses.example: As soon as I figure out what is wrong with my car, I will fix it.

senses.definition: To calculate.
senses.example: We'd already figured out that the trip would cost $1,000.

core.definition: To understand something, solve a problem or find an answer after thinking about it; or to calculate an amount.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on out. Say figure with a weak middle syllable, and link the r smoothly into out.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive, showing problem solving or understanding.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use figure out constantly for problems, directions, instructions, math and people's behavior: 'I can't figure him out.' It is informal but appropriate at work too. A natural reply is 'Yeah, took me a while to figure it out' or 'Let me know if you figure it out.'

distinctions.note: Solve is more formal and usually for a problem with a clear answer; figure out is more informal and can also mean understanding a person.
Understand is neutral and can describe comprehension at any time; figure out emphasizes the process of working something out.

examples.everyday: I can't figure out how this coffee machine works, so can you help me?
examples.professional: Let's figure out why the deployment failed before we schedule the next release.
examples.analytical: Readers must figure out the author's intention from the structure of the argument rather than from explicit claims.

nuance.analogy: To figure out a problem is like untangling a knotted string until the loose end appears.
nuance.etymology: Figure is from Latin figura, meaning shape; out is from Old English ūt, meaning outside or away.
common_mistakes: Placing an object between figure and out in the wrong way; say 'figure it out' or 'figure out the answer,' not 'figure out it' without the pronoun order.
Using figure out to mean just 'think about,' when it usually means reaching an answer or understanding.

conversation.text: I can't figure out how to turn on this TV.
Don't worry, we'll figure it out together.
I can't figure him out; one day he's friendly, the next he's cold.

senses.definition: One who files something.
A software program for managing files.

core.definition: A person or entity who files official papers, such as a tax return, or a program for managing computer files.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, FY. The final -er is a weak, r-colored vowel, so say FY-ler, not FY-lay.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a practical term used in government, tax, and software contexts.
nuance.usage_note: Americans most often hear filer in tax contexts, as in tax filer, joint filer, or single filer. In computing, a filer can be a file manager program. You would not usually say filer for a clerk who files papers in an office; you would say file clerk or filing clerk.

distinctions.note: A taxpayer is anyone who pays taxes, while a filer is someone who submits the required tax return, so a taxpayer may or may not be a filer in a particular year.
A filing clerk is a job title for a person who sorts and stores papers, while a filer is the person or entity submitting official documents.

examples.everyday: My sister is a single filer this year, so her tax return is simpler than mine.
examples.professional: The software update adds a new filer role, so administrators can control who submits reports.
examples.analytical: The policy distinguishes between filers and non-filers, which affects who appears in the official statistics.

nuance.analogy: A filer is like a person who hands the completed paperwork to the front desk: the job is to submit the file properly, on time.
nuance.etymology: From the verb file, with the agent suffix -er.
common_mistakes: Confusing filer with filter, which means a device or process that removes unwanted material.
Using filer for a file clerk or secretary who organizes papers, when the word refers to the person who submits official documents.

senses.definition: A delicate and intricate ornamentation made from platinum, gold or silver (or sometimes other metal) twisted wire.
Anything resembling such intricate ornamentation.
To decorate something with intricate ornamentation made from gold or silver twisted wire.
senses.example: She filigreed the silver locket with delicate twisted wire along its border.

core.definition: Delicate ornamental work of fine twisted wire, usually gold or silver, or anything resembling it.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and make the final syllable rhyme with 'free'. The middle syllable is a short, reduced 'ih'.

nuance.connotation: Positive, suggesting delicacy and craftsmanship.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use filigree for jewelry, metalwork, and ornate architecture, and sometimes figuratively for intricate patterns in frost, lace, or writing. It is more common in art descriptions and catalogs than in everyday talk. In casual speech, people might say 'delicate design' or 'lacy pattern'.

distinctions.note: Lace is made of thread or fine cords; filigree is made of metal wire.
Ornament is a general word for decoration; filigree names a specific, delicate type.

examples.everyday: My grandmother's earrings have tiny silver filigree on them.
examples.professional: The gallery catalog describes the lamp's filigree frame as hand-crafted.
examples.analytical: The poet's prose has a filigree of images that rewards slow reading.

nuance.analogy: Like fine threads of metal drawn into a lacework pattern.
nuance.etymology: From Italian filigrana, from Latin filum (thread) and granum (grain).
common_mistakes: Spelling it 'filligree' with a double l.
Using it for any decoration, when it specifically means delicate wire work.

filigree.etymology: From French *filigrane*, from Italian *filigrana*, from Latin *fīlum* (“thread”) + *grānum* (“grain”).

senses.definition: Resembling or made of a thin film; gauzy.
Covered by (or as if by) a film; hazy.
Filmlike; resembling a motion picture.
senses.example: A filmy layer of dust coated the windowsill, so thin it looked almost transparent.

core.definition: Thin, light and almost transparent, like a film; gauzy, or covered by a hazy layer.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The 'lm' is pronounced as one sound with no vowel between, and the final -y is a clear 'ee'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly poetic. It usually describes light, fabric or air in a soft, delicate way, though it can suggest haziness or poor vision.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use filmy mainly to describe fabrics such as stockings, veils or curtains, or things that look thin, hazy or faded, like a window covered with dust or eyes clouded by age. In everyday speech, sheer or hazy is often more natural for fabric, while filmy suggests a more delicate or slightly eerie look. Do not confuse it with filmic, which means related to movies.

distinctions.note: Sheer is the usual word for thin, see-through fabric; filmy suggests a more delicate, misty quality.
Hazy describes a lack of clarity in the air or in thinking; filmy can describe a thin layer covering something.

examples.everyday: Sunlight came through the filmy curtains and made the whole living room look soft.
examples.professional: The client complained that the screen had a filmy residue, so we need to clean the glass before the demo.
examples.analytical: The poet's filmy images of dawn suggest a world seen through memory rather than in clear outline.

nuance.analogy: Filmy is like the thin skin that forms on warm milk: you can see through it, but it covers the surface.
nuance.etymology: From film, which comes from Old English filmen, a membrane.
common_mistakes: Confusing filmy with filmic, which refers to movies.
Using filmy for any cloudy weather, when hazy or overcast is more natural.

senses.definition: Ornament; decoration; especially, excessive decoration; showy clothes; jewels.
Fine point; minute characteristic.
senses.example: The critic admired the finery of the translation, each subtle nuance carefully preserved.

senses.definition: A charcoal hearth or furnace for the conversion of cast iron into wrought iron, or into iron suitable for puddling.
senses.example: The ironworks kept a finery running day and night to make wrought iron.

core.definition: Showy, elaborate clothing and jewelry, often more decoration than an occasion calls for.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the final -ery is a reduced, unstressed vowel. Don't pronounce the second syllable as a full 'ah' sound.

nuance.connotation: Mildly negative or playful. It suggests someone is dressed up more than needed, or that the clothes are flashy. Used neutrally in fashion writing about fine clothes.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use finery mostly in the phrase 'in her finery' or 'in their Sunday finery,' describing people dressed up for a wedding, holiday, or special event. It sounds slightly old-fashioned or literary in casual talk, so in everyday speech you might say 'all dressed up' instead. It is almost always used in the plural sense of fancy clothes and accessories, not as a count noun.

distinctions.note: Clothes is the general word for anything you wear; finery specifically means elaborate, showy, dressy items.
Jewelry refers only to ornaments such as rings and necklaces, while finery can include the whole outfit plus jewelry.

examples.everyday: Look at Maria in all her finery for the cousin's wedding!
examples.professional: The gala's dress code was formal, so most guests arrived in their finery.
examples.analytical: Medieval moralists often condemned the finery of the court as a sign of pride and vanity.

nuance.analogy: Finery is like a theater costume: beautiful and eye-catching, but worn for a special occasion and not for everyday life.
nuance.etymology: From Old French 'fineure,' from 'fin' (fine), meaning refinement or fine quality.
common_mistakes: Using 'finery' as a countable noun, such as 'a finery' or 'many fineries' in ordinary speech.
Confusing it with 'fine' (good or thin) because the spelling looks similar.

senses.definition: A (usually self-sustaining) chemical reaction involving the bonding of oxygen with carbon or other fuel, with the production of heat and the presence of flame or smouldering.
senses.example: The campers built a fire from dry pine and kept it burning all night.

senses.definition: An instance of this chemical reaction, especially when intentionally created and maintained in a specific location to a useful end (such as a campfire or a hearth fire).
senses.example: We sat about the fire singing songs and telling tales.

senses.definition: The occurrence, often accidental, of fire in a certain place, causing damage and danger.
senses.example: There was a fire at the school last night and the whole place burned down.

senses.definition: The aforementioned chemical reaction of burning, considered one of the Classical elements or basic elements of alchemy.
senses.example: In medieval alchemy, fire was counted among the four elements alongside earth, air, and water.

senses.definition: The elements necessary to start a fire.
senses.example: The fire was laid and needed to be lit.

senses.definition: The bullets or other projectiles fired from a gun or other ranged weapon.
senses.example: The fire from the enemy guns kept us from attacking.

senses.definition: A planned bombardment by artillery or similar weapons, or the capability to deliver such.
senses.example: We dominated the battlespace with our fires.

senses.definition: A firearm.
senses.example: He kept his fire trained on the doorway until the sheriff arrived.

senses.definition: A barrage, volley.
senses.example: A fire of questions came from the audience after the speech.

senses.definition: An instance of firing one or more rocket engines.
senses.example: static fire

senses.definition: Strength of passion, whether love or hate.
senses.example: Her fire for justice drove her to spend years organizing tenants.

senses.definition: Liveliness of imagination or fancy; intellectual and moral enthusiasm.
senses.example: The young teacher brought real fire to every lesson she planned.

senses.definition: Splendor; brilliancy; luster; hence, a star.
senses.example: The fire of the evening star hung above the dark mountains.

senses.definition: A severe trial; anything inflaming or provoking.
senses.example: The long hospital stay was a fire that tested every part of their marriage.

senses.definition: Red coloration in a piece of opal.
senses.example: This opal has a bright red fire that catches the light when turned.

senses.definition: The capacity of a gemstone, especially a faceted, cut gemstone, that is transparent to visible light, to disperse white light into its multispectral component parts, resulting in a flash of different colors, the richness and dispersion of which increases the gemstone's value.
senses.example: The diamond's fire is impressive, scattering rainbow flashes across the white tablecloth.

senses.definition: Amazing; excellent.
senses.example: This is fire, keep up the amazing work!

senses.definition: To set (something, often a building) on fire.
senses.example: Vandals fired the old barn during the night, destroying decades of hay.
