nuance.usage_note: Americans say this at urgent care, to a pharmacist, or to a doctor, often adding how long it has lasted and whether there is fever. Be specific about the location, such as 'my throat,' so the provider knows what you mean. A typical reply from a provider is 'Let me take a look at your throat.'

distinctions.note: 'My throat is sore' describes the general state, while 'it hurts when I swallow' pinpoints the symptom that matters for diagnosis.

examples.everyday: I've had a cold for three days, and it hurts when I swallow, so I'm going to lie down.
examples.professional: I left the team meeting early because it hurts when I swallow, and I'm not sure my voice will hold up.
examples.analytical: Patients often describe pain when they swallow, and that complaint helps clinicians distinguish a simple infection from more serious conditions.

nuance.analogy: Like a sandpaper rub each time food passes, the pain tells you exactly where the trouble is.
common_mistakes: Saying 'It's hurting when I swallowing'; use the base verb 'swallow' after 'when I'.
Using 'hurt me' as the main verb when describing your own throat, which sounds awkward.

conversation.text: My throat is sore, and it hurts when I swallow.
It hurts when I swallow, so I've just been drinking soup.
It hurts when I swallow, especially in the morning.

senses.definition: Saying a game was tied at the end and played extra time.

core.definition: Said when a game is still tied after regular time and continues into extra periods; also used when any event or meeting runs longer than planned.

pronunciation.tip: Stress OH in overtime, with a lighter secondary beat on TYME. In fast speech, into sounds like IN-tuh, with the t flapped to a soft d-like sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it sounds exciting when describing sports and mildly stressful when describing work or meetings.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this for basketball, football, hockey and baseball games that are tied at the end of regulation, and they say overtime rather than the British extra time. It is also common in everyday talk about a dinner, meeting or call that ran long. A natural reply is Oh no, was it a close game?

distinctions.note: Extra time is mainly a British term for the added period in soccer; Americans say overtime for any game extended after regulation.
The same word has a work sense: I worked overtime means I earned extra paid hours, not that a game or event ran long.

collocations: tied at the end of regulation

examples.everyday: The game went into overtime, so we didn't get home until after midnight.
examples.professional: The budget review went into overtime, so let's pick up the vendor discussion on Thursday.
examples.analytical: The seminar went into overtime because the argument needed the extra time to reach a conclusion.

nuance.analogy: Like a race that is still close at the finish line, so the runners keep going for a few more laps.
nuance.etymology: Overtime comes from over, meaning beyond, plus time; the sports and work senses both mean time beyond the normal limit.
common_mistakes: Saying in overtime instead of into overtime when a game or event continues past its scheduled end.
Confusing sports overtime with paid overtime hours at work, which is a separate meaning of the same word.

conversation.text: It went into overtime, and we won by a field goal.
Sorry I'm late; it went into overtime, and I had to see the end.
It went into overtime, so I didn't go to bed until midnight.

senses.definition: Directions: the place will be on your right side.

core.definition: Used in directions to say that a place is located on your right side as you walk, drive or face a direction.

pronunciation.tip: Your is usually reduced to yer in speech, so the main stress falls on RITE. Make the r with the tongue curled back and avoid a rolled sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and helpful.
nuance.usage_note: Americans give directions this way while driving or walking, often adding a landmark, as in It's on your right, past the gas station. For a more formal tone, say on the right-hand side. A natural reply is Got it, thanks.

distinctions.note: On the right is less personal than on your right, but the meaning is the same.
To your right usually describes a direction of movement, while on your right describes a location.

examples.everyday: Turn into the parking lot, and the coffee shop is on your right.
examples.professional: The conference room is on your right when you get off the elevator.
examples.analytical: When the map says the office is on your right, it assumes you are facing the building, which is an important assumption.

nuance.analogy: Like a left and right shoe: the label depends on which way you are facing.
nuance.etymology: Right comes from Old English riht, meaning straight, correct or on the right side.
common_mistakes: Confusing on your right, meaning a location, with to the right, meaning a direction of movement.
Saying at your right instead of on your right for a place beside you.

conversation.text: Pass the gas station, and it's on your right.
"Where's the pharmacy?" "Just past the bank. It's on your right."
Keep going a little farther. It's on your right, next to the bakery.

senses.definition: Recommending a show or movie.

core.definition: Used to recommend a show, movie, documentary or video as good enough to spend your time on.

pronunciation.tip: Stress WERTH, with a clear American r, and WAH-ching, with the cot vowel ah. Worth is not pronounced like wort, and watching has no t sound in the middle.

nuance.connotation: Positive; it signals a recommendation.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say this when recommending a show, documentary, video or game, often adding a reason such as It's worth watching if you like history. It is casual and friendly. A natural reply is Thanks, I'll check it out.

distinctions.note: Worth seeing is used for places, exhibits or live events, while worth watching is used for recorded or broadcast media.
Worthwhile is broader and can describe any effort or activity, while worth watching is specific to watching something.

examples.everyday: That new documentary about the ocean is worth watching if you like nature shows.
examples.professional: The vendor's recorded demo is worth watching before Thursday's review.
examples.analytical: The lecture series is worth watching not only for its content but for how the speaker frames uncertainty.

nuance.analogy: Like a friend's book recommendation: it saves you the trouble of guessing whether the time will be well spent.
nuance.etymology: Worth comes from Old English weorth, meaning of value; watch comes from Old English wacian, meaning to stay awake.
common_mistakes: Saying worth to watch instead of worth watching.
Pronouncing worth with a long o as WORTH; the American pronunciation is WERTH.

conversation.text: It's a little slow at first, but it's worth watching.
It's worth watching, especially if you like history.
It's worth watching on the big screen.

senses.definition: Pertaining to Italy.
senses.example: Italian borders

senses.definition: Pertaining to its people or their cultures.
senses.example: Italian cuisines

senses.definition: Pertaining to their language.
senses.example: Italian verbs

senses.definition: A person from Italy or of Italian descent.
senses.example: A tour group of Italians is visiting Westminster Cathedral today.

senses.definition: A style of cuisine or individual dishes of or associated with Italy or Italian people.
senses.example: A: What's for dinner tonight? B: I don't know about you, but I'm ready for some Italian tonight!

senses.definition: Ellipsis of Italian cloth.
senses.example: They bought a bolt of the finest Italian that can be had this side of Italy.

senses.definition: Ellipsis of Italian vermouth, a dark-colored sweet or mildly bitter vermouth.
senses.example: gin and Italian

senses.definition: Ellipsis of Italian bread.
senses.example: Can I please get a meatball sub on Italian? Thank you!

senses.definition: Ellipsis of Italian sandwich.
senses.example: Can I please get an Italian and a beer? Thank you!

core.definition: Relating to Italy, its people, its language or its culture. Italian also describes food and things from Italy.

pronunciation.tip: The first syllable is a short 'ih', not 'eye', and the stress falls on TAL. The -ian ending is pronounced 'yuhn', with a y sound as in 'yes'.

nuance.connotation: Positive, usually linked to food, art and culture, though it can carry stereotypes in some contexts.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use Italian for people, the language, food and things from Italy, as in 'Italian restaurant' or 'Italian bread'. Italian-American describes Americans of Italian descent. Italianate describes architecture or art in an Italian style, and is not used for people.

distinctions.note: Italic refers to ancient peoples of the Italian peninsula, or to slanted typeface, while Italian refers to modern Italy.
Italian-American refers to Americans of Italian descent, while Italian refers to people born in or living in Italy.

examples.everyday: Do you want to grab something Italian for dinner tonight?
examples.professional: Our client is Italian, so I'll schedule the call for their morning and send the agenda in Italian.
examples.analytical: Italian Renaissance art reshaped European ideas of perspective, which is why the period is central to any history of painting.

nuance.analogy: Italian is like a passport stamp for a whole culture: it names the country, its people, its language and its food at once.
nuance.etymology: From Latin Italianus, from Italia, the Latin name for Italy.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the first syllable as 'eye', as in 'eye-TAL-yuhn', when it is a short 'ih'.
Using Italian for a language in ways that suggest the speaker is not fluent, such as saying 'Italiano' in English conversation.
Saying 'Italian' for an Italian-American without the hyphen, which blurs the difference between born and heritage identity.

italian.etymology: From Middle English *Italian*, from Medieval Latin *Italiānus*, from Latin *Italia* (“Italy”).

senses.definition: A large, extremely hard, boiled candy, typically spherical.
senses.example: My little brother clacked a giant jawbreaker against his teeth until his dad confiscated it.

senses.definition: A long, hard-to-pronounce word.
senses.example: The word “callipygous” is something of a jawbreaker.

senses.definition: A hard blow to the side of the face.
senses.example: The bouncer landed a jawbreaker on the drunk's chin, and he dropped like a sack.

core.definition: A very large, hard, round candy that dissolves slowly and lasts a long time in the mouth.

pronunciation.tip: The first syllable has the main stress, and the second has secondary stress. Keep the r in the final -er, which is a soft, reduced sound, not 'ah'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive; it is a playful, nostalgic word, especially for children's candy.
nuance.usage_note: Americans mostly use jawbreaker for the big, round candy sold in bulk at candy shops and corner stores. The 'long hard word' sense is humorous and used mainly in writing or teasing. At a candy counter, you might say 'Can I get two jawbreakers, please?'

distinctions.note: A lollipop sits on a stick; a jawbreaker is a round, hard candy usually eaten without one.
Hard candy is a broad category; jawbreakers are a specific, very large, long-lasting type.

examples.everyday: The kids spent their allowance on jawbreakers at the corner candy store.
examples.professional: For the team event, we're handing out jawbreakers as a fun giveaway that lasts through the afternoon.
examples.analytical: Philosophers love jawbreakers, and 'phenomenological' is a word that tests every reader's patience.

nuance.analogy: Like a smooth stone you can keep in your mouth for an hour, it takes forever to finish.
nuance.etymology: From jaw and breaker (from break), named for how hard the candy is.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second part as the main stress, saying 'jaw-BRAY-ker'.
Using jawbreaker for any hard candy; it refers to the big, long-lasting kind.

core.definition: In the Bible and Roman times, the southern region of Palestine centered on Jerusalem, the homeland of the Jewish people.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the middle syllable 'dee', and reduce the final syllable to 'uh'. Non-native speakers often stress the first syllable, which is incorrect.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and historical. In modern contexts it is tied to political and religious debate about the West Bank.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use Judea mainly in Bible study, history, and when discussing ancient Israel. In news and politics they may say the West Bank or the occupied territories, and terms can be politically sensitive. Use Judea with care in modern debate and say which period you mean.

distinctions.note: Judea is a region; Judah is a tribe and a kingdom named after a person.
Israel can mean the whole nation or the northern kingdom; Judea is the southern region of the land.

examples.everyday: We drove through the Judean hills last spring and the landscape looked just like the photos.
examples.professional: The project timeline covers the historical sites of Judea, from Jerusalem to Bethlehem.
examples.analytical: Luke's account places John the Baptist's ministry in the wilderness of Judea, an image central to his preaching.

nuance.analogy: Judea is like a county within a larger state, a named region with its own history and center.
nuance.etymology: From Greek Ioudaia, from Hebrew Yehudah, Judah.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable as JOO-dee-uh.
Confusing Judea with Judah, the tribe or kingdom.
nuance.biblical_note: Judea was the southern region of the land of Israel, with Jerusalem as its center. In the New Testament it is the main setting for Jesus' ministry along with Galilee. Key passages: Luke 1:65 describes news spreading through the hill country of Judea; John 3:22 places Jesus in the land of Judea; Acts 1:8 names Judea among the regions where the witnesses would testify.

senses.definition: Tells a salesperson you don't need help yet.

core.definition: A phrase you say to a salesperson to mean you don't need help yet.

pronunciation.tip: Stress 'LOOK' and keep 'just' short and light. The 'ing' is a weak 'ihng,' so the phrase sounds like 'just LUK-in.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly friendly; it politely declines help without sounding rude.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say this when a store employee greets them, so the employee knows to leave them alone for now. It is very common in clothing and electronics stores. A natural follow-up is 'Okay, just let me know if you need anything,' or the salesperson may say 'Sounds good.'

distinctions.note: Just browsing means the same thing and is equally common; just looking is slightly more common in clothing stores.
I'm all set is used when you have finished shopping or have what you need, not when you are just starting.

collocations: Just looking, I'll let you know

examples.everyday: When the clerk asked if I needed help, I said, 'Just looking, thanks.'
examples.professional: At the trade show booth, I told the vendor, 'Just looking today, but I'd like a brochure.'
examples.analytical: The phrase 'just looking' signals a boundary between the customer's autonomy and the seller's invitation to engage.

nuance.analogy: It's like putting up a small sign that says 'Not yet, thanks' so the shop staff knows you're still exploring.
common_mistakes: Saying 'I'm just look' without the -ing; the form is 'I'm just looking.'
Replying 'No' abruptly; a softer 'Just looking, thanks' sounds more natural.

conversation.text: No, thanks, I'm just looking for now.
When a salesperson offers to help, you can tell them you're just looking.
We were just looking, but then we found the perfect rug.

senses.definition: Kind of; somewhat.
senses.example: I kinda hafta do this right now.

senses.definition: Contraction of kind +‎ of.
senses.example: I kinda thought you'd bail on the hike after that rain.

senses.definition: Yes in some respects but no in other respects.
senses.example: "Are you afraid of a little bit of rain?" "Kinda, yeah."

senses.definition: A subspecies of baboon, Papio cynocephalus kindae, primarily found in Angola, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Zambia, and possibly western Tanzania.
senses.example: Field researchers in Zambia observed a kinda troop foraging near the riverbank.

core.definition: Somewhat or to some degree, used informally in speech to soften a statement, like kind of or sort of.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, KYN. The second syllable is a reduced schwa, so it sounds like 'KYN-duh,' and the final syllable is not 'dah.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral to casual. It softens a statement and can sound friendly, but it is too casual for formal writing or serious professional reports.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say kinda constantly in casual conversation to soften a claim, as in 'I'm kinda hungry' or 'It's kinda late.' Use it with friends, family, and coworkers you know well; in job interviews, emails to clients, or academic writing, use kind of or somewhat. A natural reply is 'Yeah, me too' or 'Same here.'

distinctions.note: Kind of is the fully written, slightly more formal form, while kinda is the spoken, informal reduction that appears mainly in texts and casual speech.
Somewhat is more formal and neutral in tone, while kinda is casual and often used to soften or hedge.

examples.everyday: I'm kinda tired, so let's just order pizza tonight.
examples.professional: The fix is kinda risky, so let's test it on staging before we push it to production.
examples.analytical: In the seminar, Maria said the argument was kinda circular, and the professor agreed that its premises assumed the conclusion.

nuance.analogy: Kinda is like a soft pillow placed between your words and the listener: it cushions the statement so it lands gently.
nuance.etymology: A spoken reduction of kind of, first common in writing in the 1800s for informal dialogue.
common_mistakes: Using kinda in formal writing, job applications, or academic papers, where kind of or somewhat is expected.
Confusing kinda with the noun kind, as in 'kinda of food' instead of 'kind of food.'
Pronouncing it as 'KYN-dah' with a broad ah, when the final vowel is a short schwa.

senses.definition: Clipping of kinescope (“type of recording”).
In kinesics, any of the individual movements composing a kineme.
senses.example: In the transcription, each kine of the gesture was marked separately to track the speaker's hand motions.

core.definition: Archaic plural of cow, rare outside old texts; also a short form of kinescope, an early film recording of a television broadcast.

pronunciation.tip: It is one syllable with a long i like in kite, and the final e is silent. Do not say kin-ee or keen.

nuance.connotation: Neutral, but it sounds archaic or literary, and in everyday talk it can sound quaint.
nuance.usage_note: Most Americans will never say kine. You may see it in older literature or in the old television slang for kinescope recordings, which is now dated. For cattle, say cows or cattle, and for an early TV recording, say kinescope or film recording.

distinctions.note: Cow is the normal modern word for adult female cattle, while kine is an archaic plural used in old texts.
Kinescope is the full technical term for an early film recording of a TV show, while kine is a clipped, dated form.

examples.professional: The archive team digitized a 1950s kinescope of the live broadcast and noted its early film quality.
examples.analytical: Older English translations render the plural of cattle as kine, a usage that now signals the text's age more than any difference in meaning.

nuance.analogy: Kine is like a word in a grandparent's cedar chest: you can recognize it, but nobody uses it at the dinner table anymore.
nuance.etymology: Kine is an old plural of cow formed with the -n plural ending of Middle English; kinescope comes from Greek kinēma, movement, and skopein, to look.
common_mistakes: Confusing kine with kind or kin; it is a one-syllable word with a long i.
Using kine for modern cows in everyday speech, which sounds quaint or like a joke.

kine.etymology: Middle English *kyn*, *kyne*, equivalent to *ky* + *en*, a double plural.

senses.definition: The force driving life forward.
senses.example: Philosophers and theologians have long debated whether kinesis is the vital force behind all growth.

senses.definition: The movement of an organism in response to an external stimulus.
Any energy that creates/controls movement.
senses.example: In physics class we learned how chemical kinesis drives the piston in an engine.

core.definition: In biology, movement of an organism or cell in response to a stimulus, where speed changes with stimulus intensity but direction does not.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the middle syllable, NEE, so it is not KIN-uh-sis. The final -sis is a short i, like in thesis.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical. It has no emotional coloring.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use kinesis mainly in biology, psychology and academic discussions of Aristotle's theory of change. In everyday talk it sounds odd; say movement or motion instead. The adjective kinetic is far more common in ordinary English. The broader life-force sense is archaic and should be avoided in modern writing.

distinctions.note: Kinetic describes motion and energy in general, while kinesis is a specific biological response to a stimulus.
Taxis is a directed movement toward or away from a stimulus, while kinesis is undirected and changes speed rather than direction.
Locomotion is self-directed travel from one place to another, while kinesis is a change in activity level tied to stimulus intensity.

examples.everyday: My daughter's science homework is about woodlice that move faster in dry places, and the teacher called it kinesis.
examples.professional: The lab's assay measured larval kinesis by tracking speed under three different light conditions.
examples.analytical: Aristotle used kinesis for change in place or quality more broadly, a usage that modern biology has narrowed considerably.

nuance.analogy: Kinesis is like a shopper who speeds up or slows down depending on how crowded the store is, but never heads toward a particular shelf.
nuance.etymology: From Greek kinēsis, movement, from kinein, to move.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable as KIN-ih-sis; the main stress falls on the middle syllable.
Using kinesis as a general word for physical activity; in biology it names a specific stimulus-driven movement.

senses.definition: One who kisses.
senses.example: She's a great kisser!

senses.definition: The mouth.
senses.example: Shut your kisser and let me finish, or you're walking home.

senses.definition: The face.
senses.example: He took a punch right in the kisser and stumbled backward into the crowd.

senses.definition: The kissing gourami.
A button on a bowstring that indicates consistent height when drawing a bow, for example by being placed against the archer's mouth.
senses.example: Set the kisser at the same spot every time so your anchor point stays consistent.

core.definition: A person who kisses, often used to describe a person's style of kissing, such as a good kisser or a big kisser.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, KIS. The second syllable is the reduced American r-colored sound, not a full 'ah' sound as in 'kiss-ah'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral or positive in personal contexts, as in a good kisser. The slang sense for face or mouth is humorous and dated.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use kisser mostly in casual talk, such as saying someone is a good kisser or a big kisser. The old slang sense, meaning mouth or face, is humorous and rarely heard now. In polite company, describe someone as an affectionate person instead of calling them a big kisser.

distinctions.note: Smoocher is more informal and suggests lingering, affectionate kissing, often in a playful or teasing way.
Lover usually means a romantic partner, while kisser only describes how someone kisses or how often they do.

examples.everyday: My dog is a big kisser; he greets everybody by licking their faces.
examples.professional: At the holiday party, our VP was a big kisser who hugged and kissed everyone on the cheek.
examples.analytical: Literary critics often read the kisser in romance as a figure of desire and risk rather than mere affection.

nuance.analogy: A kisser is like a welcome mat: some people give a warm, quick greeting, while others linger and make it memorable.
nuance.etymology: From kiss, the verb, with the agent suffix -er meaning one who does the action.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable, as in kiss-ER, instead of KIS-er.
Pronouncing the second syllable as 'ah' rather than the American r-colored sound.
Using kisser to mean a romantic partner, which is not its usual meaning.

senses.definition: A domestic cat (subspecies Felis silvestris catus).
senses.example: Come here, kitty-cat, and let me see whether you're hungry yet.

core.definition: A cat, especially a small or friendly one. It is a playful or affectionate word, mostly used with or about pets.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first word, KIT-ee, and the second word gets a lighter stress. The middle t is a flap, so it sounds close to a quick d, as in KID-ee.

nuance.connotation: Positive and affectionate. It can sound cute or childish when used by adults.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use kitty-cat mostly with children, in talking to a pet, or in a playful way about a cat. Among adults it may sound cutesy, so cat or kitty is the neutral choice. Your input's stress is reversed; in American speech the first syllable gets the main stress.

distinctions.note: A kitten is a young cat, while kitty-cat can refer to any cat, young or old, and is more affectionate.
Kitty alone is an informal name for a cat, and it also means a shared pot of money, such as the kitty for a group dinner.
Cat is the neutral word used in most contexts, while kitty-cat is childish and warm.

examples.everyday: Hey kitty-cat, do you want some food before I leave for work?
examples.professional: The shelter's newsletter called the adopted kitty-cat the office favorite, so we put her photo on the slide.
examples.analytical: Childish words like kitty-cat show how adults shift into a softer, more affectionate register when they talk about animals.

nuance.analogy: Like a teddy bear, kitty-cat is small, soft, and meant for affection rather than for precise description.
nuance.etymology: Cat comes from Old English catt; kitty is a pet form of uncertain origin, possibly related to kit, a young animal.
common_mistakes: Using kitty-cat in formal writing, where cat is correct.
Confusing kitty alone with a pot of money, which is a different sense of the same word.

senses.definition: A loud electric alarm or horn, especially as used in automobiles in the early 20th century.
To produce a loud, siren-like wail.
senses.example: The alarm began to klaxon as soon as the reactor pressure climbed past the safety limit.

core.definition: A loud electric horn or alarm, once common on early automobiles, ships and factories, whose sound is harsh and piercing.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the second syllable is a short, open vowel like ah. Learners often stress the second syllable or say the final vowel as a long o.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and historical, sometimes nostalgic when describing old cars.
nuance.usage_note: Americans today use horn for a car horn and alarm or siren for warning sounds. Klaxon was originally a trademark for a specific electric horn, so it is usually capitalized when it refers to that brand. You may hear it in discussions of vintage cars or historical machines.

distinctions.note: Horn is the standard American word for a car horn; klaxon is historical and refers to a particular loud, harsh type.
A siren makes a rising and falling wail, while a klaxon makes a loud, harsh, repeated buzz or bark.

examples.everyday: Grandpa still has a klaxon on his antique car, and it is so loud that the neighbors turn around.
examples.professional: The safety report noted that the warehouse klaxon was hard to hear over the forklift noise.
examples.analytical: The klaxon, once a symbol of the automobile age, now seems quaint beside modern electronic alerts.

nuance.analogy: A klaxon is like an old alarm clock with a harsh buzz: it is impossible to ignore and gets straight to the point.
nuance.etymology: Originally a trademark name for an early electric horn introduced around 1908; the word later became generic.
common_mistakes: Using klaxon for any modern car horn, when Americans would say horn.
Stressing the second syllable, as in klak-SAHN, instead of KLAK-sahn.

senses.definition: Possessing knowledge or understanding; knowledgeable, intelligent.
senses.example: She is a knowing reader of poetry who notices every allusion.

senses.definition: Deliberate, willful.
senses.example: It was a knowing lie, told to protect his brother from the consequences.

senses.definition: Shrewd or showing clever awareness; discerning.
senses.example: a knowing rascal

senses.definition: Suggestive of private knowledge or understanding.
senses.example: She gave him a knowing look across the room, and he smiled back.

senses.definition: Given my knowledge about someone or something.
senses.example: Knowing you, you would try not to be late for school.

senses.definition: The act or condition of having knowledge.
senses.example: Her knowing of the bylaws saved the committee from a costly mistake.

core.definition: Showing awareness or understanding, often in a shrewd or meaningful way, as in a knowing look or knowing smile.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The ending -ing is a short vowel, like the i in 'sit', not 'eeng'. Do not add an extra syllable at the end.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly positive. A knowing look can suggest sly amusement or a shared secret, so context decides whether it sounds friendly or teasing.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use knowing for someone who seems to understand a situation, often without words, such as a knowing glance between friends. It is rarely used to mean 'has lots of facts'; for that, say knowledgeable. Describing someone's tone as knowing is natural in casual conversation and in fiction or movie reviews.

distinctions.note: Knowing describes awareness or shrewdness in a moment; knowledgeable describes having broad information over time.
Knowing is an adjective describing a person or look; knowingly is an adverb describing how an action is done, with awareness.

examples.everyday: She gave me a knowing look when the waiter brought the dessert we both secretly wanted.
examples.professional: Our manager gave a knowing nod when someone mentioned the budget cuts, so we all knew the decision was already made.
examples.analytical: The narrator's knowing tone invites the reader into a shared irony that the characters themselves never grasp.

nuance.analogy: Like a friend who raises one eyebrow across the room, saying more with a look than with words.
nuance.etymology: From the present participle of know, from Old English cnāwan, to know or recognize.
common_mistakes: Using knowing to mean 'having many facts'; say knowledgeable instead.
Confusing the adjective knowing with the adverb knowingly, as in 'She knowing lied' instead of 'She knowingly lied'.

senses.definition: A laundering; a washing.
senses.example: In our family of five, we have to do the laundry every other day.

senses.definition: A place or room where laundering is done - including, by extension, other forms of laundering than clothes washing.
senses.example: The hotel's laundry is in the basement, next to the boiler room.

senses.definition: That which needs to be, is being, or has been laundered.
senses.example: You've left your dirty laundry all over the house.

senses.definition: A penalty flag.
senses.example: The referee threw a laundry on the play, and our touchdown was called back.

senses.definition: A business whose primary purpose is to conceal the origins of money received illegally.
senses.example: Federal agents shut down the car wash, which was really a laundry for drug money.

core.definition: Clothes, sheets, and towels that need to be washed or have just been washed; also the act or place of washing them.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. Pronounce the dr as a quick blend, not "duh," and do not add an extra syllable between n and d.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: Americans use laundry in everyday talk about washing clothes, sorting dirty items, or hanging things up to dry. Laundry is uncountable when it means clothes to wash, so people say a load of laundry. It can also mean a laundry business, as in a laundromat or dry cleaner, depending on region. Dirty laundry is a common idiom for private problems.

distinctions.note: A laundromat is a public self-service place with coin-operated machines, while laundry can refer to the clothes or the act of washing.
A dry cleaner specializes in cleaning clothes that cannot be washed normally, while laundry usually means regular washing.

examples.everyday: I have to do the laundry tonight because I am out of clean socks.
examples.professional: The office laundry room is closed for maintenance this week, so please take team towels home or use the next floor.
examples.analytical: The phrase airing one's dirty laundry suggests that private conflicts become public moral failures in ways that the speaker finds shameful.

nuance.analogy: Laundry is like a pile of past days waiting to be sorted, washed and put back into order.
nuance.etymology: From launder, from Middle English lauender, from Latin lavanda, things to be washed.
common_mistakes: Saying a laundry or laundries for clothes to wash, when the American everyday word is laundry or a load of laundry.
Pronouncing it as LAWN-dary with an extra syllable, when American English usually has two syllables.

laundry.etymology: From Middle English *lavendrie*, from Old French *lavanderie*, from Latin *lavandaria*.

conversation.text: I have a huge pile of laundry to fold.
Our building has a laundry room in the basement.
Can you throw your towels in the laundry basket?

senses.definition: Expending or bestowing profusely; profuse; prodigal.
senses.example: lavish of money; lavish of praise

senses.definition: Superabundant; excessive.
senses.example: lavish spirits

senses.definition: Unrestrained, impetuous.
senses.example: Her lavish praise of the new hire embarrassed him in front of the team.

senses.definition: Rank or lush with vegetation.
senses.example: The lavish garden was thick with ferns, vines, and tropical blossoms.

senses.definition: To give out extremely generously; to squander.
senses.example: They lavished money on the dinner.

senses.definition: To give out to (somebody) extremely generously.
senses.example: They lavished him with praise.

core.definition: Given or spent in very large amounts; generous to the point of extravagance.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the final sound is the sh in shoe, not a separate ee. Keep the vowel short, as in 'lav' in 'lavender'.

nuance.connotation: Usually positive when describing generosity or hospitality, but negative when describing spending or lifestyles that look wasteful or showy. Context decides the tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use lavish for generous hosts, gifts, and parties, and for expensive lifestyles. Calling someone's house lavish is a compliment, but calling a spending habit lavish suggests criticism. As a verb, Americans usually say lavish something on someone, for example lavish attention on a child.

distinctions.note: Extravagant focuses on spending too much money or being wasteful, and it is more negative. Lavish focuses on abundance and generosity, and can be positive.
Generous describes a giving character in general. Lavish describes the very large amount given or spent, and it sounds more emphatic.

examples.everyday: Thanks for the dinner invitation; your parents were so lavish with the food that I could barely move afterward.
examples.professional: Our marketing budget was too lavish for a product launch that small, so we cut it in half.
examples.analytical: Medieval court literature often lavishes praise on the patron, and modern readers must weigh that flattery against the historical record.

nuance.analogy: A lavish buffet is like an overflowing fountain: it keeps pouring far more than anyone needs.
nuance.etymology: From Old French lavasse, meaning a heavy downpour, from laver, to wash.
common_mistakes: Using lavish to mean luxurious only; it describes generosity or abundance, not quality alone.
Saying lavish of someone instead of lavish on someone when giving things to a person.

lavish.etymology: From Middle English *laves*, *lavas*, *lavage* (“extravagant, wasteful, prodigal”), from *lavas* (“excessive abundance”), from Old French *lavasse*, *lavache* (“torrent of rain”); possibly later conflated in some senses by Middle English *laven* (“to pour…

senses.definition: Property of being lawful, of obeying the law.
senses.example: His extreme lawfulness made him righteous, but did it make him merciful?

senses.definition: Property of operating in a manner organized by certain laws, such as laws of nature.
senses.example: Scientists trust the lawfulness of gravity, which predicts how objects fall the same way every time.

core.definition: The quality of being in accordance with the law or of obeying the law.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on LAW. The middle syllable 'ful' is weak, and the final l is often syllabic, so the word sounds like 'LAW-full-nuss' with a quick, weak second syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a precise term without emotional tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'lawfulness' in legal, political and philosophical writing, especially when discussing whether an act or government is in accordance with law. In everyday conversation people usually say 'legal' or 'following the law'. It can also be used in a broader sense when discussing whether a system is orderly and rule-based.

distinctions.note: Legality is the status of being permitted under statute, while lawfulness refers to conformity with law in a broader sense.
Legitimacy concerns whether a government or authority has a right to rule, while lawfulness concerns whether an act follows the law.

examples.everyday: My friend who is a lawyer keeps asking about the lawfulness of our landlord's entry, so I'm checking the lease.
examples.professional: Legal will review the lawfulness of our data retention policy before the audit next month.
examples.analytical: The philosopher distinguishes the lawfulness of a regime from its justice, since a law can be obeyed and still be unjust.

nuance.analogy: Lawfulness is the fit between an action and the rulebook it claims to follow.
nuance.etymology: From lawful, which comes from law plus -ful, with the noun suffix -ness from Old English -nes.
common_mistakes: Using 'lawfulness' for a person who is simply obedient; for people, say 'law-abiding' or 'obedient to the law'.
Pronouncing the middle syllable clearly as 'full'; in American speech it is weak, as in 'LAW-fuhl-nuss'.

senses.definition: A lack of law; a lack of law and order; anarchy.
senses.example: After the police withdrew, lawlessness spread through the flooded city within days.

senses.definition: Defiance of the law; outlawry, exorbitant levels of crime.
senses.example: Local officials blamed the region's lawlessness on a gang that controlled the highway.

core.definition: A state in which laws are ignored or not enforced, so that crime and disorder spread.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable only. The middle and final syllables are weak, so the ending sounds like nuhs.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it describes disorder, crime, or the breakdown of authority.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use lawlessness in news, history, and political writing, for example about a city with rising crime. In casual speech they usually say chaos, crime, or no rules. It is a strong word for a broad condition rather than a single act.

distinctions.note: Crime refers to specific illegal acts, while lawlessness describes a general condition in which law is not respected.
Anarchy is a political condition without a government, while lawlessness can exist even where a government exists but fails to enforce the law.

examples.everyday: My neighbor says the lawlessness on our street got much worse after the streetlights went out.
examples.professional: The report links the rise in theft to a broader lawlessness in the district, where enforcement has largely stopped.
examples.analytical: John describes sin as lawlessness, presenting moral failure as a rejection of the order that God's law establishes.

nuance.analogy: Lawlessness is like a dam breaking: once the barrier that holds order back gives way, disorder spreads quickly.
nuance.etymology: From lawless, plus the suffix -ness forming a noun of state.
common_mistakes: Using lawlessness for a single crime; it describes a general breakdown of order.
Confusing lawlessness with lawfulness, which describes the state of following the law.
nuance.biblical_note: The Greek word anomia, meaning lawlessness or the absence of law, appears in 1 John 3:4, where sin is described as lawlessness. In 2 Thessalonians 2:7 Paul speaks of the mystery of lawlessness already at work. In both passages the term describes a turning away from God's law rather than merely breaking a human rule.

senses.definition: A motorized garden tool that propels air out of a nozzle to move leaves and other debris.

core.definition: A motorized tool that blows air out of a nozzle to move leaves, grass clippings and other yard debris.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on BLOW, the second word, while LEAF keeps a lighter secondary stress. The final -er is a light American r-colored syllable, not a full 'air' sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in a practical sense, but often negative in daily life because the noise can annoy neighbors, especially early on weekend mornings.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use leaf blower for both gas-powered and electric or battery versions, and it is a familiar sound in suburban neighborhoods. People often say 'Can you turn off the leaf blower?' or 'Those leaf blowers are so loud.' For a machine that vacuums and shreds leaves, Americans say leaf vacuum or leaf mulcher.

distinctions.note: A rake is a hand tool that gathers leaves by pulling, while a leaf blower moves them with moving air.
A leaf vacuum sucks up leaves into a bag and often shreds them, whereas a leaf blower only pushes them along.

collocations: use a leaf blower on the driveway

examples.everyday: Our neighbor starts his leaf blower at seven every Saturday morning, so we can never sleep in.
examples.professional: Facilities ordered two cordless leaf blowers for the campus grounds crew to cut down on cleanup time.
examples.analytical: The leaf blower replaces hours of raking with a loud machine, shifting the cost of yard care onto everyone within earshot.

nuance.analogy: A leaf blower is like a hair dryer for the yard, pushing air to move things rather than picking them up.
nuance.etymology: Leaf from Old English leaf; blower from blow, from Old English blawan, plus the agent suffix -er.
common_mistakes: Saying leaves blower instead of leaf blower, since leaf is used as a modifier here.
Stressing LEAF heavily, when the main stress is on BLOW.

conversation.text: Our neighbor's leaf blower woke me up at seven on Sunday.
It's faster to use the leaf blower than to rake.
Can I borrow your leaf blower this weekend?

senses.definition: Used other than figuratively or idiomatically: see lean,‎ on.
senses.example: They sat there leaning on their elbows.

senses.definition: To depend upon for support; to require assistance from.
senses.example: When my car broke down, I leaned on my brother for rides to work.

senses.definition: To put pressure on; to attempt to compel a person to do something; to exert influence on.
senses.example: He didn't make a donation until some of his customers leaned on him.

senses.definition: To criticize or reprimand for the purpose of changing behavior.
senses.example: The coach leaned on him all season about his lazy defense.

core.definition: To depend on someone for emotional or practical support, or to pressure someone to do something.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on the particle 'on,' not on 'lean,' which is a common mistake for learners. In fast speech it sounds like 'lee-NON.'

nuance.connotation: Usually positive when it means receiving support from friends or family. Negative when it means pressuring someone to act, as in 'the boss leaned on him to sign.'
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'you can lean on me' to offer comfort, often in a friendly or caring tone. The pressure sense is common in news and business talk, for example 'lawmakers leaned on the agency.' A natural reply to someone offering support is 'Thanks, I appreciate that.'

distinctions.note: Rely on is more neutral and can be used for objects or systems; lean on usually refers to a person and suggests emotional need or closeness.
Depend on is broader and more formal, often used for conditions or financial dependence, while lean on is conversational.

collocations: lean on a colleague during a hard week

examples.everyday: When my dad passed away, my sister really leaned on me for support.
examples.professional: When the deadline slipped, the project manager leaned on the vendor to deliver the data on time.
examples.analytical: The theory leans on an unexamined assumption about rational choice that its critics have never fully addressed.

nuance.analogy: Like putting your full weight on a railing, you trust someone else to hold you up.
nuance.etymology: Formed from the verb lean and the preposition on; the phrase is recorded in English from the Middle Ages onward.
common_mistakes: Stressing 'lean' instead of 'on,' which makes the phrase sound flat.
Using 'lean at' or 'lean to' for dependence; the correct preposition is 'on.'

senses.definition: A year in the Julian or Gregorian calendar with an intercalary day added to February (in the Gregorian calendar, February 29), used to adjust for the extra hours of the solar year; a 366-day year.
Any other year featuring intercalation, such as a year in a lunisolar calendar with thirteen months instead of twelve, used to maintain its alignment with the seasons of the solar year.
senses.example: The Hebrew calendar adds an extra month in a leap year, so Passover shifts later in the calendar.

core.definition: A year with an extra day added on February 29, which keeps the calendar aligned with the solar year. It has 366 days.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on 'leap,' the first word, and 'year' is a reduced, r-colored syllable. Don't shorten 'leap' to 'lap.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a practical calendar term, though it can be playful when people talk about birthdays or proposals.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'Is this a leap year?' when talking about February or birthdays. The extra day is 'February 29,' often called 'leap day.' The term refers to the calendar year, so it is not used for other calendars in everyday speech.

distinctions.note: Leap year is the whole 366-day year, while leap day is the single extra day, February 29, within it.
A common year has 365 days and no extra day; the term is used in calendar explanations.

examples.everyday: Is this a leap year? My daughter says her birthday is on February 29.
examples.professional: Our billing system has to handle a leap year, so we added a check for February 29.
examples.analytical: A leap year is a calendar rule that reconciles the solar year with an integer number of days, not an astronomical event itself.

nuance.analogy: Like a small adjustment to a piano, the leap day keeps the calendar in tune with the seasons.
nuance.etymology: Leap comes from Old English hlēapan, to jump, and the name refers to the date 'leaping' an extra day.
common_mistakes: Saying 'leap' as 'lap,' with a short vowel.
Using 'leap year' to mean any year with a special event, when it only refers to an extra day in the calendar.

leap-year.etymology: From Late Middle English *lepe-yer*, *lep-yer* (“a year with 366 days, leap year”), from *lep*, *lepe* (“act of jumping, jump, leap”) (from Old English *hlīep*, *hlȳp*, probably ultimately from Proto-Indo-European **klewp-* (“to spring; to stumble”)) +…

senses.definition: A part of garment, such as a pair of trousers/pants, that covers a leg.
senses.example: The left leg of these jeans has a tear.

senses.definition: A rod-like protrusion from an inanimate object, such as a piece of furniture, supporting it from underneath.
senses.example: the legs of a chair or table

senses.definition: Something that supports.
senses.example: This observation is an important leg of my argument.

senses.definition: A stage of a journey, race etc.
senses.example: After six days, we're finally in the last leg of our cross-country trip.

senses.definition: One of the two sides of a right triangle that is not the hypotenuse.
One of the two equal sides of an isosceles triangle.
One of the branches of a hyperbola or other curve which extend outward indefinitely.
The ability of something to persist or succeed over a long period of time.
senses.example: This proposal has no legs. Almost everyone opposes it.

senses.definition: An extension of a steam boiler downward, in the form of a narrow space between vertical plates, sometimes nearly surrounding the furnace and ash pit, and serving to support the boiler.
In a grain elevator, the case containing the lower part of the belt which carries the buckets.
Denotes the half of the field on the same side as the batsman's legs; the left side for a right-handed batsman.
A branch or lateral circuit connecting an instrument with the main line.
A branch circuit; one phase of a polyphase system.
An underlying instrument of a derivatives strategy.
A column, as a unit of length of text as laid out.
Synonym of leg up (“forming a step for a person's feet with one's hands”).
An individual bet in a parlay (a series of bets where the stake and winnings are cumulatively carried forward).
Synonym of blackleg (“a gambling cheat”).
A limb or appendage that an animal uses for support or locomotion on land.
senses.example: Insects have six legs.

senses.definition: In humans, the lower limb extending from the groin to the ankle.
senses.example: Dan won't be able to come to the party, since he broke his leg last week and is now on crutches.

senses.definition: The portion of the lower limb of a human that extends from the knee to the ankle.
A distance that a sailing vessel does without changing the sails from one side to the other.
One side of a multiple-sided (often triangular) course in a sailing race.
A single game or match played in a tournament or other sporting contest.
An army soldier assigned to a paratrooper unit who has not yet been qualified as a paratrooper.
To remove the legs from an animal carcass.
To build legs onto a platform or stage for support.
To put a series of three or more options strikes into the stock market.
To apply force using the leg (as in 'to leg a horse').
To thrust up or raise via the legs; to give a leg-up to.

core.definition: One of the two lower limbs of the body that you use to stand and walk, from the hip down to the foot.

pronunciation.tip: It is a short vowel, like the 'e' in 'bed'. Learners often use the long 'ay' vowel from 'egg' spelling confusion or the diphthong from 'lay'; the correct vowel is the short 'eh' sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a basic body-part word, but in some contexts such as food or sport it is simply descriptive.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'leg' for the whole lower limb, and 'thigh' and 'calf' for parts of it. Common speech includes 'stretch your legs' and 'my leg is asleep' for numbness. Trousers are called 'pants' in the US, so 'pants leg' is the natural phrase, not 'trouser leg'.

distinctions.note: Limb is the general term for arms and legs; leg specifically means the lower limb used for walking.
Foot is the part below the ankle, so you stand on your foot but your leg runs from the hip to the ankle.

examples.everyday: I hurt my leg playing basketball, so I'm icing it tonight.
examples.professional: Ergonomic chairs should let your legs rest flat on the floor so your knees are at a comfortable angle.
examples.analytical: The structure of the human leg balances weight and movement, and its efficiency depends on alignment at the hip, knee and ankle.

nuance.analogy: A leg is like a pillar that holds up a building: strong, aligned and supporting the whole body above it.
nuance.etymology: From Old Norse 'leggr', related to the word for a limb or support.
common_mistakes: Saying 'lay' or 'legg' with a long vowel; the vowel is short.
Using 'leg' for the whole body or for the foot; the leg runs from the hip to the ankle.

leg.etymology: From Middle English *leg*, *legge*, from Old Norse *leggr* (“leg, calf, bone of the arm or leg, hollow tube, stalk”), from Proto-Germanic **lagjaz*, **lagwijaz* (“leg, thigh”).

senses.definition: The crime of violating majesty, an offense against the dignity of a reigning sovereign or against a state.

core.definition: A serious offense against a ruler or the dignity of a state, such as insulting a sovereign or challenging the authority of the government.

pronunciation.tip: Both words are stressed on the first syllable: 'LEEZ MAJ-ih-stee.' The 'ese' is a plain 'ee' sound, and 'majesty' has a short a and a reduced middle vowel, so the second syllable is nearly a schwa.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it refers to a serious offense, and in modern American usage it is often mentioned ironically or historically.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'lese-majesty' mainly in discussions of history, law, political theory, or foreign monarchies. The concept is not a crime in the US, so Americans often describe the idea using words like 'treason' or 'insulting the president.' Saying the phrase in casual talk may sound pretentious or joking.

distinctions.note: Treason is a specific crime against one's own country or government, while lese-majesty is an offense against a monarch's dignity.
Sedition means inciting rebellion against the government, while lese-majesty focuses on insulting or disrespecting a ruler personally.

examples.everyday: In the history class, my son said that in some old kingdoms, insulting the king could be called lese-majesty.
examples.professional: The legal memo explained that lese-majesty laws in some countries conflict with modern free speech standards.
examples.analytical: The concept of lese-majesty reveals how political authority was once personified in the sovereign, so an insult to the king could be treated as an offense against the state itself.

nuance.analogy: Lese-majesty is like damaging a sacred monument: the harm is measured not only by the object but by the authority it represents.
nuance.etymology: From French lèse-majesté, from Latin laesa maiestas, meaning 'injured majesty.'
common_mistakes: Pronouncing 'lese' with a long a or as 'less,' when Americans say 'leez' in most contexts.
Assuming it is a current criminal charge in the US, when it is mainly historical or foreign.

senses.definition: The vocabulary of a language.
A dictionary that includes or focuses on lexemes.
senses.example: The linguistics department's lexicon lists every word in the corpus with its part of speech.

senses.definition: A dictionary of Classical Greek, Hebrew, Latin, or Aramaic.
senses.example: For his seminar, she checked the Greek word in Liddell and Scott's lexicon before translating the passage.

senses.definition: The lexicology of a programming language. (Usually called lexical structure.)
senses.example: The compiler rejected the code because the lexicon of the language did not allow that character in identifiers.

senses.definition: The vocabulary used by or known to an individual. (Also called lexical knowledge.)
senses.example: Her lexicon grew quickly after she started reading novels every night in her second language.

senses.definition: A set of vocabulary specific to a certain subject.
senses.example: the baseball lexicon

senses.definition: A list thereof.
senses.example: a baseball lexicon

senses.definition: (rare) Any dictionary.
senses.label: rare

senses.definition: To add to a lexicon.
senses.example: The editors decided to lexicon the new slang terms before the next edition went to print.

senses.definition: To shorten a soundtrack to fit a shortened version of a movie.
senses.example: The studio had to lexicon the film for television, cutting dialogue so it fit the shorter broadcast slot.

core.definition: The total vocabulary of a language, a particular group, or a specific subject; also a dictionary, especially of an ancient language.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The last two syllables are reduced to a schwa, so the word ends softly as 'kun' rather than 'kon'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral, describing a set of words or a reference work.
nuance.usage_note: In American English, lexicon is common in academic, technical and business writing, as in 'the lexicon of data science'. People also use it casually to mean a set of expressions, like 'the lexicon of teenagers'. In everyday talk, 'vocabulary' is more usual.

distinctions.note: Vocabulary is the everyday word for the words a person knows or uses; lexicon is more technical and often refers to the words of a field or the words in a reference.
A dictionary is the book itself; lexicon can mean the vocabulary or, in specialized use, a dictionary of an ancient language.

examples.everyday: My daughter has picked up a whole new lexicon of gaming slang from her friends.
examples.professional: The model needs an updated lexicon of product terms so that it can classify support tickets correctly.
examples.analytical: Every theological tradition develops its own lexicon, and the meaning of a single term can shift between councils.

nuance.analogy: A lexicon is like a toolbox: it holds all the words a language or field has available to use.
nuance.etymology: From Greek lexikon (biblion), 'of words' or 'word book', from lexis, 'word'.
common_mistakes: Using lexicon as a verb in everyday speech; the verb is rare and specialized.
Confusing lexicon with lexical, which is the adjective meaning 'relating to words'.

lexicon.etymology: Through Middle French or directly from New Latin *lexicon*, from Byzantine Greek *λεξικόν* (“a lexicon, a dictionary”), ellipsis from Ancient Greek, from *λεξικός* (“of words”), from *λέξις* (“a saying, speech, word”), from *λέγειν* (“to speak”),…

senses.definition: What a police officer asks a driver for during a traffic stop.

core.definition: A request made by a police officer asking a driver to show a driver's license and the vehicle's registration during a traffic stop.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on LAI in 'license', on STRAY in 'registration', and on PLEEZ at the end. In fast speech, 'and' becomes 'uhnd' and the phrase links smoothly.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly tense. It is a routine request, but it is said in a stressful situation, so a calm, polite tone helps.
nuance.usage_note: Police officers in the United States say this during routine traffic stops. The natural reply is to say 'Sure, here you go' and hand over the documents, often with the window down. Keep your hands visible and move slowly, and do not reach into the glove box until asked.

distinctions.note: A driver's license is a specific ID for driving, while a general ID may be any government document; officers ask for the license during traffic stops.

examples.everyday: When the officer pulled me over, he just said, License and registration, please, and I handed them over.
examples.professional: Before the audit, we made sure every company vehicle had current license and registration on file.
examples.analytical: Traffic-stop procedures rely on a simple request such as License and registration, please, which establishes identity and vehicle ownership quickly.

nuance.analogy: It works like a checkpoint at an airport: a quick, routine document check that happens before anything else can move forward.
nuance.etymology: License comes from Latin licentia, meaning permission; registration comes from Latin registrum, meaning a record.
common_mistakes: Saying 'driver's license and registration' when the officer just says 'license'; both forms are used.
Stressing 'reg-is-TRA-tion' with the wrong syllable; the stress falls on STRAY in American speech.

conversation.text: The officer walked up to my window and said, "License and registration, please."
"License and registration, please." "Sure, officer, it's in the glove compartment."
When the officer says "License and registration, please," keep your hands where he can see them.

senses.definition: Thread or cloth made from flax fiber.
Domestic textiles, such as tablecloths, bedding, towels, underclothes, etc. that are made of linen or linen-like fabrics of cotton or other fibers; linens.
senses.example: She put the freshly cleaned linens into the linen closet.

senses.definition: A light beige color, like that of linen cloth undyed.
senses.example: linen:

senses.definition: Made from linen cloth or thread.
senses.example: She bought a linen tablecloth for the holiday dinner, embroidered with small blue flowers.

senses.definition: Having the color linen, light beige.
senses.example: He painted the nursery walls a soft linen color that looked warm in the afternoon light.

core.definition: Cloth or thread made from flax fiber, or household textiles such as sheets, tablecloths, and towels made from it.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on the first syllable, and both syllables are short. Many learners say the second syllable as a long ee, but it is a short, reduced vowel.

nuance.connotation: Positive; linen suggests quality, natural fiber, and comfort, especially for summer clothes and bedding.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use linen for clothing, tablecloths, bed sheets, and hotel towels. In plural, linens usually means household items such as sheets and towels, as in 'Can I get fresh linens?' Linen is more expensive than cotton, so it often signals high quality.

distinctions.note: Cotton is a different plant fiber, usually softer and cheaper; linen is stronger, more absorbent, and wrinkles more easily.
Lace is a delicate openwork fabric, which may be made of linen, cotton, or silk; linen describes the material itself.

examples.everyday: I'm packing a light linen shirt for our trip to Florida because it stays cool in the heat.
examples.professional: Housekeeping will restock the linens on each floor before check-in starts at three.
examples.analytical: In the Gospel of Mark, the young man who flees naked leaves behind a linen cloth, a detail that scholars have discussed at length.

nuance.analogy: Like the sheets you slept in as a child at a summer cabin: crisp, breathable, and a little rough the first time.
nuance.etymology: From Old English linen, from Proto-Germanic linam, related to the Latin linum, flax.
common_mistakes: Using linen as a countable noun in everyday speech; say a linen or the linens, not a linens for one item.
Pronouncing the second syllable as long ee, as in LIN-een.
nuance.biblical_note: In Hebrew the usual word is bad (בַּד), used for the white linen garments of priests and for other linen cloth, while the Greek byssos (βύσσος) names the fine linen of the New Testament. Linen is often a sign of purity, ritual cleanness, or rich dress. Revelation 19:8 describes the bride of the Lamb clothed in fine linen, bright and pure, and Proverbs 31:22 describes the capable wife making fine linen and purple garments. In Mark 14:51 a young man flees naked after leaving behind a linen cloth, a notoriously obscure detail.

senses.definition: Well-educated, erudite, literary people; intellectuals who are interested in literature.

core.definition: Well-educated people, especially writers, scholars and critics who are interested in literature and ideas.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on the third syllable, the 'rah' sound. Don't say 'lit-uh-RAH-ty'; the ending is a clear 'tee'. It is a plural noun used with plural verbs.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly admiring; sometimes ironic, implying snobbishness.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'literati' mostly in writing and conversation about book culture, criticism, or intellectual circles, such as 'the New York literati'. It is a formal, slightly playful word and sounds out of place in casual talk. A plain alternative is 'intellectuals' or 'writers and critics'.

distinctions.note: Intellectuals is broader and more common; literati specifically focuses on literary culture and erudition.
Elite refers to social power or status; literati refers to learned and literary people.

examples.everyday: My sister is always reading, so she hangs out with a group that calls itself the local literati.
examples.professional: Our editorial board is full of literati, so the review comments tend to be long and detailed.
examples.analytical: The eighteenth-century literati shaped public taste by debating novels, essays and poetry in salons and journals.

nuance.analogy: The literati are like the gardeners of a culture's libraries, tending the books and ideas that others come to admire.
nuance.etymology: From Latin litterati, plural of litteratus, 'educated, lettered', from littera, 'letter'.
common_mistakes: Using 'a literati' as singular; the word is plural, so say 'one of the literati'.
Pronouncing the final syllable as 'tie'; it is 'tee'.

senses.definition: A figure of speech whereby something is stated by denying its opposite.
The negation of a negative quality to assert a positive.
senses.example: Saying the team's results were not bad is litotes for a genuinely impressive outcome.

core.definition: A figure of speech that makes a point by denying its opposite, such as saying 'not bad' to mean good.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, LY, and the final syllable is pronounced 'teez' rather than 'tee-tees'. Non-native speakers often stress the second syllable or add an extra vowel in the middle.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It can be used to soften a claim or to create dry, understated humor, depending on the context.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this term mainly in literature classes, rhetoric, and writing discussions rather than in everyday talk. In conversation, people usually just say 'not bad' or 'not unlike' without naming the device. It is useful to recognize in essays and speeches, where it often appears as understatement.

distinctions.note: Understatement is a broader term for presenting something as less significant than it is, while litotes specifically uses a double negative or negated opposite.
Irony means saying the opposite of what is meant in a way that signals a contrast, while litotes is a direct but restrained affirmation through negation.

examples.everyday: When my friend tasted the soup, she said it was not bad at all, which meant she really loved it.
examples.professional: In the performance review, the manager wrote that the project was not without merit, a bit of litotes that signaled strong approval.
examples.analytical: The author's use of litotes allows the narrator to assert a positive judgment while avoiding the appearance of enthusiasm.

nuance.analogy: Litotes is like a dimmer switch for praise: you turn the light up by turning the opposite down, so the glow feels softer but still clearly there.
nuance.etymology: From Greek litotēs, meaning plainness or simplicity, from litos, meaning smooth or meager.
common_mistakes: Using litotes to mean any kind of understatement, when it specifically involves negating the opposite.
Mispronouncing the word with a stress on the second syllable, as in lye-TOH-teez.

litotes.etymology: Late Latin *lītotēs*, from Ancient Greek *λιτότης*, from *λιτός* (“simple”).

senses.definition: A word directly taken into one language from another one.
senses.example: "Calque" is a loanword with French origins, and "loanword" is a calque with German origins.

core.definition: A word taken from one language and used in another, such as sushi, which English borrowed from Japanese.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, with a lighter secondary stress on word. End the second syllable with the American r-colored vowel, which sounds like ur.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and descriptive.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use loanword mainly in linguistics, teaching and writing about language. In casual talk, people often say borrowed word or just name the language, as in 'that's a French word.' The word does not imply that the word must be returned.

distinctions.note: Borrowing is the general process of taking words from another language, while loanword names the individual word that was taken.
A calque translates the parts of a foreign word into native words, while a loanword keeps the foreign form, at least partly.

examples.everyday: Sushi is a Japanese loanword, but most Americans say it without thinking about where it came from.
examples.professional: Our localization guide lists loanwords like bazaar so translators keep the original form.
examples.analytical: A loanword enters a language with its sound and spelling partly intact, which shows how borrowing and adaptation happen together.

nuance.analogy: A loanword is like a guest who keeps some of their home clothes while adapting to the house rules.
nuance.etymology: A calque of German Lehnwort, from loan plus word.
common_mistakes: Assuming a loanword must be returned, because the word loan suggests borrowing with an obligation to repay.
Stressing word too strongly, when the main stress falls on loan.

senses.definition: A building for recreational use such as a hunting lodge or a summer cabin.
Ellipsis of porter's lodge: a building or room near the entrance of an estate or building, especially as a college mailroom.
A local chapter of some fraternities, such as freemasons.
senses.example: My grandfather was an active member of the local Masonic lodge for forty years.

senses.definition: A local chapter of a trade union.
senses.example: The machinists' lodge voted to strike after the contract talks broke down.

senses.definition: A rural hotel or resort, an inn.
senses.example: We spent the weekend at a rustic mountain lodge with no cell service.

senses.definition: A beaver's shelter constructed on a pond or lake.
senses.example: Beavers built a lodge of sticks and mud in the middle of the pond.

senses.definition: A den or cave.
senses.example: The wolf retreated to its lodge in the rocky hillside to nurse her pups.

senses.definition: The chamber of an abbot, prior, or head of a college.
senses.example: The abbot received the visiting bishop in his lodge overlooking the gardens.

senses.definition: The space at the mouth of a level next to the shaft, widened to permit wagons to pass, or ore to be deposited for hoisting; called also platt.
senses.example: The miners waited at the lodge near the shaft until the ore cart was hoisted.

senses.definition: A collection of objects lodged together.
senses.example: A lodge of driftwood was jammed under the bridge after the flood.

senses.definition: A Native American home, such as teepee or wigwam.
senses.example: The tribe consists of about two hundred lodges, that is, of about a thousand individuals.

senses.definition: The people who live in one such home; a household.
senses.example: The whole lodge gathered for dinner, from the grandparents down to the toddlers.

senses.definition: A family of Native Americans, or the persons who usually occupy an Indian lodge; as a unit of enumeration, reckoned from four to six persons.
senses.example: The tribe consists of about two hundred lodges, that is, of about a thousand individuals.

senses.definition: To be firmly fixed in a specified position.
senses.example: The bullet missed its target and lodged in the bark of a tree.

senses.definition: To firmly fix in a specified position.
senses.example: I've got some spinach lodged between my teeth.

senses.definition: To stay in a boarding-house, paying rent to the resident landlord or landlady.
senses.example: The detective Sherlock Holmes lodged in Baker Street.

senses.definition: To stay in any place or shelter.
senses.example: We lodged with my cousin's family for three weeks while our apartment was repaired.

senses.definition: To drive (an animal) to covert.
senses.example: The hunters lodged the deer in the thicket before the dogs arrived.

senses.definition: To supply with a room or place to sleep in for a time.
senses.example: The church lodged the traveling families in its basement for the week.

senses.definition: To put money, jewelry, or other valuables away for safety.
senses.example: She lodged her grandmother's jewelry in the bank's safe deposit box.

senses.definition: To place (a statement, etc.) with the proper authorities (such as courts, etc.).
senses.example: to lodge a complaint

senses.definition: To become flattened, as grass or grain, when overgrown or beaten down by the wind.
senses.example: The heavy rain caused the wheat to lodge.

senses.definition: To cause to flatten, as grass or grain.
senses.example: Heavy rain lodged the wheat, so the harvest will be slower this year.

core.definition: A building for recreation, such as a hunting, ski or mountain lodge, or a small resort building for guests.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the single syllable, and make the vowel short like in 'dodge'. Do not use the long oh of 'lode'.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral; it suggests a cozy place in nature or a retreat.
nuance.usage_note: Americans commonly use lodge for a rustic hotel or cabin in the mountains, woods or ski areas. It also appears as a fraternal chapter, such as a Masonic lodge. In a hotel context, Americans usually say hotel or inn for a standard building. A natural reply to 'where are you staying?' is 'a lodge up near the lake.'

distinctions.note: A cabin is a small, simple house, while a lodge is larger and often offers services like meals and rooms.
A hotel is a commercial building with many rooms, while a lodge suggests a rustic or recreational setting.

examples.everyday: We're staying at a ski lodge near the summit this weekend.
examples.professional: Please book the lodge for our team offsite retreat in October.
examples.analytical: The Masonic lodge's rituals reflect its historical role as a fraternal community bound by shared values.

nuance.analogy: A lodge is like a big cabin with a fireplace and dinner served, a place to rest in the woods.
nuance.etymology: From Old French loge, meaning hut or shelter.
common_mistakes: Using lode vowel sound for lodge.
Using lodge to mean hotel in a city, where Americans would say hotel.

lodge.etymology: From Middle English *logge*, from Old French *loge* (“an arbour, a covered walk-way”).

conversation.text: We stayed at the lodge inside the park, and it was beautiful.
Let's grab lunch at the ski lodge.
The lodge was booked, so we ended up camping.

senses.definition: Synonym of log out.
senses.example: Please log off the shared computer before you leave the library so others can use it.

senses.definition: To depart from any conversation, online or in person; to say goodbye.
senses.example: It was getting late, so I logged off and told everyone goodnight.

core.definition: To sign out of a computer, app, website or online account, ending your session.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on 'off', so 'log' is the lighter word. Say the g clearly, and don't blend it into a sound like 'loff'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and practical, used in technical and everyday contexts alike.
nuance.usage_note: In American tech use, 'log off' and 'log out' mean the same thing, and both are common, with 'sign out' also used. The sense of saying goodbye at the end of an online chat is informal, while face-to-face conversation would use 'bye' or 'talk to you later'. Remember that you log off a session, not a whole machine.

distinctions.note: Log out and log off are nearly identical in US usage, though 'log out' is slightly more common for websites and apps.
Shut down ends the whole computer or program, while log off only ends your user session and leaves the machine running.

examples.everyday: Don't forget to log off the shared computer before you leave the library.
examples.professional: Please log off the VPN once you finish the database migration.
examples.analytical: Each session ends when a user logs off, so the server can record the exact duration of each visit.

nuance.analogy: Logging off is like locking your front door when you leave, so nobody else can walk in.
nuance.etymology: From the computing sense of 'log' (a record of activity) plus 'off'.
common_mistakes: Using 'log off' to mean 'turn off' a computer; logging off ends your session but does not shut the machine down.
Saying 'log off from' a website; 'log out of' or simply 'log off' is more standard in writing.

senses.definition: A form of rhetoric in which the writer or speaker uses logical argument as the main form of persuasion.
senses.example: In her debate essay, she relied mostly on logos, using data and careful reasoning to persuade.

core.definition: In Greek philosophy, reason or the rational order of the world. In John's Gospel, the divine Word, a title for Christ.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. Both vowels are long, and the final 's' is a simple 's' sound, not a 'z'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It names a central idea in philosophy and theology, and is respected in academic circles.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use logos in philosophy, rhetoric, theology, and literary study, most often with a capital L when it refers to Christ. In rhetoric classes, it means the appeal to logic, distinct from ethos and pathos. In church settings, speakers often say 'the Word' rather than 'Logos' in ordinary conversation.

distinctions.note: Logic is the formal study of valid reasoning, while logos is a broader idea that includes reason, speech, and, in theology, the divine Word.
Ethos is persuasion through the speaker's character and credibility, while logos is persuasion through reasoned argument.
Pathos is persuasion through emotion, while logos is persuasion through logic and evidence.

examples.everyday: My friend says the best arguments have strong logos, so she always asks for the data before she gets emotional.
examples.professional: When we pitch this to the board, we should lead with logos, showing the numbers, before we tell the customer stories.
examples.analytical: In John's Gospel, the Logos is both with God and is God, which joins the Greek idea of reason to the Hebrew idea of the creative word.

nuance.analogy: Logos is like the architectural plan behind a building: the hidden order that makes its parts fit together into a meaningful whole.
nuance.etymology: From Greek logos, 'word, speech, reason', from legein, 'to speak, gather'.
common_mistakes: Confusing logos with logo, the company symbol, which is a different word with a different stress pattern in conversation.
