Using it for logic in general; logos is the rhetorical or philosophical appeal to reason.
nuance.biblical_note: The Greek word logos means word, speech, or reason. In John 1:1-14 it names the eternal Word, who was with God and was God and who became flesh in Jesus Christ. The term also appears in Hebrews 4:12, where the word of God is described as living and active, cutting between soul and spirit. Behind logos lies the Hebrew idea of dabar, the powerful spoken word through which God creates and speaks to his people. Key passages: John 1:1-14 describes the Word's eternal relation to God and his incarnation; Hebrews 4:12 describes the living and active word of God; Romans 10:8 describes the word of faith near to the believer.

logos.etymology: From Ancient Greek *λόγος* (“speech, oration, discourse, quote, story, study, ratio, word, calculation, reason”).

senses.definition: A casual greeting to someone you haven't seen for a long time.

core.definition: A casual greeting used when you meet someone you have not seen for a long time.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on SEE. Link 'long time' and 'no see' smoothly, and keep the 'n' in 'no' clear. Many learners pronounce 'time' too short; keep the diphthong 'aɪ' long.

nuance.connotation: Positive and friendly. It expresses warmth at a reunion.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say this casually to a friend, coworker, or neighbor they have not seen in a while. It is often playful and sometimes used humorously, and it can sound a bit old-fashioned or pidgin-like to some people, so keep it light. A natural reply is 'Yeah, it's been forever! How have you been?'

distinctions.note: This is more polite and neutral, suitable for formal settings; the expression is playful and informal.
It's been ages is a conversational comment about time passing, often said with the reply, while the expression is a greeting.

collocations: Long time no see, how have you been?
a long time no see reunion

examples.everyday: Long time no see! I didn't know you were back in town. How's the family?
examples.professional: Long time no see, Priya. I saw your name on the conference agenda, so let's catch up before the keynote.
examples.analytical: The phrase 'long time no see' reflects a conversational convention that marks an interval of absence and signals renewed social contact.

nuance.analogy: It is like a greeting card that says 'I remember you,' delivered out loud.
nuance.etymology: An informal English greeting, widely used in English since the twentieth century, whose exact origin is uncertain.
common_mistakes: Writing 'long time not see' with 'not' instead of 'no'; the standard casual form is 'long time no see'.
Saying it to someone you saw last week; it is only for longer gaps.

conversation.text: Hey, James! Long time no see! How have you been?
Long time no see! I think the last time was at your wedding.
"Long time no see!" "I know! It's been, what, three years?"

senses.definition: A peer of the realm, particularly a temporal one.
One possessing similar mastery in figurative senses (esp. as lord of ~)
senses.example: The Tobacco Lords were a group of Scottish merchants and slave traders who in the 18th century made enormous fortunes by trading in tobacco.

senses.definition: A magnate of a trade or profession.
senses.example: The Tobacco Lords were a group of Scottish merchants and slave traders who in the 18th century made enormous fortunes by trading in tobacco.

senses.definition: The heavenly body considered to possess a dominant influence over an event, time, etc.

(historical) One possessing similar mastery over others; any feudal superior generally; any nobleman or aristocrat; any chief, prince, or sovereign ruler; in Scotland, a male member of the lowest rank of nobility (the equivalent rank in England is baron)
senses.label: historical

senses.definition: (historical) A feudal tenant holding his manor directly of the king.
senses.label: historical

senses.definition: To domineer or act like a lord.
To invest with the dignity, power, and privileges of a lord; to grant the title of lord.

core.definition: A ruler or master with authority over others; in Christian usage, a title for God or Jesus Christ.

pronunciation.tip: In General American the vowel is the 'aw' of 'law', the same as 'caught', not the long 'o' of 'load'. Pronounce the 'r' clearly, since American English is rhotic.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in most uses. In religious contexts it is reverent, and in exclamations like 'Oh Lord' it is informal and sometimes exasperated.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use 'lord' for a real nobleman, since the United States has no aristocracy, so it sounds British or historical when used that way. In church and Bible study, 'the Lord' is the normal title for God, and it is capitalized. In casual speech, 'Oh, Lord' or 'good Lord' expresses surprise or frustration, especially in the South.

distinctions.note: King is the sovereign head of a nation, while lord is a broader word for any ruler, master, or noble with authority.
Master usually means someone who controls people or things directly, while lord suggests higher rank or a sense of authority over a domain.
God is the general name for the divine being, while Lord is a title used especially for God in Christian and Jewish practice.

examples.everyday: Oh Lord, I left my wallet at the restaurant again.
examples.professional: Our CTO is the lord of the data platform, so every schema change has to go through her team.
examples.analytical: Scripture calls Jesus Lord, a title that claims his authority over every human ruler and power.

nuance.analogy: Like a captain of a ship: the title signals who is in charge and whose word settles the matter.
nuance.etymology: From Old English hlāford, from hlāf (loaf, bread) plus weard (keeper), meaning keeper or guardian of bread.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the vowel like the 'o' in 'load' instead of the 'aw' in 'law'.
Using 'lord' for American political or social leaders, which sounds odd since the US has no lords.
nuance.biblical_note: In the Bible, Lord translates Hebrew YHWH (the divine name, shown as LORD in small capitals in the RSV) and adonai (my lord, a respectful title used in place of the divine name). The Greek word is kyrios (lord, master), used for Jesus in the New Testament. Key passages: Deuteronomy 6:4 declares that the LORD alone is God and Israel's central confession; Psalm 110:1 describes the LORD speaking to the psalmist's lord, a passage Jesus later cites; Philippians 2:9-11 says God exalted Jesus and that every tongue will confess that Jesus Christ is Lord.

lord.etymology: From Middle English *lord* and *lorde* (attested from the 15th century), from earlier (14th century) *lourde* and other variants which dropped the intervocalic consonant of earlier *lowerd*, *louerd*, *loverd*, *laford*, and *lhoaverd*; from Old English…

senses.definition: In a loyal manner, faithfully.
senses.example: The old dog loyally followed his master even if he didn't really want to go out.

core.definition: In a faithful, supportive way toward a person, group, cause or country, without switching sides.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on LOY, and the middle syllable reduces to uh. The final -ly is a clear lee sound, not lay.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It praises steady, faithful commitment.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use loyally less often than phrases such as stuck by or stayed loyal, which sound more natural in conversation. The adverb appears in news, sports writing and formal speeches to describe someone who supported a person or team through hard times. In casual talk, say she stuck by him instead.

distinctions.note: Faithfully emphasizes keeping promises and routines, often in daily duties; loyally emphasizes support and allegiance to a person or cause.
Devotedly is warmer and more emotional; loyally is more about reliability and commitment.

examples.everyday: My old neighbor has rooted for the Cubs loyally since he was a kid, even through the bad years.
examples.professional: The team loyally stuck with the project even after the budget was cut.
examples.analytical: The writer argues that many intellectuals loyally served the regime even while doubting its methods.

nuance.analogy: Like a compass needle that keeps pointing north no matter how the ship turns.
nuance.etymology: From loyal (from Old French loial) plus the adverb suffix -ly.
common_mistakes: Misspelling it as loyaly; keep the double l: loyally
Using loyally as a verb
Stressing the final syllable instead of LOY

senses.definition: To make slippery or smooth (normally to minimize friction) by applying a lubricant.
senses.example: If your bicycle chain is squeaking you should lubricate it.

senses.definition: To cause someone to become drunk, especially to make them more sociable or talkative.
senses.example: The salesman tried to lubricate the clients with free whiskey before the contract talks.

core.definition: To apply oil, grease or another substance to moving parts so they slide smoothly with less friction.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, LOO. The second syllable is reduced to a short ih, and the final syllable rhymes with late. Do not stress the final syllable, as in lu-bri-KATE.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in mechanical use; the drunk sense is informal and humorous or slightly negative.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use lubricate in manuals, engineering talk and maintenance work, while everyday speakers more often say oil or grease the hinges. The sense to make someone drunk is rare and old-fashioned, found in older fiction or jokes. In careful writing, use the mechanical sense.

distinctions.note: Grease specifically means to apply grease, while lubricate can mean applying any lubricant, including oil or spray.
Oil as a verb is informal and common at home; lubricate sounds more technical and precise.

examples.everyday: Can you lubricate that squeaky door hinge with a little oil?
examples.professional: Lubricate the rollers before the next shift to prevent overheating and premature wear.
examples.analytical: Friction must be lubricated to keep moving parts from wearing down, and every mechanical design must account for that need.

nuance.analogy: Like rubbing a little olive oil on a sticky jar lid so it turns freely.
nuance.etymology: From Latin lubricare, to make slippery, from lubricus, slippery.
common_mistakes: Using lubricate as a noun; the noun is lubricant or lubrication.
Stressing the last syllable, saying lu-bri-KATE, which is an incorrect American stress pattern.

lubricate.etymology: Borrowed from Latin *lūbricātus*, perfect passive participle of *lūbricō* (“make slippery”) (see *-ate* for more), from *lūbricus* (“slippery”).

senses.definition: The state of being luminous, or a luminous object; brilliance or radiance.
The ratio of luminous flux to radiant flux at the same wavelength; the luminosity factor.
senses.example: The lab calibrated the sensor's luminosity against the standard photopic curve at 555 nanometers.

senses.definition: The rate at which a star radiates energy in all directions.
senses.example: Astronomers estimated the star's luminosity by measuring its total radiated energy across all wavelengths.

core.definition: The degree of brightness or light emitted by something, especially a star or a light source.

pronunciation.tip: Stress NAH, the vowel in 'hot' and 'cot'. The -ity ending is unstressed and sounds like 'ih-tee'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral, technical, and precise.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use luminosity in physics, astronomy, photography, and display design. In everyday talk they would say 'brightness'. The noun also appears in literary writing about light.

distinctions.note: Brightness is what the eye perceives, while luminosity is often a measured quantity of emitted light.
Luminance is a photometric measure of light per area, while luminosity is often used more broadly or for stars.

examples.everyday: Can you turn down the luminosity on your phone? It's too bright in bed.
examples.professional: We adjusted the luminosity of the display so the charts are readable under office lights.
examples.analytical: The poet's image of the sun's luminosity suggests a God who reveals truth without hiding anything.

nuance.analogy: Like the total light a candle gives off in every direction, not just the light that reaches your eye.
nuance.etymology: From Latin luminosus 'full of light', from lumen 'light'.
common_mistakes: Using it for everyday brightness instead of 'brightness'.
Stressing the wrong syllable as 'loo-mih-NOS-ih-tee'.

luminosity.etymology: French *luminosité* or else a native formation from *luminous* + *-ity*.

senses.definition: A sudden or unsteady movement.
senses.example: the lurch of a ship, or of a drunkard

senses.definition: A predicament or difficult situation.
senses.example: to leave someone in the lurch

senses.definition: An old game played with dice and counters; a variety of the game of tables.
senses.example: Grandpa taught us the old dice game of lurch, which he played with dried beans as counters.

senses.definition: A double score in cribbage for the winner when their adversary has not yet pegged their 31st hole.
senses.example: She won the game with a lurch, pegging twice when her opponent had not reached the final hole.

senses.definition: To make such a sudden, unsteady movement.
senses.example: The bus lurched forward at the red light, throwing passengers against the seats.

senses.definition: To defeat in the game of cribbage with a lurch (double score as explained under noun entry).
senses.example: My uncle lurched me twice in cribbage last night, so I owe him dinner.

core.definition: A sudden, unsteady movement; also the idiom 'leave someone in the lurch,' meaning abandon them in trouble.

pronunciation.tip: The vowel is the American r-colored 'ur' sound, like 'her,' and the word has one syllable. Don't add an extra syllable or pronounce the 'r' as a separate sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral for the physical movement; negative for the idiom 'leave someone in the lurch.'
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'lurch' for a sudden jerk of a car, bus or boat, and 'leave someone in the lurch' is common in everyday talk for abandoning someone when they need help. A natural reply is 'Thanks for not leaving me in the lurch,' and it is often said with real gratitude. The idiom almost always requires 'in the lurch.'

distinctions.note: To stagger is to walk unsteadily from weakness or intoxication; a lurch is a sudden jerk of a moving object or person.
A jolt is a sharp shake from an impact; a lurch is a more sudden, unsteady sway or jerk in motion.
A lunge is a deliberate forward thrust; a lurch is an unsteady movement that is often unintended.

examples.everyday: The bus lurched to a stop, and I nearly spilled my coffee.
examples.professional: Please don't leave the team in the lurch if the release slips by a day.
examples.analytical: Markets lurch between euphoria and panic, but the underlying data often moves more slowly.

nuance.analogy: A lurch is like a shopping cart with one bad wheel, jerking sideways without warning.
common_mistakes: Omitting 'the' in the idiom: it is 'leave someone in the lurch,' not 'leave someone in lurch.'
Confusing 'lurch' with 'lunge,' which is a deliberate forward thrust.
Using 'lurch' as a noun with 'a lurch of' in place of 'a lurch' in everyday speech; keep the phrase simple.

lurch.etymology: Originally a nautical term, found in *lee-larches* (“the sudden and violent rolls of a ship to the leeward in high seas”), of origin.

senses.definition: To make angry.
To make insane; to inflame with passion.
senses.example: The endless delays began to madden the already exhausted team.

core.definition: To make someone very angry or irritated, often by repeated annoyances.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The second syllable is a syllabic n with no separate vowel, so say it as a quick n after the d.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes a strong irritation or anger caused by someone or something.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use madden in casual speech; they prefer annoy, drive crazy, or get on someone's nerves. You will see madden in news writing, novels, and formal essays. It sounds more intense than annoy and more dramatic than irritate.

distinctions.note: Annoy is mild and everyday. Madden is stronger and more formal, suggesting real anger or frustration.
Infuriate implies sudden, intense rage. Madden can describe slow, repeated irritation that wears a person down.

examples.everyday: The constant beeping of the microwave really maddens me.
examples.professional: The flaky test results madden the whole QA team because nobody can reproduce the failures.
examples.analytical: Hume's skeptical arguments madden readers who want certainty about causation.

nuance.analogy: Madden is like a dripping faucet: each drop is small, but after hours it drives you crazy.
nuance.etymology: From Middle English maddien, from mad.
common_mistakes: Using madden to mean become insane in everyday speech; that sense is archaic.
Using madden in casual conversation where annoy is more natural.

senses.definition: Administration; the use of limited resources combined with forecasting, planning, leadership and execution skills to achieve predetermined specific goals.
senses.example: Good management of the household budget helped us save for our first house.

senses.definition: The executives of an organization, especially senior executives.
senses.example: Management announced layoffs at the plant after disappointing quarterly earnings.

senses.definition: Judicious use of means to accomplish an end.
senses.example: Excellent time management helped her succeed in all facets of her life.

senses.definition: The prosecuting side in an impeachment trial (as opposed to the respondent or defending side).
senses.example: Counsel for the management argued that the president had abused his office.

core.definition: The process of directing and organizing people, money and resources to reach a company's or team's goals; also the people who run an organization.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The middle vowel reduces to a quick 'ih', and the g sounds like 'j', so don't add an extra syllable like 'man-ah-ment'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It can sound positive when describing skilled leadership, but it often sounds negative when workers say 'management' to mean the bosses as a group.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'management' both for the activity of running a business and for the group of managers, as in 'upper management' or 'senior management.' In casual talk, 'management' is often used with a slight edge, as in 'Management won't approve that.' For a single person, say 'manager.'

distinctions.note: Administration focuses on the routine running of an institution, while management also includes planning, leadership and decisions aimed at specific goals.
Leadership is about inspiring people and setting direction; management is about organizing resources and processes to deliver results.

examples.everyday: Honestly, the store's management needs to open another checkout line before the holidays.
examples.professional: Senior management approved the budget, so we can start the migration next sprint.
examples.analytical: Weber's account of bureaucracy treats management less as personal authority than as a rational system of rules and offices.

nuance.analogy: Management is like a conductor: the musicians play the notes, but the conductor sets the tempo, balances the sections and keeps everyone aimed at the same piece.
nuance.etymology: From manage, from Italian maneggiare 'to handle, train horses', from Latin manus 'hand'.
common_mistakes: Dropping the e after the g and writing 'managment'; the correct spelling is 'management'.
Using 'management' as a countable word for one manager; say 'manager' or 'a member of management'.
Stressing the last syllable as in 'man-AJ-ment'; the stress belongs on MAN.

senses.definition: The (often sexual) enjoyment of receiving pain or humiliation.

core.definition: Taking pleasure in receiving pain or humiliation, especially in a sexual context.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, MAS. The middle syllable is a reduced uh, and the ending is -iz-um, not -ism.

nuance.connotation: Negative or clinical; it can be used playfully in casual talk about doing something painful.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use masochism in psychology and in casual joking, such as calling a hard workout masochism. In sexual contexts it is clinical and often discussed with consent in mind. Calling a person masochistic can sound insulting, so use it carefully.

distinctions.note: Masochism is taking pleasure in pain or humiliation, while sadism is taking pleasure in causing it to others.
Self-harm is injuring oneself, usually as a sign of distress, while masochism refers to pleasure in pain.

examples.everyday: Signing up for a five a.m. workout class is pure masochism.
examples.professional: Taking on three weekend deadlines in a row isn't dedication; it's a kind of masochism.
examples.analytical: Freud linked masochism to aggression turned back against the self.

nuance.etymology: Named after Leopold von Sacher-Masoch (1836-1895), an Austrian writer whose novels described such pleasure.
common_mistakes: Confusing masochism, the noun, with masochistic, the adjective.
Stressing the last syllable instead of MAS at the beginning.

masochism.etymology: From German *Masochismus*, coined alongside Sadismus in 1886 by Richard von Krafft-Ebing in his book Psychopathia Sexualis.

senses.definition: Someone who enjoys pain or humiliation, or who derives pleasure from harming oneself or being harmed by others.
Someone who puts up with teasing.
senses.example: My brother is such a masochist that he keeps asking me to tease him about his haircut.

core.definition: A person who takes pleasure in their own pain or humiliation, or in being harmed by others.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, and reduce the second syllable to a schwa. Say the final part as 'kist' with a short i, not 'keest'.

nuance.connotation: Negative or clinical. It labels a person in a way that can sound judgmental, so use it carefully.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use masochist in psychology and in casual talk, often humorously about someone who seems to enjoy hard tasks, such as 'You're a masochist for running in this heat.' In serious conversation it can be hurtful, so avoid it when discussing real people's pain. A natural reply to a joke about it is a laugh and a comment about the task.

distinctions.note: A sadist takes pleasure in causing pain to others, while a masochist takes pleasure in receiving pain.
A glutton overeats; a masochist enjoys suffering, though the word is used humorously about people who take on hard tasks.

examples.everyday: You went hiking in the middle of July? You must be a masochist.
examples.professional: Taking on the migration project alone with no support is either brave or masochistic, and we should talk about what's realistic.
examples.analytical: Freud's account of masochism explored whether the pleasure in pain reveals deeper conflicts in the human psyche.

nuance.analogy: A masochist is like someone who keeps touching a hot stove to feel the sting, finding pleasure where others feel only pain.
nuance.etymology: Named after the Austrian writer Leopold von Sacher-Masoch, whose fiction portrayed such pleasure; the term was coined in the 1880s.
common_mistakes: Using masochist as a casual insult without considering how it sounds.
Confusing masochist with masochistic, which is the adjective.

senses.definition: A social system in which the mother is head of household, having authority over men and children, and lineage is traced through the female line.
A system of government by women (particularly as a kind of polity).
senses.example: The novel imagines a future matriarchy where women hold every seat in the council.

senses.definition: The dominance of women in social or cultural systems.

core.definition: A social system in which women hold the main authority in a family or society, often with descent traced through the mother.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, MAY, and end with a clear 'ee' sound, not 'eye'. The 'ar' in the middle is an r-colored vowel, so do not pronounce it as 'ahr' followed by a separate syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. In academic writing it is descriptive, but in political debate it can be used to make a point about gender power.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'matriarchy' mainly in anthropology, history, feminist writing and discussions of family leadership. It is the counterpart of 'patriarchy', and the two are often compared. In casual talk, people more often say a family is 'run by the women' or 'led by the matriarch'.

distinctions.note: Matrilineal refers to descent through the mother's line, while matriarchy refers to the authority held by women.
A matriarch is a woman who leads, while a matriarchy is the whole system in which women hold the main authority.
Gynocracy is a rare synonym for government by women, while matriarchy is the common term in anthropology and everyday writing.

collocations: a family run as a matriarchy

examples.everyday: My aunt runs our family like a matriarchy, and nobody makes a big decision without checking with her first.
examples.professional: The company is less a matriarchy than a team led by several strong women who share decisions.
examples.analytical: Nineteenth-century theories of an ancient matriarchy were largely rejected by later archaeologists, who found little evidence for them.

nuance.analogy: A matriarchy is like a river system where the main channel runs through the women, shaping the direction of everything downstream.
nuance.etymology: From Greek mētēr, mother, and arkhē, rule, the same roots as matriarch.
common_mistakes: Using matriarchy for a single leader; a matriarch is a person and a matriarchy is a system.
Confusing matriarchy with matrilineal, which describes descent rather than authority.

matriarchy.etymology: Coined after *patriarchy*, from Latin *māter* (“mother”) and Ancient Greek *ἄρχω* (“to rule”).

senses.definition: A rectangular arrangement of numbers or terms having various uses such as transforming coordinates in geometry, solving systems of linear equations in linear algebra and representing graphs in graph theory.
senses.example: The transformation matrix rotates each point in the coordinate plane by thirty degrees.

senses.definition: The cavity or mold in which anything is formed.
senses.example: The molten metal poured into the sand matrix and cooled into the shape of the mold.

senses.definition: The metaphorical place where something is made, formed, or given birth.
senses.example: The city became the matrix of a jazz movement that changed American music forever.

senses.definition: A table of data.
A two-dimensional array.
senses.example: She stored the sensor readings in a two-dimensional matrix before running the regression.

senses.definition: A grid-like arrangement of electronic components, especially one intended for information coding, decoding or storage.
senses.example: The memory chip uses a matrix of transistors to store each bit of data.

senses.definition: The sediment surrounding and including the artifacts, features, and other materials at a site.
senses.example: The archaeologists carefully brushed away the soil matrix surrounding the pottery shards.

senses.definition: The five simple colors (black, white, blue, red, and yellow) from which all the others are formed.
senses.example: Medieval alchemists believed that every color emerged from a basic matrix of five hues.

senses.definition: A binding agent of composite materials, e.g. resin in fibreglass.
senses.example: The fiberglass hull uses epoxy resin as the matrix that holds the glass strands together.

senses.definition: Matrix clause is a clause that has another (subordinate) clause embedded within it.
senses.example: In linguistics, a matrix clause contains an embedded subordinate clause, as in 'I think she left.'

senses.definition: The material or tissue in which more specialized structures are embedded.
senses.example: Bone marrow is the soft matrix in which blood-forming stem cells develop.

senses.definition: An extracellular matrix, the material or tissue between the cells of animals or plants.
senses.example: Fibroblasts secrete collagen to build the extracellular matrix between cells in connective tissue.

senses.definition: Part of the mitochondrion.
senses.example: Enzymes in the mitochondrial matrix drive the citric acid cycle that produces energy.

senses.definition: The medium in which bacteria are cultured.
senses.example: The lab streaked the sample onto agar, a nutrient matrix where the bacteria could grow.

senses.definition: A geological matrix.
senses.example: Geologists identified quartz crystals embedded in a fine-grained volcanic matrix.

senses.definition: The environment from which a given sample is taken.
senses.example: The soil matrix affects how contaminants are measured, so we calibrate for it.

senses.definition: (rare) The womb.
senses.example: Scripture describes the child as formed in the matrix of his mother's body.
senses.label: rare

senses.definition: (historical) In hot metal typesetting, a mold for casting a letter.
senses.label: historical

senses.definition: (historical) In printmaking, the plate or block used, with ink, to hold the image that makes up the print.
senses.label: historical

core.definition: A rectangular grid of numbers or symbols arranged in rows and columns, used to organize and calculate data or equations.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, MAY. Americans pronounce the final syllable as a quick 'iks,' not 'ix.' The plural is matrices, pronounced MAY-trih-seez.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical in mathematics and data science.
nuance.usage_note: In American technical work, matrix (plural matrices) is everyday vocabulary for data tables and linear algebra. Outside math, Americans use it for a structure or framework, as in 'a matrix of options.' In conversation, a 'matrix' also suggests the film franchise, so context matters.

distinctions.note: A table is a general term for data in rows and columns; a matrix is a mathematical object with operations such as multiplication and inversion.
A vector is a single row or column of numbers; a matrix is a full rectangular array of them.

examples.everyday: My kid's math homework has a matrix on it, and I had no idea what it meant.
examples.professional: The model stores each user's features in a sparse matrix, so we can scale training to millions of rows.
examples.analytical: A linear transformation can be represented by a matrix, which reveals its effect on vectors and its eigenvalues.

nuance.analogy: Like a spreadsheet with strict rules for how its rows and columns combine.
nuance.etymology: From Latin matrix, meaning womb, breeding female, or register; in the mathematical sense it was coined in the nineteenth century by Sylvester.
common_mistakes: Using the singular matrix for more than one grid; the plural is matrices.
Pronouncing the word as 'MAT-rix' with a short a; in General American it is MAY-triks.

matrix.etymology: From Middle English *matris*, *matrice*, *matrix*, from Old French *matrice* (“pregnant animal”), or from Latin *mātrīx* (“dam, womb”), both ultimately from *māter* (“mother”).

senses.definition: Generically, the arithmetic of matrices, involving matrix addition, scalar multiplication of matrices, matrix multiplication, and matrix inversion.
senses.example: In our machine learning course, we spent weeks on matrix algebra before touching regression.

senses.definition: A matrix ring over a commutative ring.
senses.example: Students in the abstract algebra seminar proved that the matrix algebra over a field is noncommutative.

core.definition: The branch of mathematics that uses matrices to organize data, represent linear systems, and perform operations like multiplication and inversion.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable of algebra, AL-, and let matrix keep a lighter secondary stress on MAY-. The x ends as a simple 'ks' sound, and the -bra ends in a reduced 'bruh'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise technical term with no positive or negative charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use matrix algebra most often in statistics, economics, engineering, and data science courses and papers. In casual conversation people usually say linear algebra or just algebra. Students and colleagues will expect you to say matrices, the plural, rather than matrixes in technical talk.

distinctions.note: Linear algebra is the broader field of vector spaces and linear maps, while matrix algebra focuses on computations and manipulations with matrices.
Matrix calculus studies differentiation of functions that take matrices as inputs or outputs, which is a different operation from matrix algebra.

examples.everyday: My nephew is taking matrix algebra this semester, and he says the homework is brutal.
examples.professional: We used matrix algebra to vectorize the regression so the model can train on the whole dataset at once.
examples.analytical: Matrix algebra gives the proof its structure, because it lets us treat transformations as objects that can be composed and inverted.

nuance.analogy: It is like a spreadsheet where you apply rules to whole columns and grids at once, instead of changing one cell at a time.
nuance.etymology: Matrix comes from Latin for 'womb' or 'breeding female', and algebra comes from Arabic al-jabr, 'the reunion of broken parts'.
common_mistakes: Assuming matrix multiplication is commutative; in general AB is not equal to BA.
Saying matrixes in technical contexts, when the usual plural is matrices.

senses.definition: Describes food so soft and rich it seems to dissolve as you eat it.

core.definition: Describes food so soft and rich that it seems to dissolve as you eat it.

pronunciation.tip: Stress MOUTH, the last content word. The 's' on 'melts' is voiceless, like 'ts', and 'in your' should be reduced to 'in yor' quickly.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It is an enthusiastic compliment about food.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say this phrase to recommend food, often at a dinner, party, or restaurant. A natural reply is 'Really? I have to try it.' It is casual and friendly, not suited to formal writing.

distinctions.note: Delicious is a general word for tasty food; melts in your mouth describes a particular soft, rich texture.
Juicy describes moisture; melts in your mouth describes softness and richness.

collocations: the brisket melts in your mouth
the frosting melts in your mouth
the pastry melts in your mouth
the fish melts in your mouth

examples.everyday: Try a bite of this brisket; it melts in your mouth.
examples.professional: The chef says the short rib melts in your mouth, so we should describe it that way on the menu.
examples.analytical: Food writers often use the phrase melts in your mouth to suggest a texture that is almost too soft to name.

nuance.analogy: Like butter on a warm plate, the food gives way almost as soon as it touches your tongue.
nuance.etymology: From melt (verb), in, your, mouth, a descriptive expression of texture.
common_mistakes: Saying 'melts on your mouth'; the correct preposition is 'in'.
Using it for something dry or firm, which contradicts the meaning.

conversation.text: This steak just melts in your mouth.
The chocolate melts in your mouth.

senses.definition: A US holiday on the last Monday of May honoring soldiers who died; the unofficial start of summer.

core.definition: A United States federal holiday on the last Monday of May that honors military members who died in service.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on MOR in the first word and on DAY in the second. The 'or' in 'Memorial' is a clear r-colored vowel, and the final 'al' is reduced to 'uhl'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: Americans see Memorial Day as a solemn remembrance of soldiers who died, and it is also the informal start of summer with barbecues and sales. Saying 'Happy Memorial Day' is common, but many people prefer 'Have a good Memorial Day' when speaking to someone who lost a family member in service. Do not confuse it with Veterans Day, which honors all veterans, living and dead.

distinctions.note: Veterans Day honors all people who served in the military, while Memorial Day specifically remembers those who died.
Armed Forces Day celebrates the current military in May, while Memorial Day is a solemn remembrance of the dead.

collocations: visit a cemetery on Memorial Day

examples.everyday: Are you doing anything for Memorial Day weekend, or just staying home with the grill?
examples.professional: Our office will be closed on Memorial Day, so please send any urgent requests before Friday afternoon.
examples.analytical: Memorial Day began as a day of decoration for the war dead, and its shift toward a summer holiday shows how public memory can change its meaning over time.

nuance.analogy: Memorial Day is like a family's yearly visit to a grandparent's grave, where the sadness and the picnic happen in the same afternoon.
nuance.etymology: Originally called Decoration Day, the holiday was renamed Memorial Day in the 1880s after the Civil War.
common_mistakes: Saying 'Memorial Day' with equal stress on each word.
Using it for Veterans Day, which is a separate holiday in November.

conversation.text: Memorial Day weekend is when the pools open around here.
We put flags on my grandpa's grave on Memorial Day.
Are you doing anything for Memorial Day?

core.definition: In the Bible, a high priest in Jerusalem during the Maccabean crisis who bought the office from the Seleucid king and was later executed.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on LAY, the third syllable. The middle vowels are reduced, so the name sounds like 'men-uh-LAY-us'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It names a historical figure, sometimes used negatively for a corrupt priest.
nuance.usage_note: Americans mostly meet this name in Bible study, Jewish history, or ancient history classes. It appears in the Apocrypha, which Catholic and Orthodox Bibles include in the Old Testament and Protestant Bibles usually do not. Americans would not normally use it in everyday talk.

distinctions.note: The Greek hero Menelaus, husband of Helen, is a different figure from the Jewish high priest of the same name.

examples.everyday: In my Bible study group we talked about Menelaus, the priest who bought his position in Jerusalem.
examples.professional: In the lecture on the Maccabean period, I discussed how Menelaus corrupted the high priesthood.
examples.analytical: The author of Second Maccabees portrays Menelaus as the chief agent of the crisis that drove Jerusalem into revolt.

nuance.analogy: Menelaus is like a man who bought a job he was never qualified to hold, and the cost of his choice fell on everyone else.
nuance.etymology: From Greek Menelaos, a personal name.
common_mistakes: Confusing the Jewish high priest with the Greek king of Sparta, husband of Helen.
Putting stress on the first syllable (MEN-uh-lay-us).
nuance.biblical_note: Menelaus appears in the books of the Maccabees (2 Maccabees) rather than in the main Hebrew Bible. His name is Greek, a Hellenized form of the high priest's Hebrew name, and it is not a Hebrew word itself. Key passages: 2 Maccabees 4:23-26 describes him outbidding his brother Jason for the high priesthood; 2 Maccabees 4:27-50 describes his conflicts with Jerusalem and his bribery of officials; 2 Maccabees 13:3-8 describes his execution at Beroea after he was accused of causing the trouble.

senses.definition: A rectangular region of a graphical user interface where computer menus are housed.
senses.example: Click the File option in the menu bar at the top of the window.

core.definition: The horizontal strip at the top of a computer program's window that holds menu titles such as File, Edit and View.

pronunciation.tip: In this compound, the stress falls on 'MEN' in 'menu,' not on 'bar,' as with many noun compounds. 'Menu' is pronounced 'MEN-yoo,' with a short e and a 'yoo' ending, not 'men-oo.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a practical, technical term with no emotional tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'menu bar' on both Windows and Mac, though Mac users often talk about it as the strip across the top of the screen. Do not confuse it with the three-line 'hamburger menu' icon in many apps, which Americans may just call the menu. In everyday tech talk, someone might say 'Go up to the menu bar and click File.'

distinctions.note: A toolbar usually holds icon buttons for quick actions, while the menu bar holds text labels that open dropdown lists of commands.
The taskbar, usually at the bottom of the screen, shows open programs and the Start button, while the menu bar sits at the top of an application window or the top of the screen on Mac.

examples.everyday: My mom can never find the Print option, so I tell her to look up in the menu bar and click File first.
examples.professional: Export the report from the File item in the menu bar rather than from the toolbar, so the settings are saved correctly.
examples.analytical: The menu bar concentrates commands in one predictable location, which reduces the cognitive effort needed to discover what a program can do.

nuance.analogy: A menu bar is like the directory board by the entrance of a store: categories are listed in one fixed place so you can scan them before choosing.
nuance.etymology: Menu comes from French menu, meaning a detailed list; bar means a long, narrow strip.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing 'menu' as 'men-oo' or stressing the second word of the compound.
Calling the menu bar 'the menu' in technical conversation, which can be confused with a restaurant menu or the hamburger icon.

senses.definition: A person who studies methodology, or applies its principles.

core.definition: A person who studies research methods or applies methodology, especially in science or the social sciences.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on LAH, the fourth syllable. Do not pronounce the final -ist as 'ee-st'; it is a short 'ist' with a clear s.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It names a specialist role and implies expertise.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word mainly in academic, government and research settings, as in 'she is a methodologist at the Census Bureau'. In casual conversation people usually say 'a statistician' or 'a researcher'. The word specifically names someone who designs studies and decides how research should be run.

distinctions.note: A statistician works mainly with numbers and models; a methodologist also decides how a study is designed, including non-statistical choices.
A Methodist is a member of the Methodist church, stressed on METH; the words are unrelated in meaning and differ in stress.

examples.everyday: My sister is a methodologist at the Census Bureau, so she spends her days deciding how surveys should be run.
examples.professional: Please loop in our methodologist before we change the sampling plan for the Q3 experiment.
examples.analytical: A good methodologist asks what question a method can answer before asking which method to use.

nuance.analogy: A methodologist is to a research team what an architect is to a builder: the person who designs the plan before construction begins.
nuance.etymology: From methodology, from Greek methodos, 'way of inquiry', plus the suffix -ist, 'one who practices'.
common_mistakes: Confusing it with 'Methodist', which is a church member and is pronounced with the stress on METH
Using it for anyone who likes organized work; it names a specialist in research design
Putting the stress on the first syllable instead of LAH

senses.definition: A center, midpoint.
senses.example: The middle of a circle is the point which has the same distance to every point of circle.

senses.definition: The part between the beginning and the end.
senses.example: I woke up in the middle of the night.

senses.definition: The central part of a human body; the waist.
senses.example: She wrapped the scarf around her middle to block the cold wind.

senses.definition: The middle voice.
senses.example: In Greek grammar, the verb takes the middle voice when the subject acts on itself.

senses.definition: The center of the political spectrum.
senses.example: As part of his successful re-election strategy, Clinton began governing from the middle.

senses.definition: An essay on social or literary issues in a newspaper or magazine, originally placed between the leading articles and the reviews.
senses.example: Her middle in the Sunday paper argued that libraries deserve more funding.

senses.definition: The middle stump.
senses.example: The bowler's yorker sailed straight into middle and the bails fell off.

senses.definition: Located in the middle; in between.
senses.example: the middle point

senses.definition: Central.
senses.example: I took the middle seat on the flight, which was the least comfortable.

senses.definition: Pertaining to the middle voice.
senses.example: The middle form of the verb signals that the action affects the subject.

senses.definition: To strike (the ball) with the middle portion of the face of the bat.
senses.example: He middled the pitch cleanly, sending the ball over the infield for a double.

core.definition: The point or part halfway between the beginning and the end, or between two sides of something.

pronunciation.tip: It has two syllables, not three. The final -dle is a syllabic l, so there is no full vowel before it.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a basic word with no emotional tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'in the middle of' for both places and periods of time, as in 'in the middle of the night'. 'The middle' is used in everyday speech for physical centers and for the stage between start and finish. Americans also use it for waist in casual talk, though 'waist' is more precise.

distinctions.note: Center suggests the exact central point of a space or circle, while middle is looser and can refer to a time period or a stage.
Midpoint is a precise technical term used in mathematics and measurement, while middle is everyday language.

examples.everyday: Sorry I'm late, I got stuck in the middle of traffic on the bridge.
examples.professional: Let's put the budget decision in the middle of the agenda so we have time to discuss it properly.
examples.analytical: The middle of Augustine's argument reveals a deep tension between divine will and human freedom.

nuance.analogy: The middle is the spine of a book: it holds the story together between the opening and the ending.
nuance.etymology: From Old English middel, related to mid, meaning in the midst or halfway.
common_mistakes: Saying 'at the middle of the night' instead of 'in the middle of the night'.
Pronouncing it with three full syllables, as MID-dull-uh, instead of MID-uhl.

middle.etymology: From Middle English *myddel*, *middel*, from Old English *middel* (“middle, centre, waist”), from Proto-Germanic **midlą*, **midilą*, **medalą* (“middle”), a diminutive of Proto-Germanic **midjō* (“middle, midst”) (compare **midjaz* (“mid, middle”)), from…

senses.definition: A neurological condition characterized by such headaches.
senses.example: Her migraines often start with visual flashes before the pain begins.

senses.definition: A severe, disabling headache, usually affecting only one side of the head, and often accompanied by nausea, vomiting, photophobia and visual disturbances.
senses.example: He had a headache so bad that he wished he was dead, but it was the sort of migraine that promised him he would continue to suffer but not die.

core.definition: A severe, throbbing headache, often on one side of the head, with nausea or sensitivity to light.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on MY, and the word has two syllables. The final syllable rhymes with 'gain,' so avoid a schwa or a third syllable like 'MY-gruh-ayn.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral in medical contexts. The word sounds serious, and the experience is clearly unpleasant.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'I have a migraine' or 'I'm getting a migraine,' and use 'bad headache' more loosely. Migraine names a specific medical condition, so do not use it for every headache. A typical response is 'Oh no, I hope you feel better soon.'

distinctions.note: A headache is any pain in the head, while a migraine is a specific, severe kind with other symptoms.
A tension headache is usually dull and band-like, while a migraine is usually throbbing and often comes with nausea or light sensitivity.

examples.everyday: I had to lie down in a dark room because a migraine hit me after lunch.
examples.professional: I'm working from home today because I have a migraine and can't look at screens.
examples.analytical: Clinical literature treats migraine as a neurological disorder, not simply as a severe headache.

nuance.analogy: A migraine is like a storm inside the head that builds, peaks, and then passes.
nuance.etymology: From Greek hēmikrania, meaning 'half of the skull,' through Old French and Latin.
common_mistakes: Saying 'MY-grain' with a short a; the vowel is the long a of 'gray.'
Using 'migraine' for any headache, when it refers to a specific and more severe condition.

conversation.text: She gets migraines when she doesn't sleep enough.
I had a migraine, so I worked in a dark room all afternoon.
Bright lights make my migraine worse.

senses.definition: How far a car goes on one gallon of gas (MPG); the US measure of fuel economy.

core.definition: A measure of how far a car travels on one gallon of gasoline; the standard US fuel-economy rating, often shortened to MPG.

pronunciation.tip: Stress MILES and GAL. The word 'per' is unstressed and reduced to a quick 'per' or 'pur' sound, and 'gallon' is GAL-un, not GAL-ohn. The -s in 'miles' is a z sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral, used in technical and everyday talk about car efficiency.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say miles per gallon in conversation and in car advertising, often abbreviated as MPG, as in 'What's the MPG on that hybrid?' People also say 'gas mileage' informally. Europeans and others use liters per 100 kilometers instead, so the American system is a common point of confusion abroad.

distinctions.note: Gas mileage is the informal everyday phrase; miles per gallon is the precise measure or label.
Mileage is total distance traveled; miles per gallon is a rate of efficiency.

examples.everyday: This compact car gets forty miles per gallon on the highway, which is great for our commute.
examples.professional: The new engine improves combined miles per gallon by about twelve percent over last year's model.
examples.analytical: Miles per gallon is a rate, so it rewards efficiency per unit of fuel rather than total distance, which can mislead comparisons across different driving conditions.

nuance.analogy: Miles per gallon is like a grocery price per ounce: it tells you how much you get for each unit you pay for.
nuance.etymology: Miles from Old English mīl; gallon from Anglo-Norman galon; the phrase is a descriptive compound.
common_mistakes: Saying 'gallon' with a long o, as in 'GAL-ohn'.
Putting the stress evenly on every word instead of on MILES and GAL.

conversation.text: This hybrid gets about fifty miles per gallon on the highway.
"How many miles per gallon does it get?" "Around thirty in the city."
Our old truck only gets fifteen miles per gallon, so road trips are pricey.

senses.definition: Behavior that is considered to be unacceptable.
senses.example: The student was banned from using the university's computing resources for two weeks due to gross misconduct on the Internet.

senses.definition: A penalty or write-up for improper behavior.
To mismanage.
senses.example: The former treasurer misconducted the club's funds for years before anyone noticed.

senses.definition: To behave inappropriately, to misbehave.
senses.example: The boys misconducted themselves during the field trip and lost their privileges.

senses.definition: (rare) To act improperly.
senses.example: The judge warned that any lawyer who misconducted the trial would be sanctioned.
senses.label: rare

core.definition: Improper or unacceptable behavior, especially by someone in a position of trust or authority.

pronunciation.tip: The noun stresses the first syllable, MIS, and the verb shifts to the second syllable, mis-kun-DUKT. Non-native speakers often stress the verb form on the first syllable, so keep the stress shift in mind.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it implies a violation of rules, ethics, or duty.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use misconduct in professional, legal, and academic contexts, such as 'professional misconduct' or 'a misconduct hearing.' It is serious and formal, so avoid using it for minor manners. For a child or casual situation, misbehavior is more natural.

distinctions.note: Misbehavior is milder and everyday; misconduct is more formal and often involves rules, duty, or ethics.
Malpractice is specific to professional negligence, especially in medicine or law; misconduct is broader.

examples.everyday: The coach was suspended for misconduct after the game, so the team had to find a new one.
examples.professional: HR opened an investigation into possible misconduct by a senior manager.
examples.analytical: The article argues that scientific misconduct undermines public trust in research findings.

nuance.analogy: Like a referee who takes bribes: the role demands fairness, and the wrong behavior breaks the trust the role depends on.
nuance.etymology: From mis- (wrong) plus conduct, from Latin conductus (led together, managed).
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable in the noun, as in mis-KON-duct.
Using misconduct for minor rudeness, which is usually too strong.

senses.definition: The issue in a writ of right.
Contraction of might as well.
senses.example: Since the bus is gone anyway, mise grab a coffee and wait here.

senses.definition: To make a risky move with no regard for the consequences when the alternative is certain defeat.
senses.example: Down three points with a minute left, he decided to mise and shoot from half court.

core.definition: In English legal history, the issue joined in a writ of right, a rare old property term; rarely used today.

pronunciation.tip: Pronounce it as one syllable that rhymes with 'peas'. It is a long vowel with a voiced final z sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a specialized legal term with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans almost never use mise in everyday speech. It appears mainly in legal history, old law books, or discussions of medieval property disputes. The dictionary's verb sense, 'might as well' or a risky move, is informal and regional at best, so most Americans would say 'might as well' or 'go for it' instead.

distinctions.note: Issue is the everyday word for a point in dispute or a problem. Mise is a specialized legal term for a formal point joined in an old court procedure.
A writ is the formal court order that starts a case. Mise is the issue that arises from that writ.

collocations: the mise in a writ of right

examples.everyday: Most people have never heard the word mise, so I had to look it up in my law book.
examples.professional: The legal historian explained that the mise was the point the parties had to settle in that property case.
examples.analytical: The medieval pleading narrows the dispute to a single mise, which shapes the entire procedure of the writ of right.

nuance.analogy: A mise is like the single question a judge must answer before the rest of a case can move forward.
nuance.etymology: From Anglo-French mise, 'putting, placing', from mettre 'to put'.
common_mistakes: Using mise as a modern everyday word; it is almost entirely historical or legal.
Mixing it up with mess or mice in speech; the vowel is a long ee.

mise.etymology: Borrowed from French *mise* (“a putting, setting, expense”).

senses.definition: One who leads into error.

core.definition: A person who leads others into error or wrong beliefs, often by poor or deceptive guidance.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, 'MIS.' The 'lead' is pronounced like 'leed,' and the final 'er' is a reduced, r-colored vowel.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it describes someone who leads others astray, sometimes deliberately.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use misleader in everyday talk. It appears mainly in formal essays, sermons, political commentary and literary prose. In everyday speech, people say 'someone who misled you' or 'a bad guide.'

distinctions.note: A deceiver intentionally tricks people, while a misleader may lead people astray through error or poor guidance.
A demagogue manipulates public emotion for political gain, while a misleader may be any guide who leads people wrongly.
A leader guides people toward a goal; a misleader guides them wrongly.

examples.professional: One misleader in the planning meetings kept pushing estimates that no one had checked.
examples.analytical: Historians describe the demagogue as a misleader who wins trust by flattering public fears.

nuance.analogy: Like a trail guide who confidently walks the group off a cliff while claiming to know the way.
nuance.etymology: From mis- (wrongly) and leader, from Old English lædere (one who leads).
common_mistakes: Pronouncing 'lead' like the metal 'lead' (led); here it sounds like 'leed.'
Confusing misleader with 'misleading,' which is an adjective.

senses.definition: Bad placement.
senses.example: His misplacement of his foot sprained his ankle.

core.definition: The act or result of putting something in the wrong place.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on PLACE. The final -ment is a reduced syllable with a weak vowel, closer to 'muhnt' than to 'mint'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative; it names an error in placement.
nuance.usage_note: In everyday speech Americans usually say the wrong place or misplaced. Misplacement appears mainly in technical, medical, financial, and business writing, such as a misplacement of a decimal point or a misplacement of a catheter.

distinctions.note: Misplacing is the everyday verb form for losing track of something; misplacement is the noun, usually for an error of placement.
Placement is the neutral act of putting something somewhere; misplacement adds the sense of a mistake.

examples.everyday: The package ended up at the wrong house, which was just a misplacement by the driver.
examples.professional: The audit found a misplacement of funds across two accounts, and we need to correct it before the quarter closes.
examples.analytical: A misplacement of the modifier can change the entire meaning of a sentence.

nuance.analogy: Like a label stuck on the wrong jar: everything inside is fine, but the contents are misidentified.
nuance.etymology: From misplace plus the suffix -ment, which forms nouns of action or result.
common_mistakes: Using misplacement to mean a lost item; for lost things, use the verb misplace.
Putting the stress on mis- instead of PLACE.

senses.definition: Erroneous.
senses.example: A mistaken sense of loyalty.

senses.definition: Having an incorrect belief.
senses.example: I think you must be (very) much mistaken.

core.definition: Wrong about a fact, belief or identity; holding an incorrect belief, often sincerely.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, STAYK. The final -en is a syllabic n with no full vowel, so it sounds like 'un'. Don't pronounce it as 'taken'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to mildly negative; it is softer than 'wrong' and often used politely.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'mistaken' for someone who holds an incorrect belief, often politely, as in 'I think you're mistaken.' Tone matters: said coldly, it can sound dismissive. 'Mistaken identity' is common in news and movies. A natural reply is 'Maybe I'm mistaken; let me check.'

distinctions.note: Wrong is blunter and more common, while mistaken is softer and often suggests a sincere but incorrect belief.
Incorrect is neutral and often used for facts or answers, while mistaken is often used for beliefs or identities.
Misguided suggests bad judgment or poor direction, while mistaken concerns being wrong about facts.

examples.everyday: I think you're mistaken; that was the Johnsons' house, not ours.
examples.professional: The team had a mistaken assumption about user demand, so we tested the wrong feature first.
examples.analytical: A mistaken belief held in good faith is a different moral case from a deliberate lie, a distinction many ethicists stress.

nuance.analogy: A mistaken belief is like an old map: you trust it, and it sends you the wrong way.
nuance.etymology: Past participle of mistake, from Old Norse mistaka.
common_mistakes: Using 'mistaken' for a task error; it usually refers to a belief or identity, so 'I made a mistake' is better for errors in work.
Pronouncing the final syllable as a full 'taken' rather than a weak 'un'.

senses.definition: Pertaining to a current or recent time and style; not ancient.
senses.example: Our online interactive game is a modern approach to teaching about gum disease. Although it was built in the 1600s, the building still has a very modern look.

senses.definition: Pertaining to the modern period (c.1800 to contemporary times), particularly in academic historiography.
senses.example: Modern historians often question the traditional story of the Reformation's origins.

senses.definition: Someone who lives in modern times.
senses.example: Many moderns find the quiet rhythm of old hymns surprisingly comforting.

core.definition: Belonging to the present time or recent times, with current styles, technology or ideas; not ancient or old-fashioned.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, MAH, with an open 'ah' vowel, and the second syllable is a weak, r-colored schwa. Do not say MOH-dern, which is a common mistake from speakers whose vowels differ.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral. It suggests up to date and current, though a modern style can be seen as cold in some contexts.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use modern for buildings, technology, kitchens and lifestyles, usually to mean up to date. In art and design, contemporary is often used for current work, while modern refers to a specific historical movement. In historical writing, modern can mean the period after about 1500.

distinctions.note: Contemporary means existing at the same time as us, while modern can refer to a broader present or a historical style.
New means recently made or recently appeared, while modern describes current style or design, which may not be new at all.

examples.everyday: Our apartment has a modern kitchen, but the bathroom still looks like it's from 1985.
examples.professional: The modern approach is to version our models in a registry instead of saving files by hand.
examples.analytical: Many historians date the modern period from around 1500, when printing and overseas exploration transformed European thought.

nuance.analogy: Modern is the current model year of a car: newer than the classic, but not necessarily brand-new.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin modernus, from Latin modo 'just now', from modus 'measure'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it MOH-dern instead of MAH-durn
Using modern for things that are merely new, when old-fashioned is the opposite of the intended meaning

modern.etymology: From Middle French *moderne*, from Late Latin *modernus*; from Latin *modo* (“just now”), originally ablative of *modus* (“measure”); hence, by measure, "just now".

senses.definition: The quality of being modern or contemporary.
senses.example: He was impressed by the architecture's modernity.

senses.definition: Modern times.
senses.example: The organization survived from ancient times to modernity.

senses.definition: Quality of being of the modern period of contemporary historiography.

core.definition: The quality of being modern, or the condition of living in modern times, especially the social and technological changes since about the 1700s.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, -DUR. Pronounce the r clearly and reduce the first syllable to a soft uh. The final -ity is pronounced ih-tee.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in scholarly use; in everyday speech it can sound pretentious if used for ordinary newness.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use modernity mostly in history, philosophy, sociology, and literary criticism, often in phrases like the rise of modernity. In ordinary conversation they usually say modern times or the modern world. Using it in casual talk can sound stiff.

distinctions.note: Modernity is the condition or period of being modern; modernism is a movement or set of ideas that responded to it.
Modernization is the process of making something modern; modernity is the state or condition that results.

examples.everyday: My grandfather still misses the old days, but he admits that modern times have made some things easier, like video calls with the grandkids.
examples.professional: The engineering team is struggling to balance the modernity of cloud tools with the older systems our customers still depend on.
examples.analytical: Max Weber argued that modernity is marked by rationalization, the growing dominance of calculation and bureaucratic order over tradition and charisma.

nuance.analogy: Modernity is like the weather of a particular era: you live inside it so fully that you only notice it when you step outside into the past.
nuance.etymology: From modern plus the suffix -ity, from Latin modernitas, from modernus, from modo meaning just now.
common_mistakes: Using modernity for a new product, as in this phone has modernity; say modern or up to date.
Mispronouncing the first syllable as MOD-er-ni-ty or stressing the wrong syllable.

senses.definition: Forms the superlative of many adjectives.
senses.example: This is the most important example.

senses.definition: With a superlative adjective ending in -est.
senses.example: the most tallest building in the world

senses.definition: To a great extent or degree; highly; very.
senses.example: This is a most unusual specimen.

senses.definition: Clipping of almost.
senses.example: It's most done, so I'll send you the report after lunch.

senses.definition: The greater part of a group, especially a group of people.
senses.example: Most want the best for their children.

senses.definition: The greatest amount.
senses.example: The most I can offer for the house is $150,000.

senses.definition: The greater part.
senses.example: Most of the penguins were friendly and curious.

senses.definition: A record-setting amount.
senses.example: Her team's bug fixes reached a most this quarter, setting a new company record.

senses.definition: (dated) The greatest; the best.
senses.example: My grandmother always said Pastor Ellis was the most good man in town.
senses.label: dated

core.definition: The majority of a group or amount; more than half of the people or things being discussed.

pronunciation.tip: As a determiner or pronoun, 'most' is a single syllable with little stress, so it is said quickly. Keep the final 'st' cluster clean and do not add a vowel between 's' and 't'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It simply states a majority, and it is used in every kind of speech and writing.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use most constantly in everyday talk, as in 'most people' or 'most of them'. In writing and speech, the phrase 'most of' is followed by a determiner like 'the', 'my' or 'them', while 'most people' needs no 'the' for general statements. Many Americans say 'most everyone' informally, but 'almost everyone' is the standard form in careful writing.

distinctions.note: Majority is a noun used in formal or statistical contexts and strictly means more than half, while most is a flexible everyday word.
Almost means nearly all, which is different from most, so 'almost everyone' and 'most people' are not always interchangeable.
Mostly is an adverb meaning mainly, while most is a determiner or pronoun naming a larger part of a group.

examples.everyday: Most of my friends drink coffee in the morning, but I stick with tea.
examples.professional: Most of the bugs were caught in staging, which saved us from a rollback last week.
examples.analytical: Most of the variance in the model's error is explained by two features, which suggests the rest is noise.

nuance.analogy: Like a pizza cut into slices: most is the bigger share of the whole pie.
nuance.etymology: From Old English māst or mǣst, the superlative of mā, 'more'.
common_mistakes: Saying 'most of the people' with a general meaning, when 'most people' is more natural.
Using 'most' as an adverb to mean 'almost' in careful writing; 'almost' is the standard form.

most.etymology: From Middle English *most*, *moste*, from Old English *mǣst*, *māst*, from Proto-Germanic **maistaz*, **maist*.

senses.definition: Resembling or characteristic of a moth.
senses.example: The porch light drew a mothy cloud of pale insects that kept bumping against the screen.

senses.definition: Infested with moths.
Moth-eaten.
senses.example: Grandma's old cardigan was so mothy that the sleeves had holes everywhere.

core.definition: Infested with moths, or worn and shabby as if damaged by moths. It usually describes old fabric, clothes, or stored objects.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, MAH-thee. The th is voiced, as in 'the', and the final -y is a short 'ee' sound.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It suggests neglect, age, and decay, usually of fabric or stored possessions.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use this word in everyday speech and mostly use 'moth-eaten' instead. You may see 'mothy' in descriptive writing about closets, attics, or old wool. It is a descriptive adjective, so it is not used for people.

distinctions.note: Moth-eaten is the far more common term, and it can be literal or figurative; mothy is rarer and more descriptive.
Moth-like means resembling a moth in shape or movement, not infested or worn.

examples.professional: The archive boxes were mothy and need to be moved to climate-controlled storage.
examples.analytical: The essay describes the museum's mothy textile collection as a physical record of years of neglect.

nuance.analogy: Like a sweater with small holes you only notice after you lift it up.
nuance.etymology: From 'moth' with the suffix '-y', meaning characterized by or full of.
common_mistakes: Using mothy for people; it describes objects and fabric, not personality.
Pronouncing 'moth' with a long o; the vowel is short and open, as in 'cot'.
nuance.biblical_note: The Greek word is sēs (σής), meaning moth. Matthew 6:19-20 warns against storing up treasure on earth, where moth and rust destroy. James 5:2 says riches have rotted and garments have become moth-eaten, a sign of wasted wealth.

senses.definition: Describing an argumentative tactic in which someone advances a bold, hard-to-defend claim (the bailey) but, when challenged, retreats to a modest, easily defended claim (the motte), then returns to the bold claim later.
A type of medieval castle with a fortified mound (motte) and an enclosed courtyard (bailey).

core.definition: Describing an argument that swaps a bold claim for a modest, defensible one when challenged, then returns to the bold claim once the challenge passes.

pronunciation.tip: Motte sounds like 'mott' (rhymes with 'hot'); 'and' shrinks to 'un'. The main stress lands on BAY.

nuance.connotation: Negative when applied to an argument: it implies a subtle bait-and-switch.
nuance.usage_note: The term spread through online rationalist writing, especially Scott Alexander's blog, and is now used in tech, academic and debate circles. It is usually a noun modifier: 'a motte-and-bailey argument' or 'that's a motte and bailey.' Many Americans outside those circles won't know it, so explain it briefly.

distinctions.note: Equivocation shifts the meaning of one word within an argument; motte-and-bailey shifts between two whole claims of different strength.
Moving the goalposts changes the standard of proof demanded of an opponent; motte-and-bailey changes what the speaker is claiming.
A strawman distorts the opponent's claim; motte-and-bailey disguises the speaker's own.

examples.everyday: First he said all diets are scams, then he said 'I just mean some diets are overhyped.' That's a motte-and-bailey move.
examples.professional: The vendor's pitch was a motte-and-bailey: 'our AI replaces analysts' in the deck, 'it assists analysts' when we pushed back.
examples.analytical: Shackel's motte-and-bailey doctrine describes how a theorist can enjoy the excitement of a radical thesis while defending only a trivial one.

nuance.analogy: Like the castle: you live in the pleasant courtyard (the bold claim), and when attacked you run up the tower (the safe claim) until the attackers leave.
nuance.etymology: From Old French motte 'mound' and bailey, from Old French baile 'enclosure'.
common_mistakes: Mixing up which part is which: the motte is the safe, defensible claim; the bailey is the bold, desirable one.

motte-and-bailey.etymology: From the medieval motte-and-bailey castle; the argumentative sense was introduced by the philosopher Nicholas Shackel in 2005.

senses.definition: A person who climbs mountains for sport or pleasure.
A bird of the genus Oreonympha; also called the bearded mountaineer or eastern mountaineer.
senses.example: The eastern mountaineer is a rare hummingbird, found only in the Andean cloud forests.

senses.definition: (rare) A person who lives in a mountainous area (often with the connotation that such people are outlaws or uncivilized).
senses.example: The valley townsfolk called the mountaineers outlaws and refused to trade with them.
senses.label: rare

senses.definition: To climb mountains; to climb using the techniques of a mountaineer.
senses.example: My brother mountaineers every summer, climbing peaks across Colorado and Wyoming.

senses.definition: To climb as if on a mountain.
senses.example: The window washer mountaineered up the glass tower, clinging to ropes and steel brackets.

core.definition: A person who climbs mountains for sport, adventure or professional work, often with specialized training and equipment.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on the last syllable, NEER. Keep the first syllable light and rhotic, and do not add an extra syllable between mountain and -eer.

nuance.connotation: Positive: a mountaineer is seen as skilled, brave and disciplined.
nuance.usage_note: In everyday American English, mountaineer usually means a serious climber who uses ropes and technical gear, while hiker means someone walking on trails. Mountaineer can also appear in regional history, as in people who lived in the Appalachian mountains. Americans rarely use it for animals or plants in ordinary speech.

distinctions.note: A hiker walks on established trails, while a mountaineer climbs steep, technical terrain that may need ropes and ice tools.
Climber is a broader word that may refer to rock climbers or indoor climbers, while mountaineer specifically refers to mountain climbing.

examples.everyday: My brother is a serious mountaineer, so he spends most summers climbing in Colorado and Wyoming.
examples.professional: Our safety team asked the mountaineer to confirm the route before the guided expedition began.
examples.analytical: The mountaineer's ethic of risk and restraint has been read as a model of moral seriousness in some recent philosophical writing.

nuance.analogy: A mountaineer is like a careful chess player on a rock face, planning each move before committing to the next.
nuance.etymology: From mountain, with the suffix -eer meaning a person connected with something.
common_mistakes: Using mountaineer for any hiker who walks on a trail.
Stressing the first syllable as in MOUN-tih-neer, when the strongest stress is on the last syllable.

senses.definition: A soldier or a subordinate civil officer who executes orders of a superior without protest or pity (sometimes applied to bailiffs, constables, etc).
senses.example: The governor's myrmidons seized the protesters and carried out the eviction without hesitation.

core.definition: A loyal, unquestioning follower who carries out a superior's orders, often harshly and without conscience.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, 'MUR'. The last syllable rhymes with 'con' (dahn), not 'den', and the middle syllable is a short, weak 'ih'.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it suggests blind obedience and a lack of moral judgment.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word mainly in literature, history and political commentary, drawing on Homer's Iliad. In everyday speech they would use 'henchman', 'goon' or 'yes-man'. It is a precise word for someone who carries out harsh orders without question.

distinctions.note: Henchman is more common and often suggests a criminal boss's aide; myrmidon stresses mindless obedience.
Minion is lighter and sometimes comic; myrmidon is harsher.
Lackey suggests servility; myrmidon suggests carrying out brutal orders.

examples.everyday: Don't be his myrmidon; say no if he asks you to lie for him.
examples.professional: The vice president relies on a few myrmidons who never push back on his decisions.
examples.analytical: The novel portrays the regime's myrmidons as men who traded conscience for obedience.

nuance.analogy: A myrmidon is like an ant following the colony's chemical trail without asking where it leads.
nuance.etymology: From Greek Myrmidones, the warriors who followed Achilles in Homer's Iliad; the name was later linked to myrmex, 'ant'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the middle syllable as 'mur-MID-un'; the stress falls on the first syllable.
Using it for any soldier or helper; it implies unquestioning and often harsh obedience.

myrmidon.etymology: From *Myrmidon*, from Latin *Myrmidones*, from Ancient Greek *Μυρμιδόνες*.

senses.definition: To identify specific people, especially people involved in misdeeds or other secretive activity.

core.definition: To publicly identify other people as guilty of a crime or wrongdoing, often to win leniency for oneself.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second word, NAMES, so the first word is lighter. The final z of names is voiced, and the two words link smoothly, so say it as one flowing phrase.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It suggests betraying associates, although people may be forced to do it under legal pressure.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this phrase for informing on accomplices to police or prosecutors, and for witnesses in famous congressional hearings and mob trials. In casual talk, people more often say 'rat someone out' or 'snitch.' A natural exchange: 'Did he name names?' 'No, he refused to.'

distinctions.note: To inform on someone is to report their actions to authorities, while to name names is to list others, often under pressure during an investigation.
Snitch is informal and insulting and can describe any small tattling. Name names sounds more formal and is typical in news and legal settings.

collocations: name names to the grand jury
name names in exchange for leniency

examples.everyday: The cops offered him a deal if he'd name names, but he wouldn't do it.
examples.professional: Our compliance lead warned that if the audit finds fraud, some employees may be asked to name names.
