examples.analytical: Historians still debate whether those who named names during the hearings were protecting their families or betraying their colleagues.

nuance.analogy: Like pointing at the whole crowd instead of the one person who broke the window.
nuance.etymology: Name from Old English nama, 'name'; the phrase is an idiom from legal and political settings.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'name names' (identify wrongdoers) with 'call someone names' (insult them).
Using 'name names' for simply listing people; it always implies accusation or disclosure.

senses.definition: Able to be traversed; navigable.
senses.example: After the spring floods, the old logging road was barely negotiable for our pickup truck.

senses.definition: Able to be transferred to another person, with or without endorsement, in exchange for money.
senses.example: The bank promised that the cashier's check was negotiable as soon as we endorsed it.

senses.definition: Open to negotiation or bargaining.
senses.example: Salary is negotiable, according to education and experience.

senses.definition: Something that is open to negotiation.
senses.example: Our salary is listed as a range, but the bonus and vacation days are negotiable.

core.definition: Open to discussion, so the terms, price, or details can be changed through bargaining.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, 'GOH.' The 'sh' sound is in the middle, and the final syllables reduce to 'uh-bul.'

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral, suggesting flexibility and willingness to compromise.
nuance.usage_note: Americans often say a price or salary is negotiable in shopping, job offers, and real estate. It is a friendly way to signal you are open to a deal. The word 'negotiable' is also used in finance for instruments that can be transferred, but in everyday talk it means open to bargaining.

distinctions.note: Flexible describes a person or plan that adapts easily, while negotiable specifically means terms can be bargained over.
Non-negotiable means the terms are fixed and will not be changed, which is the opposite of negotiable.

examples.everyday: The used bike was listed at two hundred dollars, but the seller said the price was negotiable.
examples.professional: The start date is negotiable, but the salary band is not, so let's discuss flexibility on the schedule.
examples.analytical: Whether a moral claim is negotiable depends on whether it rests on a principle that the parties accept as binding.

nuance.analogy: A negotiable price is like a rubber band: it stretches when both sides pull, but it has a limit.
nuance.etymology: From Latin negotiari, 'to carry on business,' from negotium, 'business.'
common_mistakes: Saying 'the price is negociable' with a spelling or pronunciation error; the stress is on 'GOH.'
Using it for a person; say 'open to negotiation' rather than 'he is negotiable' in formal settings.

senses.definition: Any plant whose foliage is covered with stinging, mildly poisonous hairs, causing an instant rash.
senses.example: Wear long sleeves when hiking, because the trail is lined with nettle that stings bare skin.

senses.definition: Especially, most species of herb genus Urtica, stinging nettles:
senses.example: Stinging nettles grew thick along the creek, so we crossed the field instead.

senses.definition: Most, but not all, subspecies of Urtica dioica (common nettle),
senses.example: The common nettle is an ingredient in some spring soups, after its sting is cooked away.

senses.definition: Urtica incisa (Australian nettle);
senses.example: Hikers in Queensland were warned about the Australian nettle, whose sting can last for days.

senses.definition: Wood nettle (Laportea canadensis);
senses.example: A patch of wood nettle grew in the shaded ravine behind our cabin in the Appalachians.

senses.definition: Bull nettles and spurge nettles (Cnidoscolus spp.):
senses.example: Ranchers in West Texas often complain about bull nettles and spurge nettles spreading across their pastures.

senses.definition: Bull nettle, spurge nettle (Cnidoscolus stimulosus)
senses.example: The field guide warned that spurge nettle has prickly stems that sting when touched.

senses.definition: Texas bull nettle (Cnidoscolus texanus),
senses.example: Texas bull nettle covered the abandoned lot, its pale spines catching on our jeans.

senses.definition: Bull nettle (Cnidoscolus urens),
senses.example: The botanist pressed a sample of bull nettle, noting its dense, needle-like stinging hairs.

senses.definition: Nettle trees or tree nettles:
senses.example: Nettle trees in the rainforest towered above us, their leaves carrying a painful stinging fuzz.

senses.definition: Various species of the genus Dendrocnide:
senses.example: The Dendrocnide nettle, a tree of Southeast Asian forests, has a sting lasting weeks.

senses.definition: Small-leaved nettle (Dendrocnide photinophylla).
senses.example: The small-leaved nettle along the rainforest trail stung my arm through my shirt.

senses.definition: Scratchbush (Urera baccifera)
senses.example: Scratchbush is a nettle with berries, and its leaves sting anyone who brushes against them.

senses.definition: Tree nettle (Urtica ferox);
senses.example: The tree nettle of New Zealand, Urtica ferox, is among the most painful plants in the world.

senses.definition: Rock nettles (Eucnide spp.);
senses.example: Rock nettles grow on the cliffs above the gorge, where few hikers dare to climb.

senses.definition: Certain plants that have spines or prickles:
senses.example: Our guide pointed out a nettle with spines along its stem, warning us not to touch it.

senses.definition: Ball nettle (Solanum carolinense);
Bull nettle, silver-leaf nettle, white horse-nettle (Solanum elaeagnifolium);
Western horse-nettle, robust horse-nettle (Solanum dimidiatum);
Horse-nettle (Solanum rostratum);
Hackberries (Celtis spp.).
Certain non-stinging plants, mostly in the family Lamiaceae, that resemble the species of Urtica:
Dead nettles, dumb nettles (Lamium spp.), particularly Lamium album, white nettle;
False nettles (Boehmeria spp. family Urticaceae);
Flame nettles or painted nettles (Coleus spp.);
Hedge nettles (Stachys spp.);
Hemp nettles (Galeopsis spp.);
Horse nettle Agastache urticifolia,
Nilgiri nettles, Himalayan giant nettles (Girardinia diversifolia, family Urticaceae spp.).
Loosely, anything which causes a similarly stinging rash, such as a jellyfish or sea nettle.
Of the nettle plant and similar physical causes, to sting, causing a rash in someone.
senses.example: The children were badly nettled after playing in the field.

senses.definition: To pique, irritate, vex or provoke.

core.definition: A plant whose leaves and stems have stinging hairs that cause a painful, itchy rash when touched.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The middle t is a flap in American speech, so it sounds like a quick 'd', and the final syllable is a weak 'ul' with no separate vowel.

nuance.connotation: Negative
nuance.usage_note: Americans use nettle mainly for the stinging plant, especially stinging nettle, in gardens, hiking or foraging. The verb form is more formal and is used figuratively for irritating someone. Stinging nettle is the usual phrase in conversation.

distinctions.note: A thistle has spiky, prickly leaves and purple flower heads, while nettle has tiny stinging hairs on its leaves and stems.

examples.everyday: Watch out for that nettle patch by the fence, it will sting your legs.
examples.professional: The landscape crew removed the nettle patch near the playground for safety.
examples.analytical: The nettle's defense is a physical one, its hairs delivering irritants that make the plant unpleasant to touch.

nuance.analogy: Like a plant that looks harmless but has tiny needles that break off in your skin.
nuance.etymology: From Old English netele, a word related to the root of 'net' because of the plant's woven fibers.
common_mistakes: Confusing nettle with thistle or poison ivy, which cause different kinds of irritation.
Pronouncing the middle t as a hard 't' instead of the American flap that sounds like 'd'.

nettle.etymology: From Middle English *netle*, *netel*, from Old English *netle*, *netele*, *netel*, from **natilā* (cognate with, Middle ), a diminutive of Proto-Germanic **natǭ* (of unknown origin, perhaps from the same source as *net*).

senses.definition: A person from New England.

core.definition: A person from New England, the northeastern U.S. region of six states including Maine, Vermont, and Massachusetts.

pronunciation.tip: Main stress falls on ING in England, while New is secondary. The final syllable is a reduced r-colored vowel, not ay.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; many people from the region take pride in the identity.
nuance.usage_note: Locals often use this word to describe themselves, especially in Massachusetts or Maine. Some people also say Yankee, but outside the Northeast that term can sound like a mild regional insult when used by Southerners. New Englander is the precise and neutral choice.
word_family: New England (adjective, as in New England clam chowder)

distinctions.note: Yankee is broader and can mean any Northerner, and it may sound insulting in the South; New Englander is the precise regional term.
Northeasterner covers New York and Pennsylvania too; New Englander is limited to the six New England states.

examples.everyday: Don't mind her accent; she's a New Englander through and through.
examples.professional: Our regional office is in Boston, so most of our senior staff are New Englanders.
examples.analytical: Historians often describe the New Englander as shaped by Puritan town governance, though this image simplifies the region's diversity.

nuance.analogy: Like a Texan or a Californian, a New Englander takes a label from the place they come from, not from their accent.
nuance.etymology: From New England, the name John Smith gave the region in the early 1600s, plus the agent suffix -er.
common_mistakes: Putting the strongest stress on New, when in New England the main stress falls on ENG.
Ending the word with an ay vowel instead of a reduced er.

senses.definition: Penultimate, one before the end of a series, placed immediately before the end in a sequence.
senses.example: Go ahead and rest. We board the plane next to last.

core.definition: Second from the end; just before the final one in a series.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress is on LAST, and 'next' has a lighter secondary stress. The word 'to' is weak, so say it as 'nekst-tuh-LAST.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral.
nuance.usage_note: In writing Americans often hyphenate it as 'next-to-last' for a stop, page, or round. In casual speech, 'second to last' is even more common, and Americans would not normally say 'last but one,' which sounds British.

distinctions.note: Second to last is more common in everyday American speech; next to last is slightly more traditional and typical in writing.
Penultimate is formal or technical and appears mainly in literary or academic writing.

examples.everyday: Our stop is the next-to-last one on this bus route.
examples.professional: The next-to-last slide should summarize the main risks before the appendix.
examples.analytical: In the next-to-last chapter, the author returns to the question of divine justice raised at the start.

nuance.analogy: Next to last is like the second-to-last step on a staircase: one more step before the top.
nuance.etymology: Compound of 'next,' 'to,' and 'last,' literally 'nearest to the last.'
common_mistakes: Saying 'last but one,' which sounds British; Americans say 'next to last' or 'second to last.'
Pronouncing 'to' with full vowel strength; in speech it is weak, as in 'nekst-tuh-LAST.'

senses.definition: To take a small, quick bite, or several of such bites, of (something).
senses.example: The rabbit nibbled the lettuce.

senses.definition: To lightly bite (a person or animal, or part of their body), especially in a loving or playful manner; to nip.
senses.example: The puppy nibbled gently on my fingers while we played in the backyard.

senses.definition: To make (a hole in something) through small bites.
senses.example: The mice had nibbled a small hole through the bottom of the flour bag.

senses.definition: To make (one's way) through or while taking small bites.
senses.example: Before he realized it, he had nibbled his way through a whole bag of potato chips.

senses.definition: Chiefly followed by into or to: to cause (something) to be in a certain state through small bites.
senses.example: The rain had nibbled the old wooden fence down to splinters over the years.

senses.definition: Followed by away, off, etc.: to remove (something) through small bites.
senses.example: She nibbled off the crust and left the soft bread in the middle.

senses.definition: To remove (small pieces) from glass, tile, etc. with a tool; also, to remove small pieces from (glass, tile, etc.) with a tool.
senses.example: The glazier nibbled away at the jagged edge of the windowpane with pliers.

senses.definition: To fidget or play with (something), especially with the fingers or hands.
senses.example: Nervously, she nibbled at the loose thread on her sleeve during the speech.

senses.definition: To catch (someone); to nab.
senses.example: The sheriff's deputies nibbled the fugitive at a diner outside Tulsa.

senses.definition: To steal (something); to pilfer.
senses.example: Someone had nibbled a few dollars from the petty cash drawer again.

senses.definition: Chiefly followed by at, away, or on: to take a small, quick bite, or several of such bites; to eat (at frequent intervals) with small, quick bites.
senses.example: The rabbit nibbled at the lettuce.

senses.definition: To lightly bite, especially in a loving or playful manner.
senses.example: He nibbled at my neck and made me shiver.

senses.definition: Chiefly followed by at: to show slight interest in something, such as a commercial opportunity or a proposal.
senses.example: The investors nibbled at the proposal but asked for more detailed projections.

senses.definition: Followed by away at: to reduce or use up gradually; to eat.
senses.example: Inflation has nibbled away at our savings every year since we retired.

senses.definition: Synonym of tramline (“of a vehicle: to tend to follow the contours of the ground with its wheels”).
senses.example: Because of the worn tires, the truck nibbled along the grooved highway in the rain.

senses.definition: To fidget or play, especially with the fingers or hands.
senses.example: She nibbled idly on the strap of her backpack while the bus crawled forward.

senses.definition: Chiefly followed by at: to make insignificant complaints; to carp, to cavil, to find fault.
senses.example: Stop nibbling at every little detail of the plan; it's working fine.

senses.definition: To engage in sexual intercourse.
senses.example: The bawdy sailors in the old novel bragged about who had nibbled with the barmaids.

senses.definition: Followed by at: of a batter: to make an indecisive attempt to bat a ball bowled outside the off stump.
senses.example: The batter nibbled at a wide delivery outside off stump, and the keeper took the catch.

senses.definition: An act of taking a small, quick bite, or several of such bites, especially with the front teeth; the bite or bites so taken.
senses.example: He took a quick nibble from the corner of the cracker before answering.

senses.definition: A light bite of a person or animal, or part of their body, especially one which is loving or playful; a nip.
An amount of food that is or can be taken into the mouth through a small bite; a small mouthful.
A slight show of interest in something, such as a commercial opportunity or a proposal.
A unit of memory equal to half a byte, or chiefly four bits.

core.definition: To eat something by taking small, quick bites, often slowly or without much appetite.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The final syllable is a weak schwa followed by l, so say it as a soft 'uhl' with no extra vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to mildly positive; it suggests small, pleasant bites of food.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use nibble for small bites of snacks, cookies, or cheese, especially at parties or while cooking. It is casual and friendly. Saying someone is nibbling on food at a formal dinner can sound slightly impolite, since it implies eating very little.

distinctions.note: A bite is a single action of biting, while nibble means small repeated bites over time.
Snack is a noun for a small meal between main meals; nibble is an action of taking small bites.

examples.everyday: I'm just nibbling on some chips while I wait for the pizza.
examples.professional: Let's keep the snack table simple so people can nibble between sessions.
examples.analytical: The essay describes how the author nibbles at the edges of the argument without committing to a clear position.

nuance.analogy: Like a mouse working at a piece of cheese, you take small bites bit by bit.
nuance.etymology: From Middle English nibben or nibblen, probably of Low German or Dutch origin, related to nib.
common_mistakes: Using nibble for one big bite; use bite instead.
Stressing the second syllable, saying ni-BULL instead of NIB-uhl.

nibble.etymology: The verb is derived from Late Middle English *nebillen*, *nebyll* (“to peck away at, nibble; to attempt to sing”); further etymology uncertain, possibly from *nibbelen* (“to eat in small bites, peck”) (modern, *gnibbeln*, *knibbeln*), possibly a variant of…

conversation.text: I'm not hungry, so I'll just nibble on some bread.
She nibbled at her salad and barely ate.
Do you want to nibble on some cheese while we wait?

senses.definition: A doctrine that universals do not have an existence except as names for classes of concrete objects.

core.definition: The philosophical view that general terms and universals name classes of particular things and have no existence apart from those names.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, and let the final -ism be a weak 'um' sound. The middle syllables are reduced to a quick 'muh' and 'nuh'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; a technical term in philosophy with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Used almost only in philosophy, theology and intellectual history courses or writing. Americans often contrast it with realism and conceptualism when discussing the medieval problem of universals.

distinctions.note: Realism holds that universals exist independently of our naming them; nominalism denies this.
Conceptualism places universals in the mind as concepts, whereas nominalism locates them only in language.

examples.everyday: My roommate is a philosophy major and keeps arguing about nominalism over dinner.
examples.professional: In the data science team's design review, someone joked that our feature labels were nominalism in practice: just names for groups of rows.
examples.analytical: Nominalism in its strict form holds that the apparent universal 'humanity' is nothing over and above the individual human beings we name with that word.

nuance.analogy: Like calling a flock of birds 'the flock': the word is useful, but there is no extra bird hiding inside it.
nuance.etymology: From Latin nomen 'name', with the suffix -ism.
common_mistakes: Saying 'NOM-in-al-ism' with stress on the second syllable; the stress falls on the first syllable.
Confusing nominalism with nominal, which means 'in name only' or 'small' in an economic sense.

senses.definition: Adhering or relating to nominalism.
senses.example: Her nominalist view held that general categories like justice are just names we apply.

senses.definition: An adherent of any of the various kinds of nominalism.
senses.example: As a nominalist, he argued that universals exist only as words in our minds.

core.definition: A person who holds nominalism, the view that universals are only names and have no existence apart from particular things.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The second vowel is a short, reduced 'ih', so the word has only three clear beats.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; a descriptive label for a philosophical position.
nuance.usage_note: Used as a noun for a person in philosophy discussions, and as an adjective for ideas or arguments. Americans rarely use it outside academic or intellectual contexts.

distinctions.note: A realist about universals holds they exist independently of language; a nominalist denies this.
A conceptualist places universals in the mind, while a nominalist treats them as mere names.

examples.everyday: My professor says he's a nominalist, which means he doesn't believe in abstract things apart from words.
examples.professional: Our team lead is a nominalist about categories, so she always asks us to define our labels by the data points they name.
examples.analytical: Ockham is the classic medieval nominalist, insisting that universals are signs predicated of many individuals rather than real entities.

nuance.analogy: A nominalist is like someone who says 'the team' is just the people on it, not a separate thing floating above them.
nuance.etymology: From nominalism, from Latin nomen 'name'.
common_mistakes: Using the adjective form as a noun, as in saying 'he is a nominalism'.
Stressing the second syllable, as in 'nom-ih-NAL-ist'.

senses.definition: Having a nominalist character.
senses.example: His philosophy of mathematics was nominalistic, treating numbers as mere names rather than real entities.

core.definition: Of or relating to nominalism, the view that general terms name individual things but do not refer to real universal essences.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on LIS, the same place as in realistic. Keep the middle vowels as quick schwas rather than full ee or ih sounds.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical; in debates it can be used dismissively to suggest someone reduces ideas to labels.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word almost only in philosophy, theology and the history of ideas. It describes a tendency or outlook rather than a named school, so 'a nominalist' is more common when referring to a person. In casual talk, say 'too literal' or 'just a label' instead.

distinctions.note: Nominal means in name only or relating to names; nominalistic describes a philosophical stance that denies abstract universals.
In philosophy, realism holds that universals exist; nominalistic is the opposite stance, so the everyday meaning of realistic does not apply here.

examples.everyday: My roommate is so nominalistic; she says the word love is just a label and nothing more.
examples.professional: Our product team took a nominalistic approach, so a customer is whatever the database tag says, not a concept we model.
examples.analytical: Ockham's nominalistic reduction of universals to individual terms reshaped later accounts of meaning and reference.

nuance.analogy: Like insisting that the word dog is only a sound on a label, with no shared dogness behind the individual dogs.
nuance.etymology: From nominalism, from Latin nominalis, from nomen 'name'.
common_mistakes: Confusing it with nominal (in name only); nominalistic refers specifically to a philosophical view of universals.

senses.definition: Having restrictions on smoking.
senses.example: We want a table in the non-smoking section.

senses.definition: Using no tobacco products.
senses.example: We have a room for a non-smoking tenant.

senses.definition: The act of abstaining from smoking; a policy of doing so.
senses.example: Yes, your Honor: non-smoking has been our policy in all of our hotel rooms for at least twenty years, and Mr Jones clearly knew that.

core.definition: Free of smoking; restricting or banning smoking in a place such as a building, vehicle, or section of a restaurant.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on SMOKE, the root word, while non- is weak or secondary. Keep the final ng sound and do not add a hard g after it.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it describes a rule or area without judgment. Calling a person non-smoking is unusual, so the word mostly applies to places.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use it for places and rules, such as a non-smoking section, room, or policy, and on signs and hotel bookings. Many Americans now say smoke-free instead, especially for indoor areas where laws ban smoking. For a person who doesn't smoke, say nonsmoker. A natural reply to 'Is this area non-smoking?' is 'Yes, it is' or 'Sorry, this is the smoking section.'

distinctions.note: Smoke-free is more common on American signs and in policy talk, and it suggests that the whole area is free of smoke, sometimes even outdoors.
Nonsmoker is a noun for a person who does not smoke; non-smoking describes places, rules, or sections.

examples.everyday: Could we get a table in the non-smoking section, please?
examples.professional: The new office lease requires a non-smoking policy in all shared spaces, including the parking garage.
examples.analytical: Public health researchers often measure whether a non-smoking rule in apartment buildings changes respiratory illness among children who live there.

nuance.analogy: A non-smoking room is like a quiet library: the rule applies to the space itself, not to the people inside it.
nuance.etymology: From non- (Latin for 'not') and smoking, from smoke (Old English smoca).
common_mistakes: Saying a no smoking section in speech; Americans say non-smoking section or no-smoking sign, depending on the phrase.
Stressing non- instead of SMOKE, which makes the phrase sound unnatural.

senses.definition: Indifference, unconcern; carelessness; coolness; disregard, detachment.
senses.example: She shrugged off the criticism with remarkable nonchalance and kept presenting.

core.definition: A calm, casual lack of concern; an easy, relaxed air of not caring about something that might seem important.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the final syllable, LAHNS, and the ch is pronounced sh. The word ends in a nasal -ahns, not a hard -ance as in 'chance'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly negative. It can describe admirable composure, but it often suggests carelessness about things that matter, so context decides.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use nonchalance for someone who handles a serious or stressful situation with apparent ease, usually in writing or polished speech. Saying a boss responded with nonchalance to a problem can sound critical. In casual talk, 'laid-back' or 'cool about it' is more natural, and a typical reply is a shrug and 'Yeah, no big deal.'

distinctions.note: Indifference is simply not caring; nonchalance adds a visible show of calm, often a deliberate pose.
Apathy is a lasting lack of interest or energy; nonchalance is usually a momentary, outward air of ease.

examples.everyday: She said she had lost her keys again with total nonchalance, like it was no big deal.
examples.professional: The manager described the missed deadline with a nonchalance that worried the whole team.
examples.analytical: Stoic writers praised a nonchalance toward fortune that was less indifference than a disciplined refusal to let outcomes govern the will.

nuance.analogy: Like a duck gliding calmly across a pond while its feet paddle furiously underwater.
nuance.etymology: From French nonchalance, from nonchaloir 'not to care', from Latin non 'not' and calere 'to be warm'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable; the main stress is on the final syllable LAHNS.
Pronouncing the ch as in 'chair'; it is pronounced sh.
Using it for a warm, friendly manner; it implies a lack of concern.

senses.definition: Not any of a given number or group.
senses.example: None of those is a good example. None are even acceptable.

senses.definition: No one, nobody.
senses.example: None of those people is my father.

senses.definition: No person.
senses.example: None of those people are my parents. None shall pass.

senses.definition: To no extent, in no way.
senses.example: I felt none the worse for my recent illness.

senses.definition: Not at all, not very.
senses.example: He was none too pleased with the delays in the program that was supposed to be his legacy.

senses.definition: A person without religious affiliation.
senses.example: On the survey, a growing share of young adults identified as none.

senses.definition: Synonym of midafternoon: the time around or following noon or nones.
senses.example: We usually eat lunch at noon, but on Sundays we wait until none.

core.definition: Not any; not one, or not a single one, of a group, amount or number.

pronunciation.tip: Rhymes with 'fun' and 'sun.' Don't say it like 'nin' or 'noh-neh.' It sounds exactly like 'nun,' the religious woman, so context carries the meaning.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a plain, everyday word and carries no emotional weight.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'none' constantly in speech, often with a plural verb when the group is countable ('None of the cookies are left'). Formal writing often prefers a singular verb ('None of the data is missing'). Both are accepted, so pick whichever sounds natural in context. In answers, 'None for me, thanks' is a polite, common reply.

distinctions.note: 'None' refers to a number or amount from a group, while 'no one' refers only to people and is more general.
'Nobody' is informal and refers only to people, while 'none' can refer to things, numbers or amounts.
'No' is a determiner placed before a noun ('no time'), while 'none' stands alone in place of a noun ('none of the time').

examples.everyday: Do you want more coffee? None for me, thanks, I'm good.
examples.professional: We checked the forty support tickets, and none of them had the error logs attached.
examples.analytical: None of the premises in the argument, taken alone, is sufficient to establish the conclusion.

nuance.analogy: Like an empty chair at a full table: the seat is there, but nobody is in it.
nuance.etymology: From Old English nān, from ne ('not') plus ān ('one').
common_mistakes: Using a singular verb automatically, when a plural verb is common with countable nouns in speech.
Confusing 'none' with 'nun' in pronunciation; 'none' has a short 'u' sound like 'fun.'
Writing 'none of the time' as 'none the time' or using 'none' before a noun instead of 'no.'

none.etymology: From Middle English *none*, *noon*, *non* (“not one”), from Old English *nān* (“not one, not any, none”), from **nain*, from Proto-Germanic **nainaz* (“none, nought, nothing”), equivalent to *ne* + *one*.

senses.definition: Inequivalence.
senses.example: The lawyer argued that the nonequivalence of the two contracts meant the court should not combine them.

core.definition: The condition of not being equivalent; two things do not have the same value, meaning or logical truth.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on KWIV, not on NON; 'non' has a secondary stress. Reduce the 'e' in 'ih' and the final 'ance' to a soft 'uhns.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise technical term with no emotional tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word mainly in mathematics, logic, statistics and philosophy. In everyday talk they would say 'the two aren't the same' or 'they don't match.' In logic, 'inequivalence' is also used, and both mean the negation of equivalence.

distinctions.note: 'Difference' is a general word for unlikeness, while 'nonequivalence' is a precise claim that two things fail a specific test of equal value or truth.
'Inequivalence' is more common in formal logic texts, while 'nonequivalence' is more common in general mathematical and statistical writing; both mean the same thing.
'Inequality' compares sizes or values with less than or greater than, while 'nonequivalence' concerns whether two statements or objects are equivalent in a defined sense.

examples.everyday: I thought the two phone plans were the same, but the fine print shows a real nonequivalence in the data limits.
examples.professional: The validation test flagged nonequivalence between the two survey versions, so we can't compare their scores directly.
examples.analytical: A proof of nonequivalence requires a single case in which the two statements differ in truth value, not just a general impression of difference.

nuance.analogy: Like two keys that look alike but do not open the same lock.
nuance.etymology: From non- ('not') plus equivalence, from Latin aequivalere, 'to have equal value.'
common_mistakes: Misspelling it as 'nonequivalance' with an 'a' in the final syllable.
Placing the main stress on NON instead of KWIV.
Using it for ordinary differences where 'different' or 'not the same' is more natural.

senses.definition: Without stopping; without interruption or break.
senses.example: There's a nonstop flight to Mauritius, but I'm not sitting on the same plane for thirteen hours.

senses.definition: Describing a point mutation within a stop codon that causes the continued translation of an mRNA strand.
senses.example: The researcher identified a nonstop mutation that allowed the ribosome to read past the stop codon.

senses.definition: Without stopping; without interruption or break.
senses.example: He worked nonstop for fourteen hours yesterday, just so he could get today off.

senses.definition: A nonstop journey, especially a nonstop flight.
senses.example: We booked a nonstop to Denver because I hate changing planes in Chicago.

senses.definition: A convenience store in parts of Europe, open 24 hours a day.
senses.example: On our trip to Lisbon, we grabbed snacks from the nonstop down the street at midnight.

senses.definition: A linguistic sound that is not a stop; a continuant.
senses.example: The phonetics lecture contrasted stops like p and t with nonstop sounds like s and f.

core.definition: Continuing without any stop, break or interruption, especially for a long time.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on STOP, the second syllable, with the short American ah sound like the vowel in cot. Say it as one smooth word and do not split it into non-stop with an extra beat.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive for flights and service; negative when it describes exhausting work or annoying noise.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use nonstop for flights with no connection, for a person who talks constantly, or for things that never end, like nonstop rain or nonstop work. For flights, nonstop is the precise term, while direct can still include stops. The word is fine in both casual and business speech.

distinctions.note: A direct flight may stop at one or more airports while keeping the same flight number; a nonstop flight never stops between the two cities.
Continuous is neutral and technical, while nonstop adds an informal sense of energy or annoyance, as in nonstop chatter.

examples.everyday: The kids have been talking nonstop since we left the house.
examples.professional: The team has been running deployments nonstop all week, so we need a break before the release.
examples.analytical: A nonstop process of revision can produce a text that never reaches a settled final form.

nuance.analogy: Like a river that never runs dry, always moving forward without a pause.
nuance.etymology: Stop from Old English stoppian, 'to stop up'; nonstop from non- plus stop.
common_mistakes: Saying direct when you mean nonstop; a direct flight may still have a stop.
Writing non stop as two words in formal writing; the standard form is nonstop.

senses.definition: Providing goods or services, but not for the purpose of making a profit.
senses.example: The community clinic is a not-for-profit provider offering low-cost care to uninsured residents.

senses.definition: A not-for-profit company or organization.
senses.example: Our foundation awards grants to each not-for-profit that completes the annual reporting requirements.

core.definition: Operating to serve a cause or the public, not to earn profits for owners or shareholders.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on 'PROF' in 'profit', and 'for' is weak, closer to 'fer'. The final syllable of 'profit' is a reduced 'uht', not 'fit'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive; it signals public benefit and legal status, especially in organizations and documents.
nuance.usage_note: Americans most often say 'nonprofit' in everyday and business speech, and 'not-for-profit' is more common in formal documents or in Canada, the UK and Australia. As a noun, 'a not-for-profit' means such an organization. Use 'nonprofit' in most American conversations and reserve 'not-for-profit' for formal or international writing.

distinctions.note: 'Nonprofit' is the standard American term; 'not-for-profit' is more formal and is more common in international writing.
'For-profit' is the opposite type, a company that distributes earnings to owners or shareholders.

examples.everyday: My sister volunteers at a not-for-profit that delivers meals to older neighbors.
examples.professional: Our client is a not-for-profit, so we need to report the grant funds separately.
examples.analytical: A not-for-profit organization may accumulate surpluses, but it may not distribute them to its members as dividends.

nuance.analogy: Like a bakery that gives its bread to the neighborhood instead of selling it for gain.
nuance.etymology: Compound of 'not', 'for' and 'profit'; 'profit' from Old French profit, from Latin profectus, 'progress, advantage'.
common_mistakes: Omitting the hyphens in the adjective form, as in 'not for profit organization'.
Confusing 'not-for-profit' with 'unprofitable', which means a business that loses money.

senses.definition: Present; current.
senses.example: The now management team is very different from the one that founded the company.

senses.definition: Fashionable; popular; up to date; current.
senses.example: I think this band's sound is very now.

senses.definition: At the present time.
senses.example: Now I am six.

senses.definition: Used to introduce a point, a qualification of what has previously been said, a remonstration or a rebuke.
senses.example: Now, we all want what is best for our children.

senses.definition: Differently from the immediate past; differently from a more remote past or a possible future; differently from all other times.
senses.example: Now I am ready.

senses.definition: At the time reached within a narration.
senses.example: Now he remembered why he had come.

senses.definition: Used to indicate a context of urgency.
senses.example: Now listen, we must do something about this.

senses.definition: At the present point of a recurring cycle or event.
senses.example: I always used to do my shopping now, to avoid the rush.

senses.definition: Used to address a switching side, or sharp change in attitude from before.
senses.example: Now, you want to protect me. An hour ago, you were mercilessly bullying me!

senses.definition: Sometimes; occasionally; used to list a series of often assumed states.
senses.example: His face fit his roles: now smiling, now earnest, now glowering, now raging.

senses.definition: Since, because, in light of the fact.
senses.example: Now all the children have grown up and left, the house is very quiet.

senses.definition: Indicates a signal to begin.
senses.example: Now! Fire all we've got while the enemy is in reach!

senses.definition: The present time.
senses.example: Now is the right time.

senses.definition: The state of not paying attention to the future or the past.
senses.example: She is living in the now.

senses.definition: A particular instant in time, as perceived at that instant.
senses.example: Every moment felt suspended in the now, with nothing before or after it.

core.definition: At the present moment; at this time, as opposed to earlier or later.

pronunciation.tip: This is a diphthong that starts open and glides to an 'oo' sound. Do not say a pure 'no' vowel, which would make it sound like 'know'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: 'Now' is one of the most common words in American speech. Americans use it for the present moment, for urgency ('Do it now'), and as a discourse marker ('Now, wait a minute'). 'Right now' is more emphatic and common in casual talk, while 'currently' is more formal and used mostly for states or conditions.

distinctions.note: Now refers to the exact moment; currently is more formal and describes a state that is true for the present period.
Now points to a specific moment; nowadays refers to the general present period and is often used with contrast to the past, as in 'Nowadays everyone has a phone.'

examples.everyday: Sorry, I can't talk now because I'm driving, so I'll call you back later.
examples.professional: We're now rerunning the model on the full dataset, so the results should be ready by three.
examples.analytical: The argument now rests on an assumption that the author never tested.

nuance.analogy: Like a photograph that freezes one moment: 'now' is the frame you are in at this instant.
nuance.etymology: From Old English nū, from a Germanic root meaning 'now'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it as 'no' with a pure vowel; the American sound is a clear 'ow' diphthong.
Using 'now' for the general present, as in 'I now live in Ohio' when you mean 'nowadays' or 'currently'.

now.etymology: From Middle English *nou*, *nu*, from Old English *nū*, from **nū*, from Proto-Germanic **nu* (“now”), from Proto-Indo-European **nū* (“now”).

senses.definition: The null hypothesis.
A non-existent or empty value or set of values.
senses.example: The function returns null when the requested record does not exist in the database.

senses.definition: Zero quantity of expressions; nothing.
senses.example: The team's final score was a null, since neither side scored a single point.

senses.definition: Something that has no force or meaning.
The null character; the ASCII or Unicode character (␀), represented by a zero value, which indicates no character and is sometimes used as a string terminator.
senses.example: Older C programs end each string with a null, which tells the computer where text stops.

senses.definition: The attribute of an entity that has no valid value.
senses.example: Since no date of birth was entered for the patient, his age is null.

senses.definition: One of the beads in nulled work.
senses.example: Each small null in the nulled work catches the light, creating a glittering pattern across the fabric.

senses.definition: Having no validity; "null and void".
senses.example: The judge declared the contract null and void because one signature had been forged.

senses.definition: Insignificant.
senses.example: For the executives, the rumor was null, not worth any attention at all.

senses.definition: Absent or non-existent.
senses.example: After the layoffs, the company's commitment to training was effectively null.

senses.definition: Of the null set.
senses.example: The measure of the set of rational numbers in that interval is null, as the lecture showed.

senses.definition: Of or comprising a value of precisely zero.
senses.example: The regression coefficient for the new variable was null, so it contributed nothing to the model.

senses.definition: Causing a complete loss of gene function; amorphic.
senses.example: The mutant mouse carried a null allele, so the protein was completely absent from its cells.

senses.definition: Neutral.
senses.example: The judge kept a null expression throughout, revealing nothing about her verdict.

senses.definition: To return to the null position, setting, etc.
senses.example: Before measuring, the technician nulled the instrument so the needle rested at zero.

senses.definition: To form nulls, or into nulls, as in a lathe.
senses.example: The turner nulled the wooden spindle, cutting small beads along its length.

senses.definition: To crack; to remove restrictions or limitations in (software).
senses.example: Someone nulled the license check in the pirated copy of the program.

core.definition: Nothing, or having no value or legal force (null and void); in statistics, the null hypothesis: the default claim that there is no effect or difference, which a test tries to reject.

pronunciation.tip: This is a single syllable that rhymes with 'dull' and 'hull'. Do not add a vowel after the l, and remember the vowel is the short 'uh' sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical. In statistics it is a precise term, and in everyday talk it means something empty or without effect.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use null hypothesis mainly in statistics, data science, and research methods courses. In casual talk, people use null to mean 'zero' or 'no value,' as in a null response. When speaking to colleagues, say 'the null' in technical discussions, but explain 'the null hypothesis' to non-specialists.

distinctions.note: Zero is a number, while null often means an absent or missing value, which is not the same as the number 0.
The alternative hypothesis is the claim a test supports if the null is rejected, while the null is the default claim being tested.

examples.everyday: The scientist said the drug had no effect, so we're starting from the null.
examples.professional: We can't reject the null hypothesis at the 0.05 level, so the difference between the two versions is not statistically significant.
examples.analytical: Fisher's framework treats the null as a conservative default, which makes its rejection an evidential claim rather than a proof.

nuance.analogy: The null hypothesis is like a defendant's presumption of innocence: it stands until the evidence is strong enough to overturn it.
nuance.etymology: From Latin nullus, 'not any,' from ne, 'not,' and ullus, 'any.'
common_mistakes: Saying 'accept the null hypothesis' instead of 'fail to reject the null hypothesis', since a test does not prove it true.
Confusing null with zero; a null value is missing or undefined, while zero is a real number.
patterns: null and void (not before a noun)

null.etymology: Borrowed from Middle French *nul*, from Latin *nūllus*.

senses.definition: In an obscure manner.

core.definition: In a way that is hard to see, understand or notice; vaguely, unclearly, or in an unknown way.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on SKYOOR, like obscure, and -ly is one light syllable, lee. Say the r clearly, since American English is rhotic, and do not drop it.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes something unclear or hidden, without strong praise or blame.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use obscurely in writing, reviews and formal speech to describe something unclear, such as an obscurely worded sign, or something unknown, such as an obscurely famous band. In conversation, people often prefer 'hard to follow' or 'not well known'. The word is more common in writing than in speech.

distinctions.note: Vaguely suggests a lack of detail, while obscurely suggests something hidden or hard to perceive.
Ambiguously means open to two or more meanings, while obscurely means hard to see or understand at all.

examples.everyday: The sign at the trailhead was obscurely worded, so we ended up on the wrong path.
examples.professional: The error message is obscurely worded, so users keep opening tickets instead of fixing their configuration.
examples.analytical: The argument is obscurely phrased in the second chapter, which makes its central premise hard to identify.

nuance.analogy: Like a face seen through frosted glass: you know someone is there, but you cannot make out the details.
nuance.etymology: From obscure, from Latin obscurus 'dark, hidden', plus the adverb suffix -ly.
common_mistakes: Confusing obscurely with obscenely, which means excessively or offensively.
Using obscurely for vaguely; obscurely suggests something hidden or hard to perceive.

senses.definition: Closed or obstructed.
Forced upwards by colder, denser air.
senses.example: Meteorologists tracked the front after the cold air overtook it, so the warm air became occluded.

core.definition: Blocked or closed off; in weather, a front where cold air lifts warmer air up and away from the ground.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the middle syllable, KLOO, and reduce the final -ed to a short 'id' sound. Non-native speakers often add an extra syllable or stress the first syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in technical use; can be somewhat dark or ominous in literary description.
nuance.usage_note: In American speech occluded appears mainly in medicine, meteorology, and literary writing. A weather forecaster might mention an occluded front, and a doctor might describe an occluded artery. In casual talk people say blocked or closed. It sounds too technical or stylized in ordinary conversation.

distinctions.note: Blocked is everyday and general; occluded is technical or literary and usually describes an opening or passage that is closed off.
Closed describes a state of being shut; occluded implies something has been obstructed, often by an outside object or process.

examples.everyday: My sinuses felt occluded after the flight, so I took a decongestant.
examples.professional: The weather service issued an update when the occluded front moved across the Midwest.
examples.analytical: The narrator describes a mind so occluded by grief that it can no longer see the world clearly.

nuance.analogy: Like a drain clogged with leaves, the passage is still there but no longer lets anything through.
nuance.etymology: From the past participle of Latin occludere, 'to shut up, close up.'
common_mistakes: Using occluded as a casual word for busy or blocked, as in 'the street is occluded'; blocked is more natural.
Stressing the first syllable instead of the middle one.

senses.definition: The process of occluding, or something that occludes.
senses.example: The occlusion of the sun by the moon during the eclipse lasted nearly three minutes.

senses.definition: An occluded front.
senses.example: The weather service warned that an occlusion would bring heavy rain by Thursday morning.

senses.definition: A closure within the vocal tract that produces an oral stop or nasal stop.
senses.example: My phonetics professor showed how the tongue creates an occlusion before the T sound.

senses.definition: The blocking of the view of part of an image by another.
senses.example: Our graphics engine handles occlusion so hidden polygons behind the car never get drawn.

senses.definition: Anything that obstructs or closes a vessel or canal.
senses.example: Doctors found a blockage that caused occlusion of the left coronary artery.

senses.definition: The alignment of the teeth when upper and lower jaws are brought together.
senses.example: The orthodontist said my occlusion was off, so I needed braces to correct my bite.

senses.definition: The absorption of a gas or liquid by a substance such as a metal.
senses.example: Palladium's occlusion of hydrogen gas makes it useful for storing fuel safely.

core.definition: The act of blocking or closing off something, or a blockage itself; in phonetics, a closure of the vocal tract.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on KLOO, and the -sion ending sounds like 'zhun', as in 'vision.' Learners often pronounce the s as a hard 's' sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; a technical term with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use occlusion mainly in medicine, dentistry, meteorology, and phonetics. In dentistry it refers to how the upper and lower teeth fit together. A doctor might talk about an arterial occlusion, while a friend would just say a blockage. The word is rarely used in casual talk.

distinctions.note: Blockage is the everyday word for something that stops flow; occlusion is more technical and often refers to a closing or closure.
Obstruction suggests something in the way; occlusion emphasizes the process or state of closing an opening.

examples.everyday: My dentist said my bite is off, and she wants to check my occlusion before the filling.
examples.professional: The monitoring system raises an alert when the occlusion of the pipeline reaches a critical level.
examples.analytical: In phonetics, a stop consonant is defined by a complete occlusion of the airflow followed by a release.

nuance.analogy: Like a dam across a river, it stops the flow and lets pressure build behind it.
nuance.etymology: From Latin occlusio, from occludere, 'to shut up, close up.'
common_mistakes: Confusing occlusion with occasion or occupation in spoken English.
Pronouncing the final -sion as 'shun' in every context; the standard form here is 'zhun.'

occlusion.etymology: Borrowed from Late Latin *occlūsiō* (“occluding, obstruction”), from the Classical Latin *occlūdō* (“to shut up or close up; to restrain”), from *ob* + *claudō* (“to shut or close”).

senses.definition: The part of the year when business is most slack and there are fewest clients or visitors.
senses.example: Seaside resorts in the off-season are really depressing.

senses.definition: A period of time when regular competitions are not being held, or when an athlete is not participating in competitions.
senses.example: Many players take a second job during the off-season to cover their living expenses.

senses.definition: During the off-season.
senses.example: Cyclists train hard off-season, then ease into races once spring weather arrives.

core.definition: The part of the year when a business, sport, or destination has the fewest customers, visitors, or competitions.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on the first part of 'season', so 'SEE' is strong and the last syllable is a weak 'un'. Keep the 'off' vowel short and pronounce the 'r' in neither word, as there is none here.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It can be positive when it means cheaper prices or quieter times, and negative when it means slow business.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'off-season' when talking about travel, sports, or businesses, such as 'Hotels are cheaper in the off-season.' It is common in everyday conversation about vacations and in work contexts about slower periods. In sports, it refers to the time between competitions. The adverb form, as in 'We went off-season,' is less common and more informal.

distinctions.note: Low season is a common alternative in travel and hospitality; off-season is more general and common in everyday American speech.
Slow season focuses on reduced business activity, while off-season also refers to the time without events or competitions.

examples.everyday: We're going to the beach in February because it's the off-season and the hotels are cheaper.
examples.professional: Our sales team uses the off-season to train new hires and clean up the customer database before the spring rush.
examples.analytical: The off-season reveals structural patterns in demand that are hidden during peak months, which is why economists often study it closely.

nuance.analogy: The off-season is like a quiet winter for a garden, when the ground rests and gets ready for the next bloom.
nuance.etymology: From off (away from the main activity) and season (a period of the year).
common_mistakes: Writing 'off season' without a hyphen in formal writing, where 'off-season' is standard.
Using the adjective 'off-season' with the wrong part of speech; as a noun it is common, and the adverb use is less natural.
Pronouncing 'season' as two strong syllables instead of a reduced second syllable.

conversation.text: The beach is way cheaper in the off-season.
A lot of restaurants close during the off-season.
We like to travel in the off-season to avoid the crowds.

senses.definition: An elderly person, especially one who holds old-fashioned views.
senses.example: My grandfather is an old fart who still insists the newspaper is better than any website.

core.definition: An older person, often a man, who is seen as stubborn or set in old-fashioned ways, used as an insult or a joke.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on FART, and the r is clearly pronounced in American speech, so the word does not sound like 'faht' with no r. Keep the vowel open and short.

nuance.connotation: Negative and rude. It mocks an older person's habits or opinions, though friends sometimes use it affectionately.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use old fart informally, often among friends, or about a specific difficult person such as a boss or neighbor. Saying it to someone's face is insulting, and in workplaces it can get you in trouble. For a neutral or respectful alternative, people say 'old-timer', 'senior colleague' or 'longtime employee'.

distinctions.note: Old-timer is neutral or warm and praises long experience, while old fart is rude and mocks stubbornness or old-fashioned habits.
Curmudgeon is a more literary word for a grumpy, cranky person, while old fart focuses on age and old-fashioned habits.
Senior is a polite, formal term for an older or higher-ranking person, and it avoids the insult of old fart.

examples.everyday: My neighbor is a grumpy old fart who yells at kids on bikes, but he's basically harmless.
examples.professional: Some of the older folks in finance still want paper reports, so let's print the summary for Thursday's meeting.
examples.analytical: Dismissing a critic as an old fart attacks the speaker's age instead of the reasoning, which is a common form of ad hominem argument.

nuance.analogy: Like a weathered fence post: solid and dependable, but stuck in the ground in the same spot for decades.
nuance.etymology: Informal slang in which fart, a vulgar word for gas from the bowels, is used as a rude term for a person.
common_mistakes: Using it as a polite term for elderly people, which can offend and sounds rude
Pronouncing the r as silent, which makes the word sound like a different word

senses.definition: From or reminiscent of an earlier time or era; old-fashioned.
senses.example: He likes to listen to old-time music.

senses.definition: Ancient; persisting since ancient times.
senses.example: The villagers still follow old-time customs that began long before recorded history.

core.definition: From an earlier era, or in the traditional style of the past; old-fashioned in a warm or nostalgic way.

pronunciation.tip: TIME gets the main stress, and OLD has a lighter secondary stress. Pronounce the l in 'old' clearly, and do not let the d disappear before the t.

nuance.connotation: Usually positive or nostalgic, as in 'old-time music' or 'old-time religion.' It can be mildly dismissive when describing a person's ideas.
nuance.usage_note: Americans often use 'old-time' for folk music, country music, traditional crafts, and church traditions, such as 'old-time gospel.' It is warmer than 'old-fashioned' and suggests fondness. It is usually used before a noun.

distinctions.note: Old-fashioned can be neutral or critical, while old-time usually suggests nostalgia or affection, especially for music, customs, or traditions.
Ancient refers to very distant history, often thousands of years ago. Old-time refers to a more recent past within living memory or family memory.
Vintage refers to something valued for its age and quality, often an object. Old-time describes a style, custom, or era.

examples.everyday: We went to a little dance hall with old-time music, and everyone was singing along.
examples.professional: The product team wants an old-time feel for the new packaging, so we are testing vintage-style fonts.
examples.analytical: The essay treats the old-time revival meetings as a religious practice shaped by longing for a lost community.

nuance.analogy: Like a family photo album: the pictures show a world that feels warm and familiar, even if it no longer exists.
nuance.etymology: Compound of 'old' and 'time,' from Old English 'eald' and Old English 'tima.'
common_mistakes: Using 'old-time' for a person to mean 'elderly,' which can sound odd or rude.
Overstressing OLD and making the word sound like two unrelated words.
Confusing it with 'oldtimer,' which is a noun for a person.

senses.definition: Old; advanced in age.

core.definition: Old, or advanced in age; used when talking about someone who is elderly, often in a polite or formal way.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on YEARS, and 'on' and 'in' are weak and quick. Pronounce the r in 'years' and keep the vowel short, not a long 'yeers'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to gentle, sometimes slightly old-fashioned. It is a more polite way of saying old.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this phrase mostly in formal, written or polite speech, such as an obituary, a news story or a respectful description of a family member. In everyday conversation, people more often say 'elderly,' 'older' or 'getting on.' Do not use it for objects or young people. A natural reply is simply to ask about the person or continue the conversation.

distinctions.note: Elderly is the most common everyday term and is neutral; on in years is more formal and a little more literary.
Aged can describe something that has been around a long time, such as wine, or a person; on in years focuses specifically on a person's age.
Senior is often used as a polite noun or adjective for older adults in American services, such as senior discounts.

collocations: on in years but still active

examples.everyday: My grandmother is well on in years, but she still plays bridge every Tuesday.
examples.professional: We need staff who can help clients who are on in years and may struggle with the new app.
examples.analytical: Philosophers have long asked whether someone who is on in years has earned the wisdom that age was once thought to confer.

nuance.analogy: Like a well-loved book, its pages worn by time but still valuable to read.
nuance.etymology: An idiom built from the everyday words on, in and years, meaning well advanced in life.
common_mistakes: Using 'on in years' for young people or things; it means old.
Saying 'in years old' or 'of years' instead of the fixed phrase 'on in years'.

senses.definition: On call.
senses.example: The hospital pays the on-call surgeon extra for every night she stays available.

core.definition: Available to be contacted and to start work quickly, usually outside normal hours, in case of an emergency.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on CALL, and the vowel in 'on' is the American open vowel shared with 'cot'. Do not add an extra syllable between the two words.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a duty or availability, sometimes implying stress or inconvenience.
nuance.usage_note: In American tech and healthcare, people say 'I'm on-call this week' to mean they must respond to alerts or emergencies. A natural reply is 'Okay, text me if anything breaks.' The adjective is often hyphenated before a noun, as in 'on-call engineer', but the adverb form is 'on call' without a hyphen.

distinctions.note: Standby suggests waiting ready to act, often with less formality; on-call is a formal duty arrangement, often with pay or rotation.
Available is a general state of being free; on-call is a specific work duty to respond when needed.

examples.everyday: I can't make the movie tonight because I'm on-call at the hospital.
examples.professional: The on-call engineer got paged at 2 a.m. when the database stopped responding.
examples.analytical: An on-call system distributes responsibility, but it also transfers the costs of fatigue to individuals who may never have chosen it.

nuance.analogy: Like a fire station crew that waits ready to respond the moment the alarm sounds.
common_mistakes: Writing 'on call' with a hyphen when it follows a verb, as in 'I am on call'; the adjective form before a noun is hyphenated.
Mispronouncing 'on' as 'ohn' with a rounded vowel; American speakers use an open vowel.
patterns: be on call (not before a noun)

senses.definition: Subject to oppression.
senses.example: politically oppressed

core.definition: Treated cruelly or unjustly by people in power; suffering under unfair authority, cruelty or control.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on PREST, the second syllable. The -ed sounds like a plain final t, so the word is one stressed syllable, not 'uh-PRESS-ed'. Keep the r clearly at the start of the stressed syllable.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes suffering and injustice.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'oppressed' mainly for groups or people treated unjustly by power: 'oppressed minorities' or 'oppressed workers'. In everyday talk people might say 'treated unfairly' or 'stepped on'. 'Oppressed' sounds serious, so reserve it for real injustice rather than small annoyances.

distinctions.note: Persecuted focuses on being harmed for beliefs or identity; oppressed covers a wider range of unjust control and mistreatment.
Repressed describes suppressed emotions or desires; oppressed describes people subjected to unjust power.

examples.everyday: Many people in that town felt oppressed by the landlord's constant threats.
examples.professional: Our nonprofit trains community leaders to speak for oppressed workers in local factories.
examples.analytical: Liberation theologians argue that God takes the side of the oppressed, reading the Exodus as a story of liberation from bondage.

nuance.analogy: Like a plant pressed under a heavy stone: it can still grow, but it cannot rise freely.
nuance.etymology: From Old French oppresser, from Latin opprimere 'to press down'.
common_mistakes: Using 'oppressed' for minor annoyances, which sounds exaggerated.
Confusing it with 'depressed' or 'repressed', which have different meanings.

senses.definition: A spherical body; a sphere, especially one of the celestial spheres; a sun, planet, or star.
senses.example: The astronomer described the bright orb rising above the eastern horizon at dawn.

senses.definition: Celestial sphere; one of the azure transparent spheres conceived by the ancients to be enclosed one within another, and to carry the heavenly bodies in their revolutions.
senses.example: Medieval cosmologists imagined each orb as a crystalline sphere carrying a planet.

senses.definition: A structural motif or finial in the shape of a sphere.
senses.example: The stone gatepost was topped with a carved orb that caught the morning light.

senses.definition: An orbit of an heavenly body.
senses.example: The satellite completed one full orb around the planet every ninety minutes.

senses.definition: A globus cruciger; a ceremonial sphere used to represent royal or imperial power.
senses.example: The king held the orb and scepter during the coronation ceremony at Westminster.

senses.definition: A translucent sphere appearing in flash photography (Orb (optics)).
senses.example: Dust particles near the lens produced a faint orb in my flash photos from the cave.

senses.definition: Amount of deviation from the closest perfect aspect.
senses.example: The astrologer said the Mars and Venus conjunction fell within a three-degree orb.

senses.definition: A body of soldiers drawn up in a circle, as for defense, especially infantry to repel cavalry.
senses.example: The infantry formed an orb with pikes facing outward to repel the cavalry charge.

senses.definition: A blank window or panel.
senses.example: The software displayed a blank orb in the corner until the data finished loading.

senses.definition: (rare) The time period of an orbit.
senses.example: The probe's orb around the comet lasted nearly eleven months.
senses.label: rare

senses.definition: (poetic) The eye, seen as a luminous and spherical entity.
senses.example: Her luminous orb gazed at him across the crowded hall.
senses.label: poetic

senses.definition: (poetic) Any revolving circular body, such as a wheel.
senses.example: The old mill's great wooden orb turned slowly in the rushing stream.
senses.label: poetic

senses.definition: (rare) A sphere of action.
senses.example: Her influence extended well beyond her own orb, into the affairs of the whole county.
senses.label: rare

senses.definition: (poetic) To form into an orb or circle.
senses.example: The dancers orbed their arms overhead until they formed a single glowing circle.
senses.label: poetic

senses.definition: (poetic) To become round like an orb.
senses.example: As the bread dough rested, its edges slowly orbed into a smooth, plump ball.
senses.label: poetic

senses.definition: (poetic) To encircle; to surround; to enclose.
senses.example: Mountains orb the valley, shielding the village from storms off the Pacific.
senses.label: poetic

core.definition: A round, glowing object, such as the sun or moon, or a ball-shaped ornament or symbol of power.

pronunciation.tip: It is one syllable with the 'or' vowel and a clear final b. Do not make it sound like 'orbit', which has its stress on OR and a separate second syllable.

nuance.connotation: Positive or poetic. It suggests beauty, light or power, and it is rarely used in plain speech.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use orb mostly in poetry, fantasy writing, descriptions of royal regalia, or lyrical description, as in 'a glowing orb'. In everyday talk they would say 'ball', 'sphere' or simply 'the moon' or 'the sun'. The orb of a crown or scepter is an ornament, so context shapes its meaning.

distinctions.note: Sphere is the general or technical term for a perfectly round three-dimensional shape; orb is more poetic and often suggests light or glow.
A globe is a round model of the Earth or a large round object; orb is more literary and often used for the sun, moon or royal symbols.

examples.everyday: The moon looked like a huge orange orb over the lake last night.
examples.professional: The new logo is a simple blue orb, which fits the brand's clean style.
examples.analytical: Medieval rulers were often painted holding an orb, a sign that earthly power imitated the order of the heavens.

nuance.analogy: An orb is a ball that has been given a glow and a crown.
nuance.etymology: From Latin orbis, 'circle, disk, ring'; related to orbit.
common_mistakes: Confusing orb, the round object, with orbit, the path around it.
Using orb in casual talk; 'ball' or 'sphere' is more natural for ordinary objects.

orb.etymology: From Middle English *orbe*, from Old French *orbe*, from Latin *orbis* (“circle, orb”).

senses.definition: A secret rite or ceremony, typically involving riotous and dissolute behavior, including dancing, drunkenness and indiscriminate sexual activity, undertaken in honor of various pagan gods or goddesses (such as Attis, Bacchus, Ceres, Dionysus, Osiris, etc).
senses.example: Early Christian writers condemned the orgy held in honor of Dionysus as scandalous.

senses.definition: A gathering of people to engage in group sex.
senses.example: The novel's wild party quickly turned into an orgy that the police later raided.

senses.definition: An instance or period of excessive indulgence in a specified activity; spree.

core.definition: A wild, drunken party with uncontrolled sexual activity, or any period of excessive indulgence in something.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, and the 'or' sounds like 'awr' with a clear r. The final -gy is pronounced 'jee', not 'gee' or 'gy' as in 'my'.

nuance.connotation: Strongly negative. It implies moral excess, loss of control, and disorder.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use orgy for sensational or disapproving descriptions, often in news, movies, or moral criticism, and it is considered explicit. In polite conversation people usually say 'wild party' or 'debauchery' instead. Use it carefully, since it can sound judgmental or shocking in ordinary talk.

distinctions.note: A party is a neutral social gathering, while an orgy is a sexual or wildly excessive gathering with strong moral disapproval.
A spree is an excessive but usually non-sexual binge, such as a shopping spree, while orgy can name sexual excess or a lurid gathering.

examples.everyday: My neighbor's party turned into a wild orgy of drinking and loud music, and the cops came by around midnight.
examples.professional: The company's final quarter became an orgy of spending on unnecessary software licenses before the budget freeze.
examples.analytical: Critics of the ancient cults argued that their rituals degenerated into an orgy of excess that threatened civic order.

nuance.analogy: An orgy is like a fire that spreads out of control: what started as a spark of pleasure becomes a destructive blaze.
nuance.etymology: From Greek orgia, meaning secret rites, especially those of Dionysus.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the final -gy as 'gee' or 'guy'; it is 'jee'.
Using orgy as a neutral word for any large party, when it carries strong sexual and moral connotations.
nuance.biblical_note: The English word orgy does not appear in the Revised Standard Version. Scripture describes similar excesses with words such as carousing and drunkenness. Galatians 5:19-21 lists drunkenness and carousing among the works of the flesh that exclude one from the kingdom of God. Romans 13:13 urges believers to avoid reveling and drunkenness, and to live decently in the daylight.

orgy.etymology: Originally in plural from French *orgies*, from Latin *orgia*, from Ancient Greek *ὄργια* (“secret rites, mysteries”).

senses.definition: Someone who originates, creates or founds something.

core.definition: A person or group that creates, starts or founds something, such as an idea, product or method.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on RIJ. The final -or is a reduced 'er' sound, not the 'or' of 'door', and the -ate syllable is pronounced 'nay'.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It usually gives credit to the person who first came up with something, though it can be neutral in legal or patent contexts.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use originator in business, patents, media and academic writing ('the originator of the concept'). In casual talk, they usually say 'the person who came up with it' or 'who started it'. Use it only for the first creator, not for someone who copied an idea.

distinctions.note: An inventor creates a new device or process, while an originator may create ideas, styles or works of any kind, not necessarily machines.
Creator is broader and warmer, while originator stresses being the first to start or propose something, often in a business or intellectual context.

examples.everyday: Do you know who the originator of this recipe was? My mom swears it's hers.
examples.professional: Please credit the originator of the framework on the slide deck.
examples.analytical: The originator of the doctrine matters less than the tradition that later developed and defended it.

nuance.analogy: It is like the first person to clear a path through a forest: others follow the path, but the first footsteps started it.
nuance.etymology: From originate, plus the agent suffix -or, one who does the action.
common_mistakes: Using 'originator' to mean a place or origin, as in 'the originator of the river'; it refers to a person.
Pronouncing the final syllable as a stressed 'or' instead of a reduced 'er'.

senses.definition: That oscillates; oscillating.
Capable of sustaining oscillations.

core.definition: Swinging or moving back and forth in a regular, repeated pattern around a central point.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable (OS-), and the middle syllables reduce to 'suh-luh', not 'oh-sih-LAY'. The ending is 'tor-ee' with a clear American r.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it describes a motion or pattern without judgment.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word mainly in science, engineering, and math to describe back-and-forth motion, such as oscillatory currents or oscillatory behavior in a system. In everyday speech they would say 'swinging,' 'back and forth,' or 'vibrating.' It is more precise than 'oscillating' because it describes the nature of the motion rather than the object moving.

distinctions.note: Vibratory suggests rapid, small, fast shaking, while oscillatory suggests a slower, wider swing back and forth around a center.
Periodic means repeating at regular intervals, which may describe any event; oscillatory specifically describes motion that swings back and forth.

examples.everyday: That desk fan has an oscillatory swing, so it keeps blowing air back and forth across the room.
examples.professional: The accelerometer picks up oscillatory vibrations from the motor, so we need a filter before we analyze the data.
examples.analytical: Some historians describe the reform era as an oscillatory movement between centralization and decentralization rather than a steady march forward.

nuance.analogy: Like a pendulum in a grandfather clock, swinging back and forth around a fixed point.
nuance.etymology: From Latin oscillare, 'to swing.'
common_mistakes: Saying 'oh-sih-LAY-tor-ee' with stress on the second syllable.
Using 'oscillatory' for a person's indecision in casual talk; it sounds technical and odd there.

senses.definition: The tensor product of two vectors.

core.definition: In mathematics, the product of two vectors that forms a matrix whose entries are all the pairwise products of their components.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on PROD in product, and the first word has a lighter secondary stress on OUT. Say 'OUT-er', not 'OTH-er' (the th-sound is a common error), and keep the American r in the final syllable of outer.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise technical term with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this term in linear algebra, statistics, machine learning and physics, usually in writing or in technical talk. You will hear it in a meeting about a model, but it never comes up in casual conversation. In data science it is often written as x times y transpose, and the outer product is one of several 'products' of vectors, so say which one you mean.

distinctions.note: The dot product of two vectors is a single number (a scalar), while the outer product is a full matrix.
The cross product is defined only in three dimensions and gives a vector perpendicular to both inputs, while the outer product works in any dimension and gives a matrix.
The Kronecker product combines two matrices into a larger block matrix; the outer product of two vectors is a special case of this idea.

collocations: outer product of the column vectors

examples.everyday: My coworker tried to explain the outer product to me over lunch, and I just nodded along.
examples.professional: We can estimate the covariance matrix as a sum of outer products of the residual vectors, which is much faster in NumPy.
examples.analytical: Each rank-one term in the singular value decomposition is the outer product of a left singular vector and a right singular vector.

nuance.analogy: Multiplying a column of numbers by a row of numbers fills a grid with every possible pairwise product, like a multiplication table built from two lists.
nuance.etymology: From Old English ūtera (outer) and Latin productum (something brought forth), so a result 'brought forth' from two inputs.
common_mistakes: Confusing the outer product (a matrix) with the dot product (a single number).
Pronouncing outer like other, with a th sound.

senses.definition: Beyond normal, expected, or reasonable limits; outrageous.
Delivered across the Internet to a television or similar device.
senses.example: We canceled cable and now stream our shows through over the top apps on the TV.

senses.definition: Downward onto plants in the field, as contrasted with other routes of administration.
senses.example: over-the-top dicamba for dicamba-tolerant crops

senses.definition: Egregiously; beyond compare.
senses.example: That band was over the top amazing last night, honestly.

senses.definition: Over the parapet of a trench, especially at the start of a futile attack.
senses.example: The men were sent over the top to their certain death.

senses.definition: Used other than figuratively or idiomatically: see over,‎ the,‎ top.
