senses.definition: Salacious, scandalous; concerning oneself with lurid or lascivious substance.
senses.example: The tabloid built its success on scabrous gossip about celebrities' private affairs and sordid scandals.

senses.definition: Of music, writing, etc.: lacking refinement; unmelodious, unmusical.
senses.example: The critic called the new album scabrous, with clumsy lyrics and harsh, unmelodious noise throughout.

senses.definition: Difficult, thorny, troublesome, requiring tact.
senses.example: Negotiating the union contract proved scabrous, since every clause touched on sensitive issues requiring careful tact.

senses.definition: Covered with a crust of dirt or grime.
senses.example: The mechanic wiped the scabrous bolts, which were crusted with dirt and grime from years underground.

senses.definition: Having scabers.
senses.example: The entomologist described the beetle's scabrous wing cases, which bore rough, scaly ridges under the lens.

core.definition: Dealing with indecent, shocking or scandalous subjects in a way that feels sleazy or lurid.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The final 'ous' is a reduced 'uhs', not a full 'us' or 'ous'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It suggests indecent, sordid or disgusting material.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely say scabrous in speech. It appears in book reviews, literary criticism and formal writing. In everyday talk people say lurid, sleazy or scandalous instead.

distinctions.note: Salacious focuses on sexual suggestion; scabrous covers a wider range of sordid or disgusting material.
Scandalous describes shocking behavior; scabrous describes the lurid, sleazy quality of the material.

examples.everyday: I stopped reading that tabloid; the stories are too scabrous for me.
examples.professional: The editor cut the scabrous passages before the book went to print.
examples.analytical: The novel's scabrous wit exposes the hypocrisy of the court beneath its polished surface.

nuance.analogy: Like a rough, stained page that you don't want to touch.
nuance.etymology: From Latin scaber 'rough'.
common_mistakes: Confusing scabrous with scary or scrabble.
Using it in everyday speech where lurid or sleazy sounds more natural.

senses.definition: Having sides all unequal in length.
senses.example: scalene triangle

senses.definition: Of or pertaining to the scalene muscle.
senses.example: The physical therapist palpated the scalene muscles to ease his neck pain.

senses.definition: Ellipsis of scalene muscle.
Ellipsis of scalene triangle.

core.definition: Having three sides that are all different lengths.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, SKAY. The ending is a light, unstressed vowel, so do not stress the last syllable as 'skay-LEEN'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise geometric term with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans mainly meet this word in geometry classes and math textbooks. In anatomy and physical therapy, 'scalene' is also a noun for the neck muscles. Outside those settings, most people would just say 'a triangle with no equal sides'.

distinctions.note: An isosceles triangle has exactly two equal sides, while a scalene triangle has no equal sides.
An equilateral triangle has three equal sides and is the opposite extreme from a scalene triangle.
Irregular is a general everyday word for uneven shapes, while scalene is a precise term for triangles with three unequal sides.

examples.everyday: My daughter asked what to call a triangle with three different sides, and I told her it's scalene.
examples.professional: The sensor layout forms a scalene triangle, so our localization math cannot assume symmetric distances.
examples.analytical: Since no two sides of a scalene triangle are equal, none of its angles are equal either.

nuance.analogy: A scalene triangle is like three sticks of different lengths: no two are alike.
nuance.etymology: From Greek skalēnos 'uneven, unequal', via Late Latin scalenus.
common_mistakes: Calling any triangle without a right angle scalene; a triangle with two equal sides is isosceles.
Stressing the last syllable as 'skay-LEEN'.

scalene.etymology: Borrowed from Late Latin *scalēnus* (“of unequal sides”), from Ancient Greek *σκᾰληνός* (“uneven, unequal”).

senses.definition: A sheet of paper (or similar) on which score is kept.
A list of people who have scored.
senses.example: The coach checked the scoresheet to see which players had scored in the first half.

core.definition: A paper or record on which points, goals or scores in a game or contest are written down as the game goes on.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on SKOR, with lighter stress on SHEET. The sh sound in the second part is a clear 'sh', and the vowel in sheet is long.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it describes an official record.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use scoresheet for the official record in many sports and games, especially in basketball, volleyball and tournament play. For golf or baseball, many people say 'scorecard' instead. A scoresheet can also mean a list of people who have scored, as in 'Check the scoresheet for the goal scorers.'

distinctions.note: A scorecard is a printed card often used in golf and baseball, while a scoresheet is a general record sheet for many sports and contests.
A scoreboard is a large display for spectators to see, while a scoresheet is the written record kept by officials or scorekeepers.

examples.everyday: Can you check the scoresheet and tell me who won the last round?
examples.professional: Attach the signed scoresheet to the tournament report before you submit it to the league office.
examples.analytical: The scoresheet records outcomes, but it cannot show how the points were earned or what strategy produced them.

nuance.analogy: Like a ledger for a game, a page where every entry is written down in order.
nuance.etymology: From score plus sheet, a sheet of paper for recording scores.
common_mistakes: Confusing scoresheet with scoreboard; the sheet is the paper record, and the board is the display.
Using scoresheet for a golf card; in golf, the usual term is scorecard.

senses.definition: A mean, worthless fellow; a rascal; a villain; a person without honor or virtue.
senses.example: The bank manager turned out to be a scoundrel who had been stealing from his own customers for years.

core.definition: A dishonest, untrustworthy man who behaves badly; a rascal or villain.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, and let the 'ow' glide smoothly into the n. The d is often nearly silent, so say 'SKOWN-drul' with a soft r and a reduced final vowel.

nuance.connotation: Negative, often with a humorous or affectionate tone when used playfully among friends.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'scoundrel' in older-sounding or playful speech, such as 'You little scoundrel!' said to a mischievous child or pet. In serious contexts, it sounds dramatic, like something from a novel or a movie. For a stronger, plainer insult today, many people say 'jerk' or 'crook.'

distinctions.note: 'Rascal' is milder and often playful, suited to naughty children, while 'scoundrel' is stronger and suggests real dishonesty.
'Villain' is stronger and often refers to a major evil character or criminal, while 'scoundrel' suggests a lower-level, less dangerous bad man.

examples.everyday: You little scoundrel, you ate the last cookie and blamed the dog!
examples.professional: That vendor is a scoundrel who hid the defects until after we signed the contract.
examples.analytical: Many classic novels present the scoundrel as more charming than the honest hero, which makes moral judgment harder.

nuance.analogy: A scoundrel is like a shadow that sticks to a crowd, looking respectable at first but never trustworthy.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the middle as 'SKOWN-dehl' with a full 'e' vowel.
Using 'scoundrel' for a minor mistake, when it means a truly dishonorable person.

senses.definition: One who searches.
senses.example: The searcher combed the forest until dusk, but found no trace of the lost hiker.

senses.definition: A customs officer responsible for searching ships, merchandise, luggage, etc.
An implement for sampling butter.
senses.example: The dairy inspector pushed a searcher into the butter barrel to test its quality.

senses.definition: A sieve or strainer.
senses.example: Sift the flour through a searcher before measuring it for the cake.

senses.definition: (historical) An instrument for examining the bore of a cannon, to detect cavities in its surface.
senses.example: The artillery officer used a searcher to check the cannon bore for cracks.
senses.label: historical

senses.definition: (historical) An instrument for feeling after calculi in the bladder, etc.
senses.example: The surgeon inserted a searcher into the bladder to locate the stone.
senses.label: historical

core.definition: A person who looks carefully for something or someone; in customs, an officer who inspects ships, cargo, or luggage.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, and let the second syllable be a light r-colored vowel, not a full 'ur' sound. Don't add an extra vowel between the 'ch' and the 'er'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. The word is simply descriptive and carries no judgment about the person.
nuance.usage_note: Americans most often use searcher for someone looking for something specific, such as a bargain searcher or a treasure searcher. For a job, Americans say job seeker more often. At airports, people say customs officer or CBP officer rather than searcher. For internet search, the word is search engine, not searcher.

distinctions.note: A seeker pursues something deeper or more purposeful, such as truth or meaning. A searcher usually looks for a concrete object or person.
An investigator conducts a formal inquiry into a crime or problem. A searcher may simply be someone looking for a lost item.

examples.everyday: My sister is a serious bargain searcher, so she always knows which store has the best sales.
examples.professional: The rescue team needs two more searchers to cover the northern grid before dark.
examples.analytical: For Pascal, the modern searcher after truth often finds that each answer opens a new question.

nuance.analogy: A searcher is like a metal detector walking a beach: focused on a target, scanning every stretch of sand.
nuance.etymology: From search (verb) plus the agent suffix -er; search comes via Old French from Latin circare, to go around.
common_mistakes: Using searcher for an internet search tool; the correct term is search engine.
Stressing the second syllable; American speakers say SURCH-er.

searcher.etymology: From Middle English *serchour*, *sercher*, from Old French *cercheor*; equivalent to *search* + *-er*.

senses.definition: In the second place.

core.definition: Used to introduce the second point in a list or argument, after 'firstly' or 'first'.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The middle syllable is often reduced to almost nothing, so say it as two quick beats, 'SEK-nd-lee', not three full syllables.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It signals an organized argument and sounds formal, so it is most natural in writing or structured speech.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'secondly' in essays, speeches, and presentations, but in casual talk they usually say 'second' or 'and second.' Use 'secondly' only if you have already said 'firstly' or 'first.' You will rarely need a reply, because the listener simply waits for your next point.

distinctions.note: 'Second' is the everyday spoken form and sounds more natural in conversation; 'secondly' is more formal.
'Furthermore' adds a point that supports the previous one, while 'secondly' just marks the next item in an ordered list.

examples.everyday: I'm not going tonight, and secondly, I'm really tired.
examples.professional: First, the migration finished on schedule; secondly, the error rate dropped by half.
examples.analytical: Secondly, the argument assumes that moral choice is purely rational, a premise that deserves scrutiny.

nuance.analogy: Like a numbered sign on a trail: 'secondly' marks the next stop in a planned route.
nuance.etymology: From 'second' (Latin secundus, 'following'), with the adverb suffix '-ly'.
common_mistakes: Using 'secondly' in casual speech where 'second' sounds more natural.
Misspelling it as 'secondley' or 'secondy'.

senses.definition: Piously self-assured and smugly moralistic.
senses.example: His self-righteous lecture about everyone else's habits annoyed the whole team.

senses.definition: Patronizingly moralizing and rebuking.
senses.example: She gave her son a self-righteous scolding about his messy room.

core.definition: Convinced you are morally better than others, and showing it by judging or lecturing them.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on 'RYE' in 'righteous', and the word has two syllables, not three, so 'righteous' sounds like 'RYE-chus'. The 'ch' sound is a single consonant, and the final 'ous' is reduced to 'us'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It implies smugness and hypocrisy, and calling someone self-righteous is an insult.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this often in conversation, the news and social commentary to criticize people who lecture others while claiming moral superiority. It is a pointed criticism, so avoid calling a friend or coworker self-righteous unless you mean it as a real complaint. A natural reply to such a comment might be 'Yeah, I know, I shouldn't have lectured them.'

distinctions.note: Righteous can be sincere praise for moral integrity; self-righteous carries the sense of smugness and an unearned sense of superiority.
Pious describes sincere devotion to religion; self-righteous describes smug, judgmental moral certainty, often without real humility.
Sanctimonious is very close in meaning and stresses a showy, hypocritical display of piety; self-righteous emphasizes the inner feeling of being morally superior.

examples.everyday: Mark kept lecturing everyone about recycling, and it got a little self-righteous after a while.
examples.professional: Please keep the code review comments constructive, because a self-righteous tone makes people defensive and slows the team down.
examples.analytical: The Pharisees in the Gospels are often portrayed as self-righteous, confident in their obedience while looking down on those who fail to keep the law.

nuance.analogy: Like someone wearing a 'I'm the good one' badge everywhere they go: the badge is what others notice first.
nuance.etymology: From 'self' and 'righteous' (from Old English rihtwis, 'just, upright'); the compound dates to the 1600s.
common_mistakes: Saying 'self-righteous' with three syllables, as in 'self-RIGHT-ee-us'.
Using it as a neutral word meaning 'principled'; it is almost always negative.

senses.definition: The quality or state of being selfless.
senses.example: Her selflessness showed when she gave up her weekends to tutor struggling students.

core.definition: The quality of caring about others more than yourself, giving time or resources without expecting anything back.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on SELF. The final syllable is short, /nɪs/, like 'kiss' with an n, not a long 'nes' with an 'ay' sound.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It names an admirable virtue, usually in praise of someone's character or service.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'selflessness' in speeches, obituaries, letters of recommendation and religious or ethical discussions. In everyday talk people often say 'she's so selfless' instead. It is a respectful word, so it is rarely used to tease or joke.

distinctions.note: Altruism is a principle or theory of concern for others' welfare, often studied in psychology and philosophy, while selflessness describes a personal quality shown in action.
Humility is an accurate, modest view of oneself, while selflessness is focused on putting others first in practice.
Generosity is the habit of giving, often of money or things, whereas selflessness involves setting aside your own interests more broadly.

examples.everyday: Her selflessness during the flood made the whole neighborhood proud of her.
examples.professional: Her selflessness in sharing credit made her the most trusted lead on the team.
examples.analytical: Christian ethics often treats selflessness as the fruit of love rather than merely the absence of greed.

nuance.analogy: Like a lighthouse that shines for ships it will never see.
nuance.etymology: From selfless + -ness.
common_mistakes: Misspelling it as 'selflessnes' or 'selfness'; there are two s's before the -ness ending.
Pronouncing the final syllable as a long 'nes' instead of a short /nɪs/.
nuance.biblical_note: Scripture does not use one exact word for selflessness, but the Greek agapē (ἀγάπη, love) and kenōsis (κένωσις, self-emptying) describe it. Philippians 2:3-8 calls believers to humility and presents Christ emptying himself as the model. John 15:13 says there is no greater love than laying down one's life for one's friends. Mark 10:45 teaches that the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve.

senses.definition: Someone who sends.
senses.example: The package was addressed to someone we didn't know, so we returned it to the sender.

senses.definition: A device or component that transmits, as in telegraphy or computer networks.
senses.example: The network switch failed, so the sender kept retransmitting packets to the server.

core.definition: A person or device that sends a message, email, package, or signal to someone who receives it.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, and make the final -er a light American r-colored sound, not 'ah'. Keep the d, which is pronounced even though it sits between n and er.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a plain, factual word in both everyday and technical settings.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use sender in emails, texts, and packages, such as 'Check the sender before you open the attachment.' In software and networks it refers to a device or program that transmits data. For mail, the return address on a package names the sender, and 'Return to sender' is a common stamp. A natural reply in casual talk is 'Oh, I know them, thanks for the heads-up.'

distinctions.note: Transmitter refers specifically to a device that emits signals, such as radio equipment, while sender can be a person or a more general device.
Originator is the person who created the content, while sender is the one who transmitted it, and the two may be different people.

examples.everyday: Wait, who's the sender on this text? I don't recognize the number.
examples.professional: Please add the sender's address and a message ID to the log so we can trace the failed deliveries.
examples.analytical: In communication theory, the sender encodes a message, and noise in the channel can distort what the receiver finally decodes.

nuance.analogy: Like the person who drops a letter in the mailbox, the sender starts the message on its way.
nuance.etymology: From send (Old English sendan) with the agent suffix -er.
common_mistakes: Mixing up sender with sander, which is a machine for smoothing wood.
Using sender only for people, when in technology it often means a device or program.

senses.definition: A sentry, watch, or guard.
A unique value recognized by a computer program for processing in a special way, or marking the end of a set of data.
senses.example: The <xmp> tag is a sentinel that suspends web-page processing and displays the subsequent text literally

senses.definition: A sentinel crab.
senses.example: Along the mangrove shore, a sentinel crab waved its large claw at passing tourists.

senses.definition: A sign of a health risk (e.g. a disease, an adverse effect).
senses.example: Sentinel animals can be used to explore endemic diseases.

senses.definition: To watch over as a guard.
senses.example: He sentineled the north wall.

senses.definition: To post a guard for.
senses.example: He sentineled the north wall with just one man.

core.definition: A soldier or guard posted to watch for danger and give warning; also a person or thing that keeps watch over something.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The second syllable is a reduced tih, and the ending is a weak nuhl, not a strong nell or a stressed tin.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive; suggests vigilance, responsibility and protection.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use sentinel mostly in writing, news and fiction, often for a guard figure or for something that stands watch, like a lone sentinel on a hill. In everyday speech they usually say guard or lookout. In software, sentinel also has a specialized meaning for a marker value in data.

distinctions.note: A sentry is a guard on duty at a fixed post; sentinel is more literary and can describe a non-human watcher.
Guard is the everyday word for someone who protects people or property; sentinel suggests a lookout role.

examples.everyday: That huge oak by the mailbox is like a sentinel; it has been standing guard over the street for a century.
examples.professional: The monitoring script raises an alert whenever the sentinel value appears in the data stream.
examples.analytical: The poem casts the lighthouse as a sentinel, a figure that keeps faithful watch over a world it cannot save.

nuance.analogy: A sentinel is like a smoke detector: it stays quiet until danger arrives, then sounds the warning.
nuance.etymology: From Italian sentinella, of uncertain origin.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable, as in sen-TIN-el.
Using sentinel where guard or lookout is more natural in everyday speech.

sentinel.etymology: from Middle French *sentinelle* (“watch or guard kept by a soldier”), from *sentinella*, probably from *sentina* + *-ella*, from *sentire* (“perceive, watch, hear”), from *sentiō* (“feel, perceive by the senses”).

senses.definition: To speak in the manner of a sermon; to preach; to propagate one's morality or opinions with speech.
To preach a sermon to (somebody); to give (somebody) instruction or admonishment on the basis of one's morality or opinions.
To say in the manner of a sermon or lecture.
To inculcate rigid rules.

core.definition: To lecture someone about morals or behavior in a preachy, unwelcome way.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, 'SUR', and keep the middle syllable very short. The ending '-ize' is pronounced 'yze' with a long 'i' sound.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It implies moralizing that the listener does not want.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'sermonize' in writing or formal speech to describe someone who keeps giving moral advice. In everyday speech, people more often say 'lecture', 'preach', or 'moralize'. Use it with 'about' or 'to' rather than as a direct object in casual American English.

distinctions.note: Lecture is neutral and common. Sermonize suggests a moralizing tone and is more formal.
Moralize means to comment on right and wrong, often in a judgmental way. Sermonize emphasizes the preachy, lecturing style.
Preach can be positive, for example in a church, while sermonize is almost always negative in everyday use.

examples.everyday: Please don't sermonize me about my diet, because I already know what the doctor said.
examples.professional: In the meeting, Dan kept sermonizing about work ethic, which didn't help us fix the outage.
examples.analytical: Mill's essay sometimes sermonizes about virtue, though his argument for liberty stands without the moral lecturing.

nuance.analogy: Like a radio stuck on one station of moral advice that plays whether or not anyone asked for it.
nuance.etymology: From 'sermon' (from Latin sermo, 'discourse') plus the verb-forming suffix -ize.
common_mistakes: Using a direct object as in 'sermonize me' without sounding stiff. Americans more often say 'sermonize about X' or 'sermonize to someone'.
Confusing 'sermonize' with 'sermonic'. Sermonize is a verb; sermonic is an adjective.

senses.definition: Used with the adverb sense of about.
senses.example: She set about cleaning the kitchen before her parents arrived for dinner.

senses.definition: Used with the preposition sense of about.
senses.example: Two youths set about him.

senses.definition: To start doing or to devote oneself to some task; to set upon.
senses.example: He set about designing his homepage.

core.definition: To begin working on a task, usually with determination or effort.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable of about: set uh-BOWT. The t of set links into the vowel of about, so say it as seh-tuh-BOWT.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It suggests purposeful effort on a task.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use set about in formal writing or formal speech, but more often say get started, start on, or get down to. You can say set about cleaning the kitchen in writing or a formal speech, but in casual talk use get to work on it.

distinctions.note: Get down to is more informal and focuses on finally doing the real work, while set about is more formal and literary.
Set out to emphasizes the intention or goal, while set about emphasizes the act of starting the work.

examples.everyday: Once the dishes were done, I set about cleaning the kitchen floor.
examples.professional: Our team will set about migrating the database once the code freeze ends.
examples.analytical: Historians note that the reformers set about dismantling the old system piece by piece, not all at once.

nuance.analogy: Like rolling up your sleeves before a big job.
nuance.etymology: From set and about, in the sense of around, meaning to put oneself to work on something.
common_mistakes: Saying set about to doing; the correct form is set about doing.
Confusing set about with set off, which means to begin a journey or trigger something.

senses.definition: To pay what one owes (a debt, a bill etc.)

core.definition: To pay the money you owe, such as a bill, a shared expense, or a debt, often between friends or at the end of a trip.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on UP, which is the particle, so do not stress SET. The 'settle' syllable has a light, reduced vowel followed by syllabic l, and the final p in 'up' is unreleased in fast speech.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It sounds friendly and practical, used to keep shared accounts fair.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say settle up when dividing costs with roommates, friends, or colleagues, and at the end of a group trip or dinner. At a restaurant, 'Can we settle up?' is less common than 'Can we split the check?', but both are used. A natural reply is 'Sure, I'll Venmo you' or 'Let me grab my wallet.'

distinctions.note: Pay up often implies reluctance or pressure, as when someone finally has to pay a debt, while settle up is neutral and cooperative.
Split the bill focuses on dividing the cost of a meal, while settle up covers any kind of shared expense or account between people.

collocations: settle up at the end of the trip

examples.everyday: Let's settle up before we leave; I'll send you my half of the Uber.
examples.professional: Can you settle up with the vendor by Friday so the invoice can close out this quarter?
examples.analytical: Accounting texts explain that a debt remains an open obligation until both parties actually settle up.

nuance.analogy: Like balancing a shared checkbook, you add up what each person paid and then transfer money until everyone is even.
nuance.etymology: From settle (to pay or arrange) and up (completely), used for paying accounts in full.
common_mistakes: Using 'settle up' without a clear object when the money is unclear; say 'settle up the bill' or 'settle up with me'.
Mispronouncing UP with a weak vowel, which makes the phrase less clear in conversation.

senses.definition: Having acute vision; having good eyesight.
senses.example: The sharp-eyed birdwatcher spotted the tiny warbler hidden high in the old oak tree.

senses.definition: Attentive, given to noticing things, aware.
senses.example: The sharp-eyed detective noticed things the ordinary patrolman missed.

core.definition: Able to see clearly and to notice small details quickly and accurately.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second word, EYED, and give sharp a lighter secondary stress. Say the two words as one phrase with a clear r and a clean final d.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It praises someone's attention to detail or ability to spot problems.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use sharp-eyed in everyday praise, such as 'my sharp-eyed daughter caught the mistake,' and in workplace settings to thank someone for catching an error. It is friendly and natural in both speech and writing.

distinctions.note: Observant is a general word for noticing things; sharp-eyed adds the sense of seeing small details clearly and quickly.
Keen-eyed is a close synonym with a similar meaning; sharp-eyed is more common in everyday American speech.

examples.everyday: My sharp-eyed daughter spotted the typo on the menu before I did.
examples.professional: Our sharp-eyed QA engineer caught the time zone bug before the release went out.
examples.analytical: A sharp-eyed reader will notice that the author's definition of justice shifts between chapters.

nuance.analogy: Like a hawk circling high above a field, able to pick out a small movement on the ground.
nuance.etymology: Compound of sharp and eye; sharp comes from Old English scearp.
common_mistakes: Dropping the hyphen or writing 'sharp eyed' as two separate words in formal writing.
Stressing both words equally instead of putting the main stress on the second word, eyed.

senses.definition: One who, or that which, shells.
senses.example: a corn sheller

core.definition: A person or machine that removes shells or husks from nuts, corn, peas, or similar food.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The second syllable is a reduced 'er' sound, not 'ah' or 'uh' stressed, so keep it short and weak.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It names a tool or worker and carries no emotional tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'sheller' mainly in agriculture, food processing, and equipment descriptions, such as a pecan sheller or corn sheller. In everyday speech people more often say 'nutcracker' for a hand tool or 'peeler' for removing skins. Using 'sheller' in casual conversation can sound overly technical.

distinctions.note: A nutcracker is a hand tool for breaking nut shells, while a sheller is often a machine or a person who removes shells in bulk.
A peeler removes skins from fruit or vegetables, while a sheller removes hard shells or husks.

examples.everyday: My grandfather used a hand-crank corn sheller every fall.
examples.professional: The processing line includes a pecan sheller and an automatic grader before packaging.
examples.analytical: The economic value of a sheller depends on how much labor it saves relative to the kernels it damages.

nuance.analogy: Like a nutcracker built for a factory, a sheller removes shells in volume instead of one nut at a time.
nuance.etymology: From shell (verb) plus -er, meaning one who or that which shells.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'sheller' with 'shelter', which sounds similar in many speakers' speech.
Stressing the second syllable or giving it an 'ah' vowel, as in 'shel-AH'.

core.definition: An ancient town in the hill country of Ephraim where the tabernacle and the ark of the covenant were kept for a long period.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, SHY, with a long i like 'sigh'. The final syllable is a clear 'oh' vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: Americans know Shiloh from the Bible and also from the Battle of Shiloh, a major Civil War battle in Tennessee in 1862. Many American towns and churches are named Shiloh, so the word is common in place names. In Bible study, it is simply the ancient sanctuary town.

distinctions.note: Shiloh is the place; a Shilonite is a person from there.

examples.everyday: We drove through Shiloh on the way to the Civil War park, and it's a nice quiet place.
examples.professional: Our church plant is named Shiloh, after the Old Testament town where the tabernacle stood.
examples.analytical: Shiloh served as Israel's central sanctuary before Jerusalem, so Jeremiah's warning about its destruction carries a sharp message about God's judgment on false worship.

nuance.analogy: Like a historic capital that held a country's most important treasures before the seat of government moved elsewhere.
nuance.etymology: From Hebrew Shiloh, of uncertain meaning, possibly 'place of rest' or 'tranquil'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable as 'shy-LOH'.
Confusing it with Shilonite, which refers to a person.
nuance.biblical_note: Hebrew Shiloh (שִׁילֹה), of uncertain meaning. Joshua 18:1 records the assembly of Israel at Shiloh, where the tent of meeting was set up. First Samuel 1:3 and 3:21 show the Lord's house at Shiloh, where Eli served and Samuel grew up. Genesis 49:10 is read by Christians as a messianic promise about one 'to whom it belongs', while Jeremiah 7:12 recalls God's judgment on the place.

senses.definition: (Apparently) shimmering, or shining with a faint, or intermittent or trembling gleam or light.
senses.example: The lake looked shimmery under the late afternoon sun, rippling with faint gold light.

senses.definition: (Apparently) shaking or trembling.
senses.example: Heat rising off the asphalt made the highway look shimmery in the August afternoon.

core.definition: Having a soft, shimmering shine, often used of fabric, makeup, or surfaces with a light sparkle that moves when you turn.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The middle vowel is a reduced schwa, not 'ee,' and the r is clear in American speech. End with a long EE sound.

nuance.connotation: Positive; it suggests something pretty, glamorous or fun.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use shimmery mostly in shopping, fashion and beauty talk, such as 'a shimmery top' or 'shimmery lip gloss.' It is casual and descriptive. In formal writing, shimmering is the more standard form.

distinctions.note: Shimmery is more casual and product-oriented, while shimmering is more descriptive and literary.
Glossy describes a smooth, reflective surface, while shimmery implies a soft, moving light on the surface.

examples.everyday: Do you think this shimmery top is too much for a birthday dinner?
examples.professional: Marketing wants the packaging to look shimmery, but the print vendor says the foil finish is expensive.
examples.analytical: The shimmery surface of the lake seems to dissolve the boundary between water and sky.

nuance.analogy: Like a sequined dress that catches the light only when you move.
nuance.etymology: Formed from shimmer with the adjective suffix -y.
common_mistakes: Using shimmery in very formal writing where shimmering is more standard
Stressing the second syllable, as in shi-MER-ee

senses.definition: To shoplift.
senses.example: If you detect a person shop stealing, report it to the police.

core.definition: To take merchandise from a store without paying for it and leave with it. The standard American word is shoplift.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on "steal," and the vowel is long, as in "feel." Many learners say "still" by mistake, so keep the vowel tense and clearly long.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes theft and carries a legal and moral charge.
nuance.usage_note: In American English the standard verb is written as one word, "shoplift," and the noun is "shoplifter." "Shop steal" is a nonstandard spelling and should not be used in writing. Americans say "He got arrested for shoplifting" in conversation and news reports.

distinctions.note: "Steal" is the general word for taking something illegally, while "shoplift" refers specifically to taking goods from a store.
"Theft" is a general noun used in legal and formal contexts, while "shoplifting" is the everyday word for stealing from stores.

examples.everyday: The guy got caught shoplifting a phone charger at the mall.
examples.professional: Our loss-prevention team reports a rise in shoplifting at the downtown store this quarter.
examples.analytical: Is shoplifting by a desperate person morally equivalent to organized theft? The law often treats them the same way.

nuance.analogy: Like slipping a candy bar into your pocket while the clerk is looking the other way.
nuance.etymology: Compound of "shop" and "steal."
common_mistakes: Writing "shop steal" in formal writing instead of "shoplift"
Saying "steal" as "still" with a short vowel

senses.definition: Time measured by the apparent diurnal motion of the vernal equinox; approximated by that based on the rotation of planet Earth relative to the seemingly fixed stars.
senses.example: The observatory's telescope tracks stars using sidereal time rather than solar time.

core.definition: Time measured by Earth's rotation relative to distant stars; a sidereal day is about 23 hours 56 minutes.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on DEER, the middle syllable. The first syllable is sy, like sigh, and the word ends with ee-ul, not eh-al. Do not say sid-EER-eal.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a precise technical term with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Astronomers, navigators and telescope operators use sidereal time in technical settings, and you rarely hear it in everyday talk. It is about four minutes shorter than a solar day, because Earth moves around the Sun as it turns. In the US it appears in observatory software and star charts. For everyday time, the word you need is standard time or local time.

distinctions.note: Solar time is based on the Sun's position, so a solar day is about four minutes longer than a sidereal day.
Mean solar time averages the Sun's motion over the year and is the basis of our clock time, while sidereal time is measured against stars.

examples.everyday: My telescope app shows sidereal time, so I can tell which stars will be up tonight.
examples.professional: The observatory's software converts UTC to local sidereal time before it points the telescope.
examples.analytical: Sidereal time, unlike solar time, measures Earth's rotation relative to distant stars rather than the Sun.

nuance.analogy: Like timing a lap against fixed stadium lights instead of the sun, which slowly shifts across the sky.
nuance.etymology: From Latin sidereus, of the stars, from sidus, sideris, star.
common_mistakes: Confusing it with standard time or local time, which follow the Sun rather than the stars.
Pronouncing the first syllable as seh, as in seh-DEER-ee-ul, instead of sy.

senses.definition: Mud or fine earth deposited from running or standing water.
Any material with similar physical characteristics, regardless of its origins or transport.
senses.example: The lab sorted the sample into sand, clay, and silt before running the analysis.

senses.definition: A particle from 3.9 to 62.5 microns in diameter, following the Wentworth scale.
senses.example: The soil report classified the sample as roughly 40 percent silt by weight.

senses.definition: To clog or fill with silt.
senses.example: Heavy runoff began to silt the reservoir, slowly reducing its capacity every spring.

senses.definition: To become clogged with silt.
senses.example: The irrigation canals silted up quickly after the spring floods swept through the valley.

senses.definition: To flow through crevices; to percolate.
senses.example: Rainwater slowly silted through the cracks in the limestone toward the cave below.

core.definition: Fine mud or soil particles carried and deposited by flowing or standing water, such as in rivers and lakes.

pronunciation.tip: It is one syllable with a short i, a clear l, and a crisp t at the end. Do not add a vowel after the l, and do not confuse it with 'salt' or 'sit'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a natural or engineering condition, often with a hint of trouble when it builds up in harbors, reservoirs, or channels.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use silt mostly in geology, environmental news, water management, and talk about rivers, lakes, or flooding. In casual speech people often say mud or dirt when the setting is not technical. Silt is also a verb, so a reservoir can silt up over decades.

distinctions.note: Mud is any wet mixture of soil and water, while silt is a specific grain size that can be dry or wet.
Sand particles are coarser than silt and feel gritty, while silt feels smooth or floury.
Clay particles are finer than silt and become sticky when wet, whereas silt is coarser and less sticky.

examples.everyday: After the flood, there was a thick layer of silt on the basement floor.
examples.professional: The sensor data shows silt building up near the intake pipe, so we need to schedule dredging before summer.
examples.analytical: Hydrologists treat silt concentration as a key variable when they predict how quickly a reservoir will lose its storage capacity.

nuance.analogy: Like the fine dust that settles at the bottom of a glass of muddy water.
nuance.etymology: Middle English, probably from Scandinavian or Low German roots; the exact origin is uncertain.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it like 'salt' or 'sit'; the vowel is a short i.
Using silt for any kind of dirt, when it names a specific particle size.

silt.etymology: From Middle English *silte*, *cilte*, *cylte*, perhaps from Middle English *silen* "to filter; strain"; equivalent to *sile* + *-t*, or cognate with Norwegian and Danish *sylt* (“salt marsh”), ultimately from Proto-Germanic **sultijō* (“salty water; brine”).

senses.definition: Sixpence coin.
senses.example: Grandad slipped a shiny simon into my palm for sweets, the way he always did.

senses.definition: A US dollar.
senses.example: Lend me a simon till Friday, and I'll pay you back with interest.

core.definition: In the Bible, a common name for several men, most importantly Simon Peter, the disciple whom Jesus called the rock on whom he would build his church.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and make the last syllable a reduced 'un'. Americans use 'eye' in the first syllable, not 'sim'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral, a common first name with religious associations
nuance.usage_note: Simon is a common first name in the United States and is also the name of Simon Peter in the Gospels. In church, it is the normal English form, and Americans will recognize Simon Peter immediately.

distinctions.note: Simon is the common English name for Peter's brother and for several other men, while Simeon is the form for Jacob's son and the man in Luke 2.

examples.everyday: My neighbor's son is named Simon, after his great-grandfather.
examples.professional: The curriculum includes a lesson on Simon Peter's role in the early church.
examples.analytical: Matthew's Gospel presents Simon, whom Jesus renames Peter, as the first of the twelve disciples to confess him as the Christ.

nuance.analogy: Simon is like a family name that appears in many branches of the Bible, each person carrying the same name but a different story.
nuance.etymology: From Greek Simon, from Hebrew Shim'on, meaning 'hearing'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it like 'Simeon'
Confusing Simon Peter with Simon the sorcerer
Using a long 'ee' vowel in the first syllable
nuance.biblical_note: Greek Simon, from Hebrew Shim'on (from shama, 'to hear'). Matthew 16:17-18 records Jesus calling Simon Peter a rock on which he will build his church. Mark 15:21 names Simon of Cyrene, who was made to carry the cross. Acts 8:9-24 describes Simon Magus, a sorcerer in Samaria who tried to buy the Holy Spirit.

simon.etymology: From Middle English *Simon*, *Symond*, *Symounde*, from Anglo-Norman *Simon*, *Simond*, *Simund*, a conflation of two unrelated names: one from Latin *Simon*, from Koine Greek *Σίμων*, strictly from Ancient Greeklikely *σῑμός* (“snub-nosed”)but used for…

senses.definition: A set of one, an item not part of a larger set, particularly:
senses.example: The lone coin in the drawer was a singlet, unmatched by any other.

senses.definition: A person who does not have a form of multiplicity; a single self or personality occupying one human body.
senses.example: Unlike her friends with plural systems, Mara is a singlet who experiences one consistent self.

senses.definition: A single piece of clothing, particularly:
senses.example: I wore a thin cotton singlet under my shirt on the hot summer day.

senses.definition: A multiplet having a single member, especially a single spectroscopic peak.
senses.example: The spectrum showed a singlet peak, meaning the nucleus had no neighboring protons.

senses.definition: A quantum state having zero spin.
senses.example: The electron pair formed a singlet state with total spin of zero.

senses.definition: A one-piece, tight-fitting uniform, usually made of spandex or nylon, required in wrestling and powerlifting.
senses.example: Before the match, the wrestler pulled on his red singlet and warmed up.

core.definition: A tight, sleeveless, one-piece athletic garment worn by wrestlers and by some track and weightlifting athletes.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The 'gl' cluster is pronounced together, with no vowel between the g and l, so it is 'SING-glit,' not 'sin-guh-let.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a technical clothing term with no negative or positive weight.
nuance.usage_note: Americans most often use 'singlet' for a wrestling uniform. In British English 'singlet' means a sleeveless undershirt, which Americans call a tank top or an undershirt. If you say 'singlet' to mean an undershirt in the US, people may be confused.

distinctions.note: A tank top is a casual sleeveless shirt, while a singlet is a close-fitting, one-piece athletic uniform.
A unitard covers both the torso and legs in one piece, while a singlet covers only the torso and has leg openings that end at the upper thigh.

examples.everyday: My son's wrestling singlet was still in the wash when the tournament started.
examples.professional: Our sports science team specified a lighter fabric for the new team singlets to reduce drag.
examples.analytical: The singlet, by minimizing fabric, shows how sport rules and bodily visibility shape what athletes are required to wear.

nuance.analogy: A singlet is like a second skin for an athlete: it is designed to stay out of the way so the body can move freely.
nuance.etymology: From 'single' (one layer) with the suffix -et; the exact development of the sense is uncertain.
common_mistakes: Using 'singlet' to mean a tank top or undershirt; in American English these are different garments.
Mispronouncing the middle as 'sin-guh-let'; it is one syllable, 'SING-glit.'

senses.definition: The property of being sinuous.
That which is sinuous.

core.definition: The quality of having many curves or bends, as in a winding river, road, or coastline, or of moving in a snaking way.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on the AH syllable, with light secondary stress on sin. The -ity ending is reduced to a short ih, and the t between vowels is usually a flap, so it sounds close to tee.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a physical or abstract property without judgment.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use sinuosity mainly in geography, hydrology, and literary description of rivers, roads, or coastlines. In everyday speech people say winding or curvy. In geography, a sinuosity index compares a channel's actual length to its straight distance, so the word sounds bookish in casual conversation.

distinctions.note: Curvature is the degree of bending at a point, while sinuosity describes the overall winding of a whole path.
Winding is a common everyday word for something that turns, while sinuosity is more technical and abstract.
Meander refers to a river that loops back and forth, while sinuosity is the general property of having many bends.

examples.everyday: Those mountain roads have so many curves that the sinuosity makes the drive take twice as long.
examples.professional: The engineers measured the sinuosity of the drainage channel to decide whether to straighten it.
examples.analytical: The sinuosity of Melville's sentences mirrors the drifting, unresolved quality of his moral argument.

nuance.analogy: Like a garden hose lying loosely on the grass, the path has far more bends than its straight length suggests.
nuance.etymology: From Latin sinuosus, full of curves, from sinus, a curve, fold, or bend.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the first vowel as long, as in sign; it is short, as in sin.
Using sinuosity for a single bend; it describes overall winding, not one curve.

senses.definition: The state or condition of being sinuous.

core.definition: The quality of being full of curves or bends, or of moving in a smooth, winding, graceful way.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable. The middle syllables are reduced, with the y sound before oo, and the final -ness is a light, unstressed ending.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It emphasizes elegance, curves, and flowing grace.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use sinuousness mainly in literary or descriptive writing about movement, lines, rivers, or roads. In speech they usually say curves or grace. It can sound poetic, so use it sparingly in conversation.

distinctions.note: Sinuosity is the more technical term for winding paths or channels, while sinuousness is the more literary term for graceful movement and form.
Grace is a general word for elegance, while sinuousness specifically emphasizes curves and flowing motion.
Curviness is casual and often used for shapes or bodies, while sinuousness is more literary and elegant.

examples.everyday: I loved the sinuousness of the road along the lake, though it made me a little carsick.
examples.professional: The designer wanted to emphasize the sinuousness of the bridge's curves in the presentation.
examples.analytical: The poem's sinuousness of syntax carries the reader through its doubts without ever settling them.

nuance.analogy: Like a ribbon blown across a field, the form owes its beauty to continuous, flowing bends.
nuance.etymology: From sinuous, from Latin sinuosus, full of curves, with the suffix -ness.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the middle syllables as oo-ous; the word is SIN-yoo-us-nus.
Using it for the technical sense of channel bends, where sinuosity is the standard term.

senses.definition: Syllabic abbreviation of situation comedy.
senses.example: My favorite sitcom airs on Thursday nights, and we never miss an episode.

senses.definition: Acronym of single income, two children, oppressive/outrageous mortgage.
senses.example: Dad joked that our life was pure sitcom, with one paycheck, two kids, and a crushing mortgage.

core.definition: A television show with a recurring cast of characters in a series of humorous, self-contained episodes.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, SIT, and make the second syllable a short, reduced 'kahm'. The vowel is the American 'ah', the same as in 'cot' under the cot-caught merger.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to light; it describes a genre of entertainment and can be used affectionately or mildly dismissively.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say sitcom for a half-hour comedy series, such as the classic TV comedies many people grew up watching. It is used in everyday talk, media, and entertainment writing. The longer phrase situation comedy is used in formal or industry contexts.

distinctions.note: Situation comedy is the full formal term; sitcom is the informal short form used in everyday speech.
A drama is a serious show focusing on plot and emotion, while a sitcom is comic and usually has short episodes.

examples.everyday: We're going to watch a sitcom after dinner, something light and funny.
examples.professional: The studio is pitching a new sitcom, and the writers are working on the pilot script this month.
examples.analytical: The modern sitcom often uses the family unit as a framework for exploring social expectations, which makes it a useful object of cultural analysis.

nuance.analogy: A sitcom is like a comfortable recurring visit with familiar friends who get into predictable, funny trouble each week.
nuance.etymology: A shortening of situation comedy.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable, as in 'sit-COM', instead of the first.
Treating sitcom as a countable noun in the wrong form; say 'a sitcom' or 'sitcoms', not 'sitcom's' for the plural.

conversation.text: It's a sitcom about a family in Chicago.
I love old sitcoms; they always make me laugh.
Sitcoms are perfect when you just want something light.

senses.definition: A sensation, pleasant or unpleasant, detected by inhaling air (or, the case of water-breathing animals, water) carrying airborne molecules of a substance.
senses.example: I love the smell of fresh bread.

senses.definition: A conclusion or intuition that a situation is wrong, more complex than it seems, or otherwise inappropriate.
senses.example: Something about the contract's fine print gave me a smell of trouble, so I asked a lawyer.

senses.definition: The sense that detects odours.
senses.example: After the flu, my sense of smell disappeared for weeks, and I could not taste my coffee.

senses.definition: To sense a smell or smells.
senses.example: I can smell fresh bread.

senses.definition: To detect or perceive; often with out.
senses.example: The bloodhound could smell out the hidden cache of evidence buried deep in the basement.

senses.definition: Followed by like or of if descriptive: to have a particular smell, whether good or bad.
senses.example: The roses smell lovely.

senses.definition: To smell of; to have a smell of.
senses.example: The kitchen smells of cinnamon and fresh bread every Sunday morning when my mother bakes.

senses.definition: To smell bad; to stink.
senses.example: Ew, this restroom smells (loathsomely).

senses.definition: To have a particular tincture or smack of any quality; to savor.
senses.example: A report smells of calumny.

core.definition: The quality of something detected through the nose, such as a pleasant odor or an unpleasant stench.

pronunciation.tip: It is one syllable with a short e like bed. Do not add an extra vowel after the m or split the l into a separate syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; the feeling depends on the adjective, as in a good smell or a bad smell.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use smell as both a noun and a verb for everyday sensing, as in what's that smell? or it smells good. Because smell can mean a bad odor, people often add good, nice or bad to avoid confusion. Informally, a smell can also mean a feeling that something is wrong, as in something smells fishy.

distinctions.note: Odor is the more formal or technical word for smell; smell is everyday and neutral.
Scent often suggests a pleasant smell, like perfume or flowers, while smell covers both good and bad.
Stench is a strong, bad smell; use it when you want to stress unpleasantness.

examples.everyday: What's that smell? Did somebody burn the popcorn?
examples.professional: Something smells off in these numbers, so let's check the data pipeline before the meeting.
examples.analytical: Philosophers warn that a bad smell in an argument is not proof that the argument itself is bad.

nuance.analogy: Like an alarm that goes off in the nose before the eyes can see anything.
nuance.etymology: Middle English smellen, from Old English smyllan, to smell.
common_mistakes: Using smell as a transitive verb without a clear object; say smell the coffee, but use smells of or smells like for descriptions.
Saying it smells like good; use it smells good, because the adjective follows smell.

smell.etymology: From Middle English *smellen*, *smillen*, *smyllen*, *smullen*, from Old English **smyllan*, **smiellan* (“to smell, emit fumes”), from **smallijan* (“to glow, burn, smoulder”), from Proto-Indo-European **smel-* (“to burn, smoke, smoulder; tar, pitch”).

senses.definition: A facial expression comprised by flexing the muscles of both ends of one's mouth, often showing the front teeth, without vocalisation, and in humans is a common involuntary or voluntary expression of happiness, pleasure, amusement, goodwill, or anxiety.
senses.example: She's got a perfect smile.

senses.definition: Favor; propitious regard.
senses.example: the smile of the gods

senses.definition: (dated) A drink bought by one person for another.
senses.example: Back in the 1920s, a gentleman might buy his friend a smile at the bar.
senses.label: dated

senses.definition: To have (a smile) on one's face.
senses.example: When you smile, the whole world smiles with you.

senses.definition: To express by smiling.
senses.example: to smile consent, or a welcome

senses.definition: To express amusement, pleasure, or love and kindness.
senses.example: The toddler began to smile when her grandmother walked through the door.

senses.definition: To look cheerful and joyous; to have an appearance suited to excite joy.
senses.example: The sun smiled down from a clear summer sky.

senses.definition: To be propitious or favorable; to countenance.
senses.example: The gods smiled on his labors.

senses.definition: Of ackee fruit: to open fully, indicating that it is no longer toxic, and ready to be picked.
senses.example: In Jamaica, my aunt waits until the ackee fruit begins to smile before picking it.

core.definition: A facial expression made by curving the lips upward, often showing the teeth, to show happiness, friendliness or amusement.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the single syllable and make the diphthong glide from the 'ah' sound toward 'ee'. Be sure the final 'l' is clear, since learners often drop it or add a vowel after it.

nuance.connotation: Strongly positive. A smile signals warmth, goodwill and approachability, though a forced or thin smile can signal discomfort.
nuance.usage_note: Americans smile at strangers often, in shops, on elevators and on walks, and a brief smile with eye contact is a normal, friendly gesture. Saying 'Smile!' before a photo is common, and 'Keep smiling' is a friendly way to say goodbye in tough situations. Replies to a smile are usually another smile or a short 'hi' or 'thanks'.

distinctions.note: A grin is broader and often shows many teeth, and it can suggest mischief or delight, while a smile is usually calmer.
A smirk is a smug or self-satisfied half-smile, usually with negative overtones, while a smile is generally sincere and friendly.
To beam is to smile very brightly and widely, showing great happiness, and it is usually used as a verb rather than a noun.

collocations: with a smile on her face

examples.everyday: The cashier gave me a big smile when I said I'd found the last loaf of bread.
examples.professional: Her warm smile and clear agenda made the difficult budget meeting feel much less tense.
examples.analytical: Philosophers have long asked whether a smile expresses an inner feeling or simply performs a social role.

nuance.analogy: A smile is like a small lamp turned on in a room: it lights up the face and tells people they are welcome.
nuance.etymology: From Middle English smilen; the origin is uncertain, possibly from Scandinavian or Low German roots.
common_mistakes: Saying 'smile to someone' instead of 'smile at someone'.
Treating 'smile' as a count noun in a way that sounds odd, as in 'I gave him a smile' is fine but 'smiles of happiness' should be used carefully to avoid overstatement.

smile.etymology: From Middle English *smilen* (“to smile”), from **smîlen* (“to smile”), from Middle High German *smielen*, from Old High German *smielēn*, from **smilēn*, from Proto-Germanic **smilāną* (“to smile”), from Proto-Indo-European **smey-* (“to laugh, be glad,…

senses.definition: Someone who smiles.

core.definition: A person who smiles, especially one who smiles often or easily.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. In General American the final syllable is a reduced, rhotic 'er' sound, so do not say a full 'ah' or 'uh' vowel there.

nuance.connotation: Positive. Calling someone a smiler is a friendly compliment, though it is less common than phrases like 'a happy person'.
nuance.usage_note: Americans more often say 'a big smiler' or 'a happy person' than 'a smiler' by itself. It sounds natural when describing children, pets or a friendly coworker. Using it for a stranger can sound slightly odd unless you are commenting on their friendly manner.

distinctions.note: Smiley can mean a cheerful person or the yellow smiling face symbol, while smiler refers more directly to someone who smiles a lot.
A grinner smiles broadly, often showing many teeth, and may suggest mischief, while a smiler is a more general term.

examples.everyday: Our new barista is such a big smiler that I always feel better after I get my coffee.
examples.professional: She is a natural smiler on video calls, which helps customers feel comfortable right away.
examples.analytical: In the study, the smilers were rated as more trustworthy by strangers, though the effect was modest.

nuance.analogy: A smiler is like a sunny window in a house: people feel warmer simply by being near them.
nuance.etymology: Formed from the verb 'smile' with the agent suffix '-er'.
common_mistakes: Using 'smiler' for an emoji or a cheerful symbol, which is usually called a smiley.
Pronouncing the final syllable as a full vowel instead of a reduced rhotic 'er'.

senses.definition: One who sneaks; one who moves stealthily to acquire an item or information.
senses.example: My little brother is such a sneak; yesterday I caught him trying to look through my diary.

senses.definition: The act of sneaking.
A cheat; a con artist.
senses.example: I can't believe I gave that sneak $50 for a ticket when they were selling for $20 at the front gate.

senses.definition: An informer; a tell-tale.
A sneaker; a tennis shoe.
A play where the quarterback receives the snap and immediately dives forward.
Ellipsis of sneak preview.
An unworthy or deceptive entry in a list of high-ranking people or things.
To creep or go stealthily; to come or go while trying to avoid detection, as a person who does not wish to be seen.
senses.example: He decided to sneak into the kitchen for a second cookie while his mom was on the phone.

senses.definition: To take (something) in a surreptitious manner, so as to avoid being noticed.
senses.example: I went to sneak a chocolate but my dad caught me.

senses.definition: To stealthily bring someone something.
senses.example: She asked me to sneak her a phone next month.

senses.definition: To inform an authority of another's misdemeanors.
senses.example: If you sneak on me I'll bash you!

senses.definition: (dated) To hide, especially in a mean or cowardly manner.
senses.label: dated

senses.definition: In advance; before release to the general public.
senses.example: The company gave us a sneak look at their new electronic devices.

senses.definition: In a stealthy or surreptitious manner.
senses.example: I was able to get a sneak peek at the guest list.

core.definition: To move quietly and secretly so you are not seen or heard, or to do something without being noticed.

pronunciation.tip: It is one syllable with a long 'ee' vowel and a final k. Say the s, ee and k as one smooth sound, without adding a vowel before the s or after the k.

nuance.connotation: Usually negative or sly, but positive in the phrase sneak peek, meaning an exciting early look at something.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use sneak for quietly leaving or entering a place, or for slipping a treat to a pet or child. In marketing, a sneak peek or sneak preview is an early look before public release, and that use is friendly and positive. Calling someone sneaky is mildly negative, while sneaking out late at night is often said playfully.

distinctions.note: Tiptoe focuses on walking softly on your toes, while sneak covers any quiet, secret movement or action meant to avoid notice.
Creep stresses slow, cautious movement, while sneak adds the idea of hiding or avoiding notice and is more common in everyday speech.
Slip means moving quietly or quickly, often out of a room, without much planning; sneak implies deliberately hiding the action.

examples.everyday: I'm going to sneak a cookie before dinner, so don't tell Mom.
examples.professional: We can give the design team a sneak preview of the dashboard before the official launch next week.
examples.analytical: Many moral arguments turn on the difference between open persuasion and attempts to sneak a conclusion past the reader.

nuance.analogy: Sneak is like a cat crossing a room, quiet and unseen, until it is already at the door.
nuance.etymology: From Old English snican, meaning to creep.
common_mistakes: Saying sneak on when you mean sneak out; in American English sneak on someone means to tattle on them.
Using a past tense inconsistently; sneaked and snuck are both used, with snuck more common in informal American speech.

sneak.etymology: Possibly from Middle English *sniken* (“to creep, crawl”), from Old English *snīcan* (“to creep, crawl”), from **snīkan*, from Proto-Germanic **snīkaną* (“to creep, crawl”), of origin; compare formally unrelated *snake*, *snoop*, *snook*, *snoke* and *snoot*.

senses.definition: Synonym of social contract.
senses.example: Many political theorists argue that a social compact binds citizens to obey laws in exchange for protection.

core.definition: An agreement, often unspoken, in which members of a society accept shared rules in exchange for order and protection.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable of compact, KAHM, which is a noun here. The ct at the end is a plain /kt/ cluster, so do not add a vowel between the c and t.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a philosophical and political term.
nuance.usage_note: Americans hear social compact mostly in political philosophy, civics classes, and speeches about government and rights. In everyday talk, people say we all agree to play by the rules. Social contract is the more common phrase in academic writing, while compact sounds a little more formal.

distinctions.note: The two terms are close synonyms; social contract is more common in modern political philosophy, while compact sounds slightly more formal.
A legal contract is written and enforceable; a social compact is a broad, often implicit understanding about how society is organized.

examples.everyday: Most of us have an unspoken social compact: we wait in line, we don't cut, and everyone benefits from that.
examples.professional: The new retirement proposal reflects a social compact between employers and workers about long-term security.
examples.analytical: Hobbes and Locke both describe a social compact, but they disagree about whether citizens can ever rightfully revoke it.

nuance.analogy: Like the unwritten rules of a shared apartment building: nobody signed anything, yet everyone depends on it.
nuance.etymology: Compact from Latin compactus, pressed together, from compacere, to bind together.
common_mistakes: Stressing compact on the second syllable; as a noun it is KAHM-pakt.
Confusing compact (agreement) with compact (small); in this phrase it means agreement.

senses.definition: A person (often a woman) of social prominence, considered to be an influential figure.
senses.example: The socialite arrived at the gala in a silver gown, greeting donors and photographers alike.

senses.definition: A person who goes to fashionable parties and is often written about in the newspapers, etc.

core.definition: A wealthy and well-known person who often attends fashionable parties and events and is frequently covered in newspapers, magazines, and gossip columns.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, SOH. The final syllable rhymes with light, and the middle syllable is weak and reduced to a schwa.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to somewhat negative. It can suggest glamor, but it often implies a focus on parties and appearances rather than serious work.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use socialite mainly for wealthy people in New York, Palm Beach, or other fashionable cities who appear in society news and gossip. It is common in media and everyday talk about celebrities and rich families. Calling someone a socialite may be a compliment for style or a mild jab at frivolity, so context matters. It is rarely used for ordinary people at parties.

distinctions.note: A celebrity is famous for entertainment, sports, or achievement, while a socialite is known mainly for wealth, social events, and presence in fashionable circles.
A philanthropist is known for giving money to causes, while a socialite may be known for attending parties and charity galas without being a major donor.

examples.everyday: My aunt loves reading about the socialites in the Sunday paper, especially who wore what at the gala.
examples.professional: Our PR team wants a socialite at the product launch so the event gets attention in the society pages.
examples.analytical: The figure of the socialite reveals how modern status depends on visibility, since wealth alone is not enough without public display.

nuance.analogy: Like a bright light in a crowded room: people notice the socialite because she is always where the attention is.
nuance.etymology: From social plus -ite, a suffix denoting a member of a group or a follower of a movement.
common_mistakes: Confusing socialite with socialist, which is a political term.
Using socialite for any friendly or outgoing person, when it usually means a wealthy, well-known member of high society.

socialite.etymology: From *social* + *-ite*, perhaps as a play on social light, in imitation of words in *-ite*.

senses.definition: In a social manner; sociably.
In social contexts.
senses.example: socially awkward

core.definition: In a way that involves other people or friendly interaction; in social situations, not professional or personal ones.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the final syllable is a short, light 'ee', not 'eye'. The 'ci' is pronounced sh, not s.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; the phrase 'socially awkward' is mildly negative, while 'socially active' is positive.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use socially in phrases such as socially acceptable, socially awkward, and socially distanced, which became common during COVID-19. It is also used for relationships outside work, as in 'I know him socially.' Do not use it to mean 'on social media'; say 'on social media' instead.

distinctions.note: Sociably describes a person's friendly, pleasant manner; socially describes the context or setting in which something happens.
Social is an adjective used before nouns (social life); socially is an adverb that modifies adjectives or verbs (socially awkward).

examples.everyday: I see my coworkers mostly at work, but I don't really know them socially.
examples.professional: Our team has lunch together, but we keep things professional and only connect socially at the holiday party.
examples.analytical: Categories such as class and race are socially constructed, which is why sociologists study how they change over time.

nuance.analogy: Socially is like a stage direction: it tells you the setting where the action happens, not the personality of the actor.
nuance.etymology: From social (Latin socialis) plus the adverb suffix -ly.
common_mistakes: Confusing socially with sociably: 'He behaved sociably at the party' describes friendliness, while 'socially' describes the setting.
Pronouncing the 'ci' as s (SOH-see-uh-lee) instead of sh.

senses.definition: Encoded computer instructions, usually modifiable (unless stored in some form of unalterable memory such as ROM).
senses.example: Some software will only run on a particular platform.

senses.definition: Soft goods, such as textiles.
senses.example: The old drapery shop sold linens, lace, and other software alongside its buttons and thread.

senses.definition: The human beings involved in warfare, as opposed to hardware such as weapons and vehicles.
senses.example: The general said training the software mattered more than buying new hardware for the army.

senses.definition: (dated) Recorded music content, as opposed to the hardware necessary for reproducing it.
senses.example: My grandfather's software was a shelf of records and tapes that he played every Sunday.
senses.label: dated

core.definition: Computer programs and instructions that tell hardware what to do, such as apps, operating systems and other digital tools.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, and the second syllable is a lighter secondary. The t is often silent in fast speech, and the ending has a clear r, so say WAIR, not soft-wahr or soft-wear.

nuance.connotation: Neutral.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use software in everyday talk for apps and programs, as in 'I need a software update' or 'This software is slow.' It is normally uncountable, so you say 'a piece of software' or 'a software package', not 'softwares'. In technical settings, software is contrasted with hardware and firmware.

distinctions.note: Hardware is the physical machines and components; software is the instructions that run on them.
Firmware is software stored permanently on a device's chip, such as a router's startup code; software is the broader category.
An app is a type of software designed for a specific task, usually on a phone or computer; software is the general term.

examples.everyday: My phone needs a software update, so it'll restart tonight while I'm asleep.
examples.professional: We need to ship the new billing software by Friday, so let's cut anything nonessential from the sprint.
examples.analytical: Software mediates our reasoning in ways philosophers have only begun to examine, since code encodes assumptions about what counts as relevant.

nuance.analogy: Software is the recipe; hardware is the kitchen and its appliances.
nuance.etymology: Coined in the 1950s from soft, meaning non-physical, plus ware, meaning goods, in contrast with hardware.
common_mistakes: Making software plural as softwares; it is usually uncountable, so say pieces of software or software packages.
Pronouncing the final syllable as wahr or wear; the American form is WAIR, with a clear r.

software.etymology: Computing sense from *soft* + *-ware*, by contrast with *hardware* (“the computer itself”).

senses.definition: Comfort or consolation in a time of loneliness or distress.
senses.example: You cannot put a monetary value on emotional solace.

senses.definition: A source of comfort or consolation.
To give solace to; comfort; cheer; console.
senses.example: Her grandmother's gentle voice solaced her after the funeral, though nothing could ease the grief.

senses.definition: To allay or assuage.
senses.example: The cold compress solaced the burn on his hand and eased the stinging.

senses.definition: To take comfort; to be cheered.
senses.example: After the loss, she solaced herself in her garden and her old books.

core.definition: Comfort or consolation that relieves sadness, loneliness, or distress; something that brings such comfort.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and make the second syllable a short, reduced i, so it sounds like SAH-lis, not suh-LAYCE. The final s is soft, not a z.

nuance.connotation: Positive; it suggests comfort in grief or hardship, and it is gentle rather than cheerful.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use solace in writing, sympathy cards, and speeches about loss, and it sounds warm and serious. In everyday talk, people more often say 'comfort' or 'a little relief.' A natural reply to someone who offers solace might be 'Thanks, that helps.'

distinctions.note: Comfort is the everyday word for physical or emotional ease; solace is more formal and suggests consolation in sorrow or loss.
Consolation is the act or thing that consoles, and can be a small prize or silver lining; solace stresses the feeling of relief in distress.

examples.everyday: I found some solace in my dog's company after the move.
examples.professional: Our team found some solace in the fact that the outage affected only one region, although the customers were still upset.
examples.analytical: The poem finds solace in the rhythm of the seasons rather than in any promise of heaven, so its consolation stays within nature.

nuance.analogy: Like a warm blanket on a cold night: it does not remove the cold, but it makes the night bearable.
nuance.etymology: From Latin solacium, comfort, related to solari, to comfort.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it as suh-LAYCE, which is not standard American English; say SAH-lis.
Confusing it with solitude, which means being alone; solace means comfort.
nuance.biblical_note: The Bible does not often use the English word solace, but it describes comfort in grief. Psalm 23:4 says the shepherd's rod and staff comfort the psalmist in the valley of death. 2 Corinthians 1:3-4 calls God the God of all comfort, who comforts believers in their affliction. The Hebrew naḥam (נָחַם) and the Greek paraklēsis (παράκλησις) carry the idea of comfort or consolation.

solace.etymology: From Old French *solas*, from Latin *sōlācium* (“consolation”), root from Proto-Indo-European **selh₂-* (“mercy, comfort”).

senses.definition: Only.
Unmarried (especially of a woman); widowed.
senses.example: Her great-aunt remained sole after her husband's death in 1952, never remarrying.

senses.definition: Unique; unsurpassed.
senses.example: The sole brilliance of this gem.

senses.definition: With independent power; unfettered.
senses.example: A sole authority.

senses.definition: The bottom of a shoe or boot.
senses.example: The sole of my hiking boot came loose halfway up the trail.

senses.definition: Solea solea, a flatfish of the family Soleidae; a true sole.
senses.example: Pan-fried sole with lemon butter is the chef's most popular dish tonight.

senses.definition: A flatfish resembling those of the family Soleidae.
senses.example: Flounder and sole look alike, but the fishmonger swore this one was a sole.

senses.definition: The bottom or lower part of anything, or that on which anything rests in standing.
senses.example: Check that the sole of the wooden stand can bear the weight of the statue.

senses.definition: The bottom of the body of a plow; the slade.
senses.example: The blacksmith replaced the worn sole of the plow before spring planting.

senses.definition: The bottom of a furrow.
senses.example: The plow cut a deep furrow, leaving the sole packed hard beneath the soil.

senses.definition: The end section of the chanter of a set of bagpipes.
senses.example: The piper's chanter had a cracked sole, so the lowest notes wouldn't sound.

senses.definition: The horny substance under a horse's foot, which protects the more tender parts.
senses.example: The farrier trimmed the hoof and checked the sole for bruising.

senses.definition: The seat or bottom of a mine; applied to horizontal veins or lodes.
senses.example: The miners reached the sole of the coal seam at about 400 feet.

senses.definition: The bottom or plantar surface of the foot.
senses.example: The podiatrist examined the sole of his foot for blisters after the marathon.

senses.definition: The bottom of an embrasure.
senses.example: Musket fire from the sole of the embrasure covered the bridge approach.

senses.definition: A piece of timber attached to the lower part of the rudder, to make it even with the false keel.
senses.example: The shipwright bolted a new sole to the rudder before launching the sloop.

senses.definition: The floor inside the cabin of a yacht or boat.
senses.example: We stowed the life jackets beneath the sole of the cabin before the storm hit.

senses.definition: To put a sole on a shoe or a boot.
