senses.example: The cobbler will sole the boots and stitch the torn leather by Friday.

core.definition: Being the only one of its kind; the only person or thing involved.

pronunciation.tip: Sole sounds exactly like soul, so context matters. Make the final l clear and avoid adding a vowel, so it is 'sohl', not 'soh-luh'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; emphasizes exclusivity and often has a formal or legal tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'sole' in formal writing, legal and business documents, and careful speech, as in 'sole owner' or 'sole responsibility'. In casual conversation most people say 'only' or 'just', as in 'I'm the only one who can go'. 'Sole' usually comes directly before a noun.

distinctions.note: 'Only' is more flexible and everyday, and can go before or after a word; 'sole' is more formal and comes almost always before a noun.
'Single' stresses that there is one, often among many; 'sole' stresses that there is no other.
'Solo' means performed or done alone; 'sole' means the only one of its type, not necessarily alone.

examples.everyday: I'm the sole driver in our house, so I'll take you to the airport.
examples.professional: I'm the sole reviewer for the model change, so send it to me before Thursday.
examples.analytical: Descartes made the thinking self the sole foundation of certainty, a move that has shaped modern epistemology.

nuance.analogy: Like the only key that opens a particular lock, a sole person or thing has no rival.
nuance.etymology: From Latin solus, alone; the same root gives 'solo' and 'solitary'.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'sole' (only) with 'soul', which sounds the same and is spelled differently.
Placing 'sole' after the noun, as in 'the reason sole', which sounds wrong.
Confusing 'sole' (only) with 'solo' (performed alone).

sole.etymology: From Middle English *sole*, *soule*, from Old French *sol*, *soul* (“alone”), from Latin *sōlus* (“alone, single, solitary, lonely”).

senses.definition: A person who lives alone; a recluse or hermit.
senses.example: The old man was a solitaire who rarely left his cabin at the edge of the forest.

senses.definition: A game for one person, played on a board with pegs or balls, in which the object is, beginning with all the places filled except one, to remove all but one of the pieces by "jumping", as in draughts.
senses.example: Grandpa played peg solitaire on the wooden board, carefully jumping pegs until only one remained.

senses.definition: Any of various card games that can be played by one person.
senses.example: On slow afternoons at the front desk, I play solitaire on the computer to pass time.

senses.definition: Ellipsis of Rodrigues solitaire (Pezophaps solitaria), an extinct bird related to the dodo.
Ellipsis of Réunion solitaire (Raphus solitarius, now Threskiornis solitarius), an extinct bird formerly believed to be related to the dodo.
One of several American species of bird in the genus Myadestes in the thrush family.
senses.example: Birders in the Ozarks hoped to spot a solitaire perched in the hemlocks along the creek.

senses.definition: A single gem, usually a diamond, mounted in a piece of jewelry by itself.
senses.example: She wore her grandmother's engagement ring, a simple solitaire set in thin gold.

senses.definition: Living or being alone; solitary.
senses.example: After the divorce, he preferred a solitaire existence, reading and walking alone on weekends.

core.definition: A card game for one player, usually Klondike, in which the player arranges cards in a set order; also a single-player board game with pegs.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on the last syllable, TAIR, which rhymes with 'air.' The first two syllables are weak, so 'sah-luh' is spoken quickly and the 'r' is clearly pronounced.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a common word for a familiar game, and a diamond solitaire is a positive term for a ring.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'solitaire' for the one-player card game that comes on most computers, and they also use it for a diamond ring with a single stone. In British English the card game is called 'patience,' which Americans would not naturally use. If you say 'solitaire' at an American office, people will know you mean the card game on the computer.

distinctions.note: 'Solitary' is an adjective meaning alone or single, while 'solitaire' is a noun for a particular game or ring.
'Patience' is the British name for the one-player card game; Americans use 'solitaire' instead.

examples.everyday: I'm playing solitaire on my phone while I wait for the bus.
examples.professional: During the long build, I play a quick round of solitaire to clear my head before the next code review.
examples.analytical: The solitaire game models a closed system in which every move must reduce the number of pieces, which is why it has a unique winning path.

nuance.analogy: Like a puzzle book you finish at your own pace: no opponent, just you and the cards on the table.
nuance.etymology: From French 'solitaire' (solitary), from Latin 'solitarius' (alone).
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it as 'SOL-ih-tair' with stress on the first syllable; Americans stress the last syllable.
Using 'patience' in American conversation, where people will think you mean something else.

senses.definition: Aloneness; the state of being alone, solitary, or by oneself.
A lonely or deserted place.
senses.example: The hermit built his cabin in a remote solitude high above the timberline.

core.definition: The state of being alone, often peacefully, without other people nearby.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on the first syllable, SAHL. The final syllable rhymes with 'food', not with 'put' or 'cut'.

nuance.connotation: Usually positive or neutral, suggesting peace, reflection, or restful quiet. It can become negative if the aloneness feels unwanted or lonely.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use solitude in conversation about retreats, nature, prayer, or taking time for oneself, for example 'I need some solitude after work.' It is a bit more formal than 'time alone', which is the everyday choice. In a sad context, people often say 'loneliness' instead, since solitude suggests a chosen state.

distinctions.note: Solitude is being alone, often by choice and without distress; loneliness is the painful feeling of wanting company.
Isolation usually implies being cut off from others, often against one's will; solitude is a more positive, voluntary state.

examples.everyday: I like to get up early and enjoy a little solitude with my coffee before the kids wake up.
examples.professional: Our architect designed the reading room to give researchers some solitude while still being close to the main floor.
examples.analytical: For the Desert Fathers, solitude was not an escape from others but a discipline that opened the heart to God.

nuance.analogy: Solitude is like a quiet room in a busy house: you are alone, but the walls are there to give you rest, not to shut you out.
nuance.etymology: From Latin solitudo, from solus 'alone'.
common_mistakes: Using 'a solitude' as a countable noun; in the general sense it is usually uncountable, though 'a solitude' is acceptable for a remote place.
Confusing solitude with solitary as an adjective; 'solitude' is the noun.
Pronouncing the last syllable as 'tyood' or 'tude' rhyming with 'rude'; the usual American form rhymes with 'food'.
nuance.biblical_note: The Greek word behind many passages about solitude is erēmos (ἔρημος), meaning 'desert, wilderness, or lonely place'. Mark 1:35 says Jesus went out to a lonely place to pray early in the morning. Luke 5:16 says Jesus often withdrew to lonely places to pray. These passages show Jesus taking time apart to pray, a practice Christians often follow in their own solitude.

solitude.etymology: From Middle English *solitude*, from Old French *solitude*, from Latin *sōlitūdō*.

senses.definition: Initialism of state of the art.

core.definition: Short for 'state of the art', meaning the most advanced level of performance or technology at present.

pronunciation.tip: Most American AI and machine learning practitioners say SOTA as one word, SOH-tuh, though some spell out S-O-T-A. Stress falls on the first syllable, and the final vowel is reduced.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It signals that a result or system is among the best available, but it can sound boastful if overused.
nuance.usage_note: In American research labs, startups, and engineering meetings, 'SOTA' is a fast, informal shorthand. In formal writing, use 'state of the art' or 'the current best results'. Saying 'We're at SOTA on this benchmark' is normal among specialists, but a general audience may need the full phrase.

distinctions.note: 'State of the art' is the full phrase and is suitable for any audience. 'SOTA' is a shorthand used mostly by specialists and in papers.
'Best-in-class' compares products or companies within a market. 'SOTA' describes the highest technical level reached in a research field.

examples.everyday: My friend says his new phone has a SOTA camera, although I'm not sure what that really means.
examples.professional: Our model beats the previous SOTA by three points on the held-out benchmark, so we'll write it up next week.
examples.analytical: Reporting SOTA as a single number hides the variance across random seeds and datasets, which can mislead readers.

nuance.analogy: SOTA is like the front of a race: the leader of the pack at a given moment, and it changes as others catch up.
nuance.etymology: Initialism of the phrase 'state of the art'.
common_mistakes: Writing 'state of art' without 'the'; the correct phrase is 'the state of the art'.
Spelling it out as S-O-T-A in speech when many specialists say the word 'SOH-tuh'.

senses.definition: To make distinct or separate from what is common, particularly:
To become distinct or separate from what is common, particularly:
To focus one's study upon a particular skill, field, topic, or genre.
To focus one's business upon a particular item or service.
To be known or notorious for some specialty.
To train (someone) in a specialty.
To make distinct or separate due to form or function.
(rare) To specify: to mention specifically.
senses.label: rare

senses.definition: (uncommon) To narrow in scope.
senses.label: uncommon

core.definition: To focus your study, training, or work on one particular field, skill, product, or type of business.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the 'ci' is pronounced 'sh'. The final syllable is 'lyze', with a strong long 'eye' vowel, which is often shortened by non-native speakers to a plain 'z' sound.

nuance.connotation: Positive; it suggests expertise and dedication, though it can sound limiting if someone wants a broad career.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'specialize' in everyday talk about careers, medicine, and business, as in 'She specialized in pediatric surgery' or 'This shop specializes in vintage furniture.' It is common in both casual and professional speech. The usual preposition is 'in', not 'on'.

distinctions.note: Major is the American college term for a field of study, while specialize means to focus your work or expertise, which can happen after college.
Focus is a general word for concentrating attention, while specialize implies developing expertise or offering a limited range of products or services.

examples.everyday: That little bakery specializes in sourdough, so the cookies are only okay.
examples.professional: Our consulting firm specializes in cloud migration for healthcare companies.
examples.analytical: Scholars who specialize in one period of history often develop insights that generalists cannot reach, but they risk losing sight of broader patterns.

nuance.analogy: To specialize is like a river narrowing into a deep channel: it flows in one direction with more force, but it covers less ground than a wide delta.
nuance.etymology: From special plus the verb-forming suffix -ize.
common_mistakes: Saying 'specialize on' rather than 'specialize in', which is the standard American preposition.
Pronouncing 'specialize' with stress on the second syllable, as in 'spe-SHAL-ize'.
Using 'specialize' to mean 'specialty', which is a noun, so you should say 'her specialty', not 'her specialize'.

senses.definition: To state explicitly, or in detail, or as a condition.
To include in a specification.
senses.example: The contract specifies that all lumber must be treated against termites.

senses.definition: To bring about a specific result.
senses.example: The new policy was meant to specify faster approvals for small business loans.

core.definition: To state something clearly and in detail, especially as a requirement or condition.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The middle syllable is a reduced schwa, so say SPES-ih-fy, not SPES-ee-fy.

nuance.connotation: Neutral, neither positive nor negative.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use specify in writing, meetings, and business to ask for exact details, such as Please specify the size. In casual speech, they often say tell me exactly or let me know. Saying specify in a casual conversation can sound a little stiff but is still correct.

distinctions.note: State is general, while specify means giving details or conditions precisely.
Define gives the meaning of a term, while specify sets out particular details or requirements.

examples.everyday: Can you specify which bread you want on the sandwich?
examples.professional: Please specify the deadline and the budget in the project brief so the team can plan properly.
examples.analytical: The author fails to specify the conditions under which the principle holds, which leaves the claim open to counterexamples.

nuance.analogy: To specify is like drawing a map with exact street names instead of just pointing toward a city.
nuance.etymology: From Latin specificare, to make specific, from species (kind) and facere (to make).
common_mistakes: Using specify without an object, as in He will specify later, when the object is usually the details.
Pronouncing the middle vowel as ee instead of a reduced schwa.

specify.etymology: From Middle English *specifien*, from Old French *specifier*, *especefier*, or directly from Medieval Latin *specificō*, from *specificus* (“specific”).

senses.definition: Shaped as a sphere; being a sphere.
Of, or pertaining to, spheres.
Of a coordinate system, specifying the location of a point in a plane by using a radius and two angles.
senses.example: We converted the satellite's position from Cartesian to spherical coordinates for the model.

senses.definition: Of or relating to the heavenly orbs, or to the sphere or spheres in which, according to ancient astronomy and astrology, they were set.
senses.example: Medieval astronomers imagined the planets moving within spherical shells of crystal.

senses.definition: Of a multivariate probability distribution, to have a covariance matrix equal to the identity matrix up to a multiplicative factor.
senses.example: a spherical Gaussian distribution

core.definition: Shaped like a sphere, round like a ball or globe, with every point on the surface equally far from the center.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, SFAIR. The middle syllable is a short, weak vowel, and the final -cal is 'kul', not 'kal'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and precise. It is used in everyday description, math, and science.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say round for everyday objects like balls or fruit, and use spherical when they need precision or are discussing geometry, physics, or design. Saying spherical for a tennis ball is fine but sounds a bit technical. In a casual setting, round is the default.

distinctions.note: Round is the everyday word for shape and can describe flat shapes too. Spherical is precise and means three-dimensional and equal in all directions.
Circular describes a flat two-dimensional shape. Spherical describes a three-dimensional ball shape.
Globular means ball-shaped but may be irregular or lumpy. Spherical means truly sphere-shaped.

examples.everyday: This ice cream scoop makes a perfectly spherical ball every time.
examples.professional: The model assumes the planet is spherical, which simplifies the gravity calculation for the first pass.
examples.analytical: Plato's cosmos was spherical, with the earth at the center and the heavens revolving around it in perfect circles.

nuance.analogy: Like a basketball, where every point on the surface is the same distance from the center.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin sphaericus, from Greek sphaira, meaning 'ball' or 'sphere'.
common_mistakes: Dropping the middle syllable and saying 'sfair-kul'.
Using spherical for flat, two-dimensional shapes; use circular or round for those.

senses.definition: To rotate, revolve, gyrate (usually quickly); to partially or completely rotate to face another direction.
senses.example: I spun myself around a few times.

senses.definition: To enter, or remain in, a spin (abnormal stalled flight mode).
senses.example: The student pilot stalled the trainer and it began to spin toward the ground.

senses.definition: To cause one's aircraft to enter or remain in a spin (abnormal stalled flight mode).
senses.example: The instructor warned never to spin the plane intentionally near the ground.

senses.definition: To make yarn by twisting and winding fibers together.
senses.example: They spin the cotton into thread.

senses.definition: To present, describe, or interpret, or to introduce a bias or slant, so as to give something a favorable or advantageous appearance.
senses.example: The campaign team tried to spin the senator's vote as a win for working families.

senses.definition: To form into thin strips or ribbons, as with sugar.
senses.example: Pastry students learned to spin sugar into delicate threads for the dessert.

senses.definition: To form (a web, a cocoon, silk, etc.) from threads produced by the extrusion of a viscid, transparent liquid, which hardens on coming into contact with the air; said of the spider, the silkworm, etc.
senses.example: Each night the garden spider spins a fresh web between the fence posts.

senses.definition: To shape, as malleable sheet metal, into a hollow form, by bending or buckling it by pressing against it with a smooth hand tool or roller while the metal revolves, as in a lathe.
senses.example: The craftsman spun the aluminum disk into a bowl on the lathe.

senses.definition: To move swiftly.
senses.example: to spin along the road in a carriage, on a bicycle, etc.

senses.definition: To stream or issue in a thread or a small current or jet.
senses.example: Blood spins from a vein.

senses.definition: To wait in a loop until some condition becomes true.
senses.example: The program will spin on the lock until the other thread releases the resource.

senses.definition: To rotate into the gravel or managing to remain on the straight as a result of bad weather.
senses.example: His car spun in the rains just after finishing lap four.

senses.definition: To play (vinyl records, etc.) as a disc jockey.
senses.example: He spun vinyl records at the wedding until midnight, taking requests from the crowd.

senses.definition: To use an exercise bicycle, especially as part of a gym class.
senses.example: Every Tuesday she spins at six a.m. with a class of twenty people.

senses.definition: To ride a bicycle at a fast cadence.
senses.example: Watch how he spins up the hill, keeping his cadence high and his knees smooth.

senses.definition: To draw out tediously; prolong.
senses.example: to spin a yarn

senses.definition: To fish with a swivel or spoonbait.
senses.example: Early in the morning, I spin for bass with a small silver spoonbait near the reeds.

senses.definition: To make the ball move sideways when it bounces on the pitch.
senses.example: This pitch is usually preferred for spin than pace.

senses.definition: To move sideways when bouncing.
senses.example: Spinning the ball gave him figures of 7-48.

senses.definition: Circular motion, usually rapid.
senses.example: The car went into a spin.

senses.definition: A state of confusion or disorientation.
senses.example: My mind was in a spin.

senses.definition: A quantum angular momentum associated with subatomic particles, which also creates a magnetic moment.
senses.example: The electron's spin is a quantum property, which produces a magnetic moment.

senses.definition: A novel, creative variation of an existing thing or type; a twist.
senses.example: Her cover of the old folk song gives it a jazzy spin that surprised everyone.

senses.definition: A favorable comment or interpretation intended to bias opinion on an otherwise unpleasant situation.
senses.example: spin doctor

senses.definition: A condition of flight where a stalled aircraft is simultaneously pitching, yawing, and rolling in a spinning motion.
senses.example: The pilot recovered from the spin only after pushing the nose down and applying opposite rudder.

senses.definition: An abnormal condition in journal bearings where the bearing seizes to the rotating shaft and rotates inside the journal, destroying both the shaft and the journal.
senses.example: The engineers found a spin in the turbine's journal bearing that had scored the shaft.

senses.definition: A brief trip by vehicle, especially one made for pleasure.
senses.example: I'm off out for a spin in my new sports car.

senses.definition: A bundle of spun material; a mass of strands and filaments.
senses.example: The spinner loaded a fresh spin of wool onto the bobbin before starting the wheel.

senses.definition: A single play of a record; especially, one broadcast by a radio station.
senses.example: Let's give this classic LP another spin.

senses.definition: The use of an exercise bicycle, especially as part of a gym class.
Clipping of spinnaker.
A special interest of an autistic person.
Rotation of the ball as it flies through the air; sideways movement of the ball as it bounces.
(dated) An unmarried woman; a spinster.
senses.label: dated

core.definition: To rotate quickly around a central point, or to make something turn quickly around its center.

pronunciation.tip: Use a short i, as in sit, not a long ee. The n is clear at the end, so do not add a vowel after it.

nuance.connotation: Neutral for physical rotation. Putting spin on news means presenting facts favorably, which sounds slightly negative.
nuance.usage_note: Everyday uses include a washing machine spinning, a dancer spinning, or a wheel spinning. Americans also say the campaign put a positive spin on the news for presenting facts in a favorable way, which is informal and a little suspicious. Take the car for a spin is a casual, friendly phrase for a short drive.

distinctions.note: Turn is the general word for changing direction or position; spin implies fast, continuous rotation.
Rotate is more technical or formal and often describes steady, controlled turning around an axis.
Twirl is a playful, light movement, often of the hands or body; spin can apply to any fast rotation.

examples.everyday: The dryer is still spinning, so the towels aren't ready yet.
examples.professional: Let's spin up a new test cluster and run the training job there before we merge the branch.
examples.analytical: The dancer's spin shows how rotation can express freedom while still obeying the laws of motion.

nuance.analogy: A spinning top stays upright because it turns around a steady center point.
nuance.etymology: From Old English spinnan, to draw out thread by twisting fibers.
common_mistakes: Using a long ee vowel, as in speen; the vowel is a short i.
Saying spinned for the past tense; the correct form is spun.

spin.etymology: From Middle English *spinnen*, from Old English *spinnan*, from Proto-Germanic **spinnaną*, from Proto-Indo-European **penh₁-*.

senses.definition: A series of bones situated at the back from the head to the pelvis of a human, or from the head to the tail of an animal, enclosing the spinal cord and providing support for the thorax and abdomen.
senses.example: The chiropractor found that two vertebrae in her spine were slightly misaligned.

senses.definition: Courage or assertiveness.
senses.example: It took real spine to tell the committee chairman that his plan would fail.

senses.definition: Something resembling a backbone, such as a ridge, or a long, central structure from which other structures radiate.
senses.example: The hiking trail followed a rocky spine along the top of the mountain range.

senses.definition: The narrow, bound edge of a book that encloses the inner edges of the pages, facing outwards when the book is on a shelf and typically bearing the title and the author's and publisher's name.
senses.example: The title was printed so clearly on the spine that I found the novel instantly.

senses.definition: Ellipsis of dendritic spine.
A linear payscale operated by some large organizations that allows flexibility for local and specific conditions.
senses.example: The new pay spine gives each nurse a clear step for every year of service.

senses.definition: The stiffness of an arrow.
senses.example: The archer chose a shaft with more spine for his heavier bow.

senses.definition: A central part which supports a whole; core.
senses.example: Honesty is the spine of our company, and every decision rests on it.

senses.definition: A pointed, fairly rigid protuberance or needlelike structure on an animal, shell, mushroom or plant. The botanical term technically refers to such a structure derived from a leaf or part of a leaf.
senses.example: The cactus was covered in long sharp spines that made pruning it painful.

senses.definition: The heartwood of trees.
senses.example: Old-growth oak develops a dark spine that resists rot far better than sapwood.

senses.definition: A tall mass of viscous lava extruded from a volcano.
senses.example: Geologists climbed the crater to photograph the new lava spine rising above the dome.

core.definition: The column of bones running down the back from the skull to the pelvis, which supports the body and protects the spinal cord.

pronunciation.tip: Use a long i, rhyming with mine. The final n is clear, and you should not add an ee sound after the i.

nuance.connotation: Neutral for the anatomical sense. As courage, spine is positive and admiring.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say spine for the back's bones in medical or everyday talk, but backbone is more common in speech. Spine meaning courage is informal: she finally found the spine to speak up is a natural phrase. In plants and animals, spine means a sharp point, like a cactus spine.

distinctions.note: Backbone is the more common everyday word; spine is more anatomical, though both can also mean courage or determination.
A thorn is a sharp woody point on a plant; a spine is a sharp point on a plant or animal, like a cactus or hedgehog.

examples.everyday: She finally had the spine to tell her boss the schedule was unfair.
examples.professional: The spine of the project is the shared data pipeline that every team depends on.
examples.analytical: The argument's spine is a single claim: that moral worth depends on the capacity to suffer.

nuance.analogy: The spine is like the central beam of a building, holding up the rest of the structure.
nuance.etymology: From Latin spina, thorn or backbone, through Old French espine.
common_mistakes: Confusing spine with spinal; spine is the noun, and spinal is the adjective.
Using spine to mean a bad temper; the common figurative meaning is courage, not anger.

senses.definition: Filled with, or showing, spite; having a desire to annoy or harm.
senses.example: She sent a spiteful email to her former roommate after the argument about rent.

core.definition: Showing a deliberate desire to annoy, hurt or get back at someone, often in a petty way.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, SPITE. The final -ful is unstressed and reduced to a short vowel, so say SPITE-ful, not SPITE-fool.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it describes people, remarks or acts meant to hurt in a petty way.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use spiteful for people, comments and acts that are meant to hurt in a petty way, such as 'a spiteful comment' or 'a spiteful ex.' It is stronger than mean but softer than vicious. In formal writing, use malicious when the intent is serious harm. The word is common in everyday speech, news and online comments.

distinctions.note: Malicious implies intent to cause serious harm, while spiteful describes smaller, petty meanness meant to annoy or thwart.
Vindictive suggests revenge for a real or perceived wrong, but spiteful can involve no provocation at all.
Mean is broader and milder, covering everyday unkindness, while spiteful stresses a deliberate wish to hurt or irritate.

examples.everyday: That was a spiteful thing to say, especially in front of the kids.
examples.professional: Please keep the review comments constructive, because spiteful remarks hurt morale and slow the team down.
examples.analytical: A spiteful act differs from a vengeful one because it need not respond to any prior injury at all.

nuance.analogy: Like a sour note played on purpose just to irritate the whole room.
nuance.etymology: Formed from spite, itself shortened from despite, plus the suffix -ful, meaning full of.
common_mistakes: Spelling it spitefull with a double l; the correct spelling is spiteful.
Pronouncing the final syllable as fool, when it is a short, reduced vowel.

senses.definition: A person in a marriage or marital relationship.
senses.example: People should treat their spouses with respect.

senses.definition: (dated) To wed; to espouse.
senses.example: The young couple hoped to spouse before the harvest, as their parents wished.
senses.label: dated

senses.definition: Someone or something that squeezes.
senses.example: I made juice with a lemon squeezer.

senses.definition: A piece of foundry apparatus for shaping a ball of puddled iron.
senses.example: The foundry worker fed the glowing ball of puddled iron into the squeezer to shape it.

senses.definition: A playing card that has its value shown in a corner such that a closely arranged hand may be studied (originally designed for poker but now standard).
senses.example: Before betting, she tucked the squeezer into her hand and studied its corner indices carefully.

senses.definition: Someone or something that coerces; one who puts the squeeze on someone.
senses.example: The loan shark was a brutal squeezer who never let his debtors breathe.

senses.definition: A hand job, an instance of male masturbation, or manual sex performed on a man.

core.definition: A kitchen tool or a person that squeezes, especially a hand tool for pressing juice from citrus.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The final -er is a weak, r-colored vowel, so it sounds like 'zur' and not a strong 'air'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a practical, everyday word for kitchen tools.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use squeezer mostly for kitchen tools such as a lemon squeezer or garlic squeezer. For a person, it sounds odd, so say 'someone who squeezes' instead. You will rarely hear it in other senses.

distinctions.note: A juicer extracts juice from whole fruit, often with a motor; a squeezer is usually a simple hand tool for citrus halves.
A reamer is a cone-shaped citrus tool that you twist into the fruit; a squeezer presses the fruit between two parts.

examples.everyday: Hand me the lemon squeezer so I can make some lemonade for the kids.
examples.professional: The kitchen team ordered a commercial citrus squeezer for the new café opening next month.
examples.analytical: The garlic squeezer, a small mechanical device, shows how kitchen design turns physical effort into efficiency.

nuance.analogy: Like a hand wringing out a sponge, turning pressure into juice.
nuance.etymology: From the verb squeeze, with the -er suffix for a tool or agent.
common_mistakes: Using squeezer for a person who squeezes, which sounds unnatural
Stressing the final syllable instead of the first

senses.definition: An unsteady movement of the body in walking or standing as if one were about to fall; a reeling motion.
senses.example: the stagger of a drunken man

senses.definition: Bewilderment; perplexity.
senses.example: Faced with the sudden price hike, the shoppers stood in silent stagger.

senses.definition: The spacing out of various actions over time.
senses.example: The team used a stagger in release dates so servers would not all update at the same moment.

senses.definition: The difference in circumference between the left and right tires on a racing vehicle. It is used on oval tracks to make the car turn better in the corners.
senses.example: The race engineer adjusted the stagger on the front tires to help the car turn left.

senses.definition: The horizontal positioning of a biplane, triplane, or multiplane's wings in relation to one another.
senses.example: The vintage biplane's wings had a noticeable stagger, with the upper wing set ahead of the lower.

senses.definition: A disease of horses and other animals, attended by reeling, unsteady gait or sudden falling.
senses.example: parasitic staggers

senses.definition: To sway unsteadily, reel, or totter.
senses.example: She began to stagger across the room.

senses.definition: In standing or walking, to sway from one side to the other as if about to fall; to stand or walk unsteadily; to reel or totter.
senses.example: She began to stagger across the room.

senses.definition: To cause to reel or totter.
senses.example: The powerful blow of his opponent's fist staggered the boxer.

senses.definition: To cease to stand firm; to begin to give way; to fail.
senses.example: The enemy staggers.

senses.definition: Doubt, waver, be shocked.
senses.example: He will stagger the committee when he presents his report.

senses.definition: To begin to doubt and waver in purposes; to become less confident or determined; to hesitate.
senses.example: Don't let the criticism make you stagger; keep your focus on the goal.

senses.definition: To cause to doubt and waver; to make to hesitate; to make less steady or confident; to shock.
senses.example: He will stagger the committee when he presents his report.

senses.definition: Have multiple groups doing the same thing in a uniform fashion, but starting at different, evenly spaced, times or places (attested from 1856).
senses.example: We will stagger the starting positions for the race on the oval track.

senses.definition: To arrange (a series of parts) on each side of a median line alternately, as the spokes of a wheel or the rivets of a boiler seam.
senses.example: The boilermaker staggered the rivets along the seam, alternating sides of the median line.

senses.definition: To arrange similar objects such that each is ahead or above and to one side of the next.
senses.example: We will stagger the starting positions for the race on the oval track.

senses.definition: To schedule in intervals or at different times.
senses.example: We will stagger the run so the faster runners can go first, then the joggers.

core.definition: To walk or stand unsteadily, swaying from side to side as if about to fall.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on the first syllable. The final syllable is a reduced American r-colored vowel, so do not pronounce it as a full ah or ay sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it describes unsteady movement or, in the noun sense, a schedule or sense of being overwhelmed.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use stagger for walking after a fall, illness, or too much alcohol, often as I staggered out of the room. It is also common in work contexts, such as staggering shifts or start times. Calling someone who is drunk staggering is normal, but it can sound unkind if said directly to them.

distinctions.note: Stumble means to trip or lose your footing briefly; stagger means to keep moving in an unsteady, swaying way.
Totter suggests an old or very weak person or a tall unstable object; stagger is more general and can describe anyone exhausted or drunk.

examples.everyday: After the long hike, I staggered into the cabin and collapsed on the couch.
examples.professional: We're going to stagger the release dates so the support team isn't overloaded on day one.
examples.analytical: The narrator staggers between grief and rage, and the prose itself seems to sway with him.

nuance.analogy: Like a boat rocking on rough water, moving forward but unable to hold a straight line.
nuance.etymology: From Middle English or Old Norse roots meaning to stumble or reel; the sense of spacing out things comes later.
common_mistakes: Using stagger for being slightly tired; it implies real unsteadiness.
Pronouncing the final syllable as a full ay sound.
nuance.biblical_note: Psalm 107:27 describes people who reel and stagger like drunken men at the end of their resources, and Isaiah 29:9 uses similar language about leaders who are confused and unsteady. The Hebrew words vary, and the image often points to helplessness rather than drunkenness alone.

stagger.etymology: From Middle English *stageren*, a variant of *stakeren*, from Old Norse *stakra* (“to stagger, sway, waver, swing, wobble”), frequentative of Old Norse *staka* (“to push, knock, bump into, stumble”).

senses.definition: Incredible, overwhelming, amazing.
senses.example: The army suffered a staggering defeat.

senses.definition: Lurching, floundering.
senses.example: The wounded soldier kept staggering across the field toward the medics.

senses.definition: The motion of one who staggers.
senses.example: His staggering up the stairs woke the whole house at midnight.

senses.definition: The condition of being staggered or amazed.
The spacing out of various actions over time.
senses.example: The staggering of shift start times reduced traffic jams at the hospital.

senses.definition: In animation, the repetition of a sequence of frames to show struggling effort.
senses.example: In the animation class, we studied staggering to make the lifting character look exhausted.

core.definition: Astonishing or overwhelming, so large, shocking, or impressive that it is hard to take in.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, STAG. The middle -er- is a weak, r-colored vowel in American speech, so say STAG-uh-ring, not stag-GER-ing.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to strong; it is often used for big numbers, costs, or shocking news, usually negative but sometimes positive for remarkable achievement.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use staggering for very large numbers, costs, or achievements, as in a staggering amount of debt or a staggering performance. It is a strong word, so do not use it for small surprises. The adverb staggeringly is also common, as in staggeringly expensive. A natural reply in conversation is It really is.

distinctions.note: Shocking stresses surprise or outrage; staggering stresses sheer size, scale, or force that overwhelms.
Stunning often sounds admiring and visual; staggering can be positive or negative and sounds more overwhelming.

examples.everyday: Have you seen what groceries cost now? It's staggering.
examples.professional: The migration project has a staggering number of dependencies, so we need to map them before we start.
examples.analytical: The sheer scale of human suffering is staggering, and it challenges any simple account of divine justice.

nuance.analogy: Like a punch you did not see coming, it knocks the breath out of you before you can react.
nuance.etymology: From Middle English staggeren, probably from Old Norse stakra (to push or cause to stumble).
common_mistakes: Confusing staggering with staggered; staggered means arranged at intervals or amazed, while staggering means overwhelming.
Using staggering for small or ordinary amounts; it is a strong word that needs a large scale.

senses.definition: The beginning of an activity.
senses.example: The movie was entertaining from start to finish.

senses.definition: A sudden involuntary movement.
senses.example: He woke with a start.

senses.definition: The beginning point of a race, a board game, etc.
senses.example: Captured pieces are returned to the start of the board.

senses.definition: An appearance in a sports game, horserace, etc. from the beginning of the event.
senses.example: Jones has been a substitute before, but made his first start for the team last Sunday.

senses.definition: A young plant germinated in a pot to be transplanted later.
senses.example: The tomato start was germinating in a small pot, waiting to be transplanted into the garden.

senses.definition: An initial advantage over somebody else; a head start.
senses.example: to get, or have, the start

senses.definition: An instance of starting.
senses.example: This is a fresh start, so let's leave last year's mistakes behind us.

senses.definition: A projection or protrusion; that which pokes out.
senses.example: A sharp start on the old fence post snagged my sleeve as I walked past.

senses.definition: The curved or inclined front and bottom of a water wheel bucket.
senses.example: Water pushed hard against the start of each bucket, turning the wheel slowly through the mill.

senses.definition: The arm, or level, of a gin, drawn around by a horse.
senses.example: The horse circled the field, pulling the start of the old gin around all day.

senses.definition: To begin, commence, initiate.
senses.example: to start a stream of water; to start a rumor; to start a business

senses.definition: To set in motion.
senses.example: to start a stream of water; to start a rumor; to start a business

senses.definition: To begin.
senses.example: The President fired the gun to start the footrace.

senses.definition: To ready the operation of a vehicle or machine.
senses.example: to start the engine

senses.definition: To put or raise (a question, an objection); to put forward (a subject for discussion).
senses.example: Before the meeting ends, I want to start a discussion about the new budget.

senses.definition: To bring onto being or into view; to originate; to invent.
senses.example: Our engineers hope to start a new trend in sustainable packaging next year.

senses.definition: To have its origin (at), begin.
senses.example: The speed limit is 50 km/h, starting at the edge of town.

senses.definition: To move suddenly, from a previous state of rest; to startle.
senses.example: The hounds started a fox.

senses.definition: To jerk, jump up, flinch, or draw back in surprise.
senses.example: The loud bang made me start, and I nearly dropped my coffee on the floor.

senses.definition: To awaken suddenly.
senses.example: The thunder would start me awake at three in the morning.

senses.definition: To disturb and set in motion; to alarm; to rouse; to cause to flee.
senses.example: The hounds started a fox.

senses.definition: To come loose, to break free of a firmly set position; to displace or loosen; to dislocate.
senses.example: the storm started the bolts in the vessel

senses.definition: To begin one's menstrual cycle.
senses.example: Have you started yet?

senses.definition: To put into play.
senses.example: Turn the key to start the engine, then let it warm up for a minute.

senses.definition: To pour out; to empty; to tap and begin drawing from.
senses.example: to start a water cask

core.definition: To begin doing something, or to cause an activity, process or machine to begin.

pronunciation.tip: It is one syllable with a strong r. Make the final t a crisp T, not a flap; the flap only happens before an unstressed vowel, as in 'starting', which sounds like 'STAHR-ding'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is one of the most general words in English for a beginning.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use start in almost every setting, from 'Let's start' in a meeting to 'the car won't start' at home. It can take a to-infinitive or -ing form, as in 'start to cry' or 'start crying', and both are natural. 'Commence' sounds stiff in everyday speech, so 'start' is the usual choice for meetings and classes.

distinctions.note: 'Begin' is more neutral and slightly more formal; 'start' is the everyday choice for practical beginnings, like starting a car or a meeting.
'Commence' is formal and often used for ceremonies or official proceedings; most Americans say 'start' in daily speech.

examples.everyday: Can we start with the appetizers while we wait for the rest of the group?
examples.professional: Let's start the meeting with a quick review of last sprint's bug list.
examples.analytical: Many theologians start with the nature of God, while others start with the human experience of need.

nuance.analogy: Like the starting gun at a race: the moment when everything else begins.
nuance.etymology: From Old English styrtan, meaning to leap or jump up.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the final t as a flap or dropping it, as in 'STAHR-duh' or 'STAHR', instead of a crisp T.
Using 'start' and 'start up' interchangeably, when 'start up' usually means powering on or launching something.

start.etymology: From Middle English *stert*, from the verb *sterten* (“to start, startle”).

senses.definition: Starvation.
senses.example: Rationing could not prevent the starving that swept through the villages that winter.

senses.definition: Extremely hungry.

core.definition: Extremely hungry, usually said in casual speech to mean very hungry.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable. The v is voiced, and the final ing is a short, unstressed syllable, not 'eeng.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral in casual speech, where it is hyperbole. In serious contexts, it refers to real starvation and sounds grim.
nuance.usage_note: Americans often say 'I'm starving!' as a joke about being very hungry before a meal. Used literally, starving describes people suffering from lack of food, so it should be used carefully when discussing hunger in the world. A natural reply to 'I'm starving' is 'Let's grab something to eat.'

distinctions.note: Hungry is the normal, neutral word, while starving is an exaggerated, informal way to say very hungry.
Starvation is the noun for the condition of dying from lack of food, while starving is an adjective in casual speech.

examples.everyday: Can we eat soon? I'm starving.
examples.professional: Sorry, I'm starving, can we move the meeting to lunch?
examples.analytical: Economists distinguish between chronic poverty and famine, since starving populations face different causes than the poor generally.

nuance.analogy: Saying you are starving is like saying a phone is almost dead: a vivid exaggeration of a real need.
nuance.etymology: From starve, from Old English steorfan, meaning to die.
common_mistakes: Using starving to mean just a little hungry in formal writing about real hunger.
Confusing starving with starved, which is used for being deprived of something.

conversation.text: Can we eat soon? I'm starving.
I skipped lunch, so I'm absolutely starving.
The kids were starving by the time the food came.
Hey, Mom, what's for dinner? I'm starving.
I haven't eaten all day, so I'm starving.
The kids came home from practice starving.

senses.definition: The skill of being a good statesman, the ability to perform well in political office.
senses.example: Her statesmanship during the budget crisis earned praise from members of both parties.

core.definition: The skill and wisdom of a statesman: leading a nation or government with long-term vision and principled judgment.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The -man- part is reduced to a quick 'muhn', and the final -ship has a short i.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It is high praise for principled leadership that looks beyond the next election.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use statesmanship in political writing, editorials, speeches and commentary to praise a leader who puts the country above partisan advantage. In everyday talk people say 'good leadership' or 'he handled that well.' Calling a politician a statesman is a strong compliment.

distinctions.note: Statecraft is the art of conducting government and diplomacy; statesmanship is the personal quality of wise, principled leadership within it.
Politics is the competition for power and votes; statesmanship rises above partisan advantage.

examples.everyday: Her decision to admit the mistake and apologize publicly showed real statesmanship, I thought.
examples.professional: The board needs statesmanship, not just clever tactics, to get the merger through without alienating employees.
examples.analytical: Statesmanship requires weighing the interests of generations not yet born against the pressures of the present election cycle.

nuance.analogy: Statesmanship is to politics what a good captain is to a ship: it steers for the destination, not for the next wave.
nuance.etymology: From statesman (state plus man) with -ship, meaning skill or quality of.
common_mistakes: Using statesmanlike as a noun; the noun is statesmanship
Stressing the last syllable; it is STAYTS-muhn-ship

senses.definition: A class that cannot be instantiated.

core.definition: A class in a programming language that cannot be instantiated and holds only static members, used to group related utility functions.

pronunciation.tip: In this noun phrase the main stress lands on CLASS, while static has a lighter secondary stress. The t inside static is quick and soft, almost a flap, between two vowels.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a precise technical term with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: American programmers use static class mainly in C#, where it is a language keyword. In Java, where there is no static top-level class keyword, people usually say utility class for the same idea. In team conversation you might hear someone say the helpers should go in a static class, and the others will know exactly what that means.

distinctions.note: A regular class can be instantiated with new to create objects, while a static class cannot be instantiated at all.
Utility class is a general design term for a class of helper methods, while static class is a specific language construct, especially in C#.
An abstract class can be inherited from but not instantiated directly, whereas a static class can be neither inherited nor instantiated.

examples.everyday: My coworker said the date helpers belong in a static class, so I moved them there.
examples.professional: Let's move the parsing utilities into a static class so the service layer stays clean.
examples.analytical: A static class enforces a stateless design, which makes its behavior easier to reason about but harder to replace in tests.

nuance.analogy: A static class is like a toolbox bolted to the wall: everyone can reach in and use the tools, but nobody can take the box home as a new object.
nuance.etymology: Static comes from Greek statikos, causing to stand, from histanai, to stand; class comes from Latin classis, a division or rank.
common_mistakes: Trying to write new before a static class name, which will not compile.
Saying the word class with a long a sound instead of the short a in class.

senses.definition: Synonym of stay the course.
senses.example: He was sure his girlfriend would stay the distance with her addiction treatment.

core.definition: To keep going until the end of a long or demanding task, contest, or challenge without giving up or fading.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on DIS in distance, and the word 'the' reduces to a quick 'thuh' before a consonant. The second syllable of distance is a reduced schwa, not a clear 'tance'.

nuance.connotation: Positive: it praises endurance and staying power, though it can imply doubt when used negatively, as in 'I doubt he can stay the distance.'
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this idiom for marathons, political campaigns, long projects, and tough jobs, and it often appears in sports commentary. It is a natural comment on a colleague's stamina during a long project, for example. A natural reply is 'Yeah, she's got the stamina to stay the distance.'

distinctions.note: Stay the course stresses following a plan steadily, while stay the distance stresses lasting until the end of a grueling contest or hard task.

collocations: stay the distance in a marathon
stay the distance in a negotiation
doubt he can stay the distance
stay the distance through the playoffs

examples.everyday: Our neighbor trained all year for the half marathon, and he really stayed the distance.
examples.professional: We need a team that can stay the distance through the full integration, not just the kickoff.
examples.analytical: Many reform movements begin with enthusiasm but only a few can stay the distance long enough to change institutions.

nuance.analogy: Like a marathon runner who keeps a steady pace and still finishes strong after the crowd has thinned.
nuance.etymology: Idiom from boxing and racing, where the distance is the full length of a bout or race.
common_mistakes: Using it for a short, single task, when it is meant for long or grueling efforts.
Saying 'stay on the distance' instead of 'stay the distance'.

inflections: stays the distance, staves the distance
stayed the distance, staid the distance

senses.definition: Having a manner that stimulates; serving to stimulate.
senses.example: The seminar on machine learning ethics was stimulating, and we talked until midnight.

core.definition: Interesting and energizing; mentally engaging, or causing new ideas, energy or activity.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. Reduce the middle 'ul' to a quick 'yuh' and finish with a short, light '-ing', not 'eeng'.

nuance.connotation: Positive: it praises something that makes you think or feel energized. It can be used politely to describe something that is not very exciting but is still good.
nuance.usage_note: Americans often say 'stimulating conversation', 'stimulating job', or 'mentally stimulating' to praise an experience. It is a polite word, so it can soften a comment about something you did not fully enjoy. The opposite of a friendly compliment would be 'boring' or 'tedious'.

distinctions.note: 'Interesting' is neutral and general; 'stimulating' adds the idea that it makes you think or energizes you.
'Exciting' is about strong emotion or thrills; 'stimulating' is about mental or intellectual energy.
'Thought-provoking' is more serious and specific about making you reconsider beliefs; 'stimulating' is broader.

examples.everyday: Our book club has been really stimulating this year, and I always leave with new ideas.
examples.professional: The retrospective was stimulating, and we left with three concrete experiments to try.
examples.analytical: Kant's argument is stimulating precisely because it refuses easy answers about moral duty.

nuance.analogy: Like a strong cup of coffee for the mind, it wakes up your thinking.
nuance.etymology: From stimulate plus the adjective ending -ing.
common_mistakes: Using 'stimulated' to describe a thing, as in 'The movie was stimulated'. Use 'stimulating' for things and 'stimulated' for how a person feels.
Confusing it with 'stimulant' (a substance) when describing an interesting talk.

senses.definition: A seat, especially for one person and without armrests.
A seat for one person without a back or armrests.
A footstool.
senses.example: She propped her swollen feet on a small wooden stool by the fireplace.

senses.definition: A royal seat; a chief's throne.
senses.example: The chief sat on the carved stool at the center of the village square.

senses.definition: A plant that has been cut down until its main stem is close to the ground, resembling a stool, to promote new growth.
senses.example: The farmer cut the willows back to a stool each winter so they would sprout.

senses.definition: Feces; excrement.
senses.example: I provided the doctor with stool samples.

senses.definition: An informer to the police.
senses.example: The mobster's old friend was a stool who sold him out to the police.

senses.definition: A production of feces or excrement; an act of defecation, stooling.
senses.example: The nurse recorded the patient's stool and urine output every four hours.

senses.definition: A small channel on the side of a vessel, for the deadeyes of the backstays.
senses.example: The rigger checked each deadeye seated in the stool along the ship's side.

senses.definition: (dated) A close-stool; a seat used for urination and defecation: a chamber pot, commode, outhouse seat, or toilet.
senses.example: The Victorian novel described the household servant emptying the stool each morning.
senses.label: dated

senses.definition: To cut down (a plant) until its main stem is close to the ground, resembling a stool, to promote new growth.
senses.example: Each winter the gardener stools the willows so they sprout thick new shoots.

senses.definition: To ramify; to tiller, as grain; to shoot out suckers.
senses.example: The wheat began to stool in April, sending out several shoots from each root.

senses.definition: To produce stool: to defecate.
senses.example: The infant stooled several times after the feeding, so the doctor was not worried.

senses.definition: (dated) To snitch, inform.
senses.example: Don't stool on your brother to the principal, or nobody will trust you again.
senses.label: dated

core.definition: A seat for one person, usually without a back or armrests, often with three or four legs.

pronunciation.tip: Use the vowel of 'pool' or 'school', a long u. Do not make it sound like 'stall' or 'stole'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes an everyday piece of furniture with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'stool' for a simple seat without a back, such as a bar stool or a piano stool. In medicine and nursing, 'stool' also means feces, and the term is formal and clinical, as in 'stool sample'. In a casual conversation about furniture, you might say 'Can you grab a stool from the garage?'

distinctions.note: A chair usually has a back and often armrests; a stool has no back or arms.
A bench is a long seat for several people; a stool is for one person.
A footstool is a low seat for resting the feet; a stool is a seat for sitting.

examples.everyday: Grab a stool and sit down, dinner is almost ready.
examples.professional: We need to order twenty new stools for the conference room, so please send me the dimensions.
examples.analytical: The stool, as a minimal seat without back support, reveals how furniture encodes social expectations about posture and rank.

nuance.analogy: A stool is like a chair with its back and arms taken away, leaving only a seat on legs.
nuance.etymology: From Old English stōl, meaning seat or throne.
common_mistakes: Using 'stool' to mean any chair; a stool has no back or arms.
Using the medical sense casually in everyday conversation without context.

stool.etymology: From Middle English *stool*, from Old English *stōl* (“chair, seat”), from **stōl*, from Proto-Germanic **stōlaz* (“chair”), from Proto-Indo-European, from **steh₂-* (“to stand”).

senses.definition: To build up a supply of (something), usually for use at a particular time in the future, when the time is right.
senses.example: Squirrels store up acorns in autumn so they can eat through the winter.

core.definition: To build up a supply of something to use later, when it is needed.

pronunciation.tip: Main stress falls on the particle up, while store has a weaker secondary stress. Say 'stor-UP' and keep the r in store clearly pronounced.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral. It suggests planning ahead, though it can imply hoarding in some contexts.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use store up for building supplies for a future need, such as food before a storm, energy for a hard week, or memories. It is common in both speech and writing. A natural exchange is: 'The hurricane is coming, so we're storing up water and batteries.' The phrase usually takes an object and sounds reflective with words like memories or energy.

distinctions.note: Stockpile emphasizes accumulating a large reserve, often of essentials or weapons, and can be more formal; store up is more general.
Stock up is the everyday phrase for buying a supply of goods; store up can cover any kind of saving, including experiences.
Save means keeping money or time for later; store up can apply to many resources and to abstract things like energy.

collocations: store up water before the storm

examples.everyday: Before the snowstorm, we stored up water, bread and batteries.
examples.professional: The team stored up enough test data to train the model without waiting for new logs.
examples.analytical: Many writers describe habit as a way of storing up capacities that later shape judgment in moments of pressure.

nuance.analogy: Store up is like filling a pantry before winter, so you have food when the weather turns.
nuance.etymology: From store plus up, where the particle up emphasizes building a full supply.
common_mistakes: Dropping up and saying only 'store' when you mean building a supply over time.
Stressing store equally with up; the particle up carries the main stress.
nuance.biblical_note: The Greek verb thesaurizō means to store up or treasure. In Matthew 6:19-20 the RSV has Jesus telling his hearers not to lay up treasures on earth but to lay up treasures in heaven, contrasting moth and rust with lasting reward. Luke 12:21 uses the same idea, describing a man who lays up treasure for himself but is not rich toward God.

senses.definition: To walk with long steps.
To stand with the legs wide apart; to straddle.
senses.example: Stand still and stride your legs apart so I can measure your inseam.

senses.definition: To pass over at a step; to step over.
senses.example: The runner had to stride over the hurdle without touching it.

senses.definition: To straddle.
senses.example: The bronze statue was built to stride the harbor entrance like a colossus.

senses.definition: A long step in walking.
senses.example: She set off with a purposeful stride.

senses.definition: The distance covered by a long step.
senses.example: Her stride was so long that she covered the parking lot in twelve steps.

senses.definition: The number of memory locations between successive elements in an array, pixels in a bitmap, etc.
senses.example: Each element occupies four bytes, so the stride between rows is 16 bytes.

senses.definition: A jazz piano style of the 1920s and 1930s. The left hand characteristically plays a four-beat pulse with a single bass note, octave, seventh or tenth interval on the first and third beats, and a chord on the second and fourth beats.
senses.example: She played stride piano at the bar, her left hand thumping out bass octaves.

core.definition: To walk with long, purposeful steps, often in a confident or determined way.

pronunciation.tip: This is one syllable with primary stress, and the vowel is a long i diphthong. Keep the final d voiced and clear. The past tense is strode, and the past participle stridden is rare in everyday speech.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral; it suggests confidence and purpose, though stride off can sound dismissive.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use stride for purposeful walking, such as someone striding into a meeting or across a field. In casual speech people more often say walk or march, so stride sounds vivid and slightly descriptive. The idiom take something in stride means to handle something calmly, and a natural reply to How did she handle the news is She took it in stride.

distinctions.note: Stroll means a slow, relaxed walk; stride is longer and more purposeful.
March suggests a regular rhythm, often in a group or protest; stride is individual and can be relaxed or confident.
Stomp means walking heavily, usually in anger; stride is controlled rather than heavy.

examples.everyday: He strode into the kitchen like he owned the place.
examples.professional: The product lead strode into the meeting and asked for the revised numbers before we started.
examples.analytical: The poem's speaker strides through the waking city, a figure of defiant self-possession.

nuance.analogy: Like a runner pacing a race: each step long and deliberate, covering ground with confidence.
nuance.etymology: From Old English stridan, meaning to straddle or stretch the legs.
common_mistakes: Using strided as the past tense; the correct past tense is strode.
Confusing stride, a long purposeful step, with step, which can be any single movement.

stride.etymology: From Middle English *striden*, from Old English *strīdan* (“stride”), from **strīdan*, from Proto-Germanic **strīdaną*.

senses.definition: In a stubborn manner.
senses.example: He stubbornly refused to quit trying, even after failing 20 times.

core.definition: In a way that refuses to change one's position or give in, even when there is good reason to do so.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The middle syllable is a reduced r sound, and the final -ly is a clear lee, not lih.

nuance.connotation: Usually negative, implying unreasonable refusal, though it can describe admirable persistence.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use stubbornly to describe someone who keeps doing something despite objections, as in she stubbornly refused help. It often appears with refuse, insist or cling. In formal writing it can describe persistence neutrally, such as stubbornly high unemployment.

distinctions.note: Persistently is neutral about the reason for continuing, while stubbornly implies refusal to yield to reason or pressure.
Firmly is usually positive about a steady position, while stubbornly suggests the person will not bend even when they should.

examples.everyday: She stubbornly refused to let anyone carry her grocery bags, even when her arms were shaking.
examples.professional: The team stubbornly kept the old schema despite repeated complaints about query speed.
examples.analytical: The text stubbornly resists a single reading, insisting on its paradoxes rather than resolving them.

nuance.analogy: Stubbornly is like a stone in a stream: the water keeps moving around it, but it refuses to move.
nuance.etymology: From stubborn plus the adverb suffix -ly.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it with a clear er vowel; it is a reduced schwa with r sound.
Using stubbornly for admirable effort without context; it often sounds like criticism.
nuance.biblical_note: The Hebrew shereruth lev, the stubbornness of the heart, describes a refusal to listen to God. Jeremiah 7:24 says the people walked in the stubbornness of their evil hearts instead of obeying. Psalm 81:12 says God gave them over to their stubborn hearts to follow their own counsels.

senses.definition: The state of being in a subordinate position.

core.definition: The condition of being in a lower or subordinate position within a social, political, or intellectual hierarchy.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on the -TUR- syllable, not on the first syllable. Keep the r clearly rhotic, and reduce the final -ity to a short 'ih-tee'.

nuance.connotation: Negative, because it implies marginalization and lack of voice or power.
nuance.usage_note: The word is used mainly in postcolonial studies, critical theory, and history, following the term 'subaltern' from Gramsci. Americans in everyday conversation would say 'second-class status', 'subordinate position', or 'marginalization'. Using it in a casual conversation may sound pretentious unless the topic is academic.

distinctions.note: Subordination describes any lower rank in a hierarchy, while subalternity is a more specific term for the marginalized position of groups in critical theory.
Marginalization is the everyday, widely understood word, while subalternity is more technical and tied to particular theorists.

examples.everyday: Sorry, I don't follow, what do you mean by subalternity?
examples.professional: The report's section on workers' subalternity at the plant made the case for a worker seat on the safety committee.
examples.analytical: Spivak's question about subalternity asks whether marginalized groups can speak within the categories that define their own subordination.

nuance.analogy: Like the crew below deck on a ship: everything depends on them, yet they are rarely visible in the official record.
nuance.etymology: From subaltern (Latin subalternus, 'subordinate'), from sub- 'under' plus alter 'other'.
common_mistakes: Using 'subaltern' to mean a military rank, which is a British usage; Americans rarely use it that way.
Stressing the first syllable, as in SUB-al-TER-ni-ty.

senses.definition: Synonym of sublet.
senses.example: She decided to sublease her apartment while she spent the summer abroad.

senses.definition: A lease sublet by a tenant or lessee to a subtenant.
senses.example: The sublease required written approval from our landlord before we could move in.

core.definition: To rent out all or part of a property that you lease from someone else, so another person pays you while you remain the tenant.

pronunciation.tip: As a verb, stress falls on LEES, while the noun 'SUB-lees' stresses the first syllable. Non-native speakers often use the noun stress for both forms.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a practical term about housing and business, with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use sublease mainly in legal, commercial and formal housing contexts, such as leases for offices and business space. For apartments, people often say sublet in everyday speech, and the two words are almost always interchangeable. Most leases require the landlord's written permission before you sublease, so check first.

distinctions.note: The two words are nearly synonymous in American usage, with sublease more formal and legal and sublet more common in everyday talk.
Subleasing keeps the original tenant responsible to the landlord, while assigning a lease transfers the whole lease and usually releases the original tenant.

examples.everyday: I'm going to sublease my apartment for the summer while I'm doing an internship in Boston.
examples.professional: We plan to sublease the third floor to a design firm, which will cover most of our rent for next year.
examples.analytical: A sublease creates a second contractual relationship, so the original tenant remains responsible to the landlord even after the subtenant moves in.

nuance.analogy: Like a middleman who rents a house from its owner and then rents rooms to others while staying responsible to the owner.
nuance.etymology: From sub- 'under' and lease, from Old French laissier 'to let, leave'.
common_mistakes: Stressing SUB as in the noun when using the verb.
Thinking a sublease transfers responsibility to the new tenant, when the original tenant usually remains liable.
Forgetting to get the landlord's written consent, which many leases require.

senses.definition: The act or process of subsidizing.
senses.example: Federal subsidization of rural broadband lowered monthly bills for thousands of families in Iowa.

core.definition: The act of paying part of the cost of a product, service or business so its price or survival is supported.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress is on 'ZAY', with the first syllable lighter. Non-natives often stress 'SID' with a long i, or drop the final '-shun' ending.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to contested; supporters see it as help, critics see it as distortion of the market.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use subsidization in economics, farm policy, energy and housing debates, usually when someone defends or criticizes government support. In everyday talk people say 'government help' or 'subsidies'. The noun is abstract, so you rarely need it in casual conversation.

distinctions.note: A subsidy is the money or benefit itself, while subsidization is the process or policy of providing it.
Funding is any money given to support something, while subsidization specifically means lowering the cost of something through public money or support.

examples.everyday: My sister says the bus fares are cheap because of subsidization, so riders don't pay the full cost.
examples.professional: Our budget memo should show the subsidization needed to keep the community clinic open through next year.
examples.analytical: The argument for subsidization rests on the claim that some public goods would be underprovided by the market alone.

nuance.analogy: Like a coupon someone else pays for: the item still costs money, but the cost to you goes down.
nuance.etymology: From subsidize, from Latin subsidium, meaning reserve or aid, with the -ation suffix forming the noun of action.
common_mistakes: Misspelling it as 'subsidation' or using 's' instead of 'z' in subsidize; the verb is subsidize.
Treating it as countable ('a subsidization'); it is usually uncountable, as in 'the subsidization of farms'.

senses.definition: The determination by a court that no factual issues are in dispute, and that the legal issues require the case to be decided in favor of one party or the other.

core.definition: A court ruling, before trial, that no facts are disputed, so one party wins as a matter of law.

pronunciation.tip: Primary stress is on SUM and secondary on JUDG. In the first word, 'summary' is 'SUM-uh-ree', with a clear American r and a light middle syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral: a precise legal term.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this term in US civil litigation, mostly among lawyers, judges, and legal writers. Lay speakers would say 'the judge threw out the case before trial'. It is a standard procedural motion in federal and state courts.

distinctions.note: A dismissal ends a case for procedural or legal reasons; summary judgment decides the outcome on the merits after the facts are reviewed.
A trial requires factual findings by a judge or jury; summary judgment is granted only when there are no real factual disputes.

collocations: no genuine dispute of material fact

examples.everyday: My cousin's lawyer said the case might end with summary judgment before we ever go to trial.
examples.professional: Our legal team filed a motion for summary judgment, arguing that the contract terms are clear.
examples.analytical: The court granted summary judgment because the plaintiff failed to show a genuine dispute of material fact.

nuance.analogy: Like a referee who calls the game early because the rules already decide the winner.
nuance.etymology: 'Summary' from Latin 'summarius' (concise); 'judgment' from Old French 'jugement', from Latin 'judicare' (to judge).
common_mistakes: Saying 'summary judgment' with an e; the American spelling is 'judgment'.
Confusing it with a verdict, which comes after a trial.

senses.definition: The state or quality of being sumptuous.
(rare) The result or product of being sumptuous.
senses.example: The wedding's sumptuousness, with gold chargers and orchids everywhere, astonished the modest guests.
senses.label: rare

core.definition: The quality of being rich, lavish and expensive in appearance, such as luxurious furnishings, food or clothing.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, and say the 'mp' cluster cleanly before the 'sh' sound, not 'sump-too-us'. The final syllables are reduced, so the word ends with a quiet 'nus'.

nuance.connotation: Positive for luxury and generosity, but can sound excessive or showy when used of things that seem wasteful.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word mostly in writing, reviews, and descriptions of decor, food, or fashion, rather than in casual talk. In conversation, people usually say 'luxury' or 'lavishness' instead. It is a good word for an essay or a formal review, but it would sound stiff at a dinner table.

distinctions.note: Luxury is the general state of comfort and expense; sumptuousness focuses on the rich, impressive look or feel of something.
Opulence stresses great wealth and abundance; sumptuousness stresses a sensory richness in the details.

collocations: the sumptuousness of the hotel suite

examples.everyday: I loved the sumptuousness of that hotel lobby with its velvet chairs and gold lamps.
examples.professional: The client wants the showroom to convey sumptuousness without looking cluttered, so we'll focus on fabric and lighting.
examples.analytical: The painter's sumptuousness of color and texture seeks to make the viewer feel the wealth of the court.

nuance.analogy: Like a velvet-lined jewelry box, the sumptuousness is in the rich texture you feel even before you look closely.
nuance.etymology: From sumptuous, from Latin sumptuosus, 'expensive', from sumptus, 'expense'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it 'sump-too-us-ness' with a 't' sound instead of 'sh'.
Using it for everyday food or cheap things that are merely nice; it implies a high level of richness.

senses.definition: To retire or put out of use due to age.
To show to be obsolete due to age.
To retire due to age.
To become obsolete or antiquated.
To give a pension to, on account of old age or other infirmity; to cause to retire from service on a pension.

core.definition: To retire someone, or remove something from use, because of age or because it has become outdated.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the syllable 'AN' in the middle, not the first or last syllable. The unstressed 'per' is a reduced schwa-r, and the final '-ate' rhymes with 'wait.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative; it can imply that a person or object has become too old to be useful.
nuance.usage_note: Americans seldom use this verb in conversation. They prefer 'retire,' 'put out to pasture' (informal), or 'phase out' for equipment and software. In formal or legal writing, 'superannuate' can appear, but it should be used carefully because it may sound harsh when applied to people.

distinctions.note: 'Retire' is the common everyday word for leaving work; 'superannuate' is more formal and can imply removal because of age.
'Obsolete' describes something no longer in use; 'superannuate' emphasizes that the thing or person has grown too old for its role.

examples.professional: The committee decided to superannuate the legacy reporting tools once the new dashboard was live.
examples.analytical: Critics argue that the law superannuates older workers, treating age as a reason for removal rather than a matter of competence.

nuance.analogy: Like a phone that has been left in a drawer so long that the updates have passed it by and no one uses it anymore.
nuance.etymology: From Medieval Latin superannuatus, beyond the year, from Latin super (beyond) and annus (year).
common_mistakes: Using 'superannuate' in casual speech where 'retire' would be natural.
Pronouncing the middle syllable 'NYOO' as 'NEW' or stressing the wrong syllable.

senses.definition: Susceptible to superstitions.
Arising from or having the character of superstitions.
senses.example: My roommate is superstitious, refusing to fly on Friday the thirteenth.

core.definition: Believing in or influenced by superstitions, such as luck charms, omens, or irrational fears.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on STISH. The final -ous is a reduced 'us,' not 'ooss,' and the middle syllables are quick and light.

nuance.connotation: Often mildly negative, though it can be affectionate in casual talk.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say someone is superstitious about things like lucky numbers or sports routines. It can be teasing and friendly, as in 'I'm a little superstitious about flying.' Calling a person superstitious in a serious conversation can sound dismissive, so use it carefully.

distinctions.note: Credulous means too ready to believe anything. Superstitious is narrower and refers to beliefs about luck, omens, or the supernatural.
Religious refers to faith and worship. Superstitious suggests irrational, fear-based belief, which can be a critical label for religion.
