examples.everyday: I'm in training for a 5K this spring, so I run every morning before work.
examples.professional: All new hires complete two days of safety training before they start on the warehouse floor.
examples.analytical: Training that focuses only on procedure can produce competence without understanding, which is why reflection matters.

nuance.analogy: Training is like tuning an instrument before a concert: repetition makes the skill automatic so you can focus on the music.
nuance.etymology: From the verb train, from Old French trainer 'to drag', from Latin trahere 'to drag'.
common_mistakes: Using 'trainings' as a plural; Americans normally say 'training sessions' or 'training programs'.
Saying 'practice' when you mean a structured, formal program of training.
nuance.biblical_note: In 2 Timothy 3:16 the RSV says Scripture is profitable for 'training in righteousness', translating the Greek word paideia, which means upbringing, instruction, or discipline. In Proverbs 22:6 the RSV says to train up a child in the way he should go, where the Hebrew verb hanak means to dedicate or initiate. In 1 Timothy 4:7 the Greek gymnazo, meaning to exercise or train, appears in the call to train yourself in godliness, which is an image of disciplined spiritual practice.

senses.definition: The data used to train a model.
senses.example: We cleaned the training data before fitting the logistic regression model.

core.definition: The collection of examples used to teach a machine learning model how to recognize patterns and make predictions.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on TRAY in training and DAY in data. The final syllable of data is usually a reduced 'uh' in American speech, and the t is often a flap.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise technical term in data science and AI.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use training data in machine learning, AI and data science, both in technical teams and in news reports. Data is often treated as uncountable in this phrase, so people say 'the training data is large' rather than 'the training datas'. In casual talk, people might say 'the examples the model learned from' instead.

distinctions.note: Training data is the general term for all data used in training, while a training set is a specific subset used for fitting one model.
Test data is held out to evaluate a model after training, so it must not be used to teach the model.

examples.everyday: My friend explained that the app learned from millions of photos, and those photos are its training data.
examples.professional: We need more labeled training data before the model can handle rare cases reliably in production.
examples.analytical: Biases in the training data often reappear in predictions, even when the algorithm itself is carefully designed.

nuance.analogy: Training data is like the practice problems in a textbook: the student learns patterns from them before the real exam.
nuance.etymology: Training from train (verb), from Old French trainer; data from Latin datum, given.
common_mistakes: Saying 'trainings data' or 'training datas', which are not standard.
Using training data to mean the test data, which confuses the purpose of each dataset.

conversation.text: Training data is the set of examples a model learns from.
Cleaning the training data improved results more than any architecture change.
Disclosure of training data sources is a recurring theme in AI regulation debates.

senses.definition: That which tranquillizes or soothes.
senses.example: Her doctor prescribed a mild tranquilizer to help her sleep after the stressful surgery.

senses.definition: A drug used to reduce anxiety or tension.
A gun that fires sedative darts.
senses.example: The veterinarian used a tranquilizer gun to calm the escaped bear before moving it.

core.definition: A drug that reduces anxiety, tension or agitation, or puts a person or animal into a calm sleep.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the kw is followed by a reduced vowel. The final -er is rhotic, so the r is clear, not dropped.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in medical and veterinary contexts, but it can sound negative when it implies people are drugged to avoid problems.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use tranquilizer mostly for sedating animals or, in everyday speech, for anti-anxiety medication. For ordinary anxiety medicine, people often name the specific drug or say sedative. Saying someone is on tranquilizers can sound judgmental, so use it carefully.

distinctions.note: Sedative is the broader, more clinical term for drugs that calm or induce sleep, while tranquilizer is common in everyday speech and for animal drugs.
A painkiller relieves physical pain, while a tranquilizer calms mental agitation or anxiety.

examples.everyday: My sister takes a mild tranquilizer before long flights, so she sleeps the whole way.
examples.professional: The clinical team reviewed the dose of the tranquilizer before the procedure to avoid oversedation.
examples.analytical: Some philosophers argue that a tranquilizer can dull distress but cannot resolve the questions that cause it.

nuance.analogy: A tranquilizer is like a dimmer switch on a bright light: it lowers the intensity but does not remove the source.
nuance.etymology: From tranquilize (from tranquil, Latin tranquillus, calm) plus the agent suffix -er.
common_mistakes: Confusing it with tranquility; tranquility is the noun for calm, and tranquilizer is the drug or device.
Misplacing the stress on the -ize syllable; the main stress is on TRANG.

senses.definition: In a transcendental manner.

core.definition: In a way that goes beyond ordinary experience or the physical world; in a transcendental manner.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on DEN, and the final -ly is a clear 'lee' sound. The first syllable is reduced, so say 'tran-sun' rather than 'trans-SEN'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to somewhat lofty; it is used in philosophy, religion and writing about meditation.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use this in everyday talk. It appears in philosophy papers, theology and writing about Transcendental Meditation. In casual speech, people say 'on a spiritual level' or 'beyond the physical world' instead.

distinctions.note: Means by supernatural powers, often miraculous; transcendentally means beyond sense experience, not necessarily magical.
Means surpassingly or to an extreme degree, as in transcendently beautiful; transcendentally is philosophical and not an intensifier.

examples.everyday: My yoga teacher says we should approach silence transcendentally, but honestly I mostly just check my phone.
examples.professional: Stop saying the forecast is transcendentally accurate; it's just well calibrated on our holdout set.
examples.analytical: Kant argues that the conditions of experience are transcendentally necessary, meaning they hold prior to any particular experience.

nuance.etymology: From transcendental plus -ly; transcendental from Latin transcendere, to climb over.
common_mistakes: Using it as a general intensifier, like extremely or incredibly.
Confusing it with supernaturally, which suggests miracles or powers beyond nature.

senses.definition: The conversion of one thing into something else; transformation.
The supposed transformation of one element into another, especially of a base metal into gold.
senses.example: Medieval alchemists spent centuries chasing the transmutation of lead into gold.

senses.definition: The actual transformation of one element into another by a nuclear reaction.

core.definition: The change of one thing into another, such as one chemical element becoming a different element, or a dramatic transformation.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on TAY, the -ation syllable, with a lighter stress on the first syllable. Say myoo as one syllable, and pronounce the ending as shun, not tee-un.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in science; in alchemy or literary use it can carry a sense of wonder or mystery.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use transmutation mainly in chemistry, physics, history of science and literary writing. Chemists rarely use it for ordinary reactions, which change compounds, and reserve it for nuclear changes that alter one element into another. For everyday change, Americans say transformation, change or makeover.

distinctions.note: Transformation is the general, everyday word for any major change, while transmutation is narrower and often refers to a change of substance or element.
Transmission means sending something from one place to another; transmutation means changing it into something else.

examples.everyday: Going from a messy garage to a clean home studio was almost a transmutation, and my wife couldn't believe the change.
examples.professional: The lab reported a transmutation of the sample's isotopes after the reaction, which confirmed the nuclear process we had modeled.
examples.analytical: The medieval alchemists sought the transmutation of lead into gold, but their hope rested on a theory of matter that modern chemistry has replaced.

nuance.analogy: Transmutation is like a caterpillar becoming a butterfly, but applied to matter itself: the substance is no longer what it was.
nuance.etymology: From Latin transmutatio, from transmutare, to change across.
common_mistakes: Using transmutation for an ordinary chemical reaction; say reaction or conversion instead.
Stressing the first syllable instead of TAY.

transmutation.etymology: Late 14th century, from Old French *transmutacion* (“transformation, metamorphosis”), from Late Latin *transmutationem*, from Latin *transmutare* (“to change”).

senses.definition: Of, relating to, or situated on the far side of a bridge.
Of, relating to, or situated on the far side of a sea.
(historical) Relating to the sensational melodramas presented on the south side of the Thames in the 19th century or earlier.
senses.label: historical

core.definition: Located on the far side of a bridge or sea, or relating to 19th-century melodramas staged south of the Thames.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on PON, the second syllable, and the final -tine rhymes with line. Many Americans are unfamiliar with this word, so the pronunciation is not standardized; say the middle vowel like the o in on.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a specialized literary or historical term.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use transpontine in ordinary speech. It appears mainly in literary criticism or theater history, especially about London melodrama. In general writing, use across the bridge or on the other side instead.

distinctions.note: Transatlantic refers to the far side of the Atlantic Ocean; transpontine is a rare term for the far side of a bridge or sea, or for a particular theatrical tradition.
Across is a common preposition; transpontine is a specialized adjective used in academic or historical writing.

examples.professional: The museum's exhibit on Victorian theater includes a section on transpontine melodrama.
examples.analytical: The critic argues that transpontine melodrama shaped popular taste by staging moral conflict in exaggerated, sensational forms.

nuance.analogy: Transpontine is like the far bank of a river seen from the city: it describes a place or style that lies on the other side of a boundary.
nuance.etymology: From Latin trans- (across) and pontem (bridge, pons).
common_mistakes: Using transpontine as a common everyday word for across the bridge; it is a rare, specialized term.
Assuming it always refers to bridges; the theatrical sense is important in literary history.

senses.definition: One who traps animals; one who makes a business of trapping animals, for their pelts, meat, etc.
senses.example: The trapper checked his lines before sunrise, hoping for a fox or two.

senses.definition: An ornamental covering for a horse. See trapping and caparison.
senses.example: The knight's horse wore a crimson trapper embroidered with gold thread.

senses.definition: A drug dealer.
senses.example: Police arrested the trapper after finding fentanyl hidden in his car.

senses.definition: A performer of trap music.
senses.example: The trapper's new album blends heavy 808 basslines with Southern hip-hop rhythms.

senses.definition: Synonym of catcher.
(historical) A worker (usually a child) who opens and shuts a door in a gallery or level of a mine, to manage ventilation and access.
senses.example: As a boy, he worked as a trapper in the coal mine, opening doors for the haulers.
senses.label: historical

core.definition: A person who catches wild animals in traps, usually for their fur.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The final -er is an American r-colored vowel, so curl the tongue slightly rather than saying a plain 'uh'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; the word often carries a frontier or rural image.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use trapper mainly for people who catch furbearing animals such as beaver, muskrat or coyote, often in rural or northern areas. Trapping is a regulated activity with state licenses in many places. In everyday talk someone might say 'he runs a trapline' in winter, and historical texts often mention fur trappers of the 1800s.

distinctions.note: A hunter pursues animals directly, usually with a gun or bow, while a trapper sets devices and checks them later.
A poacher hunts or traps illegally, while a trapper works within legal seasons and licenses, so the difference is legality.

examples.everyday: My grandfather was a trapper in northern Minnesota, so he always had stories about checking his lines on winter mornings.
examples.professional: Our wildlife agency licenses each trapper and requires a log of every animal taken during the season.
examples.analytical: The trapper's livelihood depended on taking enough animals to sell while leaving enough to breed, a tension early American conservation debates often ignored.

nuance.analogy: A trapper is like a fisherman who sets nets in the water and comes back later to see what they caught.
nuance.etymology: From trap (verb) plus the agent suffix -er.
common_mistakes: Confusing trapper with trapeze, which is an unrelated word
Using trapper for any hunter, when trapping is a specific method

senses.definition: An intentional interference with another's property or person.
senses.example: The landowner filed a lawsuit against the hunters for trespass on his property.

senses.definition: To commit an offense; to sin.
senses.example: Pastor reminded us that we all trespass against God daily and need grace.

senses.definition: To go too far; to put someone to inconvenience by demand or importunity; to intrude.
senses.example: to trespass upon the time or patience of another

senses.definition: To enter someone else's property illegally.

To subject [someone] to a trespass notice, formally notifying them that they are prohibited from entry to a property, such that any current or future presence there will constitute trespass, criminal trespass.
senses.example: The dean trespassed the streaker from his university.

core.definition: To enter someone else's land or property without permission or legal right.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable. The final syllable is a reduced 'us' sound, not 'pass' with an ah vowel, and the noun is pronounced the same way.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it describes breaking a rule, property boundary or social limit.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use trespass most often in legal and property contexts, such as 'No Trespassing' signs and trespassing charges. In everyday speech, people also say 'You're trespassing' or 'Get off my property.' The archaic sense 'to sin' appears mainly in Scripture and older religious writing.

distinctions.note: Encroach describes gradual intrusion into someone's rights or space, while trespass describes a specific act of unauthorized entry.
Intrude is a broader, milder word for entering where you are not wanted; trespass usually implies a legal or moral wrong.

examples.everyday: The sign says No Trespassing, so the kids should stay out of the field behind the farm.
examples.professional: Security will remove anyone who trespasses on the restricted floor without a badge.
examples.analytical: Jesus teaches that forgiveness of trespasses is bound up with the forgiveness we receive from God.

nuance.analogy: A trespass is like stepping over a fence that clearly says Keep Out; the wrong lies in crossing a line someone else has drawn.
nuance.etymology: From Old French trespasser, to pass across or beyond, from tres- (beyond) and passer (to pass).
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the final syllable as 'pass' (TRES-pass) instead of a reduced 'us' sound.
Using 'trespass' for simply being somewhere nearby; it implies unauthorized entry onto property.
nuance.biblical_note: In Scripture a trespass is a false step or offense against God or another person. The Greek words are paraptoma (a falling aside or false step) and parabasis (a stepping across a line). Matthew 6:14-15 links forgiving others' trespasses with God's forgiveness of ours. Ephesians 2:1 describes people as dead through trespasses and sins. Romans 5:15-18 contrasts the trespass of one man, Adam, with the free gift that comes through Jesus Christ.

trespass.etymology: Borrowed into Middle English *trespas*, from Old French *trespas* (“passage; offense against the law”), from *trespasser*.

senses.definition: Used so many times that it is commonplace, or no longer interesting or effective; worn out, hackneyed.
senses.example: Her speech was full of trite phrases that the audience had heard a hundred times.

senses.definition: So well established as to be beyond debate: trite law.
senses.example: It is a trite rule that contracts require mutual consent from both parties.

senses.definition: A denomination of coinage in ancient Greece equivalent to one third of a stater.
senses.example: A trite was worth one third of a stater in ancient Greece.

senses.definition: In Ancient Greek musical theory, the lower-pitched of the two movable notes in the farther tetrachord on a lyre, pitched lower than the paranete and higher than the paramese.
senses.example: In the Greek tetrachord, the trite note sits between the paranete and the paramese.

core.definition: Used so often that it has lost its freshness or meaning; stale, commonplace, or hackneyed.

pronunciation.tip: The vowel is the diphthong ai, as in bite, and the final t is a clear t at the end of the word. Do not reduce the vowel, and keep the r clearly pronounced at the start.

nuance.connotation: Negative. Calling a remark trite is a criticism that it is unoriginal or lacking insight.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use trite in writing, criticism, and thoughtful conversation to say a phrase or idea is overused. It can sound a bit stiff in very casual speech, where people say cliché or corny. Be careful not to call a person trite, as this can seem insulting.

distinctions.note: A cliché is a specific overused phrase or idea. Trite is an adjective that describes the quality of being overused or unoriginal.
Corny is informal and often humorous or sentimental. Trite is more formal and emphasizes lack of originality.

examples.everyday: My friend said the movie's ending was trite, because we had seen that twist a hundred times.
examples.professional: Please avoid trite phrases like think outside the box in the proposal, and state the actual value we deliver.
examples.analytical: The author's argument is trite, since it repeats familiar claims without testing them against the evidence.

nuance.analogy: A trite phrase is like a coin worn smooth by too many hands: the image is still there, but the detail is gone.
nuance.etymology: From Latin tritus, the past participle of terere, to rub or wear down.
common_mistakes: Using trite to mean tiny or small, which is a confusion with trivial or tiny.
Pronouncing trite with a short i as in trit, instead of the diphthong ai as in bite.

trite.etymology: From Latin *trītus* (“worn out”), perfect passive participle of *terō* (“to wear away, wear out”).

senses.definition: Relating to or involving the interpretation of literature focusing on the ethical lesson or moral of the story.
senses.example: The sermon offered a tropological reading of the parable, drawing out its moral for daily life.

senses.definition: Characterized by tropes; varied by tropes; tropical.
senses.example: The novel's tropological style leaned heavily on familiar metaphors and recycled images.

core.definition: Relating to the moral or ethical interpretation of Scripture, one of the four medieval senses of a biblical text.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on LAH, the third syllable of the main root. Americans often reduce the middle vowels to a quick 'uh' or 'ih'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; a technical term from theology and literary criticism.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word almost only in academic theology, biblical studies, and history of interpretation. Most people would not recognize it outside those fields, so in a general conversation say 'moral' or 'ethical' instead. It appears in discussions of medieval exegesis and in some Protestant writing that draws on it.

distinctions.note: The allegorical sense concerns what a text signifies about Christ or the Church, while the tropological sense concerns how the reader should act.
The anagogical sense concerns the final or heavenly reality, while the tropological sense concerns moral living now.

examples.everyday: My Bible study leader said the story of the Good Samaritan has a tropological lesson about how we treat strangers.
examples.professional: In the sermon, the pastor moved from the historical sense to a tropological application for the congregation.
examples.analytical: Medieval exegetes often read the Old Testament through the tropological sense, drawing moral instruction for the individual soul from each text.

nuance.analogy: If the literal sense is the map and the allegorical sense is the destination, the tropological sense is the set of instructions for how to walk the road.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin tropologia, from Greek tropos, 'turn' or 'figure'; the sense of moral interpretation comes from medieval exegesis.
common_mistakes: Confusing it with 'tropical', which is about climate.
Using it for any moral lesson in ordinary speech, where 'moral' or 'lesson' is more natural.
nuance.biblical_note: The tropological sense is the moral application of a biblical text to Christian conduct. It belongs to the medieval fourfold method of reading Scripture (literal, allegorical, tropological, anagogical). Paul uses similar language when he says the Old Testament events were written for instruction. 1 Corinthians 10:11 (RSV) says these things happened as a warning and were written for our instruction. Romans 15:4 (RSV) says that what was written in former days was written for our instruction, so that by steadfastness and encouragement we might have hope.

senses.definition: Distressing, worrying.
The infliction of trouble or distress.
senses.example: The troubling of the village by bandits lasted for decades.

core.definition: Disturbing or worrying; causing unease, concern, or doubt about something important.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, and let the middle syllable shrink to a quick 'l' sound. The final -ing is a short, unstressed 'ing', not 'eeng'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It signals serious concern, and Americans often use it to soften bad news politely, as in 'a troubling trend'.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use troubling in news, business reports, medicine, and everyday talk when something is more than an annoyance. Saying 'That's troubling' in a meeting is a calm way to flag a real concern without sounding dramatic. It works well with nouns like trend, sign, or report, and it is less casual than 'that's bad'.

distinctions.note: Troubling is about emotional concern or moral unease; troublesome is about practical difficulty or annoyance.
Worrying is more personal and often describes feelings; troubling sounds more objective and suits data, reports, or ethical questions.

examples.everyday: The doctor's comment about my blood work was troubling, so I'm getting a second test next week.
examples.professional: The dashboard shows a troubling drop in model accuracy for new customers, so we should pause the rollout.
examples.analytical: Hume's skepticism about causation is troubling to any rationalist, yet it leaves induction standing as a practical necessity.

nuance.analogy: A troubling sign is like a warning light on a car dashboard: it isn't an emergency yet, but you can't ignore it.
nuance.etymology: From trouble (verb) plus the suffix -ing used as an adjective, meaning 'causing trouble or distress.'
common_mistakes: Confusing it with troublesome; troubling implies worry or unease, not just inconvenience.
Pronouncing the middle syllable fully, as in 'TRUB-ul-ing'.

senses.definition: AI that is reliable, safe, fair and transparent enough to be trusted.

core.definition: AI systems that are designed to be reliable, safe, fair, transparent and accountable enough that people can reasonably trust them.

pronunciation.tip: Say the two words with stress on trust, then give the letters A-I with stress on the I. Keep the ay sound clear and say the I as eye.

nuance.connotation: Positive in most professional contexts, but critics sometimes see it as a marketing phrase that avoids harder questions about accountability.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use trustworthy AI in technology companies, government policy, research papers and corporate ethics documents. It names a set of goals such as safety, fairness and transparency. In casual conversation, people might say we want the AI to be reliable. Some critics argue that the phrase can sound like branding, so in serious discussions it is good to say what specific properties you mean.

distinctions.note: Responsible AI emphasizes accountability and ethical governance of how AI is developed and used, while trustworthy AI emphasizes properties users can rely on.
Ethical AI focuses on moral principles, while trustworthy AI usually includes measurable qualities like robustness and reliability.

examples.everyday: My bank says it uses trustworthy AI for fraud alerts, but I still want a person to check anything big.
examples.professional: Our team checklist for trustworthy AI covers bias testing, model documentation and a clear escalation path for errors.
examples.analytical: The phrase trustworthy AI invites a critical question: trustworthy in what respects, to whom, and under which institutional accountability?

nuance.analogy: Trustworthy AI is like a well-built smoke detector: you want it to work every time, and you want to know exactly how it decides when to sound.
nuance.etymology: Trustworthy is from trust plus -worthy; AI abbreviates artificial intelligence.
common_mistakes: Stressing AI on the first letter instead of the second; say ay-EYE.
Treating trustworthy AI as a single technical standard; it is a broad goal with several criteria.

conversation.text: Trustworthy AI is often described as lawful, ethical, and technically robust.
"Trustworthy AI" is a goal; trust has to be earned through evidence, not slogans.
Our trustworthy AI checklist covers fairness, privacy, security, and explainability.

senses.definition: Stout, rotund.
Resembling a tub.
Sounding dull and without resonance or freedom of sound.
senses.example: a tubby violin

senses.definition: An overweight person.

core.definition: Short and round, somewhat overweight, often in a mildly teasing or affectionate way.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, with a short 'uh' vowel. The final -y is a light 'ee', not a long 'eye'.

nuance.connotation: Mildly negative. It can be affectionate for a pet or small child but insulting for an adult.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'tubby' most often about pets, babies, or small children in a cute way, and sometimes humorously about adults. Describing an adult as tubby can sound rude or unkind, so 'a little heavier' or 'stocky' is safer. The word also appears in formal writing as a description of a comic or round figure.

distinctions.note: 'Chubby' is softer and more common for children and babies, while 'tubby' suggests a rounder, more barrel-shaped body.
'Stocky' describes a sturdy, solid build, often with muscle; 'tubby' suggests softness and roundness.
'Stout' is more formal and neutral, suggesting a sturdy, heavier build without the teasing tone.

examples.everyday: Our tubby cat thinks every bowl of food is meant for him.
examples.professional: The mascot costume gives the character a tubby, friendly look that tested well with the kids in focus groups.
examples.analytical: The author's tubby, comic narrator undercuts the sermon's solemnity by making the preacher himself the object of mockery.

nuance.analogy: Tubby is like a teapot: round, comfortable, and not built for speed.
nuance.etymology: From tub (noun) plus the suffix -y.
common_mistakes: Using 'tubby' as a polite description of an adult; it can sound rude.
Confusing 'tubby' with 'tubular', which means shaped like a tube.

senses.definition: One who twists.
One whose occupation is to twist or join the threads of one warp to those of another, in weaving.
senses.example: The old mill employed a twister to join the warp threads for the cloth.

senses.definition: An instrument used in twisting or making twists.
senses.example: He used a wooden twister to make tight cord from the hemp fibers.

senses.definition: A ball delivered with a twist, as in cricket or billiards.
senses.example: The spinner's twister bounced off the pitch and caught the batsman off guard.

senses.definition: A tornado.
A girder.
senses.example: Workers bolted a steel twister across the beams to support the new roof.

senses.definition: Any member of the species Tholymis tillarga of libellulid dragonfly, of tropical West Africa to Asia, Australia, and the Pacific Islands.
senses.example: A bright red twister perched on the reeds beside the tropical pond.

senses.definition: The party game Twister, usually capitalized, or a variant.
senses.example: At the birthday party, we played Twister until everyone collapsed laughing on the mat.

senses.definition: (dated) The inner part of the thigh, the proper place to rest upon when on horseback.
senses.example: The old rancher's twister ached after riding all day in the saddle.
senses.label: dated

core.definition: Informally, a tornado, especially a violent one; also a person or device that twists threads or objects.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable; the final -er is a reduced rhotic vowel, so say 'TWIS-ter' with no separate 'ah' or 'ee' sound. The dictionary form with a clear l-like r is not typical for American speech.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in weather talk; vivid and dramatic, sometimes alarming when describing a storm.
nuance.usage_note: In the US, especially in the Midwest and South, people say twister for a tornado in casual conversation, and the word appears in news and kids' speech. Formal weather reports say tornado. The word also appears in the game Twister, which is a family party game.

distinctions.note: Tornado is the standard word in weather forecasts and formal writing; twister is informal and common in everyday American talk.
A whirlwind is a small, usually harmless spinning wind; a twister is a dangerous tornado.
Cyclone refers to a large rotating storm system; in the US, cyclone is not used for tornadoes.

examples.everyday: We could hear the sirens, so we all went down to the basement because a twister was coming through the county.
examples.professional: The insurance team logged the claims after the twister tore through the industrial park on Tuesday.
examples.analytical: The meteorologist distinguished the twister from a straight-line wind event by the rotation visible in the radar data.

nuance.analogy: A twister is like a spinning top the size of a town, wobbling down from the clouds.
nuance.etymology: From twist with the agent suffix -er.
common_mistakes: Using 'twister' in a formal weather report, where 'tornado' is expected.
Confusing the weather sense with the game Twister, which has a capital T.

senses.definition: Lacking a definition or value.
senses.example: The variable remained undefined until the function was called, so the program crashed.

senses.definition: That does not have a logically sound meaning within a specific formal system and is thus not assigned an interpretation.
senses.example: The result of division by zero is undefined.

senses.definition: That behaves unreliably due to dependence on an uninitialized value or inconsistently ported code.
senses.example: In C, relying on a variable's value right after a malloc call is undefined behvaior.

senses.definition: An undefined value.
senses.example: Your code returns undefined whenever the API response is missing a field.

core.definition: Having no assigned value or meaning within a formal system, such as a mathematical expression or program variable.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on FYND, the root syllable of define. The vowel in fine sounds like 'fyne' and the final d is clear; avoid pronouncing it as 'fined' with two syllables.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in ordinary use, but often negative in programming, where it signals a bug or an unreliable value.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word in math, programming, and everyday speech. In everyday talk, a rule or term that is 'undefined' is vague, as in 'The contract leaves the fees undefined.' In mathematics, dividing by zero is 'undefined', which means it has no meaning in standard arithmetic. In software, 'undefined behavior' means a program can do anything, so developers avoid it.

distinctions.note: Indefinite means not fixed in amount, time, or extent, as in 'an indefinite period'; undefined means no meaning or value has been assigned.
Ambiguous means something has two or more possible meanings, while undefined means no meaning has been fixed at all.
Vague means unclear or imprecise in wording, while undefined means the term or value has not been given any definition.

examples.everyday: The lease leaves the cancellation policy undefined, so I want to ask the landlord before I sign anything.
examples.professional: Dividing by zero is undefined in our calculator spec, so the function should return an error instead of a number.
examples.analytical: Philosophers of language debate whether a sentence containing an undefined term has a truth value at all, which challenges classical bivalent logic.

nuance.analogy: Like a blank space on a map where the border was never drawn, so nobody can say exactly where one country ends.
nuance.etymology: From un- (not) plus defined, from define, from Latin definire 'to limit, bound', from de- plus finire 'to end'.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'undefined' with 'unknown'; a value can be unknown but still defined, while an undefined value has no meaning in the system at all.
Confusing 'undefined' with 'indefinite', which describes an unlimited time or amount rather than a missing definition.

senses.definition: A funeral director; someone whose business is to manage funerals, burials and cremations.

(historical) A person receiving land in Ireland during the Elizabethan era, so named because they gave an undertaking to abide by several conditions regarding marriage, to be loyal to the crown, and to use English as their spoken language.
senses.example: In 1588, Edmund Spenser became an undertaker in the first Elizabethan plantation, receiving the forfeited Irish estate of Kilcolman Castle.
senses.label: historical

senses.definition: (historical) A contractor for the royal revenue in England, one of those who undertook to manage the House of Commons for the king in the Addled Parliament of 1614.
senses.example: The royal undertaker collected customs duties and fines on behalf of the Crown in 1610.
senses.label: historical

senses.definition: (rare) One who undertakes or commits to doing something.
senses.example: She was a fearless undertaker of difficult tasks, never leaving a promise unfinished.
senses.label: rare

core.definition: A person whose job is to arrange funerals, burials and cremations and care for the dead; in the US, usually called a funeral director.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on the first syllable, UN, with a lighter secondary stress on 'take'. The final -er and the 'er' in 'under' are r-colored, not pronounced as 'uh' followed by a separate r sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to somber, but can sound old-fashioned or slightly blunt when used directly about someone who works in funeral care.
nuance.usage_note: Americans usually say 'funeral director' or 'mortician' when speaking politely about the profession; 'undertaker' is more traditional and can sound a bit old-fashioned or blunt. Many people will still use the word in casual speech, such as 'We called the undertaker after Dad passed.' Avoid making jokes about the job with strangers.

distinctions.note: Funeral director is the polite, modern American term; undertaker is older and more traditional.
Mortician is a more technical or formal term for someone who prepares bodies; undertaker covers the whole funeral business.

examples.everyday: After Grandpa died, the family called the local undertaker to handle the arrangements.
examples.professional: Our insurance claim needs a letter from the funeral director, not just from the undertaker's assistant.
examples.analytical: Historians of medicine note that the nineteenth-century undertaker gradually became a professional regulated by the state.

nuance.analogy: An undertaker is like a wedding planner for the final event, but with care for the dead and grieving families.
nuance.etymology: From the verb 'undertake' (to take on a task), in the sense of one who takes on the arrangements for a burial.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable, saying un-DER-taker; the main stress is on UN.
Using it as a casual joke in polite company; 'funeral director' is the safer term.

senses.definition: Not of the earth; nonterrestrial.
Preternatural or supernatural.
Strange, enigmatic, or mysterious.
Ideal beyond the mundane.
Ridiculous, ludicrous, or outrageous.

core.definition: Strange and eerie, as if not of this world; also used informally for an absurdly early or inconvenient hour.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on ERTH, the second syllable, not on un-. Keep the r strong, the th voiceless, and the final -ly a light lee.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative; it suggests strangeness or eeriness, and in casual use often complains about an extreme hour.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use unearthly in casual complaints such as at an unearthly hour for a very early time, and to describe strange sounds or lights. In serious contexts it means not of this world, as in ghost stories or science fiction. For a strange feeling people often say eerie or otherworldly, which are more common.

distinctions.note: Eerie describes a creepy, uneasy atmosphere, while unearthly can be eerie or simply describe a very early hour.
Otherworldly suggests a different realm and is often positive or wonderful, while unearthly often sounds strange or frightening.
Supernatural refers to powers beyond natural laws, while unearthly describes the feeling or appearance of something strange.

examples.everyday: Why does the alarm go off at an unearthly hour when I don't have any meetings this morning?
examples.professional: We got a call at an unearthly hour from the data center, and the outage was not yet understood.
examples.analytical: Philosophers of religion often describe the sense of the sacred as unearthly, suggesting that it cannot be reduced to ordinary experience.

nuance.analogy: Unearthly is like a light in the window of an empty house at midnight: it does not seem to belong to the ordinary world.
nuance.etymology: From un- (not) plus earthly, from earth; the sense not of earth is older than the informal sense of very early.
common_mistakes: Stressing the prefix un- instead of the ERTH syllable.
Confusing unearthly with earthly, which means worldly or practical and is nearly the opposite meaning.

senses.definition: Difficult, undesirable, or unpleasant; not to be envied.
senses.example: Valjean was in the unenviable position of either living with the knowledge an innocent would suffer for his crime or revealing his true identity and going back to prison.

core.definition: Difficult, unpleasant or undesirable, so that people would not want to be in that position.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on EN, the first syllable of the root 'envy', not on the un- at the start. The -iable is said 'vee-uh-bul' in General American.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it describes a situation no one would want to be in, often with dark humor or sympathy.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use it for difficult jobs, responsibilities or positions, often with sympathy or humor, as in 'You have the unenviable task of telling the client about the delay.' It is common in news, business and everyday talk. In casual speech, people might say 'a crummy job' or 'a tough spot' instead.

distinctions.note: Difficult is a neutral word for something hard to do; unenviable adds the idea that most people would not want that role or situation.
Unpleasant describes the experience itself; unenviable describes a position or job that others would not want.

examples.everyday: Telling my brother the wedding is off is the unenviable job, and I drew the short straw.
examples.professional: Our team has the unenviable task of migrating three legacy databases before the audit.
examples.analytical: Pastors occupy an unenviable position, caught between the demands of a congregation and the demands of conscience.

nuance.analogy: Like being the goalie on a losing team: somebody has to do it, but nobody lines up for the job.
nuance.etymology: From un- (not) + enviable, from envy, from Old French envie, from Latin invidia 'envy, ill will'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the un- syllable (UN-en-vee-uh-bul) when the stress belongs on EN.
Confusing it with 'unenvious', which means free of envy and describes a person, not a job or position.

senses.definition: That doesn't have a known or readily available explanation.

core.definition: Impossible or very difficult to explain; having no known or readily available explanation.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on PLAIN, with a weaker stress on un-. The -able reduces to 'uh-bul', and the 'ex' before s is 'ik', not 'eks'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it often describes strange events or behavior and can carry a sense of mystery or frustration.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use it about odd noises, symptoms, bills or events: 'an unexplainable noise in the engine'. Unexplained is more common when something is simply still unexplained. Unexplainable suggests the thing cannot be explained at all, so it fits more definitive statements.

distinctions.note: Unexplained means no explanation has been given yet; unexplainable means no explanation can be given.
Inexplicable is more formal and literary, often used for behavior or mysteries that seem beyond reason.

examples.everyday: My car makes an unexplainable clicking sound every morning, and the mechanic can't find anything.
examples.professional: We saw an unexplainable spike in latency, so we're logging every request to find the cause.
examples.analytical: Some phenomena in the data remain unexplainable within the current model, which shows where theory must extend.

nuance.analogy: Like a locked room with no visible door: the fact is clear, but no route to understanding seems to exist.
nuance.etymology: un- + explainable, from Latin explanare 'to make plain'.
common_mistakes: Using 'unexplainable' where 'unexplained' fits better, since unexplained only means no explanation has been given yet.
Pronouncing the final -able with a full vowel as 'AY-bul' instead of the reduced 'uh-bul'.

senses.definition: Remaining composed and level-headed at all times; impossible to fluster; not becoming frustrated or irritated easily.
senses.example: Our emergency room nurse stays unflappable even during the worst shifts.

core.definition: Calm and composed in difficult situations; not easily upset, rattled, or flustered.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on FLAP, and the -able ending reduces to a quick uh-bul. Do not pronounce the p as a strong sound in the middle; it is a quick, light p between the vowels.

nuance.connotation: Positive, praising someone's calm under pressure. It can sometimes suggest a lack of emotion when used about someone who seems cold.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use unflappable informally to praise a host, a pilot, a nurse, a manager, or a parent who stays calm during chaos. It is common in workplace conversation and in articles about leadership. A natural reply is I wish I were that calm.

distinctions.note: Calm describes a general state; unflappable suggests staying calm specifically under stress or pressure.
Composed is more formal and focuses on self-control; unflappable is more informal and emphasizes an unshakable temperament.
Cool can mean calm or stylish, and can also mean aloof; unflappable clearly refers to not being rattled.

examples.everyday: My sister stayed totally unflappable when the kids spilled juice all over the car seats.
examples.professional: Our release manager stayed unflappable during the outage, and she kept the team focused on one step at a time.
examples.analytical: The Stoics prized an unflappable mind, one that external events could not disturb, and they saw this calm as a sign of wisdom.

nuance.analogy: An unflappable person is like a sailor in a storm who keeps the boat steady, watching the waves without panicking.
nuance.etymology: Formed in English from flap (to agitate or upset) with un- and -able; the word is a 20th-century American coinage in its common sense.
common_mistakes: Using unflappable for a physical object; it describes temperament and composure in people.
Confusing it with unflappable's near opposite flappable, which is rare and informal.

senses.definition: Not favored by fortune.
senses.example: The unfortunate settlers had no food, no tools, and no hope of rescue.

senses.definition: Marked or accompanied by or resulting in misfortune.
senses.example: The storm brought an unfortunate series of floods that ruined the harvest.

senses.definition: Regrettable or unsuitable.
senses.example: It was unfortunate that he wore a bright orange tie to the funeral.

senses.definition: An unlucky person; one who has fallen into bad circumstances.
senses.example: The charity helps the unfortunates who lost their homes in the fire.

core.definition: Unlucky, or regrettable because it brings bad luck or undesirable results.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on FOR, and the -tune- part is pronounced 'chuh,' not 'too.' The ending is 'nit,' not 'nate.'

nuance.connotation: Mildly negative. It softens disappointment and suggests bad luck rather than blame.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'unfortunate' in polite speech and writing to describe bad luck or a regrettable situation, as in 'an unfortunate accident.' In casual talk, people often say 'unlucky,' 'too bad,' or 'that sucks.' As a noun, 'an unfortunate' for an unlucky person is literary and sounds sympathetic or old-fashioned.

distinctions.note: Unlucky describes a person's luck directly and is more casual; unfortunate can describe events, timing, or choices and sounds more formal.
Regrettable emphasizes that someone should feel regret, often for a mistake; unfortunate is milder and more neutral about blame.

examples.everyday: It's unfortunate that the store is out of your favorite bread, but they'll restock on Friday.
examples.professional: The outage happened at an unfortunate time, right before our quarterly release, so we are rescheduling it.
examples.analytical: Her reading is unfortunate, not because it is wrong, but because it ignores the historical context that shaped the author's argument.

nuance.analogy: Like missing a bus you could not have caught.
nuance.etymology: From un- (not) plus fortunate, from Latin fortuna, 'fortune' or 'chance.'
common_mistakes: Saying 'un-for-TOO-nit' with a 'too' sound; the middle is 'chuh.'
Using it as a stronger word than 'bad' in phrases such as 'an unfortunate disaster,' which is redundant.

senses.definition: Unfortunately; regrettably.
Through evil fate or chance; wretchedly.
senses.example: Unhappily, the couple's first apartment flooded just days after they moved in.

senses.definition: Without happiness; sadly.
senses.example: She sat unhappily by the window, watching the empty street for hours.

core.definition: Sadly, or unfortunately; used to introduce bad news or to describe a sad manner of doing something.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on HAP, and the un- prefix stays light. The final -ly is a short ih-lee, not lie.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It signals regret or sadness and is mildly sympathetic when used to introduce bad news.
nuance.usage_note: In American speech people usually say unfortunately to introduce bad news, and unhappily sounds more formal or written. You will see it in news reports, business letters and statements. To describe how someone did something, Americans might say sadly or with a sad look.

distinctions.note: Unfortunately is the everyday choice for introducing bad news. Unhappily is more formal and can also describe a sad manner, such as 'she spoke unhappily'.
Sadly often describes a speaker's feeling about something, while unhappily can describe the emotional state of a person or the manner of an action.

examples.everyday: We were going to eat out, but unhappily the restaurant was closed for a private party.
examples.professional: Unhappily, the deployment slipped two weeks because the staging database failed during testing.
examples.analytical: Unhappily, the argument depends on a premise that the evidence does not support.

nuance.analogy: Unhappily is like a sad note attached to bad news, telling you the feeling as well as the facts.
nuance.etymology: Formed from unhappy plus -ly; happy comes from Middle English hap, meaning 'chance' or 'luck'.
common_mistakes: Using unhappily as an adjective, as in 'I am unhappily'; the adjective is unhappy.
Starting casual sentences with unhappily, which sounds stiff; say unfortunately instead.

unhappily.etymology: From Middle English *onhappily*, *unhappili*, *unhappily*, *unhappyly*; equivalent to *un-* + *happily* or *unhappy* + *-ly*.

senses.definition: Not impressed.
senses.example: My manager stayed unimpressed by the fancy slides and asked for actual results.

core.definition: Not feeling admiration or interest; not moved or won over by something or someone.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on PREST, with a clear American r and a short e. The -ed ending is silent and sounds like a plain t after the s, so say PREST, not PRESSED.

nuance.connotation: Negative toward the thing or person; it implies the speaker felt it was not good enough.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say I'm not impressed or I'm unimpressed to show they are not wowed, often jokingly or with a mild edge. It can sound rude to someone who worked hard, so Okay, thanks or softer praise is kinder. It usually takes with or by after it, as in unimpressed with the service.

distinctions.note: Unimpressed describes a person's reaction; unimpressive describes the thing itself as not impressive.
Indifferent means having no interest or concern at all; unimpressed means you noticed and were not won over.
Disappointed implies that hopes were let down; unimpressed does not require any expectation.

examples.everyday: My son looked at the new phone, shrugged, and said he was totally unimpressed.
examples.professional: The client was unimpressed with the first draft, so we need to revise the pricing section by Friday.
examples.analytical: Readers have often been unimpressed by Kant's dense prose, yet the argument rewards patient reading.

nuance.analogy: Like a judge who has seen the same magic trick a hundred times and simply shrugs.
nuance.etymology: From un- 'not' plus impressed, from Latin impressus, past participle of imprimere 'to press into'.
common_mistakes: Using unimpressed for things; for a thing that is not impressive, say unimpressive
Using the preposition at instead of with or by after unimpressed

senses.definition: Not organized as a corporation.
Not contained in a municipality.
senses.example: The county library serves thousands of residents in unincorporated areas outside the city limits.

core.definition: Not formed into a legal corporation; of a place, not part of any incorporated city or town.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on KOR, pronounced with a strong American r, and the -ated ending is ay-tid with a short i. The word has five syllables, so keep the middle per light.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical; it describes a legal or administrative status, not a judgment about quality.
nuance.usage_note: In American English, unincorporated is most common in government, real estate, and news, as in an unincorporated area of the county, meaning it has no city government of its own. It is also used for businesses not registered as corporations, such as a sole proprietorship. In casual speech people usually say outside city limits or the county.

distinctions.note: Incorporated means formally registered as a corporation or as a city with its own government; unincorporated is its opposite.
Rural describes a type of land; unincorporated is a legal status, and a place can be urban and still be unincorporated.
Unorganized means not arranged or structured; unincorporated has a specific legal meaning.

examples.everyday: We live in an unincorporated part of the county, so our trash pickup comes from the county, not a city.
examples.professional: The unincorporated area has no town council, so the county planning department handles building permits.
examples.analytical: Her essay on unincorporated communities argues that legal status shapes who holds power in rural places.

nuance.analogy: Like a neighborhood without a town hall: it exists on the map but has no local government of its own.
nuance.etymology: From un- 'not' plus incorporated, from Latin incorporare 'to embody', from in- 'into' and corpus 'body'.
common_mistakes: Using unincorporated to mean disorganized; in the US it usually refers to legal status, as in unincorporated area
Misplacing the stress as un-in-kor-PER-ay-tid; the main stress is on KOR

senses.definition: In an unjustifiable manner.

core.definition: In a way that cannot be defended or excused; without good reason.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the 'fy' syllable, and let the '-ably' ending reduce to 'uh-blee'. The vowel in 'un' is short and light, so do not stress it.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it signals that someone's behavior or decision was indefensible.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use unjustifiably to describe a person's action or a decision that went too far, usually in news, complaints or formal disagreements. It often follows verbs like 'treat,' 'criticize,' 'accuse' or 'delay.' In everyday conversation, 'totally uncalled for' is a more natural way to say the same thing.

distinctions.note: Unfairly stresses that someone was treated unequally, while unjustifiably stresses that the act could not be defended by any good reason.
Unreasonably describes an act that goes beyond what is sensible, while unjustifiably sounds more like a moral or formal judgment.

examples.everyday: He was unjustifiably rude to the waiter, and everyone at the table noticed.
examples.professional: The vendor was unjustifiably slow to respond to our tickets, so we escalated the contract.
examples.analytical: The court held that the agency had unjustifiably delayed the hearing for more than two years.

nuance.analogy: A referee who blows the whistle for a foul that never happened: the penalty may be real, but no rule supports it.
nuance.etymology: From unjustifiable plus the adverbial ending -ly, from Latin justificare 'to make just'.
common_mistakes: Using it for mild cases where unfairly or unreasonably fits better.
Misplacing the stress as 'un-jus-TIF-ee-uh-blee' rather than stressing the 'fy' syllable.

senses.definition: Believing without question; having absolute loyalty.
Naive, blind, uncritical.
senses.example: unquestioning faith

core.definition: Accepting or following something completely, without any doubt, criticism or questions.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on KWES. The middle syllables are weak: 'chuh' is a reduced schwa, and the ending is a clear 'ning,' not 'neen.'

nuance.connotation: Often negative. It usually suggests naivety or excessive obedience, though it can be positive when describing trust or love.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'unquestioning' to describe people who follow instructions, leaders or beliefs without thinking, often with a critical tone. It can be praise in phrases like 'unquestioning love,' but it more often implies a lack of independent judgment. In speech, 'blind' or 'unthinking' are common alternatives.

distinctions.note: Unquestioning describes a person's attitude; unquestioned describes a belief or authority that is accepted without challenge.
Skeptical describes someone who doubts and asks for evidence, the opposite of unquestioning acceptance.

examples.everyday: My little brother has unquestioning trust in whatever our dad tells him.
examples.professional: We cannot rely on unquestioning acceptance of the model's output; every result needs a review.
examples.analytical: Such unquestioning obedience to authority, Arendt warns, can make ordinary people complicit in harm.

nuance.analogy: Like a compass needle that never checks the map, it simply points where it is told.
nuance.etymology: From un- plus questioning, present participle of question, from Latin quaestio, 'inquiry.'
common_mistakes: Using it for 'unquestioned' when you mean that a belief is accepted by everyone rather than that a person accepts it blindly.
Mispronouncing the middle syllables by saying them fully instead of using a weak 'chuh.'
Using it as a positive compliment without context; it often sounds critical.

senses.definition: Not receptive.
senses.example: The committee remained unreceptive to our proposal, no matter how carefully we presented it.

core.definition: Not open to new ideas, suggestions, or influence, or not responsive to something offered.

pronunciation.tip: Stress SEP, the third syllable, which is the root -cept-. The first syllable is a reduced uh, and the final -ive is a short, unstressed iv.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative. It describes a lack of openness, often in a business, medical, or social context, and can sound critical.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use unreceptive in work settings, medicine, and politics, such as 'the board was unreceptive to the proposal.' In casual talk, people more often say 'closed-minded' or 'not open to it.' The word is neutral and descriptive, which makes it useful in professional feedback.

distinctions.note: Closed-minded is a strong personal criticism, while unreceptive describes a more neutral lack of openness in a given moment.
Resistant suggests active opposition, while unreceptive suggests the absence of welcome or interest.

examples.everyday: My landlord seemed pretty unreceptive when I asked about fixing the heater.
examples.professional: The client was unreceptive to the new pricing model, so we should revisit the assumptions before the next meeting.
examples.analytical: Scripture repeatedly describes hearts that are unreceptive to the prophetic word, which suggests a condition of the will rather than a lack of information.

nuance.analogy: Like a sponge that is already full, an unreceptive listener cannot take in anything new, no matter how good the offer is.
nuance.etymology: From un- (not) plus receptive, from Latin receptivus, from recipere, 'to receive.'
common_mistakes: Using 'unreceptive' for an unknown or unconfirmed reaction, where 'no response' is more accurate.
Confusing unreceptive with 'unreceptible' or 'unreceptable' in spelling.

senses.definition: Not deserving of trust; unreliable.

core.definition: Not deserving trust; likely to lie, cheat, or fail to keep your word, so you cannot rely on the person or thing.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on TRUST, and the un- prefix is light. The final -thy is a weak 'thee' sound, not 'tee', and the middle syllable -wor- is reduced.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes character or reliability and is a serious criticism of a person, source, or product, so use it carefully in front of the person.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use untrustworthy about people, news sources, websites, and even machines. In everyday talk you might say 'I don't trust him' instead, which sounds softer. In workplace reviews, 'untrustworthy' suggests dishonesty, while 'unreliable' only suggests missed deadlines.

distinctions.note: Unreliable means it often fails to work or arrive on time; untrustworthy implies it may deliberately deceive you.
Suspicious describes your feeling that something is wrong, while untrustworthy describes an actual quality of the person or thing.

examples.everyday: I wouldn't buy anything from that website; the reviews there are untrustworthy.
examples.professional: We should remove that vendor from the list because their data has been untrustworthy for months.
examples.analytical: A historian must treat a memoir written decades later as potentially untrustworthy, since memory reshapes events.

nuance.analogy: Like a map with a few false roads drawn in: you cannot follow it, even if most of it looks right.
nuance.etymology: un- (not) + trust + worthy; 'trust' from Old Norse traust, and 'worthy' from Old English weorthig.
common_mistakes: Saying 'untrustable', which is not standard; use untrustworthy.
Stressing the last syllable, as in un-trust-wor-THY.

senses.definition: Not wavering.
senses.example: His unwavering gaze stayed fixed on the horizon as the boat drifted.

senses.definition: Always on course and steady.
senses.example: The unwavering beam of the lighthouse guided ships safely past the rocks.

senses.definition: Not doubting or unsure; decisive, firm, resolute.
senses.example: Despite the criticism, she remained unwavering in her commitment to the reform.

core.definition: Steady and firm; not changing or doubting, even when pressure or difficulty appears. Used for loyalty, belief, and commitment.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on WAY, and the un- prefix is weak. The -er- in the middle is reduced to 'ur', and the ending is '-ing', not '-een'.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It praises steadiness, loyalty, or determination.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use unwavering in speeches, news, sports coverage, and personal praise: 'unwavering support' or 'unwavering faith'. In casual talk you might say 'totally behind you' instead. It sounds sincere and a bit emphatic, so it works best for real commitment, not small preferences.

distinctions.note: Steadfast emphasizes loyalty kept over a long time; unwavering emphasizes the lack of hesitation at any moment.
Firm can describe a position or handshake; unwavering is more about a person's commitment or gaze.
Resolute stresses determination to act; unwavering stresses steadiness of belief or support.

examples.everyday: My sister has been unwavering in her support while I changed jobs.
examples.professional: The leadership gave an unwavering commitment to the migration timeline, even after the budget changed.
examples.analytical: Kierkegaard's knight of faith displays an unwavering commitment that the aesthetic life cannot sustain.

nuance.analogy: Like a lighthouse that stays in place while waves crash around it: the light holds steady.
nuance.etymology: un- (not) + wavering; 'waver' from Middle English waveren, related to 'wave'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the middle syllable, as in un-wa-VER-ing.
Using unwavering for physical steadiness of objects in everyday speech; it is mainly used for commitment or belief.

senses.definition: A popular revolt that attempts to overthrow a government or its policies; an insurgency or insurrection.

core.definition: A popular revolt against a government or its policies, usually smaller and less organized than a full revolution.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, UP, and do not stress RISE, which is often mistaken for the verb 'rise' with stress on the second syllable. The r in both syllables is pronounced in General American.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative. It is often used by governments or media to describe revolts they oppose, while supporters may call the same event a revolution or a people's movement.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'uprising' for revolts by ordinary people, such as a peasant rebellion, a prison uprising or a city-wide protest that turns violent. In news reports it is a neutral term, but commentators may choose it to suggest the revolt lacks legitimacy or organization. For a larger, more successful change of government, Americans would more likely say 'revolution'.

distinctions.note: A revolution aims to replace the political system and often succeeds; an uprising is usually a shorter revolt that may fail.
A riot is a disorderly crowd outburst, often without political goals; an uprising has an organized aim against authority.
Rebellion is a broad term for resisting authority, even by one person; uprising refers specifically to a collective revolt by a group of people.

examples.everyday: Did you see the news about the uprising in that prison? It's all over the TV.
examples.professional: Our risk team flagged the uprising in the region as a possible threat to our supply chain.
examples.analytical: Historians still debate whether the peasant uprising was driven mainly by economic grievance or by religious conviction.

nuance.analogy: Like a pot that boils over: pressure builds beneath the surface until it breaks through.
nuance.etymology: From up plus rise, from Old English upp and rīsan.
common_mistakes: Saying 'uprising to' the government instead of 'uprising against' it.
Stressing the second syllable, as in 'up-RIS-ing', which blurs it with the verb 'rise'.

senses.definition: With great haste, with a sense of urgency, because it is very important.
senses.example: We all urgently need to apply solutions to the problem of pollution.

senses.definition: Continuously. With insistence.
senses.example: He pleaded urgently for release from what he considered to be an unjust imprisonment.

core.definition: In a way that shows the need for quick action, or with strong insistence.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on the first syllable, and the 'ntl' cluster is pronounced quickly, with a clear 'lee' at the end. Do not insert an extra vowel between 't' and 'l'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative; it signals pressure or serious concern.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say urgently when they want to show that something needs quick action, as in 'We urgently need volunteers'. In casual speech people often say 'really need' or 'need it ASAP' instead. It can sound formal in a text message, but it is natural in email, news, and requests for help.

distinctions.note: Quickly describes speed, while urgently describes the sense that something must be done soon because it matters.
Desperately suggests hopelessness or extreme need, while urgently is more neutral and practical.

examples.everyday: The restaurant called me urgently because they had mixed up my order.
examples.professional: Please review the security patch urgently, since the vulnerability is already being exploited.
examples.analytical: The author argues that the church must urgently reconsider its response to poverty in the modern city.

nuance.analogy: Urgently is like a fire drill: everyone moves at once because the situation can't wait.
nuance.etymology: Formed from urgent, from Latin urgens, meaning pressing.
common_mistakes: Using urgently to mean quickly with no sense of importance, when quickly is more natural.
Pronouncing the middle as 'UR-gent-lee' with a hard 'g' sound.

senses.definition: Of, relating to, occurring in, or affecting urine, its production, function, or excretion.
senses.example: Persistent urinary problems can sometimes be an early sign of kidney disease.

senses.definition: Of, relating to, occurring in, or affecting the organs involved in the production, function, or excretion of urine.
senses.example: Persistent urinary problems can sometimes be an early sign of kidney disease.

core.definition: Relating to urine or to the organs that produce, store, and release it, such as the bladder and kidneys.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable YOOR, with a lighter secondary stress on NAIR. Many learners say yoo-RIN-ary or drop the final ee, so keep the -ary ending clear.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and clinical. Doctors use it calmly, and patients may find it awkward if discussed bluntly.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use urinary most often in medical contexts, such as a urinary tract infection or urinary symptoms. In everyday talk people often say bladder problems or going to the bathroom more often. Doctors in the US say urinary frequently, and UTI is a common shorthand. A natural reply when a doctor asks about urinary symptoms is to describe what you have noticed plainly.

distinctions.note: Uric refers specifically to uric acid or substances derived from urine, while urinary describes organs, tract, or functions.
Urine is the noun for the liquid, while urinary is an adjective describing things connected with urination or the system.
Urinal is a noun for a fixture or device, although it can be used as an adjective with a rare meaning close to urinary.

examples.everyday: My doctor asked whether I've noticed any urinary symptoms, like going more often at night.
examples.professional: The clinical trial tracks urinary side effects such as frequency and urgency for every participant.
examples.analytical: Urinary function is a useful window into kidney health, because changes in output often appear before measurable damage.

nuance.analogy: Urinary function is like a home's drainage system: when the flow changes, it signals a problem somewhere in the pipes.
nuance.etymology: From Latin urina meaning urine, with the English adjective ending -ary.
common_mistakes: Saying yoo-RIN-ary with the stress in the wrong place
Using urinary for the fixture in a men's room, where urinal is the correct word

senses.definition: Making an AI system's goals and behavior match human values.
senses.example: Our research team spent months on value alignment, testing whether the chatbot respected users' ethical limits.

core.definition: In AI, designing systems so their goals and behavior reliably match what humans actually want and value.

pronunciation.tip: Value has the stress-free VAL-yoo pattern, and alignment has its main stress on LINE. The final -ment is weak and sounds like mint, with a reduced vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a technical term in AI research and policy, and it carries serious but not emotional weight.
nuance.usage_note: Value alignment is used mainly by AI researchers, engineers, and policy writers, especially in discussions of AI safety. It is not a casual phrase, so you would rarely hear it at a restaurant or during small talk. In a team meeting, it is natural to say we need to check value alignment before launch.

distinctions.note: AI safety is the broader field of making AI systems safe, while value alignment is one specific problem within it.
Value learning is a method for inferring human values from data, while value alignment is the goal of matching those values.
Alignment alone can mean any kind of lining up; value alignment specifically concerns human values and goals.

examples.everyday: My friend works on AI safety, and she says value alignment is harder than it sounds.
examples.professional: Our roadmap includes value alignment tests before any model goes into customer-facing use.
examples.analytical: Value alignment is hard not only because human values conflict, but because we often cannot specify them precisely enough to optimize.

nuance.analogy: Like a GPS that reaches the destination you typed but takes a route you would never want, because the map was never truly tied to your goal.
nuance.etymology: Value from Latin valere, to be worth; alignment from French aligner, to line up.
common_mistakes: Using value alignment to mean team members sharing company values; in AI it refers to machine goals matching human values.
Stressing the second syllable of alignment; the main stress is on LINE.

conversation.text: Value alignment asks whose values an AI system should reflect and how to instill them.
Value alignment is hard because people disagree, and values vary across cultures.
We frame value alignment as learning from human preferences rather than hard-coding rules.

senses.definition: Taking a variable number of arguments; especially, taking arbitrarily many arguments.
senses.example: C's printf is one of the most widely used variadic functions.

senses.definition: Belonging to a variadic function.
senses.example: each variadic argument

senses.definition: A function that takes a variable number of arguments.
senses.example: We wrote a variadic that sums any number of sensor readings passed in.

core.definition: Describing a function that can accept a variable, unlimited number of arguments in a call.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, "ad." The first vowel is the vowel in "bet," and the final syllable is short, like "ik."

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical, with no emotional coloring.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use variadic mainly in programming discussions, especially with languages such as C, C++, Python, and JavaScript. Engineers say a function is variadic when it takes an unknown number of arguments. In general conversation, people would not use the word, and they might say takes any number of arguments instead.

distinctions.note: An overloaded function has multiple definitions with different parameter lists; a variadic function has one definition that accepts a variable number of arguments.
Polymorphic refers to functions or types that work with multiple types; variadic refers specifically to variable argument counts.

examples.everyday: My friend who codes said the printf function is variadic because you can pass any number of values.
examples.professional: Make the logging helper variadic so developers can pass any number of fields without writing new overloads.
examples.analytical: A variadic function raises interesting questions about type safety, since the compiler cannot always check the arguments in advance.

nuance.analogy: A variadic function is like a bag that can hold any number of groceries: the bag stays the same, but the number of items inside can change.
nuance.etymology: Formed from variable and the -adic ending of dyadic, from Greek dyas, meaning two.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable instead of the second.
Assuming a variadic function accepts arbitrary types, when it usually accepts a variable count of arguments.
Pronouncing the final syllable as "ick" instead of a short "ik."

senses.definition: Greatly, in a vast manner.
senses.example: The company's revenue grew vastly after the new product launched in Ohio.

core.definition: By a very large amount or to a very great degree.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, VAST, and the final syllable is a light 'lee'. Do not add a vowel between s and t, and keep the -ly ending as a simple 'lee' sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral, but it signals a strong contrast or difference, so it can sound emphatic.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use vastly with comparatives and with words like different, better or more, as in 'vastly better'. In casual speech, people more often say 'way better' or 'so much better', so vastly sounds slightly more formal or polished. It is rarely used for physical size; 'hugely' or 'enormously' is more natural there.

distinctions.note: Very intensifies an adjective modestly, while vastly signals a huge gap or difference between two things.
Greatly is general and neutral, while vastly emphasizes a large size of difference or effect.

examples.everyday: The new pizza place down the street is vastly better than the old one.
examples.professional: Our second-quarter forecast was vastly more accurate after we added the seasonality term.
examples.analytical: The two interpretations are vastly different in their implications for free will, even though they share the same premises.

nuance.analogy: Vastly is like the gap between a bicycle and a jet: they both move you, but the difference in scale is so large it changes the whole comparison.
nuance.etymology: From vast, from Latin vastus, empty, huge, with the English suffix -ly.
common_mistakes: Using vastly for small differences, which sounds exaggerated.
Using vastly to describe physical size where 'hugely' or 'enormously' would sound more natural.

senses.definition: Someone who vaticinates; a prophet.

core.definition: A person who foretells the future; a prophet or predictor, usually in a grand or solemn style.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, TIS, and the last syllable is a reduced 'er', not 'or'. Learners often stress the final syllable or give the first syllable a long 'a' sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to mildly mocking, depending on context; calling someone a vaticinator can suggest pompous or self-important prediction.
nuance.usage_note: This is a rare, bookish word that Americans mostly meet in old novels, essays or humorous writing. In everyday speech you would say forecaster, predictor, prophet or fortune-teller. Using it in conversation will sound deliberately literary.

distinctions.note: A prophet in the religious sense claims divine inspiration; a vaticinator is simply someone who predicts, and the word is lighter and broader.
A forecaster works from data and methods; a vaticinator makes bold or oracular pronouncements about what will happen.

examples.everyday: My uncle fancies himself a vaticinator, and he has predicted a stock market crash every year for a decade.
examples.professional: The consultant acted like a vaticinator, promising a revenue jump that none of our data could support.
examples.analytical: Ancient vaticinators were valued less for accuracy than for the authority their words conferred on the listener.

nuance.analogy: A vaticinator is a weather forecaster who speaks from a mountaintop, as if the future were already decided.
nuance.etymology: From Latin vaticinari, 'to prophesy,' from vates, 'prophet, seer.'
common_mistakes: Stressing the last syllable (vuh-tis-ih-NAY-ter) instead of TIS.
Confusing the spelling with 'vaccinator' when writing from dictation.
Using it in everyday conversation where 'forecaster' or 'predictor' is natural.

senses.definition: Having a vibe; atmospheric and trendy.
Having positive vibes. (Can we add an example for this sense?)
senses.example: The coffee shop had a warm, vibey feel with string lights and mismatched couches.

core.definition: Having a relaxed, appealing atmosphere, a trendy feel, or a positive, good-energy mood.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and keep the final sound as a clear 'ee'. Don't say 'VIE-bay' or 'VY-bay-ee', which sounds unnatural to American ears.
